t: 1.1 Origins and meaning of the word "Education"
x: The English word education has three commonly cited Latin roots. Each one carries a different idea of what education does, so it is worth knowing all three for examinations and for opening an answer well. Latin root Literal meaning Implied view of education Educare to bring up, to nourish, to rear Education as nurturing: the adult cultivates the child, much as a gardener tends a plant Educere to lead out, to draw out Education as unfolding: drawing out the innate potential already within the learner Educatum the act of teaching or training Education as deliberate instruction, which emphasises the teacher's role The two dominant roots point to a long-running tension in educational thought. Educare implies that something is put in from outside (knowledge, culture, values), while educere implies that something already present is drawn out. Most modern definitions try to hold both: education transmits a cultural inheritance and develops the individual's own capacities. "Shikkha" (শিক্ষা) The Bangla word shikkha comes from the Sanskrit root shas (শাস্), meaning to discipline, to govern, to control or to instruct. In the classical Indian tradition the related word vidya (from vid , to know) refers to knowledge or learning that liberates (" sa vidya ya vimuktaye ", that is knowledge which liberates). The root meaning of shikkha therefore stresses disciplined, guided learning, while vidya stresses the liberating purpose of knowledge. Key Point Examiners often ask you to compare "educare" and "educere". Say that educare is the narrow, outside-in view (instruction and rearing) and educere is the broad, inside-out view (unfolding of latent powers), then argue that a complete definition combines both.

t: 1.2 Narrow and broad concepts of education
x: Narrow (specific) concept. Education means the deliberate, planned instruction given in a school or other institution, over a limited period, according to a set curriculum, by qualified teachers, and certified by examinations. It is easy to measure, but it ignores most of what people actually learn. Broad (general) concept. Education is a lifelong process covering every experience that shapes a person's knowledge, skills, attitudes and character, from the family, the community, work, media, religion and play as well as the school. As J. S. Mackenzie put it, in the wider sense education is "a process that goes on throughout life and is promoted by almost every experience in life". Basis Narrow concept Broad concept Time span Limited to years of schooling Lifelong (womb to tomb) Place School, college, university Everywhere: home, community, workplace, media Agency Teacher-led, deliberate Deliberate and incidental, many agents Content Prescribed curriculum All life experiences Outcome measured by Examinations, certificates Growth, adaptation, quality of life

t: 1.3 Definitions of education: perspectives and contexts
x: No single definition is accepted by everyone, because a definition always reflects a view of human nature, knowledge and society. The table groups classic definitions by perspective. Learn the author and the key phrase. Thinker Definition (key phrase) Perspective Plato Education is "the capacity to feel pleasure and pain at the right moment" and develops in the body and soul all the beauty and perfection of which they are capable Idealist / moral Aristotle "The creation of a sound mind in a sound body" Realist / holistic Rousseau Education of the child according to nature; "Everything is good as it comes from the hands of the Author of Nature" Naturalist Pestalozzi "The natural, harmonious and progressive development of man's innate powers" Developmental Froebel "A process by which the child makes the internal external" Developmental / idealist Swami Vivekananda "The manifestation of the perfection already in man" Spiritual / idealist M. K. Gandhi "An all-round drawing out of the best in child and man: body, mind and spirit" Holistic Rabindranath Tagore "The highest education is that which does not merely give us information but makes our life in harmony with all existence" Humanist / naturalist John Dewey "The reconstruction or reorganization of experience which adds to the meaning of experience, and which increases ability to direct the course of subsequent experience" Pragmatist Émile Durkheim "The influence exercised by adult generations on those that are not yet ready for social life" Sociological R. S. Peters Initiation into worthwhile activities in a morally acceptable manner Analytic / philosophical Peters' three criteria of education The analytic philosopher R. S. Peters (1966) argued that a process counts as "education" only if it meets three criteria. This is one of the most examinable ideas in the course. Normative (worthwhileness) criterion. Education implies the transmission of what is worthwhile to those who become committed to it. Training a pickpocket is not education. Cognitive (knowledge) criterion. Education must involve knowledge and understanding and some "cognitive perspective", not just inert skills. Procedural criterion. Education rules out procedures that lack wittingness and voluntariness on the part of the learner, so indoctrination and conditioning do not qualify. "To be educated is not to have arrived at a destination; it is to travel with a different view." R. S. Peters (1965), Education as initiation Bipolar and tripolar views John Adams described education as a bipolar process between the educator and the educand: one personality acts on another in order to modify its development. Dewey added society and described a tripolar process involving the teacher, the child and the social environment (curriculum). Later writers added further components, which leads to the five-component model in Unit 5. Figure 1. From bipolar to tripolar: how definitions widened the components of education

Drawing these definitions together, education can be characterised as: A purposeful process. It is directed towards desirable goals. A lifelong process. It is not confined to childhood. A bipolar or tripolar process. It involves the learner, the teacher and society. Holistic. It develops the cognitive, affective and psychomotor domains. Social and cultural. It conserves, transmits and renews culture. Dynamic. Its aims and methods change with society, knowledge and technology. A human right and a public good. Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and Article 17 of the Constitution of Bangladesh both recognise it. Bangladesh Context Article 17 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh obliges the State to adopt effective measures for (a) a uniform, mass-oriented and universal system of education and free and compulsory education for all children up to a level determined by law, (b) relating education to the needs of society and producing properly trained and motivated citizens, and (c) removing illiteracy within a time determined by law. Article 15 lists education among the basic necessities of life.

Education is both a right in itself and an "enabling right" that unlocks other rights such as health, work and political participation. The key instruments are: UDHR (1948), Article 26: everyone has the right to education; it shall be free at least in the elementary stages and compulsory. ICESCR (1966), Articles 13–14: progressive introduction of free secondary and higher education. CRC (1989), Articles 28–29: the right of the child to education, and the aims of education (development of personality, respect for human rights, preparation for responsible life). UNCRPD (2006), Article 24: inclusive education for persons with disabilities. Katarina Tomaševski's 4-A framework (2001) is the most widely used way of assessing whether the right is realised: education must be Available , Accessible , Acceptable and Adaptable . Figure 2. Tomaševski's 4-A framework for the right to education

t: 1.6 Modes of education: informal, non-formal and formal
x: The influential typology comes from Philip Coombs and Manzoor Ahmed's work for the World Bank and the International Council for Educational Development (Coombs, Prosser & Ahmed, 1973; Coombs & Ahmed, 1974). Definition Formal education : The hierarchically structured, chronologically graded education system running from primary school through university, including specialised programmes and institutions for full-time technical and professional training. Definition Non-formal education : Any organised educational activity outside the established formal system, operating separately or as part of a broader activity, that is intended to serve identifiable learning clienteles and learning objectives. Definition Informal education : The truly lifelong process whereby every individual acquires attitudes, values, skills and knowledge from daily experience and the educative influences and resources in his or her environment: family, neighbours, work, play, the market place, the library and the mass media. Feature Formal Non-formal Informal Organisation Highly structured, graded Organised but flexible Unorganised, incidental Curriculum Fixed, centrally prescribed Need-based, learner-relevant None Entry and age Age-specific, entry requirements Open, any age Everyone, always Duration Long, full-time Short, part-time Lifelong Certification Degrees, certificates Sometimes (equivalency possible) None Teacher Trained professional Facilitator, often from the community Anyone (parents, peers, media) Bangladesh example Government primary school, public university BRAC schools, BNFE literacy centres, Second Chance programmes Learning farming from parents, learning from television Figure 3. The three modes of education overlap in a lifelong learning system Note Alan Rogers (2005) argues that the three modes are better seen as a continuum than as separate boxes. A school field-trip is formal education using informal learning; a literacy centre that follows a national curriculum with equivalency is "formalised" non-formal education. Rogers distinguishes "flexible schooling" (NFE as a cheaper alternative route to formal outcomes) from "participatory education" (NFE built from learners' own needs). Exam Focus Likely questions: "Define education from different perspectives." "Distinguish between formal, non-formal and informal education with Bangladeshi examples." "Explain Peters' criteria of education." Study tip Before reading this unit, write your own one-sentence definition of education, then decide whether it leans towards "educare" or "educere". It turns the etymology into a reflection on your own assumptions.

t: 2.1 Literacy, functional literacy and basic education
x: Literacy. UNESCO's 1958 definition is still the reference point: "A person is literate who can with understanding both read and write a short simple statement on his or her everyday life." Functional literacy. UNESCO (1978): "A person is functionally literate who can engage in all those activities in which literacy is required for effective functioning of his group and community and also for enabling him to continue to use reading, writing and calculation for his own and the community's development." Functional literacy therefore links the 3Rs to life skills, livelihood and civic participation. Contemporary thinking speaks of literacies in the plural (digital, financial, health, media and environmental literacy) and of literacy as a continuum of proficiency rather than a literate/illiterate dichotomy (UNESCO, 2006, EFA Global Monitoring Report: Literacy for Life ). Paulo Freire's idea of critical literacy (reading the word and the world) adds a political dimension. Basic education. The World Declaration on Education for All (Jomtien, 1990) defined it in terms of basic learning needs : the essential learning tools (literacy, oral expression, numeracy and problem solving) and the basic learning content (knowledge, skills, values and attitudes) that people need to survive, develop their capacities, live and work in dignity, participate fully in development, improve their quality of life, make informed decisions and continue learning. In Bangladesh, primary education (and, under the National Education Policy 2010, an extension to Class VIII) is the core of basic education, supplemented by non-formal routes for out-of-school children and adults.

General education: broad, liberal education in languages, sciences, social sciences and humanities, the common foundation for all citizens. Professional education: preparation for a profession with a specialised body of knowledge and a code of ethics, such as medicine, law, engineering or teaching. Religious education: education about and in a faith tradition. In Bangladesh it is a compulsory school subject (Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Christianity) and is the core of madrasah education. Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET): education for occupational skills, from basic trade courses to diploma engineering, regulated in Bangladesh through the Bangladesh Technical Education Board and the National Skills Qualification Framework.

Universal education: education available to every child of the relevant age, without discrimination. Universal Primary Education (UPE) was a Millennium Development Goal (MDG 2). Compulsory education: education that the law requires every child to attend. In Bangladesh the Primary Education (Compulsory) Act 1990 made primary education compulsory; the National Education Policy 2010 envisaged extending it to Class VIII. Education in Emergencies (EiE): quality learning opportunities for all ages in situations of crisis such as conflict, natural disaster and pandemics. EiE provides physical, psychosocial and cognitive protection. The Inter-agency Network for Education in Emergencies (INEE) Minimum Standards (2010) set the global benchmark. Bangladesh examples include education for Rohingya children in Cox's Bazar under the Learning Competency Framework and Approach (LCFA) and later the Myanmar Curriculum Pilot, and school continuity during floods and COVID-19 (television and radio lessons such as Amar Ghore Amar School ).

t: 2.4 EFA, mass, second chance, continuing and lifelong education
x: Education for All (EFA): the global movement launched at Jomtien (1990) and renewed in the Dakar Framework for Action (2000) with six goals: early childhood care and education, universal primary education, youth and adult learning needs, a 50% improvement in adult literacy, gender parity and equality, and quality of education. Mass education: education for the general population, especially adults who missed schooling, often through literacy campaigns and media. In Bangladesh the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education carries the term in its title. Second Chance Education (SCE): flexible programmes that let out-of-school children, youth and adults re-enter learning and, ideally, obtain equivalency with formal qualifications. Continuing education: learning after initial education, for further personal, professional or community development, such as post-literacy, skills upgrading or continuing professional development. Lifelong education / lifelong learning: the organising principle that learning takes place across the whole life span (lifelong) and in every setting (life-wide). The Faure Report Learning to Be (UNESCO, 1972) and the Delors Report Learning: The Treasure Within (UNESCO, 1996) made it central to global policy. The four pillars of learning (Delors Report, 1996) Figure 4. The four pillars of learning for the 21st century (Delors et al., 1996)

t: 2.5 Indicators of educational participation and efficiency
x: These terms appear in BANBEIS and DPE statistical reports. You must be able to define each and, ideally, to calculate it. Indicator Definition Formula / note Catchment area The geographical area from which a school draws its pupils; used for school mapping and planning e.g. a 2 km radius for a primary school Gross Enrolment Rate (GER) Total enrolment at a level, regardless of age, as a percentage of the official age-group population for that level (Enrolment at level ÷ population of official age) × 100; can exceed 100% because of over-age and under-age pupils Net Enrolment Rate (NER) Enrolment of the official age group at a level as a percentage of that age-group population (Enrolled of official age ÷ population of official age) × 100; maximum 100% Dropout rate Proportion of pupils who leave school in a given year without completing the cycle Pupils leaving ÷ enrolment × 100 Repetition rate Proportion of pupils enrolled in a grade who study in the same grade the following year Repeaters in year t+1 ÷ enrolment in grade in year t × 100 Cycle completion rate Percentage of a cohort entering grade 1 who complete the final grade of the cycle Measures internal efficiency Survival rate Percentage of a cohort reaching a given grade Survival to grade 5 is a key primary indicator Transition rate Number of new entrants to the first grade of a higher level as a percentage of pupils in the final grade of the lower level in the previous year e.g. primary to secondary transition Key Point GER > 100% does not mean every child is in school; it signals over-age or under-age enrolment, often caused by late entry or repetition. The gap between GER and NER is a quick measure of age-grade distortion.

Curriculum comes from the Latin currere , "to run", and curriculum , a racecourse. In the narrow sense it means the subjects taught; in the broad sense it is "all the learning which is planned and guided by the school, whether it is carried on in groups or individually, inside or outside the school" (Kerr, 1968). Kelly (2009) distinguishes the planned (official) curriculum from the received (actual) curriculum and draws attention to the hidden curriculum. Syllabus is narrower: a list or outline of topics and content for a particular subject or course within the curriculum, usually with time allocation and assessment information. Curriculum Syllabus Broad: aims, content, methods, materials, assessment, co-curricular activities Narrow: topics and content of one subject Prescriptive at national or institutional level Descriptive, subject-specific Covers the whole educational programme A part of the curriculum Developed by national bodies (NCTB in Bangladesh) Often prepared by subject teachers or boards

Pedagogy (Greek paidos , child, and agogos , leader): the art and science of teaching children. It is teacher-directed and the teacher decides what, when and how. Andragogy (Greek aner/andr- , man or adult): popularised by Malcolm Knowles (1980) as "the art and science of helping adults learn". Knowles' assumptions are that adults (1) need to know why they learn, (2) have a self-directing self-concept, (3) bring rich experience, (4) are ready to learn what helps them cope with real-life tasks, (5) are problem- or life-centred in orientation, and (6) are driven mainly by internal motivation. Heutagogy (Greek heutos , self): introduced by Hase and Kenyon (2000) as self-determined learning, where the learner decides what and how to learn, develops capability rather than just competence, and engages in double-loop learning (questioning their own assumptions). Blaschke (2012) presents pedagogy, andragogy and heutagogy as a continuum of increasing learner autonomy. Figure 5. The pedagogy, andragogy, heutagogy continuum: learner autonomy and maturity increase towards the base (after Blaschke, 2012) Basis Pedagogy Andragogy Heutagogy Learner Dependent Self-directed Self-determined Role of teacher Director, transmitter Facilitator Coach, co-learner Use of experience Little Rich resource Basis for reflection and capability Orientation Subject-centred Problem-centred Learner-defined, capability-centred Motivation External (grades, praise) Internal Internal, self-efficacy

Gender parity: equal numbers of girls and boys enrolled, measured by the Gender Parity Index (GPI = female value ÷ male value; 0.97–1.03 is treated as parity). Bangladesh achieved gender parity in primary and secondary enrolment in the 2000s, helped by the Female Secondary School Stipend Programme. Gender equality: equal rights, opportunities, treatment and outcomes for all genders, in and through education. Equity: fairness, which means giving more support to those who need more so that outcomes can be equal. Equality treats everyone the same; equity treats people according to need. Inclusion: "a process of addressing and responding to the diversity of needs of all learners through increasing participation in learning, cultures and communities, and reducing exclusion within and from education" (UNESCO, 2005, Guidelines for Inclusion ).

Figure 6. Four responses to learner diversity Special education: specially designed instruction for learners with disabilities, traditionally in separate institutions. Integrated education: placing children with disabilities in mainstream schools, often with resource support, while expecting the child to fit the system. Inclusive education: restructuring curricula, pedagogy, assessment and the school environment so that all children learn together. The Salamanca Statement (UNESCO, 1994) declared that "regular schools with this inclusive orientation are the most effective means of combating discriminatory attitudes, creating welcoming communities, building an inclusive society and achieving education for all."

Value education: the deliberate cultivation of moral, social, aesthetic and spiritual values such as honesty, empathy, tolerance and respect for diversity. It is treated in depth in PC 121. Citizenship education: preparing learners to participate as informed, responsible and active citizens, with knowledge of rights, duties, democratic institutions and civic skills. Global Citizenship Education (GCED) extends this to a sense of belonging to a common humanity (SDG target 4.7). Exam Focus Practise calculating GER and NER from a small table, and practise distinguishing pairs: literacy/functional literacy, equality/equity, integration/inclusion, curriculum/syllabus, pedagogy/andragogy.

u: Unit 3: Aims, Purposes and Functions of Education
x: An aim is a broad, long-term statement of intent that gives direction (for example, "to develop responsible citizens"). A goal is more specific and attainable within a programme or level. An objective is a precise, observable and usually measurable statement of what a learner should be able to do after instruction. Aims answer the question "why educate?", while objectives answer "what exactly should learners achieve?" Figure 7. The hierarchy from philosophy to classroom objectives

u: Unit 3: Aims, Purposes and Functions of Education
x: Approach Key thinkers Aim of education Implication Idealist Plato, Hegel, Froebel, Vivekananda Self-realisation; development of the spiritual and moral self; pursuit of eternal truth, beauty and goodness Teacher as moral exemplar; emphasis on humanities, ethics and religion Realist Aristotle, Comenius, Locke, Herbart Preparing the learner for real life; knowledge of the physical and social world as it is Science, mathematics, vocational subjects; objective, systematic teaching Pragmatist Peirce, William James, Dewey Growth, social efficiency and the creation of values through experience; education has no end beyond more education Activity, project and problem-solving methods; school as a miniature democratic society Naturalists (Rousseau) add the aim of free, natural development of the child, which influenced child-centred education.

u: Unit 3: Aims, Purposes and Functions of Education
x: Objectives are usually classified into three domains, following Bloom's and later taxonomies: Cognitive: acquisition of knowledge and intellectual skills (remembering to creating; Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001). Affective: attitudes, values, ideals and appreciation (receiving to characterisation; Krathwohl, Bloom & Masia, 1964). Psychomotor: mental-motor and manual skills (imitation to naturalisation; Dave, 1970; Simpson, 1972).

u: Unit 3: Aims, Purposes and Functions of Education
x: The individual aim (associated with Rousseau, Froebel and T. P. Nunn) holds that education should develop the unique potential of each person; Nunn (1920) wrote that education should help "the fullest development of individuality". The social aim (Plato, Durkheim, Bagley) holds that the individual exists in and for society, so education should produce socially efficient citizens. Dewey's synthesis is that individual growth and social progress are interdependent: education should develop each individual's powers through participation in social life, and that is the meaning of social efficiency .

u: Unit 3: Aims, Purposes and Functions of Education
x: Individual development: physical, intellectual, emotional, social, moral and spiritual development. Social efficiency: the ability to contribute productively to society and to cooperate with others. Economically productive skills: education as investment in human capital (Schultz, 1961; Becker, 1964), raising productivity and earnings. Raising consciousness (conscientisation): Freire's (1970) aim of enabling learners to perceive social, political and economic contradictions and act against oppression. Promoting social understanding and cohesion: tolerance, peace and respect for diversity. Nationalism and patriotism: love for the nation, its language, culture and history. In Bangladesh this is tied to the spirit of the Liberation War, the Language Movement and the four founding state principles. Internationalism: understanding of global interdependence and shared human values; UNESCO's 1974 Recommendation on Education for International Understanding.

u: Unit 3: Aims, Purposes and Functions of Education
x: Biesta (2010) offers a modern three-part framework of the functions (purposes) of education: qualification (knowledge, skills and dispositions to do something), socialisation (becoming part of social, cultural and political orders) and subjectification (becoming an autonomous, responsible subject rather than simply a copy of the existing order). Good education keeps all three in balance. Figure 8. Biesta's three overlapping functions of education Other functions commonly listed in textbooks: Conservation and transmission of culture. Reconstruction and renewal of culture (innovation). Socialisation and citizenship training. Human resource development for the economy. Selection and allocation of people to occupational roles (a functionalist idea; Parsons, 1959). Social mobility and the reduction of inequality. Development of national identity and integration.

u: Unit 3: Aims, Purposes and Functions of Education
t: 3.7 Education for a civil, democratic and inclusive society
x: Dewey (1916) argued that democracy is "more than a form of government; it is primarily a mode of associated living, of conjoint communicated experience", so schools must practise democracy by valuing shared interests and free interaction between groups. Education supports a civil and democratic society by: teaching knowledge of rights, laws and institutions; developing critical thinking, deliberation and tolerance of dissent; providing experience of participation, for example through student councils, debate and community service; removing barriers so that marginalised groups (girls, ethnic minorities, children with disabilities, the urban poor) are full participants. An inclusive society needs an inclusive school.

u: Unit 3: Aims, Purposes and Functions of Education
x: UNESCO (2015) defines GCED as aiming to empower learners "to assume active roles to face and resolve global challenges and to become proactive contributors to a more peaceful, tolerant, inclusive and secure world". It works across three learning domains: Figure 9. The three domains of Global Citizenship Education (UNESCO, 2015) SDG Target 4.7 asks that by 2030 all learners acquire the knowledge and skills needed to promote sustainable development, including through education for sustainable development, human rights, gender equality, a culture of peace and non-violence, global citizenship and appreciation of cultural diversity.

t: 3.9 National and international policy, laws and acts
x: Instrument Year Key provision Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Art. 26 1948 Right to free, compulsory elementary education Constitution of Bangladesh, Arts. 15, 17, 28 1972 Education as a basic necessity; free, compulsory, uniform mass-oriented education; non-discrimination and special provision for women, children and backward sections Qudrat-e-Khuda Education Commission Report 1974 First national commission; secular, science-oriented, work-oriented education; 8-year compulsory primary Convention on the Rights of the Child 1989 Right to education and its aims (Arts. 28–29) Primary Education (Compulsory) Act 1990 Compulsory primary education in Bangladesh Jomtien World Declaration on EFA 1990 Meeting basic learning needs Salamanca Statement 1994 Inclusive education Dakar Framework for Action 2000 Six EFA goals by 2015 National Education Policy (Kabir Chowdhury Committee) 2010 Primary to Class VIII, one-year pre-primary, common core curriculum, creative questions, strengthened TVET Persons with Disabilities Rights and Protection Act 2013 Inclusive education rights Non-Formal Education Act 2014 Legal basis for NFE and the Bureau of Non-Formal Education Incheon Declaration / Education 2030 Framework 2015 SDG 4: inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning for all National Curriculum Framework 2021 Competency-based curriculum from pre-primary to Class XII Bangladesh Context The draft Education Act (various versions since 2013) seeks to consolidate the legal framework, including regulation of coaching centres, guidebooks and private institutions. Check the latest status before your exam, because it is a common exam and viva question. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Discuss the idealist, realist and pragmatist aims of education." "How can education build a democratic and inclusive society?" "What is Global Citizenship Education? Discuss its relevance for Bangladesh."

u: Unit 4: Maxims and Principles of Learning
t: 4.1 What is a maxim of teaching?
x: A maxim is a general, experience-based guideline for organising teaching so that it suits the learner's psychology. Maxims come from the work of Comenius ( Didactica Magna , 1657), Pestalozzi, Froebel, Herbart and Herbert Spencer ( Education: Intellectual, Moral and Physical , 1861). They are not scientific laws, but they are consistent with modern cognitive psychology, especially schema theory, cognitive load theory and Bruner's spiral curriculum.

u: Unit 4: Maxims and Principles of Learning
x: Maxim Meaning Classroom example Modern support Simple to complex Present easy elements before difficult combinations Single-digit addition before carrying Cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988) Known to unknown Start from what pupils already know and link the new to it Teach "map" through the classroom layout Ausubel's (1968) meaningful learning: "ascertain what the learner already knows and teach him accordingly" Whole to parts Present the whole first, then analyse the parts Read a whole poem before analysing lines Gestalt psychology Particular to general Give specific examples before the general rule Several examples of nouns before defining a noun Inductive concept formation Inductive to deductive Derive a rule from examples, then apply it to new cases Discover the angle sum of a triangle by measuring, then apply it Bruner's discovery learning Concrete to semi-concrete to abstract Real objects, then pictures, then symbols Counting sticks, then dots, then numerals Bruner's enactive, iconic, symbolic modes; Piaget's stages Definite to indefinite Begin with clear, certain facts before vague or debatable ideas Facts of a historical event before interpretations Building secure schemas Analysis to synthesis Break a problem into parts, then recombine them into a solution Analyse a geometry problem, then build the proof Problem-solving heuristics (Polya) Empirical to rational From observation and experience to reasoned explanation Observe evaporation, then explain the kinetic theory Scientific method Psychological to logical Order material by learner readiness first, then the logical structure of the discipline Start with pupils' interests, end with systematic knowledge Dewey's "psychologising" of subject matter Figure 10. Bruner's modes of representation underpin the maxim "concrete to abstract"

u: Unit 4: Maxims and Principles of Learning
x: J. P. Guilford (1967) distinguished convergent thinking (working towards a single correct answer, as in most examination questions) from divergent thinking (generating many varied and original ideas, the basis of creativity). Good teaching needs both: divergent tasks such as brainstorming, open-ended questions and "how many uses can you think of" stimulate fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration, while convergent tasks consolidate accuracy and logic. Figure 11. Convergent and divergent thinking

u: Unit 4: Maxims and Principles of Learning
x: Learning by doing / activity-based learning. Learners construct knowledge through action and experience (Dewey; Kilpatrick's project method; Froebel's "gifts"). Edgar Dale's "cone of experience" suggests retention increases with direct, purposeful experience. Treat the percentages often attached to the cone with caution, because Dale never published them. Learning through joyful experience. Positive emotion enhances attention and memory; fear and anxiety inhibit learning (the Yerkes–Dodson relationship). In Bangladesh, "joyful learning" is a stated principle of the primary curriculum. Child-centric learning. The child's interests, needs, abilities and developmental stage determine content and method (Rousseau, Montessori, Dewey). The teacher is a facilitator. Use of life experience. Linking content to learners' daily lives makes it meaningful and transferable (situated learning; Lave & Wenger, 1991). Teacher-pupil rapport. A warm, trusting relationship is a strong predictor of engagement and achievement. Hattie's (2009) synthesis found teacher-student relationships among the high-effect influences (d ≈ 0.72). Learning how to learn rather than what to learn. In a knowledge-rich, fast-changing world the key outcome is metacognition and self-regulation: planning, monitoring and evaluating one's own learning (Flavell, 1979; Zimmerman, 2002). Key Point Link each maxim and principle to a theory when you answer. "Known to unknown" connects to Ausubel's advance organisers and Piaget's assimilation; "learning by doing" to Dewey and constructivism; "learning how to learn" to metacognition. That linkage is what distinguishes a high-scoring answer from a textbook list. Study tip To remember the maxims, picture a lesson taught in reverse order (abstract to concrete) and then correctly (concrete to abstract), and ask yourself which would work better for learners and why.

u: Unit 5: Components of the Education System
x: An education system can be analysed with an input–process–output–outcome model. Its core components (learner, teacher, curriculum, institution and environment) interact continuously. A weakness in any one component limits the whole system. Figure 12. The five interacting components of the education system

u: Unit 5: Components of the Education System
x: Innate endowments: heredity sets potential in intelligence, aptitude, temperament and physical capacity. Social and cultural environment: family income, parental education, language spoken at home, gender norms and community values shape readiness and opportunity. Bourdieu's concept of cultural capital explains why children from educated families tend to do better at school. Individual differences: learners differ in ability, learning pace, prior knowledge, interests, motivation and needs. Teaching must therefore be differentiated. Modern education places the learner at the centre: the learner is an active constructor of knowledge, not a passive receiver.

u: Unit 5: Components of the Education System
x: Personality: warmth, enthusiasm, fairness, patience, emotional stability and humour. Education: subject content knowledge, pedagogical knowledge, and pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) , Shulman's (1986) "special amalgam of content and pedagogy" that is unique to teachers. Roles: instructor, facilitator, guide and counsellor, assessor, role model, manager, researcher (the reflective practitioner; Schön, 1983) and a link between school and community. Responsibilities and commitment: to learners, to the profession, to parents and society, and to their own professional development. "No education system can rise above the quality of its teachers." This line, often attributed to the McKinsey report (Barber & Mourshed, 2007), summarises the evidence that teacher quality is the most important in-school factor in student learning.

u: Unit 5: Components of the Education System
x: The curriculum is the vehicle through which aims become learning experiences. An appropriate curriculum is relevant to learners' needs and society's goals, matched to developmental stages, balanced across domains, flexible and inclusive. Co-curricular activities (sports, debate, cultural programmes, scouting, Girl Guides, Red Crescent, science fairs) develop leadership, cooperation, creativity and values that are hard to achieve in the classroom. They are part of the curriculum, not extras.

u: Unit 5: Components of the Education System
x: Origin: schools arose when societies became too complex for informal transmission of culture. In Bengal this ran from tols , pathshalas , maktabs and madrasahs to the modern school system established under colonial rule. Functions: instruction, socialisation, certification, custody and care, and community service. The school as a society: Dewey (1899) called the school "an embryonic community life". In Democracy and Education (1916) he set out its three functions: to provide a simplified environment, to purify (eliminate unworthy features of the existing environment) and to balance (give each individual an opportunity to escape the limitations of their social group). Management and leadership: effective schools have strong instructional leadership, a clear shared vision, high expectations, a safe orderly climate, frequent monitoring of progress and good home–school partnerships (the "effective schools" research of Edmonds, 1979, and later work).

u: Unit 5: Components of the Education System
x: Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory (1979) is a powerful lens for analysing how environments surrounding the learner influence learning. Figure 13. Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems model applied to the learner Natural environment: climate, geography, flooding and river erosion in Bangladesh (which affect attendance and school buildings). Physical facilities: classrooms, light, ventilation, water and sanitation (WASH), separate toilets for girls, ramps, furniture, libraries and laboratories. Learning environment: psychological safety, positive teacher-pupil relationships, a print-rich classroom and opportunities for participation. Responding to diversity: recognising and valuing differences in language, ethnicity, religion, gender, ability and socio-economic background, and adapting teaching accordingly (Universal Design for Learning; CAST, 2018). Exam Focus Likely questions: "Analyse the interrelationship among the components of education." "Evaluate the role of the school as a social institution." "How does the environment influence learning? Use Bronfenbrenner's model."

A discipline is a branch of knowledge that is taught and researched at university level, with its own subject matter, concepts, methods of enquiry and community of scholars. Becher and Trowler (2001) describe disciplines as "academic tribes and territories": communities with shared norms and cultures that occupy particular intellectual territories. King and Brownell (1966) identified characteristics of a discipline, which can be summarised as: A community of scholars. An expression of human imagination . A domain , or a defined subject matter. A tradition and a history. A syntactical structure : its own methods of enquiry and rules of evidence. A substantive structure : its concepts, principles and theories. A specialised language and symbol system. A heritage of literature and an artefact network (journals, books, conferences). A valuative and affective stance . An instructive community , with programmes that train new members.

This is a classic debate and a favourite viva question. The "field" or "applied" view. In the 1960s and 1970s (Tibble, 1966; Hirst, 1966), education was often described as a field of study to which the foundation disciplines (philosophy, psychology, sociology and history of education) contribute. On this view education has no distinctive methods of its own. The "discipline" view. Today education meets most criteria of a discipline: It has a distinct subject matter : teaching, learning, curriculum, assessment and the organisation of education across the life span. It has developed its own theories and concepts , such as curriculum theory, pedagogical content knowledge, the theory of formative assessment and educational leadership models. It has its own and adapted research methods : action research, design-based research, classroom observation systems, educational measurement and evaluation. It has a scholarly community : faculties and institutes (such as IER, University of Dhaka, established 1959), professional associations (AERA, BERA, WERA) and thousands of peer-reviewed journals. It has professional application in teacher education, policy and leadership. Furlong (2013) describes education as a discipline that must hold together academic, professional and policy knowledge. A balanced answer is that education is an interdisciplinary, applied discipline : it borrows from the foundation disciplines but integrates them around its own problems of teaching and learning, much as medicine draws on biology and chemistry. Figure 14. Education as an interdisciplinary discipline: contributing fields around a distinctive core

t: 6.3 Configuration of education as a discipline
x: Education as a discipline can be configured along three axes: Foundations: philosophy, psychology, sociology, history, economics and comparative education. Professional studies: curriculum, pedagogy and subject methods, assessment, guidance, management and leadership, educational technology. Research and enquiry: quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods; measurement and evaluation; policy analysis.

t: D. Model answer outline: "Is education a discipline?"
x: Introduction: define a discipline (Becher & Trowler; King & Brownell) and note the debate. Arguments that it is a field: dependence on the foundation disciplines (Tibble, 1966; Hirst, 1966); eclectic methods. Arguments that it is a discipline: distinct subject matter; its own theories (curriculum, PCK, formative assessment); its own research methods (action research, design-based research, measurement); an institutional and scholarly community; professional application. Synthesis: an interdisciplinary applied discipline, comparable to medicine or engineering (Furlong, 2013). Scope: level-wise and area-wise. Conclusion: significance for Bangladesh (teacher education, IER, policy research).

u: Unit 1: Education as a National System
t: 1.1 Concept of a national system of education
x: A national system of education is the organised whole of institutions, programmes, laws, policies, curricula, personnel and financing through which a state provides education to its population in line with its national philosophy and development goals. It has a common legal basis, a defined structure (levels and streams), governance (ministries, directorates, boards), standards (curricula, examinations, qualifications) and financing mechanisms. A national system is not uniform, but it is coherent: its parts are linked through recognised equivalences and pathways. Components of a national system Figure 1. Components of a national system of education Types of national systems Centralised (France historically; Bangladesh largely): curriculum, textbooks, examinations and teacher recruitment controlled nationally. Decentralised (USA, Germany by state): states or local authorities control most decisions. Mixed / semi-centralised : national frameworks with local implementation (England after 1988; Bangladesh's school management committees and upazila education offices are an element of this).

u: Unit 1: Education as a National System
t: 1.2 Historical development of education in Bengal and Bangladesh
x: Figure 2. Milestones in the history of education in Bengal and Bangladesh Ancient period (Vedic/Aryan, c. 1500 BCE onward) Education was religious and residential, organised in the gurukul (the pupil lived in the teacher's home), tol and chatuspathi (centres of Sanskrit learning). The curriculum covered the Vedas, grammar, logic, philosophy and astronomy, with oral memorisation and upanayana initiation. It was restricted largely to upper castes and to boys. Buddhist period (c. 6th century BCE to 12th century CE) Monastic viharas became great universities open to all castes: Nalanda, Vikramashila, Odantapuri and, in present-day Bangladesh, Somapura Mahavihara (Paharpur, Naogaon), Shalban Vihara (Mainamati, Cumilla) and Jagaddala. Teaching used discussion and debate, and the curriculum combined religion with logic, medicine and the arts. Muslim period (13th to 18th century) Elementary maktabs attached to mosques taught reading of the Qur'an, writing and arithmetic; madrasahs offered higher learning in theology, law, logic, Arabic and Persian. Persian was the court language, and patronage came from sultans, nawabs and landlords. Pathshalas continued as indigenous elementary schools. British colonial period (1757 to 1947) Year Event Significance 1780 Calcutta Alia Madrasah (Warren Hastings) Origin of the Alia madrasah stream 1813 Charter Act First government allocation (Rs. 1 lakh) for education 1835 Macaulay's Minute English-medium Western education; "downward filtration" theory 1854 Wood's Despatch "Magna Carta of English education in India": departments of education, grants-in-aid, universities 1857 University of Calcutta Affiliating, examining university 1882 Hunter Commission Emphasis on primary education under local bodies 1917–19 Sadler (Calcutta University) Commission Recommended a teaching and residential university at Dhaka 1921 University of Dhaka First university in present-day Bangladesh 1930 Bengal (Rural) Primary Education Act Early compulsory education legislation Pakistan period (1947 to 1971) Commissions included the Akram Khan Committee (1949), the Ataur Rahman Khan Commission (1957), the Sharif Commission (1959) , whose recommendations on fees and a three-year degree triggered the 1962 student movement, the Hamoodur Rahman Commission (1964) and the Nur Khan proposals (1969). The Language Movement (1952) made the medium of instruction a national political question. Bangladesh (1971 to present) Year Commission / policy Key recommendations 1974 Qudrat-e-Khuda Education Commission Secular, science- and work-oriented education; free, compulsory 8-year primary; Bangla medium; one stream 1979 Interim Education Policy Reorganisation of primary and secondary levels 1983 Mazid Khan Commission Structural reforms (controversial, not implemented) 1988 Mofiz Uddin Commission Comprehensive reform proposals 1997 Shamsul Haque Committee Basis for the 2000 policy 2000 National Education Policy 2000 Approved but later suspended 2003 Moniruzzaman Miah Commission Proposals during 2001–06 2010 National Education Policy (Kabir Chowdhury Committee) One-year pre-primary; primary to Class VIII; secondary IX–XII; common core in all streams; creative questions; TVET expansion; permanent education commission 2021 National Curriculum Framework Competency-based, experiential curriculum from pre-primary to Class XII Note Policy in Bangladesh has changed quickly since 2023. The competency-based NCF 2021 curriculum was rolled out from 2023, and after the political transition of 2024 the authorities announced a return to a revised version of the 2012 curriculum for secondary classes from 2025 while a new reform is prepared. Always check the latest NCTB and Ministry announcements before your exam, because examiners like to ask about current reforms.

u: Unit 1: Education as a National System
t: 1.3 Goals, philosophy, policies and constitutional provisions
x: Bangladesh's educational philosophy draws on the four founding state principles of the 1972 Constitution (nationalism, socialism, democracy and secularism), the spirit of the Liberation War and the Language Movement, and a commitment to science, humanism and social justice. NEP 2010 lists 30 aims and objectives, including: reflecting the spirit of the Liberation War and developing patriotism; developing a humane, rational, scientifically minded and creative citizenry; ensuring equal opportunity regardless of gender, religion, ethnicity, location or disability; building skilled human resources to meet the needs of a knowledge economy; promoting moral and religious values and respect for all faiths. Constitutional provisions. Article 15 (education as a basic necessity), Article 17 (free and compulsory education; relating education to the needs of society; removal of illiteracy), Article 19 (equality of opportunity), Article 23 (preservation of culture), Article 28 (non-discrimination and special provisions for women, children and backward sections) and Article 41 (religious education must not be imposed on a person of another faith). Legal framework Primary Education (Compulsory) Act 1990 Private University Act 1992, replaced by the Private University Act 2010 University Grants Commission of Bangladesh Order 1973 (President's Order No. 10) Non-Government Teachers Registration and Certification Authority (NTRCA) Act 2005 Persons with Disabilities Rights and Protection Act 2013 and the Neuro-Developmental Disability Trust Act 2013 Non-Formal Education Act 2014 Bangladesh Accreditation Council Act 2017 National Skills Development Authority Act 2018 Al-Haiatul Ulya Lil-Jamiatil Qawmia Bangladesh Act 2018 (recognition of the Qawmi Dawra-e-Hadith degree) Draft Education Act (pending)

u: Unit 1: Education as a National System
x: Figure 3. The structure of formal education in Bangladesh (indicative ages) Key structural features: Three main streams (general, madrasah and technical-vocational) plus the independent Qawmi madrasah and English-medium (O/A level) schools. Public examinations at the end of Class X (SSC/Dakhil/SSC Vocational) and Class XII (HSC/Alim/HSC Vocational), conducted by 11 education boards : 9 general boards (Dhaka, Rajshahi, Cumilla, Jashore, Chattogram, Barishal, Sylhet, Dinajpur, Mymensingh), the Bangladesh Madrasah Education Board and the Bangladesh Technical Education Board. Terminal examinations at Class V (PECE) and VIII (JSC/JDC), introduced in 2009–10, have not been held since 2020. Non-formal routes under the Bureau of Non-Formal Education provide second-chance and literacy programmes, with equivalency under the NFE Act 2014.

u: Unit 1: Education as a National System
x: SDG 4: "Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all" (United Nations, 2015; UNESCO, 2016). Target Focus 4.1 Free, equitable, quality primary and secondary education with relevant learning outcomes 4.2 Quality early childhood development, care and pre-primary education 4.3 Equal access to affordable, quality TVET and tertiary education 4.4 Increase youth and adults with skills for employment, decent jobs and entrepreneurship 4.5 Eliminate gender disparities; equal access for the vulnerable, persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples 4.6 Youth and a substantial proportion of adults achieve literacy and numeracy 4.7 Knowledge and skills for sustainable development, global citizenship and a culture of peace 4.a Build and upgrade safe, inclusive, effective learning environments 4.b Expand scholarships for developing countries 4.c Increase the supply of qualified teachers Key Point Remember "7 + 3": seven outcome targets (4.1–4.7) and three means of implementation (4.a–4.c). The Education 2030 Framework for Action recommends spending 4–6% of GDP and/or 15–20% of public expenditure on education. Bangladesh has spent roughly 2% of GDP on education in recent years, one of the lowest shares in South Asia, so this is a standard "issue" point in any essay. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Trace the historical development of education in Bangladesh." "Describe the present structure of the education system." "Explain SDG 4 and assess Bangladesh's progress."

Primary education (Classes I–V, official age 6–10) is free and compulsory, and is administered by the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education (MoPME) through the Directorate of Primary Education (DPE) . One year of pre-primary education (age 5) was introduced nationally in government primary schools from 2010 following NEP 2010; NCF 2021 envisages two years (ages 4+ and 5+). Primary education is delivered by government primary schools, newly nationalised schools (about 26,000 registered non-government schools were nationalised in 2013), ebtedayee madrasahs, kindergartens, NGO schools (such as BRAC) and community schools. The goals of primary education (NEP 2010; National Primary Education goals) are to develop foundational literacy and numeracy, physical and mental development, moral and human values, patriotism and the spirit of the Liberation War, scientific and creative thinking, environmental awareness and readiness for further learning.

Bangladesh has made major progress since 1990: Near-universal access : primary net enrolment has exceeded 95% in recent Annual Primary School Census (APSC) reports. Gender parity achieved : girls' enrolment now equals or exceeds boys' at primary level. Internal efficiency improved : dropout fell from roughly 50% in the early 2000s to under 20%, and completion rates rose. Remaining equity gaps : children in urban slums, char and haor areas, hill tracts and tea gardens; working children; children with disabilities; and ethnic minority children taught in a language they do not speak at home. Note Figures change every year. Use the latest APSC (DPE) and BANBEIS reports when you cite numbers in an exam, and always give the year and the source.

Pre-primary curriculum is play-based and organised as a matrix of learning areas (physical and motor development, socio-emotional development, language and communication, early mathematics, environment and science, arts and creativity, and health and hygiene), with suggested learning activities (play, songs and rhymes, stories, drawing, games) and expected learning outcomes . Primary curriculum has been competency-based since the 1990s revisions, with terminal competencies for the end of Class V and class-wise and subject-wise learning outcomes . The 2012 revision listed 29 terminal competencies. Subjects include Bangla, English, Mathematics, Bangladesh and Global Studies, Primary Science, Religion and Moral Education, plus Physical Education, Music and Arts and Crafts. NCTB (National Curriculum and Textbook Board) develops curricula, writes and prints textbooks and distributes them free (the national Textbook Festival on 1 January), and prepares teacher guides. Assessment includes continuous assessment, term examinations and the National Student Assessment (NSA), a sample-based survey of learning outcomes in Bangla and Mathematics in Classes III and V.

Figure 4. Administrative structure of primary education MoPME sets policy, plans the budget and coordinates with development partners. It also oversees the Bureau of Non-Formal Education (BNFE) and the National Academy for Primary Education (NAPE) , Mymensingh. DPE implements programmes, recruits and posts teachers, manages stipends and school feeding, and runs teacher training through the PTIs. Financing comes mainly from the government revenue budget and the Annual Development Programme (ADP), with sector-wide support from development partners (World Bank, ADB, EU, JICA, UNICEF and others) pooled under PEDP.

Programme Period Focus PEDP I 1997–2003 Collection of project-based interventions PEDP II 2004–2011 First sub-sector-wide approach (SWAp): access, quality, management PEDP3 2011–2017 (extended) Learning outcomes, participation and disparity reduction, decentralisation; results-based financing (DLIs) PEDP4 2018–2025 (extended) Quality learning for all from pre-primary to Class V; teacher development; ICT; inclusive education Primary Education Stipend Programme ongoing Cash transfer to mothers via mobile banking School Feeding Programme ongoing Biscuits and cooked meals to improve attendance and nutrition Reaching Out-of-School Children (ROSC) 2004 onward Ananda schools / learning centres for out-of-school children Government, NGO and INGO initiatives. NGOs such as BRAC, Dhaka Ahsania Mission, FIVDB and CAMPE (Campaign for Popular Education, a network that publishes the Education Watch reports), and INGOs such as Save the Children, Plan International, UNICEF and Room to Read, contribute through non-formal schools, early-grade reading programmes, research and advocacy.

Diploma in Primary Education (DPEd): an 18-month programme launched in 2012 (replacing the one-year Certificate-in-Education) delivered in Primary Teacher Training Institutes (PTIs) with school-based practice. It was designed with IER, University of Dhaka, and NAPE. Sub-cluster training: short, regular in-service subject training for teachers of a cluster of schools, led by AUEOs. Upazila Resource Centres (URCs): in-service subject-based and ICT training at upazila level. IER, University of Dhaka and other universities: degree programmes, curriculum and research support. NAPE: national apex institution for primary teacher education, research and training of PTI instructors.

Secondary education comprises junior secondary (Classes VI–VIII) , secondary (IX–X) , ending with the SSC examination, and higher secondary (XI–XII) , ending with HSC. NEP 2010 proposed restructuring to IX–XII with primary up to VIII; this has not been fully implemented. Streams after Class VIII have traditionally been Science, Humanities and Business Studies. NCF 2021 proposed abolishing streaming until Class X, which became one of the most debated reforms. Objectives (NEP 2010): develop the creative and critical faculties of learners, prepare them for higher education and employment, ensure a common core curriculum in all streams, develop moral and patriotic values and promote science and ICT.

Since the 1990s secondary enrolment has expanded rapidly. The Female Secondary School Stipend Programme (from 1994 nationally) is internationally recognised for helping Bangladesh achieve gender parity and, at many levels, more girls than boys enrolled. Persistent challenges include high dropout (particularly for poor boys who enter work and girls affected by child marriage), low completion rates, and urban–rural and regional disparities. More than 95% of secondary schools are non-government (privately managed but receiving government salary support under the Monthly Pay Order, MPO ).

t: 3.3 Curriculum, textbooks, teachers' guides and assessment
x: NCTB develops the secondary curriculum, textbooks and teachers' guides. The 2012 curriculum emphasised learning outcomes and creative (structured) questions (CQ) , introduced from 2008 to discourage rote learning. The NCF 2021 curriculum introduced experiential learning, project work and largely school-based, competency-based assessment with "performance indicators", before the 2024–25 policy reversal noted in Unit 1. Evaluation and examination system Education boards conduct SSC and HSC examinations, issue certificates and register institutions. Results use a GPA system (introduced 2001 for SSC; 5.0 maximum). School-Based Assessment (SBA) , piloted from the mid-2000s with support from the Secondary Education Sector Improvement Project (SESIP), aimed to add continuous assessment of practical and affective learning. It faced problems of teacher capacity, workload and reliability. NAEM and BEDU (Bangladesh Examinations Development Unit) have supported training in question-setting and assessment.

Figure 5. Governance of secondary education Ministry of Education (MoE) has two divisions (since 2016–17): the Secondary and Higher Education Division (SHED) and the Technical and Madrasah Education Division (TMED) . DSHE supervises secondary schools and colleges, manages MPO, transfers and postings in government institutions, and implements projects. Other bodies: NCTB , BANBEIS (statistics), NAEM (training of managers and teachers), DIA (Directorate of Inspection and Audit), NTRCA (registration and certification of non-government teachers) and the education boards .

Project Focus TQI-SEP (Teaching Quality Improvement in Secondary Education Project), phases I and II (c. 2005–2017) In-service training, CPD for secondary teachers, strengthening TTCs and HSTTIs SESIP (Secondary Education Sector Investment Program, ADB) Sector reform: curriculum, assessment including SBA, management SEQAEP (Secondary Education Quality and Access Enhancement Project, World Bank) Stipends, tuition support, teacher incentives in poorer upazilas SEDP (Secondary Education Development Program, 2018 onward) Sector-wide programme for access, quality, governance SBA (School-Based Assessment) Continuous and formative assessment practices

IER, University of Dhaka and other university institutes: BEd (Hons), MEd, MPhil and PhD. Government Teachers' Training Colleges (TTCs): one-year BEd and MEd for in-service and pre-service teachers; private TTCs also offer BEd. Higher Secondary Teachers' Training Institutes (HSTTIs): in-service training of college teachers. NAEM: foundation and management training for education cadre officers and heads. Bangladesh Open University: distance BEd and MEd.

t: 3.7 Major issues, challenges and possible solutions
x: Quality and learning outcomes: many learners lack higher-order skills; private tutoring and guidebooks are widespread (Nath, 2008). Solutions: teacher CPD, formative assessment, regulation of coaching, better textbooks. Teacher quality and shortages: especially in English, Mathematics and Science in rural schools; untrained teachers in non-government schools. Solutions: NTRCA merit-based recruitment, subject-based training, incentives. Governance: politicisation of managing committees, irregularities in MPO and recruitment. Solutions: transparency, e-management, accountability. Equity and dropout: poverty, child labour, child marriage. Solutions: stipends, school meals, safe schools, second-chance programmes. Curriculum instability: frequent reforms reduce teacher confidence. Solutions: evidence-based piloting, stakeholder consultation, a permanent education commission (as proposed in NEP 2010).

Higher education aims to create and disseminate knowledge, produce skilled professionals and leaders, conduct research for national development, and nurture critical, ethical citizenship. The Strategic Plan for Higher Education in Bangladesh 2006–2026 (UGC) set goals of quality, relevance, research capacity, governance and financing reform.

Type Examples Features Public general universities University of Dhaka (1921), Rajshahi (1953), Chittagong (1966), Jahangirnagar (1970) Mostly autonomous; the four older universities are governed by the 1973 Acts Public science and technology / specialised universities BUET, Bangladesh Agricultural University, SUST, medical universities Professional and technical focus Affiliating universities National University (1992); Islamic Arabic University (2013) Affiliate thousands of colleges (degree pass, honours, masters) and Fazil/Kamil madrasahs Open university Bangladesh Open University (1992) Distance and open learning Private universities North South University (1992) and many others Governed by the Private University Act 2010; fee-financed Colleges and specialised institutions Government and non-government colleges, medical colleges, engineering colleges, TTCs Teaching under affiliating universities International universities Asian University for Women Regional mandates

Tertiary enrolment has expanded rapidly, with National University colleges accounting for the largest share. Access remains unequal by income, region and gender in some fields. University Grants Commission (UGC) was established by President's Order No. 10 of 1973. Its roles: allocating government grants to public universities; planning and coordinating development of higher education; approving new programmes and monitoring private universities; quality assurance (through the Quality Assurance Unit and Institutional Quality Assurance Cells, IQACs, created under HEQEP); advising the government on higher education policy. The Bangladesh Accreditation Council (BAC) , created by the 2017 Act, is responsible for programme and institutional accreditation.

HEQEP (Higher Education Quality Enhancement Project, World Bank, c. 2009–2018): competitive Academic Innovation Fund, IQACs, BdREN (Bangladesh Research and Education Network), digital library resources. HEAT (Higher Education Acceleration and Transformation project, World Bank, approved 2021): research, quality assurance, digital transformation and labour-market relevance.

Madrasah (Arabic, "place of study") refers to institutions of Islamic learning. In Bengal, madrasahs flourished under the Sultanate and Mughal rulers; the Calcutta Alia Madrasah , founded by Warren Hastings in 1780, is the origin of the government-recognised Alia stream, while the Deoband movement (Darul Uloom Deoband, 1866) inspired the independent Qawmi stream. Type Governance Curriculum Recognition Alia madrasah Bangladesh Madrasah Education Board; Directorate of Madrasah Education; TMED Islamic studies and Arabic plus general subjects (Bangla, English, Mathematics, Science, ICT) Ebtedayee = primary; Dakhil = SSC; Alim = HSC; Fazil = degree; Kamil = masters (through Islamic Arabic University) Qawmi madrasah Independent boards (e.g. Befaqul Madarisil Arabia Bangladesh) under Al-Haiatul Ulya Dars-e-Nizami tradition: Qur'an, Hadith, Fiqh, Arabic, Urdu, Persian Dawra-e-Hadith recognised as equivalent to Master's in Islamic Studies and Arabic (2018 Act)

t: 5.2 Present structure, goals, access and participation
x: Alia madrasahs run from Ebtedayee (I–V), Dakhil (VI–X), Alim (XI–XII), Fazil (degree) and Kamil (masters). Goals combine religious scholarship and moral development with general education and employable skills. Madrasahs enrol a substantial share of secondary students, disproportionately from poorer and rural households, and a high proportion of girls in Alia madrasahs.

The Alia curriculum follows the NCTB general curriculum for core subjects, alongside Qur'an, Hadith, Aqaid and Fiqh, and Arabic. The Bangladesh Madrasah Education Board conducts the JDC (historically), Dakhil and Alim examinations. Instruction often relies on recitation and memorisation; teacher training in modern pedagogy for general subjects is a known gap.

Technical and Madrasah Education Division (TMED) of MoE: policy. Directorate of Madrasah Education (established 2016): administration, MPO and monitoring. Bangladesh Madrasah Education Board : curriculum (with NCTB), registration, examinations. Islamic Arabic University (2013): affiliation of Fazil and Kamil madrasahs. Financing: almost all Alia madrasahs are non-government but receive MPO salary support; Qawmi madrasahs are financed by community donations and zakat . Bangladesh Madrasah Teachers Training Institute (BMTTI) , Gazipur: in-service training and BEd-type courses for madrasah teachers.

Quality of general subjects, especially Science, English and Mathematics: subject teachers and specialised training. Employability of graduates: integration of ICT and vocational skills. Lack of unified standards between Alia and Qawmi streams: dialogue and equivalency frameworks. Weak infrastructure and libraries: targeted investment. Perceptions and stereotypes: research-based policy and integration with the national qualifications framework.

u: Unit 6: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET)
x: TVET develops the occupational knowledge and skills needed for employment and self-employment. Its goals in Bangladesh include producing a skilled workforce for the domestic and overseas labour markets, reducing youth unemployment, supporting industrialisation and the "demographic dividend", and raising the share of TVET enrolment (the government target has been around 30% of post-Class VIII enrolment). u: Unit 6: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET)
x: TVET enrolment has grown, but its share of total secondary and post-secondary enrolment remains modest and female participation is low. TVET often carries low social esteem ("second choice"), and many institutions lack modern equipment and industry links.

u: Unit 6: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET)
t: 6.3 Curriculum and the National Qualifications Framework
x: The National Technical and Vocational Qualifications Framework (NTVQF, 2011) , developed with ILO/EU support, introduced competency-based training and assessment (CBT&A) with levels from pre-vocational to diploma. The Bangladesh National Qualifications Framework (BNQF, approved 2021) integrates general, TVET and higher education qualifications in a 10-level framework, with the National Skills Qualifications Framework (NSQF) covering skills levels. Competency standards are developed with Industry Skills Councils (ISCs) so that training reflects employers' needs.

u: Unit 6: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET)
t: 6.4 TVET for employability and sustainable development
x: TVET contributes to SDG targets 4.3 and 4.4 (skills for decent work), SDG 8 (decent work and economic growth) and to green skills for climate adaptation. Remittances from skilled migrant workers are a major source of foreign exchange, so recognised skills qualifications raise both earnings and national income.

Other ministries also run training: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare (Technical Training Centres under BMET), Youth and Sports, Labour and Employment, and Women and Children Affairs.

Refugee education is education provided for people forced to flee their country because of persecution, conflict or violence. Since the large influx of August 2017, Bangladesh has hosted roughly one million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar, mostly in camps in Ukhiya and Teknaf (Cox's Bazar) and on Bhasan Char. More than half are children. Education provides: protection from child labour, trafficking, early marriage and recruitment into armed groups; psychosocial wellbeing and a sense of normality; skills and hope for a durable solution, whether repatriation or other; social cohesion with host communities.

Right to education : the 1951 Refugee Convention (Art. 22) and the CRC guarantee education for refugee children. INEE Minimum Standards : foundational standards (community participation, coordination, analysis), access and learning environment, teaching and learning, teachers and other education personnel, and education policy. Do no harm and conflict sensitivity : education must not reinforce divisions. Protection and psychosocial support : safe learning spaces and trauma-informed teaching. Quality and relevance : recognised curricula that support future pathways (UNHCR, 2019, Refugee Education 2030 ). Inclusion and gender equality : reaching girls, adolescents and children with disabilities. Community participation : involving refugee teachers, parents and majhis (community leaders).

t: 7.3 Joint Response Plan and the education programme
x: The Joint Response Plan (JRP) for the Rohingya humanitarian crisis is prepared each year by the Government of Bangladesh and humanitarian partners, coordinated by the Inter Sector Coordination Group (ISCG) . The Education Sector , co-led by UNICEF and Save the Children with UNHCR, coordinates learning centres, teacher recruitment and training, materials and monitoring. The government's policy has been that Rohingya children learn in Burmese and English (not Bangla) and follow a Myanmar-oriented curriculum to support eventual return.

Age group Intervention 3–5 years Early childhood development and play-based learning in learning centres 4–14 years Learning Competency Framework and Approach (LCFA) , a four-level non-formal framework introduced in 2019 covering Burmese, English, Mathematics, Life Skills and Science School age (Grades 6–9 initially, then expanding) Myanmar Curriculum Pilot (MCP) , launched 2021–22, to give learners a formal curriculum recognised in Myanmar Adolescents and youth (15–24) Literacy and numeracy, life skills, basic vocational and digital skills, protection programmes Host-community children School improvement, teacher support and social-cohesion activities in Ukhiya and Teknaf Challenges include funding shortfalls, lack of accreditation, teacher quality, overcrowding, and girls' drop-out at puberty. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Explain the principles of refugee education with reference to the Rohingya response." "Describe programme interventions for different age groups in refugee education in Bangladesh."

Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Educational psychology applies psychological theory and research to teaching and learning. Woolfolk (2019) defines it as "the discipline concerned with teaching and learning processes; it applies the methods and theories of psychology and has its own as well". E. L. Thorndike, often called the father of educational psychology, launched the Journal of Educational Psychology in 1910. Its central questions are: how do people learn, why do they differ, what motivates them, and how can teaching be organised to help them learn? Definition Educational psychology : The branch of psychology that studies human learning and development in educational settings, the psychology of teaching, and the social psychology of schools as organisations.

Figure 1. The scope of educational psychology The learner: physical, cognitive, social and emotional development; heredity and environment; individual differences in intelligence, aptitude and personality. The learning process: theories of learning, memory and forgetting, transfer of learning, problem solving. The learning situation: classroom climate, group dynamics, instructional technology. The teacher: effective teaching characteristics, teacher expectations (the Pygmalion effect; Rosenthal & Jacobson, 1968), teacher stress and wellbeing. Motivation, emotion and wellbeing. Measurement and evaluation: tests of achievement, intelligence and personality. Guidance and counselling, mental health and inclusive education.

Method Description Strengths Limitations Introspection Self-observation of one's own mental processes (Wundt, Titchener) Direct access to experience Subjective; not possible for young children Observation (naturalistic, participant, structured) Systematic recording of behaviour in real settings Natural, ecologically valid Observer bias; time-consuming; cannot show causation Experimental method Manipulating an independent variable and measuring its effect on a dependent variable with control of other variables Establishes cause and effect Artificial settings; ethical limits Case study (clinical) In-depth study of one individual or group using many sources Rich detail; useful for special needs Not generalisable Survey / questionnaire Collecting self-reported data from large samples Efficient; broad coverage Response bias; shallow Correlational method Measuring the relationship between two variables Shows association and allows prediction Correlation is not causation Developmental methods: longitudinal and cross-sectional Following the same group over time, or comparing age groups at one time Show developmental change Longitudinal studies are costly and suffer attrition; cross-sectional ones have cohort effects Action research Teachers studying their own practice in cycles of plan–act–observe–reflect Directly improves practice Limited generalisability Key Point Exam answers on methods should end with a sentence on ethics : informed consent, protection from harm, confidentiality and special care with minors.

u: Unit 2: Biological Basis of Behaviour and Learning
x: Figure 2. Organisation of the human nervous system Neuron: the basic unit, with dendrites (receive signals), a cell body, an axon (sends signals, often insulated by a myelin sheath) and axon terminals. Neurons communicate across the synapse through neurotransmitters such as dopamine (reward and motivation), serotonin (mood), acetylcholine (attention and memory) and GABA (inhibition). Brain regions relevant to learning: Cerebral cortex , with four lobes: frontal (planning, reasoning, executive function and working memory, with the prefrontal cortex maturing into the mid-20s), parietal (sensory integration, spatial and numerical processing), temporal (hearing, language comprehension in Wernicke's area, memory) and occipital (vision). Limbic system: the hippocampus consolidates new memories; the amygdala processes emotion, especially fear. Cerebellum: coordination, motor learning and some cognitive functions. Brainstem: basic life functions and arousal (reticular activating system).

u: Unit 2: Biological Basis of Behaviour and Learning
x: Neuroplasticity: the brain changes its structure and function in response to experience. "Neurons that fire together wire together" (Hebb, 1949). Learning strengthens synaptic connections (long-term potentiation). Synaptogenesis and pruning: there is rapid growth of synapses in early childhood followed by pruning of unused connections ("use it or lose it"), which makes early stimulation important. Myelination: continues into early adulthood and speeds neural transmission; this helps explain developmental limits on attention and executive control. Sensitive periods: windows when certain learning, such as language phonology, happens most easily, although learning remains possible throughout life. Sleep, exercise, nutrition and stress all influence memory consolidation and attention. Chronic stress (cortisol) impairs the hippocampus and working memory. Note Beware of neuromyths : "we use only 10% of our brains", "left-brained and right-brained learners" and "learning styles (VAK) improve learning when matched" are not supported by evidence (Howard-Jones, 2014; Pashler et al., 2008). Mentioning this in an interview shows critical awareness.
