u: Unit 1: The Sociological Approach to Studying Education
t: 1.1 Concept, nature and scope of sociology
x: Sociology (from the Latin socius , companion, and Greek logos , study) was named by Auguste Comte (1838), who is called the father of sociology. It is "the scientific study of human social life, groups and societies" (Giddens & Sutton, 2021). Max Weber defined it as "a science which attempts the interpretive understanding of social action in order to arrive at a causal explanation of its course and effects." Nature: sociology is a social science (not a natural science); it is categorical (describes what is, not what ought to be), pure as well as applied, abstract (studies patterns, not individual events), generalising, and both rational and empirical. Scope: two schools of thought: Formal (specialistic) school (Simmel, Tönnies, Weber): sociology studies the forms of social relationships, such as cooperation, competition and conflict. Synthetic school (Durkheim, Hobhouse, Sorokin): sociology is a general science synthesising all social sciences to study society as a whole. Sociological imagination (C. Wright Mills, 1959): the ability to link "personal troubles" (a child dropping out) to "public issues" (poverty, child labour, policy).

u: Unit 1: The Sociological Approach to Studying Education
t: 1.2 Sociology of education and educational sociology
x: Educational sociology (early 20th century, Lester Ward, George Payne) applied sociology to solve educational problems; it was practical and reform-oriented. Sociology of education (from the 1950s) is the scientific study of education as a social institution and its relation to other institutions, structures and processes. It asks: how does education reproduce or reduce inequality? What does schooling do for society? How are knowledge and identities constructed in classrooms? Importance of the sociological approach: it reveals the social causes of educational success and failure; explains the hidden curriculum; informs policy on equity; helps teachers understand diverse learners; and connects school with the wider community.

u: Unit 1: The Sociological Approach to Studying Education
x: Figure 1. Three classic sociological perspectives on education Functionalism. Durkheim (1956) saw education as "the methodical socialisation of the young generation" to create the social solidarity a society needs. Parsons (1959) saw the school class as the main agent for transferring children from particularistic family values to the universalistic, achievement-based values of society, and for allocating them to adult roles. Davis and Moore (1945) argued that education sorts people by talent into unequally rewarded positions. Conflict theory. Bowles and Gintis (1976), Schooling in Capitalist America : the correspondence principle , according to which the social relations of school (hierarchy, obedience, external rewards) correspond to those of the capitalist workplace. Bourdieu and Passeron (1977): schools reward cultural capital (language, tastes and dispositions of the dominant class), producing cultural reproduction and symbolic violence. Collins (1979): credentialism. Symbolic interactionism. Becker's (1952) study of how teachers judge "ideal pupils"; labelling theory; Rosenthal and Jacobson's (1968) Pygmalion in the Classroom showed teacher expectations can produce a self-fulfilling prophecy.

u: Unit 1: The Sociological Approach to Studying Education
x: These are two broad ways of understanding the relationship between society and its parts, including education. Basis Inorganic (mechanical / atomistic) approach Organic approach View of society An aggregate of individuals, like parts of a machine, assembled by contract A living organism whose parts (institutions) are interdependent, like organs of a body Key thinkers Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau (social contract); individualism Herbert Spencer (organic analogy), Durkheim, Plato (the state as the individual "writ large") Primacy The individual comes first; society serves individual interests Society comes first; individuals find meaning in their social functions Education Emphasises individual development, rights and freedom Emphasises socialisation, social efficiency, duties and cohesion Durkheim's terms Closer to "organic solidarity" in a complex society of specialised individuals (Note: Durkheim's mechanical solidarity is based on likeness in simple societies; organic solidarity on interdependence in complex ones) Key Point Do not confuse the "organic approach" (society as an organism, Spencer) with Durkheim's "organic solidarity" (interdependence in modern societies with a complex division of labour). Examiners sometimes test exactly this distinction. Exam Focus Likely questions: "What is the sociological approach to education? Explain its importance." "Compare the functionalist and conflict perspectives on education." "Distinguish between the organic and inorganic approaches."

Education serves social aims when it prepares individuals to live productively and harmoniously in society. The syllabus lists nine aims; a holistic view sees them as interrelated. Figure 2. The social aims of education Aim Meaning How education achieves it Bangladesh example Physical development Health, fitness, motor skills, healthy habits Physical education, games, health education, school meals Mandatory Physical Education and Health subject; inter-school sports Development of personality Integrated growth of cognitive, emotional, social and moral traits Child-centred teaching, co-curricular activities, counselling Debate clubs, scouts, cultural programmes Democratic and intellectual abilities Critical thinking, rational discussion, tolerance, participation Discussion methods, student councils, civics Student cabinet elections in secondary schools Social competencies Cooperation, communication, empathy, leadership Group work, community service, SEL Group projects in NCTB curricula Livelihood Knowledge and skills for earning a living TVET, career guidance, entrepreneurship SSC (Vocational), skills programmes Moral development Honesty, justice, responsibility Moral and religious education, role models Religion and Moral Education subject Cultural development Understanding and transmitting heritage; respect for diverse cultures Literature, history, festivals, arts Celebrating Pohela Boishakh, Language Day Aesthetic development Appreciation and creation of beauty Music, art, crafts, literature Arts and crafts, music in primary curriculum Spiritual development Inner values, meaning, connection beyond the self Religious education, reflection, values education Religious education for all major faiths Note A balanced answer explains that these aims must be integrated. Over-emphasis on livelihood risks narrow instrumentalism; over-emphasis on spiritual or cultural aims without livelihood risks irrelevance. Dewey's idea of "social efficiency" combines individual growth with social contribution.

Agencies of education are the institutions and forces in society that educate individuals, deliberately or incidentally. They are classified as formal (deliberate, organised) and informal (spontaneous, incidental). Some writers add non-formal agencies (literacy centres, training programmes), as well as active (two-way: family, community) and passive (one-way: newspapers, radio) agencies. Figure 3. Agencies of education

School: the main formal agency. Functions: systematic instruction, socialisation, character building, transmission of culture, preparation for citizenship and work, selection and certification. Dewey: "the school is a special environment" that simplifies, purifies and balances. Madrasah: formal agency combining religious and general education, central for many rural families in Bangladesh. College and university: advanced knowledge, research, professional preparation and leadership; universities also act as centres of critical thought and social movements (the 1952 Language Movement and 1969 uprising were led by students). Other institutions: technical institutes, teacher training institutes, academies, and training centres.

Agency Educational role Home / family The first school and the mother as the first teacher; primary socialisation, language, values, habits, emotional security, attitudes to learning Community Norms, customs, festivals, occupational skills, social control; community support for schools (SMCs) State Policy, law, funding, curricula, compulsory education, regulation, civic education Organisations (clubs, NGOs, scouts) Leadership, service, specialised skills, non-formal education Religion Moral and spiritual values, rituals, community identity; mosques, temples, churches and pagodas as learning places Peer group Secondary socialisation, identity, norms of behaviour, sometimes delinquency or bullying Mass media (newspapers, magazines, radio, television, cinema, drama) Information, awareness, entertainment, shaping opinions and values; educational TV and radio (Sangsad TV lessons) Social media and the internet Instant information, networking, self-learning, online courses; risks of misinformation, cyberbullying and addiction Library and museum Self-directed learning, research, heritage (National Museum, Liberation War Museum) Tours and excursions Direct experience of places, cultures and history

The agencies complement each other; when they conflict (for example the media promoting values contrary to school teaching), learners face confusion. Effective education requires coordination , such as home–school partnerships, community participation and responsible media.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Family structure (nuclear or joint), income, parental education, especially mothers' education, and the home learning environment strongly predict school outcomes. Cultural capital (Bourdieu), social capital (Coleman, 1988) and parental involvement (Epstein, 2001, six types of involvement) explain why. In Bangladesh, first-generation learners in poor rural families face the greatest disadvantages, while urban middle-class families invest heavily in private tutoring.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Gender norms influence expectations, opportunities and treatment. Bangladesh achieved gender parity in enrolment at primary and secondary level through stipends and incentives, but girls still face early marriage, safety concerns, domestic burden and under-representation in STEM, TVET and higher education leadership. Boys in poor families face pressure to work and growing dropout rates. See PC 122.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Bangladesh is home to more than 50 ethnic minority groups (for example Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Santal, Garo, Manipuri), mainly in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and the northern plains. Barriers include language (Bangla-medium instruction), remoteness, poverty and cultural irrelevance of curricula. Since 2017 NCTB has provided pre-primary and early-grade textbooks in five ethnic languages (Chakma, Marma, Kokborok/Tripura, Garo/Achik and Sadri), an example of mother-tongue-based multilingual education (MTB-MLE) .

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Social stratification is the hierarchical arrangement of individuals and groups by wealth, power and prestige (class, caste, status). It shapes access to quality schools, private tutoring, English-medium education and higher education. Bangladesh's education system is stratified into parallel streams (English-medium, Bangla-medium general, Alia and Qawmi madrasah), which often mirror and reproduce class divisions (Bourdieu's reproduction thesis). Education can also enable social mobility (vertical mobility through credentials and occupation).

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Population size, growth, density, age structure and migration affect educational demand and planning. Bangladesh's large youth population (the demographic dividend ) creates both opportunity and pressure on schools, teachers and the labour market. High density means overcrowded classrooms; migration to cities creates demand for urban schools; climate-induced displacement affects schooling in coastal areas.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Religion shapes values, worldviews, educational institutions (madrasahs, tols, mission schools) and attitudes towards girls' education and science. Bangladesh's Constitution guarantees religious freedom; religious education is taught according to each student's faith. Education can promote interfaith understanding and tolerance.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Culture is "that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society" (Tylor, 1871). Education transmits material and non-material culture. Cultural lag (Ogburn, 1922) occurs when non-material culture (values, institutions) lags behind material and technological change; for example, online learning tools arrived faster than norms for their responsible use.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Rapid urbanisation (Dhaka is one of the world's fastest-growing megacities) creates both opportunities (more schools, colleges, jobs) and problems: overcrowding, high costs, slum children out of school, child labour, rising inequality between elite and poor schools.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Industrialisation demands a literate, skilled and disciplined workforce; it historically drove mass schooling in Europe. In Bangladesh, the ready-made garment (RMG) sector has transformed women's employment and created demand for skills and TVET, while also drawing adolescents out of school.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: National income, public spending (about 2% of GDP), household income and the opportunity cost of schooling shape participation. Human capital theory (Schultz, Becker) sees education as investment; conflict theorists highlight how economic inequality limits educational opportunity.

u: Unit 4: Social Bases of Education (with reference to Bangladesh)
x: Political ideology, stability, governance and student politics influence education policy, curriculum content (for example the history of the Liberation War), appointments and campus climate. Frequent policy changes and politicisation of institutions are recurrent issues in Bangladesh. Figure 4. Social bases that shape educational access and outcomes

Socialisation is the lifelong process through which individuals learn the culture, norms, values and roles of their society and develop a social self. Primary socialisation occurs in the family; secondary socialisation occurs in schools, peer groups, workplaces and media. Key theorists: G. H. Mead: the self develops through the "I" (spontaneous) and the "me" (socialised self) in stages of play, game and the generalised other. C. H. Cooley: the looking-glass self : we see ourselves as we imagine others see us. Durkheim: education as "methodical socialisation". Schools socialise through the formal curriculum and the hidden curriculum (Jackson, 1968): punctuality, obedience, competition, gender roles and respect for authority.

Education prepares informed, responsible and active citizens with knowledge of rights and duties, democratic values, critical thinking and participation skills. Marshall (1950) distinguished civil, political and social citizenship. Methods: civics curricula, student councils, debates, community service, mock parliaments and global citizenship education.

Education preserves the cultural heritage (language, literature, history, arts, values) and transmits it to new generations. In Bangladesh, the Language Movement, the Liberation War and Bengali festivals are deliberately taught.

Education is also a source of new knowledge and ideas through research, creativity, critical thinking and scientific inquiry. Universities, in particular, generate innovations in science, technology, arts and social thought.

Social change is the alteration of social structures, relationships and cultural patterns over time. Education is both a cause (an agent) and an effect (a consequence) of social change: it spreads new ideas, promotes modernisation and mobility, empowers women and disadvantaged groups, and supports economic development. Yet it can also preserve the status quo. The extent of education's power is debated (Counts versus reproduction theorists). Figure 5. Education as both cause and effect of social change

Education helps individuals and societies adapt to change by developing flexibility, problem-solving, digital literacy and lifelong learning; by updating curricula; and by reducing cultural lag . Examples: digital learning during COVID-19, climate adaptation education, and new skills for the Fourth Industrial Revolution. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Explain the role of education in socialisation." "Is education an agent of social change or a product of it? Discuss." "How does education conserve and transmit culture?"

u: Unit 6: Sociology of Pedagogy and Andragogy
x: Pedagogy: the art and science of teaching children; teacher-directed, subject-centred, with extrinsic motivation. Andragogy: "the art and science of helping adults learn" (Knowles, 1980); self-directed, experience-based, problem-centred, intrinsically motivated.

u: Unit 6: Sociology of Pedagogy and Andragogy
t: 6.2 Social contexts of learning and teaching
x: Social context Children (pedagogy) Adults (andragogy) Social role Dependent learners; student is the main role Multiple roles: worker, parent, citizen Reason for learning Curriculum requirements, examinations, parents Life tasks, work, social responsibilities Group dynamics Age-graded classes, peer influence Heterogeneous groups, rich experience, mutual respect Power relations Teacher has formal authority More equal relationship; facilitator Barriers Family background, child labour Time, work and family burdens, low confidence, previous negative schooling Setting Schools, formal NFE centres, workplaces, community, online Social outcomes Socialisation, preparation for adult roles Empowerment, livelihood, civic participation, social change (Freire) Social learning theory (Bandura, 1977) and situated learning in communities of practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991) show that both children and adults learn through observation and participation in social contexts.

u: Unit 6: Sociology of Pedagogy and Andragogy
x: A profession is an occupation that requires specialised knowledge and long training, provides an essential public service, has autonomy, a code of ethics, a professional association and public recognition (Lieberman, 1956; Hoyle, 1980). Teaching meets many criteria but is often called a semi-profession (Etzioni, 1969) because of lower autonomy, status and pay, and because entry standards vary. Professionalisation of teaching in Bangladesh involves NTRCA certification, the BEd/MEd qualifications, the draft National Teacher Standards and continuing professional development.

u: Unit 6: Sociology of Pedagogy and Andragogy
x: A teacher's code of ethics typically includes commitment to: Students: respect for dignity, fairness, non-discrimination, protection from harm, confidentiality, no corporal punishment, no private tutoring of one's own students for profit (a specific Bangladeshi rule under the 2012 coaching policy). The profession: competence, continuous learning, integrity, collegiality. Parents and community: honest communication, partnership. Society and nation: promoting democratic values, national integrity and human rights. UNESCO/ILO's Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers (1966) is the international reference document.

u: Unit 6: Sociology of Pedagogy and Andragogy
x: Subject mastery; pedagogical skills; communication; empathy and warmth; fairness; patience; enthusiasm; creativity; leadership; reflective attitude; integrity; and cultural sensitivity. Research consistently shows that warm, high-expectation teachers who build relationships achieve better learning outcomes.

t: 1.1 Test, measurement, assessment, evaluation and examination
x: Term Definition Key feature Test A systematic procedure or instrument for measuring a sample of behaviour (Gronlund) An instrument: a set of questions or tasks Measurement "The assignment of numerals to objects or events according to rules" (Stevens, 1946) Quantitative: answers "how much?" Assessment The process of gathering, interpreting and using information about learners' learning, through tests and other methods (observation, portfolios, projects) Broader than testing; can be quantitative or qualitative Evaluation "The systematic process of determining the extent to which instructional objectives are achieved" (Gronlund); a value judgement about worth or merit Judgement: answers "how good?" Examination A formal, usually summative assessment conducted under controlled conditions, often public (e.g. SSC, HSC) Formal, high-stakes, certification Key Point A classic formula: Evaluation = Measurement (quantitative description) or Non-measurement (qualitative description) + Value judgement (Gronlund & Linn). Assessment includes measurement and non-measurement information; evaluation adds the judgement. Figure 1. The nested relationship of test, measurement, assessment and evaluation

Curriculum (what should be learned), instruction (how it is taught) and assessment (how learning is checked) form a triangle that must be constructively aligned (Biggs, 1996): objectives, activities and assessment tasks must target the same outcomes. When assessment is misaligned, for example testing recall when the curriculum seeks problem solving, teaching and learning drift towards what is tested. Figure 2. Constructive alignment: curriculum, instruction and assessment must target the same outcomes

Assessment has a powerful backwash or washback effect on teaching and learning (Alderson & Wall, 1993). Positive washback occurs when examinations reward understanding and skills; negative washback occurs when high-stakes examinations encourage rote memorisation, guidebooks, coaching and "teaching to the test", as widely observed with Bangladesh's public examinations. Formative assessment research (Black & Wiliam, 1998) found effect sizes of 0.4–0.7 on achievement, among the largest of any intervention.

Clarity of purpose: decide what is assessed and why. Alignment with objectives and instruction. Validity: measure what it intends to measure. Reliability: produce consistent results. Fairness and inclusiveness: free from bias; accommodations for diverse learners. Variety: use multiple methods for a comprehensive picture. Transparency: criteria known to learners in advance. Practicality: feasible in time, cost and effort. Feedback: timely, specific, actionable. Continuity: ongoing, not one-off. Ethics: confidentiality, honesty, avoiding harm.
Figure 3. Steps in educational assessment

Type Purpose Timing Examples Diagnostic Identify prior knowledge, strengths, learning difficulties Before or during instruction Pre-test, diagnostic interview Formative: assessment for learning (AfL) Monitor progress and give feedback to improve learning During instruction Questioning, quizzes, exit tickets, peer feedback Assessment as learning (AaL) Students monitor and regulate their own learning (metacognition) Throughout Self-assessment, learning journals, goal setting Summative: assessment of learning (AoL) Judge and certify achievement End of unit, term or course Final examinations, SSC/HSC Placement Place learners in appropriate level or group Before instruction Admission tests Assessment for inclusion Identify and remove barriers so all learners can participate and show learning Throughout Universal design, accommodations, alternative formats Note "Assessment for inclusion" is a recent idea (Nieminen, 2022; Tai et al., 2022) that asks whether assessment designs disadvantage some learners (for example those with disabilities, or those learning in a second language) and how to design assessments that let all students demonstrate learning.

u: Unit 2: Basis of Assessment: Learning Objectives and Learning Outcomes
t: 2.1 Concept and importance of learning objectives
x: A learning objective states what learners should be able to do after instruction. Objectives guide the selection of content, methods and materials, communicate expectations to learners, and provide the basis for assessment. A learning outcome is a statement of what the learner has actually achieved or is expected to demonstrate, often written at the programme level. In practice, both are written with observable verbs.

u: Unit 2: Basis of Assessment: Learning Objectives and Learning Outcomes
x: Cognitive domain. Bloom et al. (1956) proposed six levels: Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Analysis, Synthesis and Evaluation. Anderson and Krathwohl (2001) revised it to verbs and reordered the top two levels. Figure 4. Revised Bloom's taxonomy of the cognitive domain (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001), highest level at the top The revision also added a knowledge dimension : factual, conceptual, procedural and metacognitive knowledge, creating a two-dimensional taxonomy table. Affective domain (Krathwohl, Bloom & Masia, 1964): receiving → responding → valuing → organisation → characterisation by a value complex. Psychomotor domain (Dave, 1970): imitation → manipulation → precision → articulation → naturalisation. Simpson (1972) and Harrow (1972) offered alternative models.

u: Unit 2: Basis of Assessment: Learning Objectives and Learning Outcomes
x: Mager (1962) proposed three components: performance (what the learner will do), conditions (under what circumstances) and criterion (how well). The ABCD format adds Audience . Definition ABCD objective : A udience (Class VII students) will B ehaviour (solve two-step linear equations) under C ondition (without a calculator) to D egree (with at least 8 of 10 correct). Avoid vague verbs such as "know", "understand", "appreciate" and "learn" in specific objectives; use action verbs such as "list", "explain", "calculate", "compare", "design" and "justify". SMART objectives are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

u: Unit 2: Basis of Assessment: Learning Objectives and Learning Outcomes
x: Teachers derive objectives from curriculum competencies and learner needs, and share them in student-friendly language ("I can..." statements). Students can co-construct success criteria, self-assess against them and set personal goals, which is a core practice of assessment for learning (Wiliam, 2011).

u: Unit 2: Basis of Assessment: Learning Objectives and Learning Outcomes
t: 2.5 Relationships among objectives, instruction, outcomes and assessment
x: Objectives drive instruction; instruction produces learning outcomes; assessment provides evidence of outcomes against objectives; and the results feed back to revise objectives and instruction. This is the logic of the Tyler rationale (1949) and constructive alignment.

u: Unit 3: Methods and Tools of Assessment
x: Figure 5. Methods and tools of assessment

u: Unit 3: Methods and Tools of Assessment
x: Classification of tests: By mode : written, oral, performance. By construction : teacher-made and standardised. By interpretation : norm-referenced and criterion-referenced. By purpose : achievement, aptitude, diagnostic, intelligence, personality. By time : speed tests and power tests. By format : essay (supply type, subjective) and objective (selection type).

u: Unit 3: Methods and Tools of Assessment
x: Written tests require learners to respond in writing. Nature: economical for large groups, permanent record, standardised conditions. Purposes: measure knowledge, understanding, application and higher-order thinking. Types: essay (extended and restricted response), short answer, objective (MCQ, true–false, matching, completion) and structured (creative) questions.

u: Unit 3: Methods and Tools of Assessment
x: Oral tests (viva voce): learners respond orally. They assess communication, reasoning, depth of understanding and language proficiency, and are useful for young children and learners with writing difficulties. They are time-consuming and prone to examiner subjectivity. Performance tests: learners perform a task or create a product (laboratory experiment, speech, drawing, sports skill, teaching practice). They assess skills in authentic contexts and are scored with checklists, rating scales or rubrics.

u: Unit 3: Methods and Tools of Assessment
x: Basis Norm-referenced test (NRT) Criterion-referenced test (CRT) Purpose Compare a learner's performance with others (a norm group) Determine whether a learner has mastered specified criteria Interpretation Percentile rank, standard scores, position Percentage mastered, pass/fail against standard Content Broad, samples a wide domain Narrow, well-defined domain Item selection Items of moderate difficulty that discriminate Items matched to objectives, regardless of difficulty Example Admission tests, IQ tests Driving test, competency-based classroom tests, mastery tests

u: Unit 3: Methods and Tools of Assessment
x: Accommodations that change how a learner accesses or responds without changing what is assessed: extra time, large print, Braille, a scribe, a reader, sign language interpretation, a separate room, assistive technology. Modifications that change the content or standard for learners with significant disabilities, guided by an Individualised Education Plan (IEP). Universal Design for Assessment: clear language, accessible formats, multiple ways to demonstrate learning. In Bangladesh, public examinations allow extra time and a scribe for visually impaired candidates, and the Persons with Disabilities Rights and Protection Act 2013 supports such accommodations.

u: Unit 3: Methods and Tools of Assessment
x: Alternatives to traditional paper-and-pencil tests: authentic assessment (real-world tasks; Wiggins, 1990), performance assessment , portfolios (purposeful collections of work showing growth), projects , self and peer assessment , concept maps , learning journals , presentations and e-portfolios . Strengths: assess higher-order and practical skills, promote engagement and reflection. Limitations: time, scoring reliability, need for clear rubrics.

Restricted (short-answer) response Extended response Nature Limits content and form ("Give three reasons...") Freedom to organise, integrate and express ideas ("Discuss...", "Evaluate...") Measures Understanding, application Analysis, synthesis, evaluation, creativity, writing Principles: use essays for higher-order outcomes; define the task clearly with specific directive verbs; indicate marks and time; avoid optional questions (they reduce comparability); prepare a model answer and scoring scheme in advance. Scoring: use an analytic rubric or point scheme; score question by question across all scripts, not script by script; score anonymously; ignore handwriting and irrelevant factors; use a second marker for a sample. Strengths: assess higher-order thinking and expression; easy to prepare; reduce guessing. Limitations: limited content sampling; subjective, unreliable scoring (the "halo effect", examiner fatigue, order effects); time-consuming to mark; bluffing.

Introduced in Bangladesh's SSC examinations from 2008 (and HSC from 2010), the creative question ( srijonshil prosno ) presents a stimulus (a passage, picture, graph or scenario) followed by four sub-questions at increasing cognitive levels: Part Cognitive level Marks Example verb (a) Knowledge 1 What, define, name (b) Comprehension 2 Explain, why (c) Application 3 Apply, calculate, show how (d) Higher ability (analysis, synthesis, evaluation) 4 Evaluate, analyse, compare, justify Strengths: reduces memorisation, tests multiple levels, uses unseen stimuli. Limitations: many teachers lack training to write good stimuli, so guidebooks and coaching filled the gap (Education Watch and other studies documented this); stimuli are often copied; scoring of level (d) varies widely.

A table of specification (TOS) or test blueprint is a two-way chart that relates content areas to cognitive levels (objectives) and allocates the number of items or marks to each cell according to the instructional emphasis. It is the main tool for ensuring content validity . Development process: (1) list content areas and the time or weight spent on each; (2) list cognitive levels; (3) decide total marks; (4) distribute marks across content in proportion to weight; (5) distribute each content's marks across levels; (6) decide item types for each cell. Content (weight) Remember Understand Apply Analyse/Evaluate Total Photosynthesis (40%) 4 4 4 4 16 Respiration (30%) 3 3 3 3 12 Transpiration (30%) 3 3 3 3 12 Total 10 (25%) 10 (25%) 10 (25%) 10 (25%) 40

A rubric is a scoring guide that lists criteria for a task and describes levels of performance for each criterion (Brookhart, 2013). Analytic rubric: separate scores for each criterion, giving detailed feedback. Holistic rubric: a single overall score based on a general impression, which is faster. Process of developing a rubric: identify the learning outcomes; select criteria (3–6); decide performance levels (typically 3–5); write clear descriptors for each level; pilot with sample work; revise; share with students in advance. Criterion Excellent (4) Good (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Content accuracy All facts accurate and complete Minor errors Several errors Mostly inaccurate Organisation Logical, clear structure Mostly logical Some disorganisation No clear structure Use of evidence Strong, relevant examples Adequate examples Few examples No evidence Language Clear, correct, fluent Few errors Errors affect clarity Errors impede meaning

u: Unit 5: Qualities of a Good Test
x: Validity, reliability, objectivity, usability (practicability), discrimination, comprehensiveness, adequacy, fairness and the existence of norms.

u: Unit 5: Qualities of a Good Test
x: Definition Validity : "The degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses of tests" (AERA, APA & NCME, 2014). In simple terms, a test is valid if it measures what it is supposed to measure. Type Question it answers How it is established Content validity Does the test adequately sample the content and objectives? Table of specification; expert judgement Face validity Does it look appropriate to test-takers? Superficial judgement (not a technical form of validity) Criterion-related: concurrent Does it correlate with a current criterion? Correlate with an established test given at the same time Criterion-related: predictive Does it predict future performance? Correlate with later criterion (e.g. admission test with first-year GPA) Construct validity Does it measure the theoretical construct (e.g. intelligence, anxiety)? Factor analysis; convergent and discriminant evidence Consequential validity (Messick, 1989) What are the intended and unintended consequences of using the test? Studies of impact and washback Factors that reduce validity: unclear directions; difficult vocabulary; ambiguous items; inappropriate difficulty; poor sampling of content; identifiable answer patterns; cheating; too little time; test anxiety; unreliable scoring. Ways to enhance validity: align with objectives through a TOS; clear instructions; appropriate item difficulty; adequate length; secure administration; objective scoring.

u: Unit 5: Qualities of a Good Test
x: Definition Reliability : The consistency, stability or dependability of test scores across occasions, forms, items or raters. A reliable test gives similar results under consistent conditions. Method Type of consistency Procedure Test–retest Stability over time Give the same test twice to the same group; correlate scores Parallel (equivalent) forms Equivalence Give two equivalent forms; correlate Split-half Internal consistency Split the test into halves (e.g. odd–even), correlate, then correct with Spearman–Brown : r_full = 2r_half ÷ (1 + r_half) Kuder–Richardson (KR-20, KR-21) Internal consistency for dichotomously scored items KR-20 = [k ÷ (k−1)] × [1 − Σpq ÷ σ²] Cronbach's alpha Internal consistency for any item scoring α = [k ÷ (k−1)] × [1 − Σσ²_i ÷ σ²_X] Inter-rater (scorer) reliability Agreement between scorers Correlation or Cohen's kappa between two raters Exam Focus Worked example: the odd–even halves of a test correlate at r = 0.60. Full-test reliability = 2(0.60) ÷ (1 + 0.60) = 1.20 ÷ 1.60 = 0.75 . Factors affecting reliability: test length (longer tests are more reliable); group heterogeneity (more variability gives higher reliability); item quality and difficulty; objectivity of scoring; testing conditions; time interval (for test–retest); guessing. Relationship: reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. A test can be reliable but not valid (a bathroom scale that is consistently 2 kg wrong), but it cannot be valid without being reliable. Figure 8. The target analogy for reliability and validity

u: Unit 5: Qualities of a Good Test
x: Objectivity: the degree to which equally competent scorers obtain the same results; ensured by clear keys and rubrics. Usability (practicability): ease of administration, scoring and interpretation; reasonable time and cost; availability of equivalent forms.

u: Unit 5: Qualities of a Good Test
x: Norms are statistics that describe the performance of a defined reference group (the norm group), such as age norms, grade norms, percentile norms and standard-score norms. Standardisation means that a test has uniform procedures for administration and scoring, and that its norms are established on a representative sample.

A standardised test is constructed by experts, tried out on a representative sample, and has established validity, reliability and norms, with uniform procedures for administration, scoring and interpretation. Examples: the Stanford–Binet, Wechsler scales, SAT, TOEFL and IELTS.

Basis Teacher-made test Standardised test Constructed by Classroom teacher Test experts and specialists Purpose Measure learning in a specific class or unit Compare performance across schools, regions, nations Content Local curriculum, specific instruction Broad, common content Item analysis and tryout Rarely Extensive Reliability and validity Usually not established Established and reported Norms None Established on representative samples Administration and scoring Flexible Uniform, fixed Cost Low High
Figure 9. Steps in standardising a test

Item analysis evaluates the quality of each item using students' responses. The common procedure: arrange papers by total score, take the upper 27% and lower 27% groups (Kelley, 1939), and count correct responses in each. Difficulty index (p): proportion of students answering correctly. p = (R_U + R_L) ÷ (N_U + N_L), where R = number right in each group and N = number in each group. Interpretation: p > 0.80 easy; 0.30–0.80 moderate (desirable, ideally around 0.50 for NRTs); p < 0.30 difficult. Discrimination index (D): how well the item distinguishes high from low achievers. D = (R_U − R_L) ÷ N_group. Interpretation (Ebel, 1979): D ≥ 0.40 very good; 0.30–0.39 reasonably good; 0.20–0.29 marginal (revise); < 0.20 poor (reject or revise); negative D indicates a faulty item (more low achievers answered it correctly). Distractor effectiveness: a good distractor attracts more students from the lower group than the upper group, and is chosen by at least about 5% of examinees. A distractor that nobody chooses is non-functional. Exam Focus Worked example: 30 students in each of the upper and lower groups. On Item 7, 24 in the upper group and 12 in the lower group answered correctly. p = (24 + 12) ÷ 60 = 0.60 (moderate). D = (24 − 12) ÷ 30 = 0.40 (very good). Keep the item. Option A B* (key) C D Upper group (n = 30) 2 24 3 1 Lower group (n = 30) 7 12 8 3 Interpretation Functioning Good item Functioning Weak distractor (few choose it)

Prepare the physical environment (light, seating, quiet); follow standard instructions and timing exactly; ensure test security; establish rapport and reduce anxiety; provide accommodations; avoid giving hints; monitor actively to prevent malpractice; record irregularities; collect materials systematically.

x: Measure Definition Formula (ungrouped) Best used when Mean Arithmetic average x̄ = Σx ÷ N Interval/ratio data, symmetrical distribution Median Middle score when arranged in order Value at position (N + 1) ÷ 2 Skewed data, ordinal data, outliers present Mode Most frequent score The value with highest frequency Nominal data, quick estimate Grouped data formulas: Mean = Σfx ÷ N. Median = L + [(N/2 − cf) ÷ f] × i, where L = lower limit of the median class, cf = cumulative frequency below that class, f = frequency of the median class, i = class width. Mode (empirical) ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean. Exam Focus Worked example: scores 12, 15, 15, 18, 20. Mean = 80 ÷ 5 = 16 . Median = 15 (the third score). Mode = 15 .

u: Unit 7: Statistics for Understanding Test Results
x: Range = highest − lowest score. Interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1; quartile deviation (QD) = (Q3 − Q1) ÷ 2. Variance σ² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ N (population) or s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) (sample). Standard deviation (SD) = √variance. It is the most widely used measure of spread. Exam Focus Worked example: for 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 (mean 16), deviations are −4, −1, −1, 2, 4; squared: 16, 1, 1, 4, 16; sum = 38. Population variance = 38 ÷ 5 = 7.6; SD = √7.6 ≈ 2.76 .

u: Unit 7: Statistics for Understanding Test Results
x: The normal curve is a symmetrical, bell-shaped distribution in which mean, median and mode coincide. It is asymptotic to the baseline and its total area is 100%. Approximately 68.26% of cases lie within ±1 SD, 95.44% within ±2 SD and 99.72% within ±3 SD. Figure 13. The normal probability curve with standard deviations, z-scores and T-scores Uses: interpreting standard scores and percentiles; grading on the curve; determining the relative difficulty of items; checking whether scores are normally distributed; and normalising scores.

u: Unit 7: Statistics for Understanding Test Results
x: Correlation describes the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables, from −1 (perfect negative) through 0 (no relationship) to +1 (perfect positive). Figure 14. Scatterplots showing positive, negative and zero correlation Pearson product-moment r (interval/ratio data): r = [NΣxy − ΣxΣy] ÷ √{[NΣx² − (Σx)²][NΣy² − (Σy)²]}. Spearman's rank correlation ρ (ordinal data): ρ = 1 − [6ΣD² ÷ N(N² − 1)], where D is the difference between ranks. Interpretation (rule of thumb): 0.00–0.19 negligible; 0.20–0.39 low; 0.40–0.69 moderate; 0.70–0.89 high; 0.90–1.00 very high. Correlation does not imply causation. Exam Focus Worked example (Spearman): five students ranked in Bangla and English. Rank differences D = 1, −1, 0, 2, −2; ΣD² = 1 + 1 + 0 + 4 + 4 = 10. ρ = 1 − (6 × 10) ÷ [5(25 − 1)] = 1 − 60 ÷ 120 = 0.50 (moderate positive).

t: 8.1 Purpose of standard scores and norms
x: Raw scores are hard to interpret and cannot be compared across tests with different means and spreads. Standard scores express a score's distance from the mean in SD units, which allows comparison across tests and combining scores fairly. Norms show how a score compares with a reference group.

z-score: z = (X − x̄) ÷ SD. Mean 0, SD 1; can be negative or fractional. T-score: T = 50 + 10z. Mean 50, SD 10; avoids negatives. Other standard scores: deviation IQ = 100 + 15z; stanines (1–9, mean 5, SD ≈ 2). Exam Focus Worked example: Rina scored 70 in Mathematics (class mean 60, SD 5) and 75 in English (mean 70, SD 10). Mathematics z = (70 − 60) ÷ 5 = +2.0 , T = 70 . English z = (75 − 70) ÷ 10 = +0.5 , T = 55 . Although her English raw score is higher, her relative performance is much better in Mathematics.

Grade-equivalent score: the grade level at which a raw score is the median (e.g. 5.3 = fifth grade, third month). Age-equivalent score: the age at which a raw score is typical (e.g. mental age in Binet's tests). Cautions: they are easily misinterpreted (a Grade 3 child scoring at grade 5.3 has not mastered the Grade 5 curriculum), and they have unequal units.

Ranking orders students by score. Grading converts scores into categories (A+, A, A−...). Bangladesh uses a GPA system for SSC and HSC (introduced in 2001 for SSC and 2003 for HSC): Marks Letter grade Grade point 80–100 A+ 5.00 70–79 A 4.00 60–69 A− 3.50 50–59 B 3.00 40–49 C 2.00 33–39 D 1.00 0–32 F 0.00 Grading can be absolute (criterion-based, fixed cut-offs as above) or relative (norm-based, "on the curve").

A percentile (Pₚ) is the score below which a given percentage of scores fall. P₅₀ is the median, P₂₅ = Q1, P₇₅ = Q3. A percentile rank (PR) is the percentage of scores falling below a given score. Computation (grouped data): Pₚ = L + [(pN/100 − cf) ÷ f] × i. Percentile rank (ungrouped, simple): PR = [(B + 0.5E) ÷ N] × 100, where B = number of scores below the score, E = number equal to it. Exam Focus Worked example: in a class of 40, 30 students scored below Karim and 2 scored the same as him (including Karim). PR = [(30 + 0.5 × 2) ÷ 40] × 100 = (31 ÷ 40) × 100 = 77.5 . Karim performed better than about 77% of his class. Interpretation and use: percentiles are easy to understand and widely used in reporting; however they are ordinal (unequal units), so differences near the middle are exaggerated and differences at the extremes are compressed.

u: Unit 1: Organisation as a Social System
t: 1.1 Meaning, concept, types and functions of organisation
x: Definition Organisation : "A social unit (or human grouping) deliberately constructed and reconstructed to seek specific goals" (Etzioni, 1964). Barnard (1938) defined it as "a system of consciously coordinated activities or forces of two or more persons." Organisation also refers to the process of organising : dividing work, grouping activities, assigning authority and responsibility, and establishing relationships so that people work together towards goals. Elements: goals; people; structure (roles, hierarchy, rules); technology (methods of work); environment; and culture. Types of organisation: Basis Types Structure Formal (deliberately designed with official hierarchy and rules) and informal (spontaneous networks of personal relationships within formal organisations) Authority pattern Line (direct chain of command), line and staff (line managers advised by specialists), functional (specialists direct their function across units), matrix (dual reporting, project and function), committee Ownership / purpose (Blau & Scott, 1962: cui bono , "who benefits?") Mutual-benefit (unions), business (firms), service (schools, hospitals: clients benefit), commonweal (police, army: the public benefits) Compliance (Etzioni, 1961) Coercive (prisons), utilitarian (business), normative (schools, religious bodies) Functions of organisation: clarifying goals; dividing labour and specialising; establishing authority and accountability; coordinating; facilitating communication; using resources efficiently; providing stability and growth.

u: Unit 1: Organisation as a Social System
x: A social system is a set of interrelated parts (people, roles, groups) that interact to achieve goals within an environment. Open systems theory (Katz & Kahn, 1966) treats schools as open systems that take inputs (students, teachers, funds, curriculum), transform them through processes (teaching, learning, management), and produce outputs (educated graduates), with feedback from the environment. Figure 1. The school as an open system The Getzels–Guba model (1957) Getzels and Guba described social behaviour in an organisation as a function of two dimensions: Nomothetic (institutional) dimension: institution → roles → expectations. Idiographic (personal) dimension: individual → personality → need-dispositions. Behaviour (B) = f(R × P), the interaction of role and personality. Effective administrators balance institutional expectations with individual needs; conflict arises when the two clash. Later versions added the cultural dimension (ethos, values). Figure 2. Getzels and Guba's social systems model

u: Unit 1: Organisation as a Social System
x: Basis Organisation Institution Nature A deliberately structured group of people pursuing goals An established, enduring pattern of norms, values and practices that society regards as important Example A particular school, the DSHE Education, family, religion, marriage Formation Created deliberately Evolves over time Concreteness Concrete, with members, buildings, budgets Abstract, a system of norms Change Can be reorganised quickly Changes slowly Selznick (1957) noted that an organisation becomes an institution when it is "infused with value beyond the technical requirements of the task at hand". A school is both: an organisation (a structured unit) and part of the institution of education.

u: Unit 1: Organisation as a Social System
t: 1.4 The educational institution as a social organisation
x: Schools have distinctive features as organisations: Goals are multiple, complex and sometimes ambiguous (academic, social, moral). The "raw material" (students) is human, varied and participates in the process. The core technology (teaching) is uncertain and hard to standardise. Teachers are professionals with considerable classroom autonomy, so schools are loosely coupled systems (Weick, 1976). Schools depend heavily on their environment (parents, community, government). Schools have a strong culture and climate (Hoy & Miskel, 2013) that shape effectiveness. Key Point Weick's "loosely coupled systems" explains why a policy announced at the ministry may change little in classrooms: units are connected but retain independence. Good school leaders strengthen coupling around teaching and learning (instructional leadership) while respecting professional autonomy.

u: Unit 2: Management Structure of Educational Institutions
x: Administration is concerned with determining policy, goals and overall direction; it is a higher-level, thinking function. Management is concerned with executing policies, organising resources and directing people to achieve goals; it is a doing function. In education the terms overlap. Educational administration is "the process of integrating the efforts of personnel and of utilising appropriate materials in such a way as to promote effectively the development of human qualities" (Campbell et al.). Educational management is used increasingly in Britain and Commonwealth countries (Bush, 2020). Basis Administration Management Function Policy formulation, goal setting Implementation of policy Level Top level Middle and lower levels Nature Determinative Executive Focus What and why How Example Ministry of Education Head teacher, DEO

u: Unit 2: Management Structure of Educational Institutions
x: Fayol's 14 principles remain the classic reference: division of work, authority and responsibility, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual to general interest, remuneration, centralisation, scalar chain, order, equity, stability of tenure, initiative and esprit de corps. Principles specific to educational management: democratic participation; child-centredness; professional autonomy of teachers; equity and inclusion; accountability and transparency; flexibility; cooperation with the community; and continuous improvement.

u: Unit 2: Management Structure of Educational Institutions
x: Classical: scientific management (Taylor, 1911), administrative management (Fayol), bureaucracy (Weber: hierarchy, rules, impersonality, merit, specialisation). Human relations: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies (1920s–30s) showed the importance of social and psychological factors; McGregor's Theory X (people dislike work and must be controlled) and Theory Y (people seek responsibility and self-direction) (1960). Behavioural science / systems: Barnard, Simon, Getzels–Guba, open systems theory. Contemporary: total quality management (Deming), learning organisations (Senge, 1990), distributed leadership, school-based management.

u: Unit 2: Management Structure of Educational Institutions
x: Centralised: decisions made at the top (national level). Bangladesh's education system is largely centralised: curriculum, textbooks, examinations, MPO and recruitment rules are national. Decentralised: authority delegated to regions, districts or schools; school-based management (SBM) gives schools authority over budgets, staffing and planning (Caldwell & Spinks, 1988). Line, line-and-staff, functional and committee structures within institutions.

Main bodies in the governance of education in Bangladesh Body Main functions Ministry of Primary and Mass Education (MoPME) Policy, planning and finance for pre-primary, primary and non-formal education Directorate of Primary Education (DPE) Implementing primary programmes, teacher recruitment and training, stipends, monitoring Bureau of Non-Formal Education (BNFE) Literacy, second-chance and lifelong learning programmes Ministry of Education (MoE) Policy for secondary, higher, madrasah and technical education, through SHED and TMED DSHE Administration of secondary and higher secondary schools and colleges, MPO, inspections, projects Directorate of Madrasah Education Administration of Alia madrasahs Directorate of Technical Education (DTE) Polytechnics, TSCs, TVET teacher training NCTB Curriculum and textbooks BANBEIS Educational statistics and the Education Management Information System (EMIS) NAEM Training of education managers and teachers DIA Inspection and audit of non-government institutions Education boards Registration, public examinations, recognition of institutions, rules for managing committees UGC Higher education planning, funding and quality

u: Unit 2: Management Structure of Educational Institutions
x: E-management: digital systems for administration and data, such as EMIS (BANBEIS), the IPEMIS (Integrated Primary Education Management Information System of DPE), online admission and result systems, e-MPO, the Teachers' Portal and online attendance. Benefits: transparency, speed, data-based decisions. Challenges: connectivity, skills, data security. School Management Committee (SMC): for primary schools under DPE guidelines; members include the head teacher (member-secretary), parents, teachers, donors and local representatives. Functions: school development planning (SLIP), monitoring attendance and learning, mobilising community resources, overseeing facilities. Managing Committee (MC) / School Managing Committee: for non-government secondary schools under education board regulations (the 2009 regulations, as amended): approves budgets, appoints staff (subject to NTRCA rules), supervises finances. College Managing Committee (CMC) / Governing Body (GB): for non-government colleges, with similar functions under the National University or board regulations. Madrasah Managing Committee (MMC): for non-government madrasahs under the Madrasah Education Board. Government institutions are managed directly by the directorates, often with advisory committees. Bangladesh Context Persistent issues with managing committees in Bangladesh include political influence, irregular recruitment, weak financial accountability and limited parental voice. Reform proposals include training members, transparent elections, e-procurement and stronger oversight by boards and DIA.

u: Unit 3: The Role of Heads as Leaders in Educational Institutions
t: 3.1 Roles and responsibilities of the institution
x: Educational institutions are responsible for: delivering the curriculum and ensuring learning; holistic development of students; safety and wellbeing; inclusion; professional development of staff; partnership with parents and community; transparent use of resources; compliance with policies; and continuous improvement.

u: Unit 3: The Role of Heads as Leaders in Educational Institutions
t: 3.2 The head as leader and decision-maker
x: The head teacher, principal or vice-chancellor is the chief executive, instructional leader and public face of the institution. Main roles: Visionary: sets a clear vision, mission and goals. Instructional leader: supervises teaching, supports curriculum implementation, monitors learning outcomes (Hallinger & Murphy, 1985). Manager and administrator: organises timetable, staff, finance, facilities and records. Human resource developer: recruits, motivates, mentors and develops staff. Decision-maker and problem-solver. Communicator and public relations officer. Change agent: leads innovations such as new curricula and ICT. Guardian of discipline and culture. Decision-making models Model Description Rational (classical) Identify problem → generate alternatives → evaluate → choose optimal → implement → evaluate Bounded rationality (Simon, 1947) Decision-makers "satisfice" (choose a satisfactory option) because of limited information and time Incremental (Lindblom, 1959) "Muddling through" with small, successive changes Participative / shared Involving stakeholders improves acceptance and quality (Vroom–Yetton model on when to involve others) Garbage can (Cohen, March & Olsen, 1972) In "organised anarchies" like universities, problems, solutions and participants meet somewhat randomly Figure 5. The rational decision-making process

u: Unit 3: The Role of Heads as Leaders in Educational Institutions
x: Emergencies include natural disasters (floods, cyclones, earthquakes), pandemics (COVID-19), fires, violence and political unrest. The head's role spans the disaster management cycle : Figure 6. The head's role across the emergency management cycle Disaster: school disaster management committees, evacuation drills, safe shelters (many schools serve as cyclone shelters), keeping records safe, protecting children. Pandemic (COVID-19): organising remote learning (TV, radio, online, worksheets), maintaining contact with students, supporting teachers, safe reopening with health protocols, managing learning loss through remedial programmes and assessment. Post-pandemic: learning recovery (Teaching at the Right Level, accelerated curricula), mental health support, re-enrolling dropouts (particularly girls who married and boys who joined work), and building resilience and blended-learning capacity. Other emergencies: violence or unrest on campus, fires and accidents, and individual crises such as the death of a student. The Comprehensive School Safety Framework (GADRRRES, 2017; updated 2022) sets out three pillars: safe learning facilities, school disaster management, and risk reduction and resilience education.

u: Unit 3: The Role of Heads as Leaders in Educational Institutions
t: 3.4 Meaning, concept and styles of leadership
x: Definition Leadership : "A process whereby an individual influences a group of individuals to achieve a common goal" (Northouse, 2021). Leadership is distinct from management: Bennis and Nanus (1985) said "managers are people who do things right and leaders are people who do the right thing." Major leadership theories Theory Key idea Trait theory Leaders have innate traits (intelligence, self-confidence, integrity) Behavioural theories Ohio State (initiating structure and consideration); Michigan (job-centred and employee-centred); Blake and Mouton's Managerial Grid (concern for people × concern for production: impoverished, country club, task, middle-of-the-road, team) Contingency / situational Fiedler's contingency model; Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership (telling, selling, participating, delegating according to follower readiness); path–goal theory Transactional leadership Exchange of rewards for performance (Burns, 1978) Transformational leadership Inspires followers to transcend self-interest. Bass's "4 Is": idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration Instructional leadership Focus on improving teaching and learning (Hallinger) Distributed leadership Leadership spread across many people and roles (Spillane, 2006; Harris, 2008) Servant leadership Leader serves followers' growth first (Greenleaf, 1977) Moral / ethical leadership Leadership grounded in values and moral purpose (Sergiovanni, 1992; Fullan) Figure 7. Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership styles Key Point Leithwood, Harris and Hopkins (2008), Seven strong claims about successful school leadership : school leadership is second only to classroom teaching as an influence on pupil learning; almost all successful leaders draw on the same basic practices (building vision and setting directions, understanding and developing people, redesigning the organisation, managing the teaching and learning programme); leadership has a greater influence when it is widely distributed.

u: Unit 3: The Role of Heads as Leaders in Educational Institutions
x: Vision; integrity and fairness; communication skills; emotional intelligence; decisiveness; knowledge of curriculum and pedagogy; ability to build teams; empathy; resilience; commitment to learning; problem-solving; and the ability to manage change (Fullan, 2001).

u: Unit 3: The Role of Heads as Leaders in Educational Institutions
t: 3.6 Human relations in schools and colleges
x: Relationship Good practices Head–staff Respect, participation in decisions, recognition, fair workload, professional development, open communication, conflict resolution Head/teacher–pupil Caring, fairness, listening to student voice (student councils), safe environment, guidance School–community Involving the community in SMCs, using local resources, community service, open days School–parent Regular communication, parent–teacher meetings, home visits, involving parents in learning (Epstein's six types of involvement: parenting, communicating, volunteering, learning at home, decision-making, collaborating with the community) School–government officers Timely reporting, cooperation with inspectors and education officers, using supervision for improvement

u: Unit 4: Management of Curricular and Co-curricular Activities
x: A time-table is the instrument that translates the curriculum into the daily and weekly schedule of the school. It is the "mirror of the school" and the "second school clock". Principles of time-table construction: Follow government and board rules on subject periods and total hours. Place difficult subjects (Mathematics, Science, English) in early periods when attention is high (fatigue principle). Provide variety and alternate heavy and light subjects. Allocate time according to the importance and difficulty of subjects. Distribute workload fairly among teachers. Use facilities (laboratory, library, playground) efficiently. Include co-curricular activities and breaks. Be flexible to accommodate special events. Consider single- or double-shift arrangements. Types: master (consolidated) time-table, class-wise, teacher-wise, vacant-period (substitution) chart, and co-curricular time-table. Software tools (aSc Timetables, FET) can help.

u: Unit 4: Management of Curricular and Co-curricular Activities
x: Definition Supervision : The process of helping, guiding, advising and stimulating teachers to improve the quality of teaching and learning. Modern supervision is developmental and collegial, not fault-finding inspection. Inspection (traditional) Supervision (modern) Fault-finding Improvement-oriented Authoritarian Democratic, cooperative Focus on rules and records Focus on teaching and learning One-way, judgemental Two-way, supportive Occasional Continuous Models: clinical supervision (Goldhammer, Cogan): pre-observation conference → observation → analysis → post-observation conference → critique of the process; developmental supervision (Glickman); peer coaching; lesson study (Japan). In Bangladesh, academic supervision is carried out by heads, Upazila Academic Supervisors, AUEOs and DSHE officials, often with standardised observation forms.

u: Unit 4: Management of Curricular and Co-curricular Activities
x: Continuous professional development (CPD) through induction, in-service training (NAEM, TTCs, URCs), subject-based training, workshops, peer observation, professional learning communities (PLCs), mentoring, action research, conferences and online courses (Muktopaath). Effective CPD is sustained, collaborative, focused on subject content and student learning, and includes practice with feedback (Darling-Hammond et al., 2017).

u: Unit 4: Management of Curricular and Co-curricular Activities
x: Plan an assessment calendar; form an examination committee; set questions according to a table of specification and moderate them; maintain security of papers; arrange seating and invigilation; ensure fair marking with marking schemes; tabulate results accurately and confidentially; analyse results to improve teaching; communicate results to students and parents; keep records; and prevent malpractice. Continuous assessment records should be maintained throughout the year.

u: Unit 4: Management of Curricular and Co-curricular Activities
x: Functions: support curriculum, encourage reading habits, provide reference and research resources, promote self-directed learning. Management: an appropriate room with seating and lighting; trained librarian; selection and acquisition policy; classification (Dewey Decimal Classification) and cataloguing; circulation system (issue and return, ideally digital); reading programmes; book clubs; digital resources and e-library. S. R. Ranganathan's five laws of library science (1931): books are for use; every reader his/her book; every book its reader; save the time of the reader; the library is a growing organism.

u: Unit 4: Management of Curricular and Co-curricular Activities
x: Co-curricular activities (CCAs) include literary (debate, essay writing, wall magazines), cultural (music, drama, dance), physical (sports, games), social service (scouts, Girl Guides, Red Crescent, BNCC), scientific (science fairs, clubs) and national day celebrations. Principles: linked with curricular objectives; participation of all students; a balanced variety; teacher guidance; proper scheduling in the time-table; adequate budget; record-keeping and recognition; student leadership. Values: develop leadership, cooperation, creativity, discipline, physical health, citizenship and talent.

u: Unit 5: Management of School Funds and Other Resources
x: Definition Budget : A financial plan that estimates income and expenditure for a specific period (usually a fiscal year) to achieve the institution's goals. Sources of income: government grants (salary through MPO; development funds; SLIP grants for primary schools), tuition and session fees, examination fees, donations and endowments, community contributions, rent of facilities, and income-generating activities. Expenditure heads: salaries; maintenance and repair; teaching materials; library and laboratory; co-curricular activities; utilities; examinations; welfare and stipends; contingencies. Budget preparation process: review past budgets → estimate income → estimate expenditure by priorities → consult staff and committee → approval by SMC/MC/GB → implementation → monitoring and revision. Principles: balance, realism, priority to learning, flexibility, participation and transparency.

u: Unit 5: Management of School Funds and Other Resources
x: Accounts: cash book, ledger, receipt and payment registers, fee register, stock register, salary register and bank reconciliation. All transactions should be through bank accounts with joint signatories, and vouchers kept for every expense. Audit: an independent examination of financial records to verify accuracy and compliance. Internal audit: by the institution's own committee, continuous. External audit: by DIA (Directorate of Inspection and Audit) for non-government institutions, by the Comptroller and Auditor General's office for government funds, and by chartered accountants. Purposes: prevent fraud and misuse, ensure compliance, build public trust and improve financial management.

u: Unit 5: Management of School Funds and Other Resources
x: Facility Management considerations Site Safe, accessible, healthy location; adequate area; away from noise and hazards; flood safety Building Adequate classrooms (about 1 m² per student minimum), ventilation, light, earthquake resistance, accessibility (ramps), separate toilets for girls, WASH facilities Furniture Appropriate size for age, flexible for group work, durable Equipment Teaching aids, ICT equipment, inventory and maintenance Library See Unit 4.5 Laboratory Safety rules, equipment registers, chemical storage, first aid, trained assistants Workshop For TVET and practical subjects; safety equipment Playground and recreation Adequate space, maintenance, sports equipment, shade Plant management: a facilities committee, regular inspection, preventive maintenance, stock registers, cleanliness campaigns, involvement of students (e.g. tree planting), and use of facilities for community purposes.

u: Unit 5: Management of School Funds and Other Resources
x: Institutional planning is a programme of development prepared by an educational institution, based on its own needs and resources, for the improvement of the institution and its educational programme. It is bottom-up planning that complements national plans. Figure 8. The institutional (school development) planning cycle Areas of institutional planning: academic programmes (results improvement, remedial teaching), co-curricular programmes, physical development (buildings, furniture), staff development, community relations and student welfare. Bangladesh example: SLIP and UPEP. Under PEDP, each government primary school prepares a School Level Improvement Plan (SLIP) with the SMC and community, receiving an annual grant to implement priorities; Upazila Primary Education Plans (UPEPs) aggregate local priorities.

The practicum allows students to apply the course content in real institutions. Suggested activities (each producing a short report or portfolio entry): Organisational study of a school: draw its organisational chart, identify formal and informal structures, describe its management committee. Time-table analysis : evaluate a school's time-table against the principles in Unit 4.1 and suggest improvements. Leadership interview : interview a head teacher on leadership style, decision-making and emergency management (e.g. COVID-19 experience). Budget study : analyse a school's annual budget and accounts procedures. Facilities audit : assess buildings, WASH, library, laboratory and accessibility using a checklist. Institutional plan : prepare a one-year school improvement plan based on a SWOT analysis. Co-curricular plan : design an annual co-curricular calendar. Study tip To link theory with practice, try a mini-project with classmates: visit a local school, prepare a SWOT analysis and a one-year institutional plan, and ask the head teacher for feedback. Citing such an example strengthens any exam answer on school management.
