u: Unit 1: Concepts, Theories and Issues of Development
t: 1.1 Meaning, concept and dimensions of development
x: Development is a multidimensional process of improving people's lives: raising incomes and productivity, but also expanding health, knowledge, freedom, dignity, equity and environmental sustainability. Todaro and Smith (2020) identify three core values of development: sustenance (meeting basic needs), self-esteem (being a person, not a tool of others) and freedom from servitude (being able to choose). Amartya Sen (1999) defines development as "a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy" ( Development as Freedom ). Figure 1. Dimensions of development

u: Unit 1: Concepts, Theories and Issues of Development
x: Term Meaning Economic growth Increase in the production of goods and services (GDP), a quantitative change Economic development Growth plus structural change and improved living standards, a qualitative change Underdevelopment A condition of low income, low productivity, poverty, dependence and weak institutions Modernisation Transformation from traditional to modern (industrial, urban, rational) societies Sustainable development "Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs" (Brundtland Commission, WCED, 1987) Human development Expanding people's choices and capabilities (UNDP, 1990) Inclusive growth Growth that benefits all groups and reduces inequality Poverty line Minimum income for basic needs; the World Bank international line is US$2.15 per day (2017 PPP), revised in 2025 to US$3.00 (2021 PPP) LDC graduation Bangladesh met all three UN criteria (per-capita income, Human Assets Index, Economic Vulnerability Index) in 2018 and 2021, and was recommended to graduate from Least Developed Country status in 2026

u: Unit 1: Concepts, Theories and Issues of Development
x: The World Bank classifies economies by GNI per capita (Atlas method) into low-income, lower-middle-income, upper-middle-income and high-income countries; the thresholds are revised each 1 July. Bangladesh became a lower-middle-income country in 2015. The UN uses "developed", "developing" and "least developed" categories. Terms such as "Third World" and "Global South" are also used, with debate about their accuracy. Characteristics often attributed to developing countries: low per-capita income, high dependence on agriculture, rapid population growth, high unemployment and underemployment, dualism (modern and traditional sectors), dependence on primary exports and weak institutions.

u: Unit 1: Concepts, Theories and Issues of Development
x: Rostow's stages of economic growth (1960) W. W. Rostow's The Stages of Economic Growth: A Non-Communist Manifesto proposed five linear stages: Figure 2. Rostow's five stages of economic growth (1960) Role of education: builds the preconditions (literacy, scientific attitude, skilled labour). Critique: Eurocentric, assumes all countries follow one path, ignores external constraints and inequality. Structural change model (Lewis, 1954; Chenery) Sir Arthur Lewis's two-sector model : surplus labour moves from a low-productivity traditional (agricultural) sector to a high-productivity modern (industrial) sector; reinvested profits drive growth until surplus labour is absorbed (the "Lewis turning point"). Chenery's patterns of development show shifts from agriculture to industry and services. Education's role: skills for the modern sector. Critique: assumes full employment in the modern sector and labour-using investment; urban unemployment is common. Marxist view Development is driven by class struggle and changes in the mode of production (primitive communism → slavery → feudalism → capitalism → socialism → communism). Capitalism generates growth but also exploitation and inequality. Education is part of the superstructure that reproduces capitalist relations (Bowles & Gintis) but can also raise class consciousness. Dependency theory Developed by Latin American scholars (Raúl Prebisch, André Gunder Frank, Samir Amin, Cardoso and Faletto). Underdevelopment is not an original state but a result of the unequal integration of peripheral (poor) countries into a world economy dominated by the core (rich) countries. Frank's " development of underdevelopment ". Wallerstein's world-systems theory adds core, semi-periphery and periphery. Education: colonial and Western-oriented education can create " brain drain " and cultural dependency (Carnoy, 1974, Education as Cultural Imperialism ). Policy prescriptions: import substitution, self-reliance, South–South cooperation. Modernisation theory Associated with Talcott Parsons, Daniel Lerner, Alex Inkeles and David McClelland (1950s–60s). Development requires transformation from traditional to modern values, institutions and personalities (achievement orientation, rationality, openness to change). Inkeles and Smith's (1974) Becoming Modern found that schooling was the strongest predictor of "modern" attitudes. Critique: ethnocentric; neglects structural and international constraints. Human capital theory Theodore Schultz (1961, "Investment in Human Capital") and Gary Becker (1964) argued that education and training are investments that raise productivity and earnings, just like investment in physical capital. Evidence: the rate of return to education (Psacharopoulos & Patrinos, 2018: about 9% per extra year of schooling globally; returns highest at primary and, recently, tertiary levels). Critiques: screening and signalling theory (Spence, 1973: credentials signal ability rather than create it), credentialism (Collins) and neglect of non-economic values. Theory Cause of underdevelopment Path to development View of education Rostow Traditional economy Pass through stages, investment Builds preconditions Structural change Dual economy Transfer labour to modern sector Skills for industry Marxist Class exploitation Socialist transformation Reproduces or challenges class relations Dependency Exploitation by core countries Self-reliance, delinking Can create dependency; needs decolonising Modernisation Traditional values and institutions Diffusion of modern values, technology Creates modern attitudes Human capital Low skills and knowledge Invest in people Productive investment

u: Unit 1: Concepts, Theories and Issues of Development
t: 1.5 Recent trends: human development and sustainable development
x: Human development (Mahbub ul Haq; Amartya Sen's capability approach ): development is about enlarging people's choices and capabilities (being and doing what they value). UNDP's Human Development Report since 1990. Sustainable development : balancing economic, social and environmental goals across generations (Brundtland, 1987; Rio Earth Summit 1992; Agenda 2030). The three pillars: economy, society, environment. Figure 3. The three pillars of sustainable development

u: Unit 1: Concepts, Theories and Issues of Development
x: Development benefits are unevenly distributed among individuals , classes (rich and poor), genders (women's unpaid work, wage gaps), ethnic groups (indigenous peoples' land and language rights), regions (urban and rural, east and west) and generations (climate change). These raise questions of equity, participation and justice.

u: Unit 1: Concepts, Theories and Issues of Development
t: 1.7 Development as a whole and truncated development
x: Development as a whole (holistic, balanced) integrates economic growth with social, political, cultural and environmental progress, so that all groups benefit. Truncated development is partial, lopsided growth in which some sectors or groups advance while others are left behind, for example GDP growth without job creation ("jobless growth"), industrial growth with environmental destruction, or urban prosperity with rural poverty. UNDP's 1996 Human Development Report warned against five types of bad growth: jobless, ruthless (inequality), voiceless (no democracy), rootless (cultural loss) and futureless (environmental damage).

u: Unit 1: Concepts, Theories and Issues of Development
t: 1.8 The SDGs as targets for development
x: The 17 Sustainable Development Goals (2015–2030), with 169 targets, are the global development agenda. Education is SDG 4, but it also underpins goals on poverty (1), health (3), gender (5), decent work (8), inequality (10) and climate (13). Figure 4. SDGs most directly supported by education
An indicator is a measurable variable used to track progress towards a goal. Good indicators are valid, reliable, comparable, available and policy-relevant.

Indicator Definition GDP (Gross Domestic Product) Market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) GNP / GNI (Gross National Product / Income) GDP plus net factor income from abroad (income earned by nationals abroad minus income of foreigners at home). Remittances make GNI an important measure for Bangladesh Per-capita income GNI (or GDP) ÷ population; often adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP) Growth rate Annual percentage change in real GDP Limitations of GDP: ignores distribution, non-market work (household, care), environmental damage, informal sector, quality of life and wellbeing. Hence the search for broader measures (Stiglitz, Sen & Fitoussi, 2009). Income inequality: Lorenz curve, Gini coefficient and Gini index The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of population. The Gini coefficient = A ÷ (A + B), where A is the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve and B is the area under the Lorenz curve. It ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality) ; the Gini index is the same value × 100. Bangladesh's income Gini has been around 0.48–0.50 in recent Household Income and Expenditure Surveys (HIES), indicating rising inequality. Figure 5. The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient: the further the curve bows from the line of equality, the higher the inequality

Life expectancy at birth: a summary of health conditions. Knowledge: adult literacy rate, mean years of schooling, expected years of schooling, enrolment ratios, learning outcomes. Quality of life / standard of living: infant and maternal mortality, nutrition, access to safe water and sanitation, housing, electricity, poverty headcount. Composite indices: HDI, the Gender Development Index (GDI), the Gender Inequality Index (GII), the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI; Alkire & Foster), the Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI; Morris, 1979: literacy, life expectancy and infant mortality).

u: Unit 3: Human Resource Development and Human Development
x: HRD is the process of increasing the knowledge, skills and capacities of people so that they become productive resources for the economy. Harbison and Myers (1964) defined it as "the process of increasing the knowledge, the skills, and the capacities of all the people in a society." Population is the total number of people. Human resources are the population's productive potential (the working-age and skilled population). Human capital is the stock of knowledge, skills, health and experience embodied in people that generates economic value (Schultz, Becker). Population becomes human capital through investment in education, health and training. The World Bank's Human Capital Index (2018) measures the expected productivity of a child born today; Bangladesh's HCI was about 0.46 in 2020, meaning a child would be 46% as productive as with complete education and full health.

u: Unit 3: Human Resource Development and Human Development
x: Origin Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq (1934–1998) led the first UNDP Human Development Report in 1990, drawing on Amartya Sen's capability approach . HD was defined as "a process of enlarging people's choices". The three essential choices are to lead a long and healthy life, to acquire knowledge and to have access to resources for a decent standard of living. Relation to other concepts Basis HRD / human capital Human development View of people Means (inputs into production) Ends in themselves Goal Productivity and economic growth Expanding freedoms and choices Education valued because It raises earnings It is intrinsically valuable and enables other freedoms Measure Returns, HCI, labour productivity HDI and related indices Aspects and factors of HD The UNDP highlights four pillars: equity , productivity , sustainability and empowerment . Factors include health, education, income, gender equality, participation, human security and environment.

u: Unit 3: Human Resource Development and Human Development
x: The HDI is the geometric mean of normalised indices in three dimensions: Figure 6. The structure of the Human Development Index Dimension index = (actual value − minimum) ÷ (maximum − minimum). HDI = (I_health × I_education × I_income)^(1/3). Goalposts: life expectancy 20–85 years; mean years of schooling 0–15; expected years 0–18; GNI per capita PPP$100–75,000. Classification and profiles HDI category HDI value Asian examples Very high 0.800 and above Japan, Republic of Korea, Singapore, Malaysia (around 0.80) High 0.700–0.799 China, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Indonesia Medium 0.550–0.699 Bangladesh , India, Bhutan, Nepal, Myanmar Low Below 0.550 Afghanistan, Pakistan (around the boundary), Yemen Bangladesh's HDI has risen steadily from about 0.39 in 1990 to about 0.67–0.69 in the most recent reports, among the fastest improvements in the world, driven by gains in life expectancy and schooling. Always quote the latest UNDP report figure with its year.

u: Unit 4: Development Process and Plans in Bangladesh
x: Development planning is the deliberate, coordinated effort by the government to set goals and allocate resources over a defined period. Bangladesh uses a hierarchy of plans: a long-term perspective plan , medium-term five-year plans , and annual ADPs . Figure 7. Hierarchy of development plans in Bangladesh

u: Unit 4: Development Process and Plans in Bangladesh
x: Planning Commission: the central planning body, with divisions such as the General Economics Division (GED, which prepares perspective and five-year plans), the Programming Division (ADP), and sectoral divisions such as the Socio-Economic Infrastructure Division (covering education) and the Physical Infrastructure Division. Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED): monitors and evaluates projects. Statistics and Informatics Division (SID) / Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS). National Economic Council (NEC): the highest policy-making body for economic development, chaired by the head of government; approves the five-year plans and ADP. Executive Committee of the NEC (ECNEC): approves development projects above a cost threshold (smaller projects are approved by the Planning Minister) and reviews implementation.

u: Unit 4: Development Process and Plans in Bangladesh
x: Vision 2021 (Digital Bangladesh; middle-income status) and the First Perspective Plan 2010–2021 . Vision 2030: aligned with the SDGs (SDG Action Plan). Vision 2041 and Perspective Plan 2021–2041: aims to eliminate extreme poverty and achieve high-income status by 2041, with "Smart Bangladesh" (smart citizens, government, economy, society). Five-year plans: the 1st FYP (1973–78) was prepared under Prof. Nurul Islam; the 7th FYP (2016–2020) and 8th FYP (July 2020–June 2025) included education chapters stressing quality, equity, TVET and ICT. Delta Plan 2100 for water and climate. ADP: the annual list of development projects with allocations; education is among the largest sectors.

u: Unit 4: Development Process and Plans in Bangladesh
t: 4.4 Education ministries and agencies in development
x: Ministry / agency Development role MoPME – DPE Implements PEDP, stipends, school feeding, classroom construction, teacher recruitment MoE – DSHE Secondary and higher secondary projects: SEDP, ICT in education, infrastructure MoE – DTE TVET expansion: polytechnics, TSCs in every upazila, skills projects MoE – Directorate of Madrasah Education Madrasah infrastructure, ICT, teacher development UGC Higher education projects: HEQEP, HEAT, research grants, new universities

u: Unit 4: Development Process and Plans in Bangladesh
x: Level Programmes and projects Primary PEDP4 (2018–2025, extended), primary stipends, school feeding, ROSC, infrastructure in hard-to-reach areas Secondary Secondary Education Development Program (SEDP), secondary stipend programmes (consolidated under a national education assistance trust), school digital/ICT labs, multimedia classrooms Higher HEAT (World Bank), research grants, Bangladesh Research and Education Network (BdREN), quality assurance (IQAC) TVET ASSET, SEIP, establishment of TSCs in 329 upazilas Implementation procedure: project concept → Development Project Proposal (DPP) or Technical Assistance Project Proposal (TAPP) → appraisal by the Planning Commission (Project Evaluation Committee) → approval by the minister or ECNEC → inclusion in ADP → implementation by the agency (Project Director) → monitoring by IMED → completion report and evaluation. Impact and challenges: large gains in access, gender parity and infrastructure; weaker gains in learning quality; recurring problems of delays, cost overruns, procurement irregularities, weak monitoring and limited use of evaluation evidence.

u: Unit 5: Role of Education in Development
x: Figure 8. How education contributes to development Primary education: literacy and numeracy foundations; highest social returns; better health and nutrition; reduced fertility, especially through girls' education; the foundation of all later learning. Secondary education: skills for modern employment; delayed marriage for girls; preparation for TVET and higher education; civic knowledge. Higher/tertiary education: research and innovation; professionals and leaders; technology adoption; the knowledge economy; higher private and increasingly social returns. The evidence is strong: Hanushek and Woessmann (2015) show that cognitive skills (learning outcomes), not just years of schooling , explain differences in long-run economic growth across countries, which highlights the importance of quality.

u: Unit 5: Role of Education in Development
t: 5.2 Role of non-formal and continuing education
x: Non-formal education (NFE): literacy, second-chance education, life skills; BRAC's NFE model (from 1985) reached millions of out-of-school children. Population education: awareness of population dynamics, family planning and the relationship between population, resources and development. Bangladesh's fertility decline (TFR from about 6.3 in 1975 to about 2.0 now) was helped by education and awareness programmes. Health and nutrition education: hygiene, oral rehydration (BRAC's ORS campaign is a classic example), nutrition, maternal and child health. Programmes for youth and disadvantaged groups: skills training, entrepreneurship, financial literacy, and programmes for street children, working children, persons with disabilities and ethnic minorities.

u: Unit 5: Role of Education in Development
x: TVET builds skills for employability, productivity, self-employment and overseas employment (remittances). It supports SDG 8 and the demographic dividend. Bangladesh's priority sectors (RMG, light engineering, ICT, construction, agro-processing, health care) need middle-level technical skills.

u: Unit 5: Role of Education in Development
t: 5.4 Education in Emergencies and refugee education
x: Education in emergencies protects children, preserves human capital during crises and supports recovery. Building human resources to manage EiE requires trained teachers in psychosocial support, emergency curricula, disaster-preparedness planners and coordination capacity (the Education Cluster, INEE standards). In Bangladesh, EiE is needed for floods and cyclones, and for the Rohingya response (see PC 112, Unit 7).

u: Unit 5: Role of Education in Development
x: Women's empowerment is the expansion of women's ability to make strategic life choices (Kabeer, 1999: resources, agency and achievements). Education: increases women's earnings and labour force participation; reduces child marriage and fertility, and improves child health ("educate a woman, and you educate a nation"); raises voice and political participation; challenges gender norms. Bangladesh's female stipend programme and girls' education gains are linked to rising female employment, lower fertility and improved child survival. Challenges: continuing child marriage, low female participation in TVET and higher education leadership, harassment, and gender gaps in the labour market.

u: Unit 5: Role of Education in Development
t: 5.6 Role of education in development progress
x: Education has contributed to Bangladesh's "development surprise": rising life expectancy, falling poverty, women's empowerment and LDC graduation, despite low spending (Asadullah, Savoia & Mahmud, 2014).

u: Unit 5: Role of Education in Development
x: Low public spending (about 2% of GDP). Learning poverty (many children unable to read a simple text by age 10; World Bank, 2019). Quality and relevance gaps; graduate unemployment. Equity gaps (poor, rural, disabled, ethnic minorities, urban slums). Teacher quality and motivation. Governance, politicisation and weak accountability. Climate change and disasters. Rapid technological change and the need for digital skills. Exam Focus Likely essay: "Discuss the role of education in national development with reference to Bangladesh." Structure: (1) define development; (2) theoretical links (human capital, modernisation, human development); (3) contributions by level and type of education, with Bangladeshi evidence; (4) women's education; (5) challenges; (6) recommendations (spending, quality, TVET, equity, governance).

t: 1.1 Origin, meaning, concept, nature and scope
x: Curriculum comes from the Latin verb currere , "to run", and the noun curriculum , a "racecourse" or "running course". By analogy, the curriculum is the course that learners run to reach educational goals. Definitions illustrate the range of meanings: "All the learning which is planned and guided by the school, whether it is carried on in groups or individually, inside or outside the school" (Kerr, 1968). "A plan for learning" (Taba, 1962). "The reconstruction of knowledge and experience, systematically developed under the auspices of the school, to enable the learner to increase his or her control of knowledge and experience" (Tanner & Tanner, 1980). "An attempt to communicate the essential principles and features of an educational proposal in such a form that it is open to critical scrutiny and capable of effective translation into practice" (Stenhouse, 1975). Pinar's (1975) currere : the curriculum as the lived, autobiographical experience of the learner. Nature: dynamic, goal-oriented, planned, comprehensive, culturally situated, value-laden and subject to continuous revision. Scope: aims and objectives, content, learning experiences, teaching–learning strategies, materials, assessment, co-curricular activities, the learning environment and, in its broadest sense, all experiences under the school's guidance.

t: 1.2 Connotation of curriculum in historical perspective (narrower to wider)
x: Figure 1. The widening meaning of curriculum over time Smith (1996, 2000) distinguishes four approaches: curriculum as body of knowledge (syllabus), as product (objectives; Tyler), as process (interaction; Stenhouse) and as praxis (committed action for emancipation; Grundy, 1987).

Basis Curriculum Syllabus Scope Broad: entire educational programme Narrow: one subject or course Components Aims, content, methods, materials, assessment, co-curricular activities Topics, content outline, time allocation, sometimes assessment Developed by National bodies (NCTB), institutions Subject experts, boards, teachers Nature Prescriptive, philosophical Descriptive, subject-specific Relationship Includes the syllabus Part of the curriculum

Figure 2. The four interrelated components of curriculum (Tyler's elements) Characteristics of a good curriculum: based on clear aims and the needs of learners and society; relevant and up to date; balanced across domains and subjects; flexible and adaptable to local contexts; inclusive of diverse learners; logically sequenced (continuity, sequence and integration); feasible with available resources; aligned (objectives, content, methods and assessment cohere); and open to evaluation and revision.

Figure 3. Foundations of curriculum Philosophical foundations determine aims and values. Perennialism leads to a Great Books curriculum; essentialism to core subjects; progressivism to experience- and problem-centred curricula; reconstructionism to social-issues curricula; existentialism to choice and the arts (see PC 115). Psychological foundations guide sequence, method and level: Piaget's stages (concrete before abstract), Bruner's spiral curriculum ("any subject can be taught effectively in some intellectually honest form to any child at any stage of development"; Bruner, 1960), Vygotsky's ZPD, behaviourist objectives, and theories of motivation and multiple intelligences. Sociological foundations: curriculum must reflect society's needs, culture, values, economy and changes (technology, globalisation, climate change), and promote social cohesion and equity. Questions of "whose knowledge?" (Apple, 1979) matter. Historical foundations: knowing how curricula evolved (e.g. from colonial to national curricula; the 1976, 1995, 2012 and 2021 reforms in Bangladesh) helps avoid repeating mistakes.

Figure 4. Three levels of curriculum (IEA; Travers & Westbury, 1989) Gaps between these levels explain why reforms often fail: well-designed intended curricula can be undermined by teachers' lack of training, large classes or high-stakes examinations, so the achieved curriculum is much narrower. Goodlad (1979) proposed a similar list: ideal, formal, perceived, operational and experiential curricula.

By control Type Features Example Centralised Developed and controlled by a national authority, uniform Bangladesh (NCTB), France historically Semi-centralised National framework with local adaptation England's National Curriculum with school-based schemes Decentralised Developed by states, districts or schools USA (state and district), Finland (local curricula within a national core) By organisation and focus Content (subject)-based curriculum: organised around separate subjects and disciplines; emphasises knowledge; teacher-centred. Learner-centred curriculum: organised around learners' needs, interests and development (Rousseau, Dewey, Rogers). Activity-based curriculum: learning through activities, projects and experiences (Kilpatrick). Core curriculum: a common set of essential subjects or learning required of all students, with electives around it. NEP 2010 specified a common core across general, madrasah and technical streams. Integrated curriculum: content from different subjects combined around themes, problems or concepts (multidisciplinary → interdisciplinary → transdisciplinary; Drake, 1998). Competency-based curriculum (CBC): defines competencies (integrated knowledge, skills, attitudes and values) that learners must demonstrate; progression by mastery. Bangladesh's primary curriculum has been competency-based since the 1990s; NCF 2021 extended a competency-based approach to all levels. Outcome-based curriculum (OBE): begins with clearly defined learning outcomes and designs backward (Spady, 1994); widely used in higher education accreditation (e.g. Washington Accord in engineering; BAC requirements in Bangladesh).

Streaming means dividing learners into separate tracks (e.g. Science, Humanities, Business Studies) usually after Class VIII, based on achievement or choice. Arguments for: specialisation, efficient teaching. Arguments against: early labelling, inequity (lower-income and rural students often end up in less-valued streams), narrow education. NCF 2021 proposed postponing streaming until Class XI; this was one of the most debated reforms.

Unified curriculum: the same curriculum for all learners in a level (e.g. a common primary curriculum). Diversified curriculum: different curricula or options to meet varied abilities, interests and career goals (e.g. vocational streams, electives). The Qudrat-e-Khuda Commission (1974) recommended a unified primary and junior secondary education followed by diversification.

Hidden curriculum: the unwritten, unofficial lessons, values and norms learners acquire through school life, such as obedience, punctuality, competition and gender roles (Jackson, 1968; Apple, 1979). Example: if only boys are asked to lift benches and only girls to decorate, gender stereotypes are taught without being stated. Null curriculum: what schools do not teach, through omission, which also teaches something (Eisner, 1979). Examples: sexuality education, local indigenous histories, critical media literacy or financial literacy may be absent. Balanced curriculum: an appropriate balance across domains (cognitive, affective, psychomotor), subjects, theory and practice, local and global, core and elective, and individual and social needs. Figure 5. Layers of curriculum learners actually experience

Disciplines are organised bodies of knowledge with their own concepts and methods. Correlation means deliberately relating content across subjects so that learning in one reinforces another (e.g. teaching graphs in Mathematics at the same time as data in Geography). Herbart's followers advocated correlation and concentration (organising subjects around a central core subject).

Important themes are taught across several subjects rather than as a single subject: for example environment, gender, ICT, values, disaster risk reduction, health, citizenship and sustainable development. In Bangladesh, cross-cutting issues such as climate change, gender equality and ICT appear across NCTB textbooks.

Activities that complement the formal curriculum (sports, debates, cultural programmes, scouts, clubs). They develop leadership, teamwork, creativity, physical health and citizenship, and are increasingly integrated into competency-based curricula and assessment.

Objectives (aims, goals, competencies, outcomes), content, learning experiences/strategies, materials, and evaluation. Development is the process of planning, implementing and evaluating these elements systematically.

Situational analysis is the systematic study of the context in which a curriculum will operate before decisions are made (Skilbeck, 1984; Print, 1993). It ensures relevance and feasibility. Component Factors to analyse Societal and cultural Values, social change, economy, labour market needs, national policies, SDGs Learners Age, developmental stage, prior learning, needs, interests, diversity, special needs Teachers Qualifications, skills, attitudes, workload, numbers Institutions Facilities, resources, class sizes, management, time Knowledge and disciplines Developments in subject areas, new knowledge Existing curriculum Strengths, weaknesses, evaluation results, public examinations Tasks of analysis: review documents and research; conduct surveys and needs assessments; consult stakeholders (teachers, parents, employers, experts); compare international curricula; identify gaps; summarise implications for curriculum design.

Objective (rational / linear) models * Ralph Tyler (1949), Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction . * The "Tyler rationale" asks four questions: What educational purposes should the school seek to attain? (objectives) What educational experiences can be provided that are likely to attain these purposes? (learning experiences) How can these educational experiences be effectively organised? (organisation) How can we determine whether these purposes are being attained? (evaluation) Objectives come from three sources (studies of the learners, studies of contemporary life, and suggestions from subject specialists) and are filtered through two screens: the school's philosophy and the psychology of learning. Figure 6. Tyler's model of curriculum development (1949) * Hilda Taba (1962), Curriculum Development: Theory and Practice . An inductive, grassroots * model: teachers, who know their students, should participate. Seven steps: Diagnosis of needs Formulation of objectives Selection of content Organisation of content Selection of learning experiences Organisation of learning experiences Determination of what to evaluate and the ways and means of evaluation Cyclical models * D. K. Wheeler (1967), Curriculum Process : extended Tyler into a cycle * of five phases, in which evaluation feeds back into objectives: (1) aims, goals and objectives; (2) selection of learning experiences; (3) selection of content; (4) organisation and integration of learning experiences and content; (5) evaluation. Figure 7. Wheeler's cyclical model (1967) * Audrey and Howard Nicholls (1978), Developing a Curriculum: A Practical Guide : added situational analysis * as the starting point of the cycle: situational analysis → selection of objectives → selection and organisation of content → selection and organisation of methods → evaluation. * Murray Print (1993), Curriculum Development and Design : a cyclical model with a curriculum presage * (the forces and people who influence developers: curriculum foundations, developers' conceptions) followed by situational analysis, aims, goals and objectives, content, learning activities and evaluation, with all elements interacting. Interactive (dynamic / naturalistic) models Decker Walker (1971), "A naturalistic model for curriculum development": describes how developers actually work. Three phases: Platform: the beliefs, theories, values and aims developers bring. Deliberation: discussion and debate to reach agreement on choices, considering alternatives. Curriculum design: the decisions are recorded in a plan and materials. Figure 8. Walker's naturalistic model (1971) * John Kerr (1968), Changing the Curriculum : an interactive model in which four elements (objectives, knowledge (content), learning experiences and evaluation *) are all interconnected so that development can begin with any element, and each influences the others. Kerr also contributed the influential broad definition quoted in 1.1. Model Type Starting point Strength Limitation Tyler Objective, linear Objectives Logical, simple, widely used Rigid, behaviourist, neglects context Taba Objective, inductive Diagnosis of needs Teacher involvement, needs-based Time-consuming, still linear Wheeler Cyclical Aims Continuous; evaluation feeds back Still objective-driven Nicholls Cyclical Situational analysis Context-sensitive Complex in practice Print Cyclical Curriculum presage and situational analysis Comprehensive, realistic Complex Walker Interactive / naturalistic Platform of beliefs Describes real practice, deliberation Little guidance on evaluation Kerr Interactive Any element Flexible Lacks clear sequence

Hierarchy: aims (broad, national) → goals (level- or programme-specific) → objectives (subject, unit, lesson) → learning outcomes. Sources: society, learners, subject matter, philosophy, national policies and international commitments (SDG 4). Classification and domains: cognitive, affective and psychomotor (Bloom and colleagues; see PC 117). Competencies and learning outcomes: competencies integrate knowledge, skills, attitudes and values to perform in real contexts. NCF 2021 defined ten core competencies for Bangladesh, such as communication, critical and creative thinking, problem solving, collaboration, digital literacy and global citizenship, and translated them into subject competencies and learning outcomes by grade.

Criteria for selecting content: significance, validity, utility, interest, learnability, feasibility, consistency with social realities and alignment with objectives (Ornstein & Hunkins, 2018). Principles of organisation: Scope: the breadth and depth of content. Sequence: the order (simple to complex, chronological, prerequisite learning, whole to part). Continuity: vertical repetition of key concepts and skills over time. Integration: horizontal linking across subjects. Articulation: vertical and horizontal coherence across grades and subjects. Balance. Patterns of organisation include logical (subject structure), psychological (learner readiness), spiral (Bruner: revisiting concepts at increasing levels of complexity), concentric and topical . Figure 9. Bruner's spiral curriculum: core ideas revisited with increasing depth

Textbooks, teachers' guides, workbooks, supplementary readers, digital content and assessment materials. Process: plan aligned with curriculum → write → expert review → try out in schools → revise → print and distribute. Quality criteria: accuracy, alignment, readability, inclusive and gender-sensitive representation, attractive design, activities for active learning.

t: 3.7 Selection and organisation of instructional strategies
x: Strategies should match objectives (e.g. discussion for attitudes, demonstration for skills, inquiry for higher-order thinking), learners and resources. A competency-based curriculum favours experiential, collaborative, project and inquiry-based strategies.

Assessment must be aligned with objectives and competencies; it should combine formative and summative assessment, use multiple methods, and assess higher-order skills and values as well as knowledge (see PC 117).

Dissemination means communicating the new curriculum to teachers, administrators, parents and the public so that they understand and accept it. Strategies: orientation and training (cascade training, which often suffers dilution), teachers' guides, media campaigns, online platforms, pilot schools as demonstration sites, and stakeholder meetings. Havelock (1971) described research–development–diffusion, social interaction and problem-solving models of dissemination.

Implementation is putting the curriculum into practice. Fullan (2007) identifies factors affecting implementation: characteristics of the change (need, clarity, complexity, quality), local factors (district, community, principal, teachers) and external factors (government, agencies). The Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM) (Hall & Hord) tracks teachers' stages of concern (from awareness to refocusing) and levels of use. Monitoring collects ongoing information on implementation (classroom observation, school visits, surveys, learning assessments) to identify problems and provide support.

Curriculum must change as society, knowledge, technology and learner needs change. Curriculum evaluation judges the worth of the curriculum. Models include Tyler's objectives model, Stufflebeam's CIPP (Context, Input, Process, Product), Stake's countenance model, Scriven's goal-free and formative/summative evaluation, and Kirkpatrick's four levels (for training). Results lead to revision, modification and renewal . Figure 10. Stufflebeam's CIPP model of curriculum evaluation

u: Unit 4: Curriculum for Pre-primary and Primary Education of Bangladesh
x: Primary curriculum: after independence, a new primary curriculum was developed by the National Curriculum and Syllabus Committee (1976–77). In 1986–1991 , a new competency-based primary curriculum was developed under the IDA/UNICEF-supported projects (introduced in schools from 1992), with 53 terminal competencies . It was revised in 2002 (50 terminal competencies) and again in 2011–2012 (29 terminal competencies; subject-wise and class-wise learning outcomes; new textbooks from 2013). Pre-primary curriculum: NEP 2010 introduced one year of pre-primary education for 5-year-olds; the Pre-primary Curriculum was developed (2011) with learning areas and a play-based approach, and expanded under the Operational Framework for Pre-primary Education (2008) and PEDP3. NCF 2021: a single framework from pre-primary to Class XII with ten core competencies; two years of pre-primary; new primary textbooks rolled out from 2023 in Class I and later grades.

u: Unit 4: Curriculum for Pre-primary and Primary Education of Bangladesh
t: 4.2 Main features of the present pre-primary curriculum
x: Play-based, child-centred, activity-oriented learning; no formal textbooks for children; materials include a learning kit, picture books, rhymes and a teachers' guide. Learning areas: physical and motor; social and emotional; language and communication; early mathematics; environment and science; creative arts; health, hygiene and safety. Daily routine with free play, circle time, storytelling, songs, drawing and outdoor play. Assessment through observation and portfolios, not written tests. Emphasis on school readiness and smooth transition to Class I.

1976: first national secondary curriculum after independence (based on the Qudrat-e-Khuda Commission's recommendations). 1995–96: revised secondary curriculum. 2012: new curriculum for Classes VI–XII aligned with NEP 2010; learning outcome–based; creative questions (introduced in 2008 for SSC); new textbooks from 2013; Science, Humanities and Business streams from Class IX. NCF 2021: competency-based, experiential learning from Class VI to XII; ten subjects common to all until Class X (no streaming); 60–70% continuous, school-based assessment; rolled out in Classes VI and VII in 2023, VIII and IX in 2024. 2024–25 reversal: after the political transition, the government announced a return to a revised version of the 2012 curriculum for secondary classes from 2025 (with streaming reintroduced from Class IX), while planning a new reform with wider consultation. Note Because of these rapid changes, examiners are likely to ask you to compare the 2012 and NCF 2021 approaches and to evaluate why the 2021 reform faced resistance. Prepare a balanced answer.

Feature 2012 curriculum NCF 2021 curriculum Orientation Learning outcomes; content-focused Competency-based; experiential learning Streaming From Class IX (Science, Humanities, Business) None until Class X (proposed from Class XI) Subjects Many subjects, heavy content Ten common subjects (e.g. Bangla, English, Mathematics, Science, History and Social Science, Digital Technology, Life and Livelihood, Wellbeing, Religion, Arts and Culture) Teaching Lecture-dominant in practice Projects, inquiry, group work, field work Assessment Term examinations, creative questions, SSC/HSC public examinations Large share of continuous school-based assessment, performance indicators, reduced public examinations Role of textbooks Central Activity books and experience-based materials

Under the 2012-based system: class tests, term (half-yearly and annual) examinations, SBA components, creative questions and MCQs; public examinations at SSC and HSC with GPA. Under NCF 2021: continuous formative assessment with performance indicators recorded in apps (e.g. "Noipunno"), summative assessment through tasks and projects, and descriptive reports rather than marks. The latter faced criticism over teacher workload, unclear indicators, parental anxiety about the loss of marks and examinations, and resource demands.

Strengths (across reforms): recognition of higher-order skills; attempts to reduce rote learning; free textbooks; inclusion of ICT and life skills; cross-cutting issues (environment, gender, values); NCF 2021's focus on wellbeing and experiential learning. Weaknesses: Frequent, rapid reforms without adequate piloting or consultation. Insufficient teacher preparation (short cascade training). Large classes, poor resources and limited laboratories. Assessment misalignment and the dominance of public examinations and guidebooks. Persistent urban–rural and public–private gaps. Textbook quality issues and content controversies. Weak monitoring and use of evaluation evidence.

Establish a stable, evidence-based reform process with a permanent curriculum commission and long-term vision. Pilot new curricula in representative schools and evaluate before scaling up. Invest heavily in teacher professional development, with school-based support. Align public examinations with curriculum competencies; strengthen the reliability of school-based assessment through moderation. Reduce class sizes and improve facilities. Engage parents and communities in understanding reforms. Ensure quality textbooks through rigorous review. Use technology to support, not replace, teacher–student interaction.

The word value comes from the Latin valere , "to be strong, to be worth". A value is an enduring belief about what is desirable, good or worthwhile that guides choices and behaviour. Definition Value : "An enduring belief that a specific mode of conduct or end-state of existence is personally or socially preferable to an opposite or converse mode of conduct or end-state of existence" (Rokeach, 1973, p. 5). Value education is the deliberate process of helping learners understand, internalise and act upon values. Halstead and Taylor (2000) define values education as "the principles and fundamental convictions which act as general guides to behaviour, the standards by which particular actions are judged as good or desirable", and their transmission in schools.

Nature: values are learned (not innate), relatively enduring, hierarchical (organised into priorities), emotionally charged, both personal and shared, culturally influenced, and expressed in behaviour. Scope: moral values, social values, civic and democratic values, cultural values, aesthetic values, environmental values, spiritual and religious values, professional and work values, and universal human values (human rights, peace, tolerance).

t: 1.3 Taxonomy of affective learning and learning values
x: Krathwohl, Bloom and Masia (1964) described how values are internalised in five levels: Figure 1. Krathwohl's taxonomy of the affective domain: internalisation increases towards the base Level What the learner does Example (value: honesty) Receiving Becomes aware of the value Listens to a story about honesty Responding Reacts, participates Answers questions about why the character was honest Valuing Accepts and prefers the value Chooses to return a lost pen and explains why Organisation Integrates it with other values Weighs honesty against loyalty to a friend who cheated Characterisation Lives by it consistently Is known by peers and teachers as reliably honest Key Point Value education succeeds only when learners move beyond receiving and responding to valuing and characterisation, which requires experience, reflection and practice, not just preaching.

t: 1.4 Differentiating values from other affective constructs
x: Construct Definition Relation to values Belief A proposition accepted as true ("Hard work leads to success") Values are beliefs about what is desirable Attitude A learned predisposition to respond favourably or unfavourably to an object, person or idea Narrower and more specific; values underlie attitudes Interest Preference for an activity Less enduring; can be shaped by values Norm A social rule or expectation about behaviour Norms are external and group-based; values are internal standards Ideal A conception of perfection or a standard to aspire to The highest form of a value Morals Principles concerning right and wrong conduct Moral values are a subset of values Ethics The systematic study of morality; codes of conduct Ethics reflects on and justifies values Virtue A settled disposition of character to act well (Aristotle) A value internalised as a character trait

Figure 2. Types of values Other classifications: Rokeach (1973): terminal values (desirable end-states, e.g. freedom, equality, wisdom, a world at peace) and instrumental values (preferred modes of behaviour, e.g. honest, responsible, courageous, helpful). Spranger (1928): theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political and religious values. Schwartz (1992): ten universal values (self-direction, stimulation, hedonism, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition, benevolence, universalism) arranged in a circle by compatibility and conflict. Intrinsic (valued for their own sake) and extrinsic/instrumental (valued as means). Universal (human dignity, truth, non-violence) and culture-specific values.

Family (the primary source); religion; school and teachers; peer group; community and culture; mass and social media; literature and the arts; national ideals and the constitution; great personalities; personal experience and reflection.

Values can compete or conflict at several levels: Intrapersonal conflict: within one person, e.g. honesty versus loyalty to a friend, or ambition versus family duty. Interpersonal conflict: between individuals with different priorities. Intergenerational conflict: between traditional values of parents and modern values of youth (e.g. arranged versus self-chosen marriage, career choices). Intercultural / social conflict: between groups, religions or cultures, or between tradition and modernity (e.g. individualism versus collectivism). Institutional conflict: between school values (cooperation) and examination culture (competition). Resolving conflicts in education: moral dilemma discussions, values clarification, perspective-taking, dialogue, reference to shared universal values and human rights, and the development of moral reasoning.

u: Unit 2: Evolution and Approaches of Developing Values
x: Greek origin Socrates: "virtue is knowledge"; the examined life; dialogue to discover moral truth. Plato: education to develop the four cardinal virtues (wisdom, courage, temperance, justice) in the ideal state. Aristotle: virtue as a golden mean developed through habituation ; moral education as character formation for eudaimonia (flourishing). This is the root of contemporary character education . Religious tradition Throughout history, moral education was inseparable from religious education: in the Vedic gurukul , Buddhist viharas , Islamic maktabs and madrasahs , and Christian church schools. Religious texts, exemplary lives and rituals were the main means of transmitting values. Secularisation in modern states led to debates about whether and how values can be taught apart from religion, and many systems (including Bangladesh's "Religion and Moral Education") combine both. Modern developments * Durkheim (1925), Moral Education : * three elements of morality: the spirit of discipline, attachment to social groups, and autonomy (understanding the reasons for rules). * Piaget (1932), The Moral Judgment of the Child : * heteronomous morality (rules as fixed, from authority; judging by consequences) moving to autonomous morality (rules as social agreements; judging by intentions). The character education movement (early 20th century and revived from the 1990s), values clarification (1960s–70s), cognitive-developmental moral education (Kohlberg), the ethics of care (Noddings), and social-emotional learning.

u: Unit 2: Evolution and Approaches of Developing Values
x: (i) Theory of social morality Morality is learned through socialisation into the norms and values of society. Durkheim saw morality as social in origin: society is the source of moral authority, and the school's task is to attach the child to society and its rules. Social learning theory (Bandura) adds that values are learned by observing and imitating models and through reinforcement. Educational implication: teachers and institutions must model values; the school's ethos and rules, the hidden curriculum, and community participation matter as much as lessons. (ii) Theory of personal development Values develop as part of the growth of the whole person and the self. Humanistic psychologists (Rogers, Maslow) argue that, in a climate of acceptance, empathy and genuineness, people naturally move towards self-actualisation and prosocial values. Erikson's psychosocial stages link virtues to resolving each stage (hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care, wisdom). Educational implication: supportive relationships, self-reflection, autonomy and opportunities for responsibility. (iii) Values clarification Developed by Louis Raths, Merrill Harmin and Sidney Simon in Values and Teaching (1966). Rather than imposing values, teachers help students clarify their own values through a seven-step valuing process : Figure 3. The valuing process in values clarification (Raths, Harmin & Simon, 1966) Strategies: clarifying responses, values continuum, rank ordering, values voting, "twenty things I love to do", and values sheets. Critique: risks moral relativism ("all values are equally valid") and gives little guidance on right and wrong (Lockwood, 1978; Kirschenbaum later proposed comprehensive values education). (iv) Kohlberg's theory of moral development Lawrence Kohlberg (1958, 1981) extended Piaget. Using moral dilemmas (e.g. the Heinz dilemma : should Heinz steal a drug he cannot afford to save his dying wife?), he analysed the reasoning behind answers and identified three levels with six stages: Level Stage Orientation Typical reasoning Pre-conventional (most children under 9) 1. Obedience and punishment Avoid punishment "He shouldn't steal because he'll go to jail." 2. Individualism and exchange (instrumental) Self-interest, fair deals "He should steal if he needs his wife." Conventional (most adolescents and adults) 3. Good interpersonal relationships ("good boy/good girl") Approval of others "A good husband would steal to save her." 4. Maintaining social order (law and order) Duty, laws, authority "Stealing is against the law; society would collapse." Post-conventional (a minority of adults) 5. Social contract and individual rights Laws are social agreements that can be changed "The right to life is above property law." 6. Universal ethical principles Justice, dignity, conscience "Life has a universal value; he must act on principle." Figure 4. Kohlberg's levels of moral reasoning, highest at the top Educational implications: moral dilemma discussions (the "Blatt effect": discussion with peers at a slightly higher stage promotes development), the just community school (democratic participation in rule-making), and attention to moral reasoning rather than indoctrination. Critiques: Carol Gilligan (1982) argued that the theory is biased towards a male "justice" orientation and neglects the "care" orientation; it focuses on reasoning rather than behaviour; and stage 6 is rarely found and may be culturally biased (Snarey, 1985). Exam Focus Kohlberg is one of the most frequently examined theories in this course. Learn the six stages with one Heinz-style example each, and Gilligan's critique. Other approaches Character education (Lickona, 1991): moral knowing, moral feeling and moral action; respect and responsibility as core values; whole-school approach. Ethics of care (Noddings, 1984): modelling, dialogue, practice and confirmation. Inculcation: direct teaching and reinforcement of values (effective for basic norms but risks indoctrination). Moral reasoning, analysis and action learning approaches (Superka et al., 1976 typology: inculcation, moral development, analysis, clarification, action learning). Living Values Education Programme (UNESCO-supported, 1996 onward): twelve values (peace, respect, love, responsibility, happiness, cooperation, honesty, humility, tolerance, simplicity, freedom, unity).

u: Unit 2: Evolution and Approaches of Developing Values
t: 2.3 Value mediation through different tiers of the curriculum
x: Figure 5. How values are mediated through different tiers of the curriculum National tier: the Constitution, National Education Policy 2010 and NCF 2021 state national values (patriotism, the spirit of the Liberation War, democracy, secularism, humanism, gender equality, respect for diversity). Curriculum tier: values are built into aims, competencies, subject outcomes and cross-cutting issues. Textbook tier: content, stories, images and activities carry values (positively or, sometimes, stereotypes). School tier: ethos, rules, assemblies, celebrations, discipline policies and the hidden curriculum. Classroom tier: teacher behaviour, relationships, methods (cooperative learning develops cooperation), and responses to students.

Person Life sketch Core values exemplified Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) (570–632 CE) The Prophet of Islam; known even before prophethood as Al-Amin (the trustworthy); established the Charter of Madinah, which guaranteed rights to different communities Truthfulness, trustworthiness, justice, mercy, compassion for the poor, orphans and animals, forgiveness (the forgiveness of the people of Makkah), tolerance, simplicity, respect for women and knowledge ("Seeking knowledge is obligatory for every Muslim") Gautama Buddha (c. 563–483 BCE) Prince Siddhartha who renounced luxury to seek the end of suffering; taught through parables (the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son) and the Sermon on the Mount Love of God and neighbour, forgiveness, humility, service to the poor and sick, peace-making, the Golden Rule Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman (1920–1975) Leader of the Six-Point Movement and the independence struggle; the 7 March 1971 speech; founding father of Bangladesh Patriotism, courage, sacrifice, democracy, secularism, love for people, commitment to justice and the mother tongue Begum Rokeya (1880–1932) Pioneer of women's education among Bengali Muslims; author of Sultana's Dream ; founded a girls' school Gender equality, courage, perseverance, social reform, the value of education Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (1820–1891) Educator and social reformer in Bengal; simplified Bangla prose and wrote Barnaparichay ; campaigned for widow remarriage (Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856) and girls' education Compassion, humanism, honesty, self-reliance, generosity, rational reform, dignity of women Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) Poet, Nobel laureate (1913), founder of Shantiniketan and Visva-Bharati; composer of the national anthems of Bangladesh and India Love of nature, humanism, creativity, freedom, internationalism, beauty, harmony Kazi Nazrul Islam (1899–1976) National Poet of Bangladesh; the "Rebel Poet" ( Bidrohi ); wrote against oppression and communalism Courage, rebellion against injustice, communal harmony, equality, love of humanity Confucius (551–479 BCE) Chinese teacher-philosopher Benevolence ( ren ), propriety, filial piety, respect, self-cultivation, lifelong learning Lalon Shah (c. 1774–1890) Baul mystic poet of Kushtia; songs questioning caste and religious divisions (" Shob loke koy Lalon ki jat songsare " – "Everyone asks what Lalon's caste is") Humanism, equality beyond caste and creed, tolerance, simplicity, spiritual search Mother Teresa (1910–1997) Founder of the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize (1979); served in Bangladesh after 1971 Compassion, service to the poorest, humility, dignity of every person Nelson Mandela (1918–2013) Anti-apartheid leader imprisoned for 27 years; first Black president of South Africa; Nobel Peace Prize (1993) Forgiveness, reconciliation, perseverance, equality, justice, leadership ("Education is the most powerful weapon which you can use to change the world") Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772–1833) "Father of the Indian Renaissance"; founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828); campaigned against sati (abolished 1829) and for modern education Rationalism, social reform, women's rights, religious tolerance, freedom of the press Figure 6. Universal values shared across great lives Study tip Study a "great life" through a story, a short video or a drama, then ask yourself discussion questions ("What would I have done?"), write a short values reflection and try a small action project (e.g. a kindness week inspired by Mother Teresa). This is how learners move up Krathwohl's taxonomy from receiving to valuing.

u: Unit 4: Development of Values from the Study of Religions
x: All major religions teach a version of the Golden Rule ("treat others as you would like to be treated"), honesty, compassion, justice, charity, self-discipline and respect for life. Teaching these shared values builds interfaith understanding and social harmony, which is vital in plural Bangladesh. Article 41 of the Constitution protects freedom of religion, and religious instruction must not be imposed on students of another faith.

u: Unit 4: Development of Values from the Study of Religions
x: Core beliefs (tenets): Tawhid (the oneness of Allah); prophethood ( Risalah ), with Muhammad (peace be upon him) as the final prophet; the Qur'an as revelation; angels; the Day of Judgement ( Akhirah ); divine decree. Five Pillars: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (obligatory charity), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage). Values: justice ( adl ), mercy ( rahmah ), honesty and trustworthiness ( amanah ), patience ( sabr ), gratitude ( shukr ), charity, brotherhood, respect for parents, knowledge, cleanliness ("cleanliness is half of faith"), moderation, care of the environment as stewardship ( khalifah ), and the sanctity of life ("whoever saves one life, it is as if he had saved all mankind", Qur'an 5:32).

u: Unit 4: Development of Values from the Study of Religions
x: Core beliefs: Brahman (ultimate reality) and Atman (the self); dharma (duty, righteousness); karma (actions and their consequences); samsara (cycle of rebirth) and moksha (liberation); scriptures including the Vedas, Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, Ramayana and Mahabharata. * Four aims of life ( purusharthas ): dharma , artha (prosperity), kama (pleasure) and moksha*. Values: truth ( satya ), non-violence ( ahimsa ), selfless action ( nishkama karma , Gita), duty, self-control, respect for parents and teachers ( matri devo bhava, pitri devo bhava, acharya devo bhava ), hospitality, tolerance (" Ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti " – "Truth is one; the wise call it by many names").

u: Unit 4: Development of Values from the Study of Religions
x: Core beliefs: the Four Noble Truths (life involves suffering; suffering arises from craving; suffering can cease; the path to its cessation) and the Noble Eightfold Path (right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration); karma ; nirvana ; the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha). * Five Precepts ( Pancha Sila ): * abstain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech and intoxicants. Values: compassion, loving-kindness, non-violence, mindfulness, equanimity, generosity ( dana ), moderation (the Middle Path).

u: Unit 4: Development of Values from the Study of Religions
x: Core beliefs: one God as the Trinity (Father, Son and Holy Spirit); Jesus Christ as the Son of God and Saviour; the Bible (Old and New Testaments); salvation by grace; resurrection. u: Unit 5: Development of Values through Schooling
t: 5.1 Values in the school curricula of Bangladesh
x: NEP 2010 aims include moral and spiritual values, patriotism and the spirit of the Liberation War, humanism, secularism, gender equality, respect for all religions and cultures, and environmental consciousness. Primary curriculum: terminal competencies include respect for parents and elders, honesty, cooperation, patriotism, respect for all religions, gender equality, environmental care and good habits. Subjects carrying values explicitly: Religion and Moral Education (Islam, Hindu, Buddhist and Christian religion and moral education), Bangladesh and Global Studies, Bangla literature. NCF 2021 includes values in its core competencies (e.g. responsible citizenship, empathy, respect for diversity) and introduced a subject on wellbeing ( Shastho Surokkha ). Integrity strategy: the National Integrity Strategy (2012) promotes ethics in education institutions (e.g. integrity units, "honesty stores" in schools).

u: Unit 5: Development of Values through Schooling
x: Stories, fables, folk tales, poems and biographies make values concrete and engaging. Examples: Aesop's fables and the Panchatantra (wisdom, honesty); Thakurmar Jhuli (Bengali folk tales); Tagore's stories and poems; Sukumar Ray's humour; Nazrul's poems for children (such as Lichu Chor ); and modern Bangla children's books. Teaching strategies: storytelling, read-aloud with discussion questions, role-play, rewriting endings, and connecting stories to students' lives.

Sex refers to the biological and physiological characteristics (chromosomes, hormones, reproductive organs) typically used to classify people as female, male or intersex. Gender refers to the socially constructed roles, behaviours, expressions, identities and relations that a society considers appropriate for women, men and gender-diverse people. Ann Oakley's Sex, Gender and Society (1972) popularised the distinction. Gender identity is a person's internal sense of their own gender; gender expression is how a person presents gender outwardly. Sexuality / sexual orientation refers to a person's emotional, romantic and sexual attraction to others. Simone de Beauvoir (1949): "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." Judith Butler (1990): gender is performative , produced through repeated acts. West and Zimmerman (1987): gender is something we "do" in everyday interaction. Sex Gender Biological Social and cultural Largely fixed at birth Learned, varies across cultures and over time Universal categories Culture-specific roles and expectations Example: only women can give birth Example: the belief that only women should cook or care for children

Transgender describes people whose gender identity differs from the sex assigned at birth. In South Asia, hijra communities have a long cultural history as a recognised third gender. In Bangladesh, the government recognised hijras as a third gender in 2013 , and from 2019 voters could register as hijra . Other related terms: intersex (variations in sex characteristics), non-binary and gender-diverse . Transgender people face exclusion from education, employment, health care and housing, family rejection and violence.

t: 1.3 Biological, psychological, social and cultural interpretations
x: Figure 1. Four interpretations of gender Biological explanations emphasise physical differences but are criticised for biological determinism (the idea that biology fixes social roles). Psychological explanations: Freud (identification), Kohlberg (cognitive-developmental gender constancy), Bandura (social learning by imitation and reinforcement), Bem's gender schema theory (1981; children organise information through gender categories). Social explanations: gender is a structure of social relations and power (Connell, 2009), sustained by institutions (family, school, workplace, state). Cultural explanations: Margaret Mead's Sex and Temperament (1935) found different gender patterns among the Arapesh, Mundugumor and Tchambuli of Papua New Guinea, showing that "masculine" and "feminine" traits are culturally shaped.

t: 1.4 Women and gender: are they synonymous?
x: No. "Gender" is not a synonym for "women". Gender refers to relations between women, men and gender-diverse people, and to the structures of masculinity and femininity. Gender analysis therefore includes men and boys (e.g. pressures of "hegemonic masculinity"; Connell), sexual and gender minorities, and the relations of power between groups. Early development policy focused on "women" (WID); later approaches shifted to "gender" (GAD) because women's disadvantage cannot be understood without analysing relations with men and social structures.

Concept Meaning Patriarchy A social system in which men hold primary power and dominate in roles of leadership, authority and property; "a system of social structures and practices in which men dominate, oppress and exploit women" (Walby, 1990) Gender role Behaviours and responsibilities a society considers appropriate for each gender Gender stereotype Generalised, often inaccurate beliefs about the traits of each gender ("boys are better at mathematics", "girls are emotional") Gender division of labour Allocation of tasks by gender: Moser's triple roles of women: productive, reproductive and community management Practical gender needs (PGNs) Needs arising from women's existing roles that improve their condition without challenging the gender order: water, health care, income (Moser, 1993; Molyneux, 1985) Strategic gender needs (SGNs) Needs that challenge women's subordinate position: legal rights, protection from violence, equal wages, control over their bodies, political voice Gender equality Equal rights, responsibilities and opportunities for all genders Gender equity Fairness of treatment according to respective needs, which may require different treatment to achieve equality Gender awareness / sensitisation Recognising that gender shapes experience and that differences in power exist; training to become sensitive to gender issues Empowerment Expanding people's ability to make strategic life choices in a context where this ability was previously denied (Kabeer, 1999): resources, agency and achievements Gender and development Approaches to development that analyse and address gender relations (see Unit 5) Gender lens A way of looking at policies, programmes or data to see their different effects on women, men and gender-diverse people Gender neutrality Policies or language that do not distinguish by gender. "Gender-neutral" policies can be "gender-blind" if they ignore real differences in needs Gender-balanced approach Ensuring the representation and participation of all genders in decision-making, staffing and content Gender audit A systematic assessment of how far an organisation's policies, programmes, budget and culture promote gender equality (e.g. the ILO Participatory Gender Audit) Intersectionality Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989): systems of oppression (gender, race, class, caste, disability, religion, ethnicity) intersect, so a poor, disabled, ethnic minority girl faces compounded disadvantage Figure 2.
