Longwe's Women's Empowerment Framework: levels of equality (highest at top) Historically, societies have also moved from strongly patriarchal arrangements towards more egalitarian ones through stages such as formal legal equality (voting rights, education rights), substantive equality (equal outcomes and opportunities) and transformative equality (changing norms and structures).

u: Unit 2: Gender Education: Concept and Vision
t: 2.1 Origin and development of gender education
x: Gender education developed from women's studies (from the late 1960s, linked to second-wave feminism) and broadened into gender studies in the 1980s–90s to include men, masculinities and sexualities. In education, early work focused on girls' access to schooling; later work examined sexism in curricula, classroom interaction and the hidden curriculum (Spender, 1982; Sadker & Sadker, 1994). International frameworks (CEDAW 1979, Beijing 1995, EFA 2000, SDGs 2015) made gender equality in and through education a global commitment. In Bangladesh, the University of Dhaka established a Department of Women's Studies in 2000 (now Women and Gender Studies).

u: Unit 2: Gender Education: Concept and Vision
x: Gender education is education about gender and for gender equality: helping learners understand how gender is constructed, recognise inequality and discrimination, and develop attitudes and skills for respectful, equal relationships. Objectives: raise awareness of gender constructions and stereotypes; promote equal opportunities and rights; prevent gender-based violence; develop critical thinking about media and culture; support all learners to achieve their potential; prepare gender-sensitive teachers and leaders. Scope: curriculum, textbooks, pedagogy, classroom interaction, school environment and safety, teacher education, leadership, policy, community and media.

u: Unit 2: Gender Education: Concept and Vision
x: Sociology (social structures), psychology (identity, socialisation), anthropology (cultural variation), economics (labour, care work), political science (power, representation), law (rights), history (women's history), health sciences (reproductive health), development studies, and literature and media studies.

u: Unit 2: Gender Education: Concept and Vision
t: 2.4 Role of family, school and society
x: Family: the first site of gender socialisation (toys, chores, freedom of movement, investment in education, inheritance). School: formal and hidden curriculum; teacher expectations and interaction; separate or mixed schooling; school safety; role models among teachers and leaders. Society: religion, media, peer groups, community norms, laws and the labour market.

u: Unit 2: Gender Education: Concept and Vision
x: Figure 5. How gender is learned through socialisation Mechanisms: manipulation and canalisation (Oakley: directing children towards gender-typed toys and activities), reinforcement (praise and punishment), modelling , verbal appellations ("good girl", "boys don't cry") and gender schemas .

u: Unit 2: Gender Education: Concept and Vision
t: 2.6 Role of the curriculum and hidden curriculum
x: Formal curriculum: textbook content and images may under-represent women, show them only in domestic roles, or ignore women's contributions. Gender-responsive curricula include diverse role models, challenge stereotypes and include gender equality content. Hidden curriculum: teachers giving boys more attention and harder questions; assigning cleaning to girls and lifting to boys; seating patterns; disciplinary practices; sexist jokes; and the gender composition of leadership (most head teachers are men while many primary teachers are women). NCTB textbook reviews have sought to remove stereotypes; studies still find persistent imbalances (e.g. more male characters and stereotyped occupations).

u: Unit 2: Gender Education: Concept and Vision
x: NEP 2010 commits to gender equality, eliminating gender discrimination in textbooks, female teacher recruitment (a 60% quota for women in government primary teacher recruitment), stipends for girls, separate toilets and safe schools. PEDP and secondary programmes include gender action plans. The Female Secondary School Stipend Programme (from 1994) is an internationally cited success in achieving gender parity.

u: Unit 2: Gender Education: Concept and Vision
x: A gender-inclusive school: ensures safety (anti-harassment committees, safe transport); provides gender-segregated and accessible toilets and menstrual hygiene management (MHM) facilities; uses inclusive language and materials; trains teachers in gender-responsive pedagogy (FAWE, 2005/2018); involves girls and boys equally in leadership and co-curricular activities; welcomes transgender and gender-diverse learners; and offers comprehensive, age-appropriate life skills and sexuality education.

t: 3.1 Marriage and family: patriarchy and matriarchy
x: Patriarchal families: authority with the father or eldest male; patrilineal descent and inheritance; patrilocal residence (the bride moves to the husband's home). This is dominant in Bangladesh. Matriarchal / matrilineal families: descent and property traced through women; examples in Bangladesh include the Garo (Mandi) and Khasi communities, where property passes through daughters and husbands often live with the wife's family. (Matrilineal does not necessarily mean women hold political power.) Issues: child marriage (Bangladesh has one of the highest rates in the world; about half of women aged 20–24 were married before 18 in recent MICS surveys), dowry, polygamy, divorce, inheritance, and women's decision-making power in households.

t: 3.2 Social values, social division of labour and participation
x: Values about modesty, honour, purdah and the "proper place" of women restrict mobility and participation. The gender division of labour assigns unpaid care and domestic work mainly to women (women do on average several times more unpaid care work than men), limiting time for education, paid work and public life.

Hijra communities in Bangladesh traditionally live in gharanas under a guru , earning through blessings at births and weddings and collecting money in markets. Despite legal recognition in 2013, they face stigma, family rejection, exclusion from education and work, violence and limited health care. Government and NGO programmes (stipends for hijra students, vocational training, employment quotas in some private firms) are steps forward, but social acceptance remains limited.

Discrimination appears across life: son preference and unequal nutrition, unequal schooling, restricted mobility, occupational segregation, wage gaps, unequal inheritance, under-representation in leadership, and stereotyped media portrayal.

Definition Gender-based violence : Harmful acts directed at an individual based on their gender, rooted in gender inequality, abuse of power and harmful norms; it includes physical, sexual, psychological and economic harm, and threats, coercion and deprivation of liberty (UNHCR; UN Declaration on the Elimination of Violence against Women, 1993). Setting Forms of violence and harassment Family Domestic violence, marital rape, dowry violence, acid attacks, child marriage, honour-related violence Workplace Sexual harassment, unequal pay, unsafe conditions (e.g. RMG factories) Peers Bullying, "eve teasing" (street sexual harassment), dating violence Educational institutions Harassment by teachers or students, corporal punishment, gendered bullying Transport Harassment on buses, trains and streets Cyberspace Cyberbullying, image-based abuse, threats, stalking, sextortion Role of media: media can instigate violence (sexual objectification, normalising violence, sensational reporting) or prevent it (awareness campaigns, exposing abuses, positive role models). Legal responses in Bangladesh: the Prevention of Oppression Against Women and Children Act 2000 (amended 2020 to include the death penalty for rape); Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010; Acid Crime Control Act 2002; Dowry Prohibition Act 2018; the High Court directive on sexual harassment (2009) , which requires complaint committees in educational institutions and workplaces; the Digital/Cyber security laws addressing online harassment; and the national helpline 109 .

t: 3.6 Gender Management System (GMS) and the role of education
x: The Gender Management System (Commonwealth Secretariat, 1999) is a network of structures, mechanisms and processes within government to integrate gender into all policies, plans and programmes ( gender mainstreaming ). Components: an enabling environment (political will, legal framework), structures (lead agency, gender focal points, inter-ministerial steering committee), mechanisms (gender analysis, gender-disaggregated data, gender budgeting, training) and processes (planning, monitoring, evaluation). Bangladesh introduced gender budgeting in 2009–10; the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs is the lead agency with gender focal points in ministries. Role of education in improving the situation: gender-responsive curricula and pedagogy; awareness of rights and laws; life skills and comprehensive sexuality education; safe schools; engaging boys and men; women teachers and leaders as role models; and critical media literacy.

u: Unit 4: Political, Economic and Legal Dimensions
x: Political rights: the Constitution guarantees equal rights (Articles 27, 28) and permits special provisions for women (Art. 28(4)). There are 50 reserved seats for women in the 350-member Jatiya Sangsad (indirectly elected) and one-third reserved seats in local government (Union Parishad). Decision-making and participation: although Bangladesh has had women heads of government for long periods, women's participation in parliament (directly elected), cabinets, local leadership, political parties and civil service leadership remains low. Barriers include patriarchal norms, money and violence in politics, and family responsibilities. Role of education: civic education, leadership training, student councils with gender balance, and role models.

u: Unit 4: Political, Economic and Legal Dimensions
x: Women's labour force participation in Bangladesh has risen (driven by the ready-made garment sector, microfinance and agriculture), but remains well below men's and is concentrated in informal, low-paid work. Issues: wage gap, occupational segregation, unpaid care work, limited access to credit, land and technology, harassment, and limited decision-making over income. The Global Gender Gap Index (World Economic Forum) measures economic participation, educational attainment, health and political empowerment. Role of education: skills and TVET for women, financial literacy, entrepreneurship, STEM education for girls, and challenging occupational stereotypes.

u: Unit 4: Political, Economic and Legal Dimensions
x: Family and personal law: marriage, divorce, maintenance, custody and inheritance are governed by religious personal laws (Muslim, Hindu, Christian, Buddhist) which contain gender inequalities; for example, under Muslim law a daughter inherits half the share of a son, and Hindu personal law in Bangladesh has historically limited women's inheritance and has no codified divorce right. Legal rights: the Constitution, the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 (registration of marriage, restrictions on polygamy), the Hindu Marriage Registration Act 2012, labour laws (maternity leave), and the 2009 amendment to the citizenship law that allows mothers to pass on citizenship to their children. Access to legal aid: the National Legal Aid Services Organisation (Legal Aid Act 2000), NGOs such as BLAST, Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK), Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association (BNWLA) and Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, and One-Stop Crisis Centres (OCCs) in hospitals for survivors of violence. Role of education: legal literacy; knowledge of rights and services; reducing fear and stigma in seeking justice.

Development policy has moved from ignoring women, to seeing them as an untapped resource, to analysing and transforming unequal gender relations. Figure 6. t: 5.2 Human development: gender perspectives and indices
x: UNDP introduced gender-sensitive indices in its 1995 Human Development Report : Gender-related Development Index (GDI): adjusts HDI for gender inequality in health, education and income. Since 2014 it is calculated as the ratio of female HDI to male HDI. Gender Empowerment Measure (GEM): measured women's participation in economic and political life (seats in parliament, managerial and professional positions, income). Replaced in 2010 by the Gender Inequality Index (GII) , which measures reproductive health (maternal mortality, adolescent births), empowerment (parliamentary seats, secondary education) and labour market participation; 0 = equality, 1 = maximum inequality. The 1995 report's message: "Human development, if not engendered, is endangered."

t: 5.4 Gender in the MDGs and SDGs; recent global policies
x: MDG 3: promote gender equality and empower women (target: eliminate gender disparity in primary and secondary education by 2005 and at all levels by 2015). Bangladesh achieved parity in primary and secondary enrolment. SDG 5: achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls (ending discrimination, violence, child marriage and FGM; valuing unpaid care work; equal participation in leadership; reproductive rights). SDG 4.5: eliminate gender disparities in education. SDG 4.7: gender equality as part of education for sustainable development. Other initiatives: UNGEI (UN Girls' Education Initiative, 2000), the Gender at the Centre Initiative (G7, 2019), "Her Education, Our Future" (UNESCO), and UNESCO's 2024 Gender Report (GEM).

The Yogyakarta Principles (2006; updated 2017) apply international human rights law to sexual orientation and gender identity. Several countries legally recognise third or non-binary genders (e.g. India's NALSA judgment, 2014, and the Transgender Persons Act 2019; Nepal, 2007; Pakistan's Transgender Persons Act 2018; Bangladesh's 2013 recognition of hijras). UNESCO's work on homophobic and transphobic bullying ( Out in the Open , 2016) highlights the need for safe, inclusive schools.

u: Unit 6: Gender and Development in Bangladesh: Issues and Status
t: 6.1 National gender policy and action plans in education
x: National Women Development Policy 2011 (earlier versions 1997, 2004, 2008): goals on women's rights, education, health, economic empowerment, political participation and elimination of violence. The National Action Plan implements it across ministries. NEP 2010: gender equality commitments in education. PEDP and secondary programmes: gender and inclusive education action plans (female teacher recruitment, girls' toilets, MHM, stipends, gender-sensitive textbooks, anti-harassment measures). National Children Policy 2011 and National Plan of Action to End Child Marriage (2018–2030) .

u: Unit 6: Gender and Development in Bangladesh: Issues and Status
t: 6.2 Policies, programmes and issues in gender and development
x: Achievements: gender parity in school enrolment; declining maternal mortality and fertility; rising female labour force participation; women's leadership in microfinance and NGOs; women's representation in local government through reserved seats. Persistent issues: child marriage; gender-based violence and harassment; low female participation in TVET, STEM and higher education faculty; wage gaps; unpaid care work; limited inheritance rights; low representation in decision-making; vulnerability to climate change and disasters.

u: Unit 6: Gender and Development in Bangladesh: Issues and Status
x: BRAC (girls' schools, adolescent clubs, legal aid, microfinance), Grameen Bank (microcredit to women), Bangladesh Mahila Parishad (women's rights advocacy), Ain o Salish Kendra (legal aid, human rights), BNWLA (legal aid against trafficking and violence), Naripokkho (feminist activism), Steps Towards Development, CAMPE (education advocacy), and international NGOs (Plan, Save the Children, CARE, ActionAid) run programmes on girls' education, life skills, child marriage prevention, GBV services and women's economic empowerment.

u: Unit 6: Gender and Development in Bangladesh: Issues and Status
t: 6.4 Acts and policies regarding transgender people
x: 2013: Cabinet decision recognising hijras as a third gender. 2015 onward: Ministry of Social Welfare programmes for hijra livelihood, stipends for hijra students and old-age allowances. 2019: Election Commission allowed registration as hijra on voter lists. Draft legislation to protect transgender rights has been discussed, but there is no comprehensive law as yet; public debate on terminology (hijra, transgender, third gender) and inclusion in textbooks continues. Check the latest developments before your exam.

u: Unit 7: Gender in Disaster, Emergency and Pandemic
x: Disasters affect women and men differently because of social inequality, not biology. In the 1991 cyclone in Bangladesh, women died at far higher rates than men; contributing factors included restrictions on mobility, lack of swimming skills, clothing, waiting for male relatives' permission, caring for children and the elderly, and cyclone warnings not reaching women. Neumayer and Plümper (2007) found that disasters reduce women's life expectancy more than men's in societies where women's status is low. After disasters, women and girls face increased risk of violence in shelters, early marriage, trafficking, loss of livelihood and school dropout. Gender-responsive disaster risk reduction: women's participation in disaster planning; warning systems that reach women; separate, safe and accessible shelters with lighting and toilets; MHM supplies; swimming and survival skills for girls; and gender-disaggregated data. The Sendai Framework (2015–2030) emphasises women's leadership in DRR.

u: Unit 7: Gender in Disaster, Emergency and Pandemic
t: 7.2 Gender in war, conflict and emergencies
x: Conflict brings sexual violence as a weapon of war (recognised in international law; e.g. the 1971 Liberation War, in which hundreds of thousands of women suffered sexual violence; Bangabandhu declared survivors Birangona , "war heroines"; they were recognised as freedom fighters in 2015), displacement, female-headed households and disrupted education. In the Rohingya refugee response, women and girls face GBV, trafficking, child marriage and limited access to learning. UNSCR 1325 calls for women's participation in peace processes and protection from GBV.

u: Unit 7: Gender in Disaster, Emergency and Pandemic
t: 7.3 Implications of the pandemic on gender
x: COVID-19 (2020–22) had gendered impacts: increased unpaid care work for women; job losses in sectors employing women (garments, domestic work); a " shadow pandemic " of domestic violence (UN Women, 2020); increased child marriage risk during school closures; girls' greater domestic burden limiting remote learning; the digital gender divide (fewer girls with phones and internet access); and women health workers on the frontline.

t: 1.1 Environment, environmental science, environmental education and environmental literacy
x: Concept Meaning Environment (French environner , to surround) The sum of all living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components and their interactions that surround and affect organisms. It includes the natural environment (air, water, land, organisms) and the human-made social, cultural and built environment. Bangladesh's Environment Conservation Act 1995 defines it as water, air, land and physical properties and their interrelationships with human beings, other living beings, plants and micro-organisms Environmental science An interdisciplinary scientific study of the environment and of solutions to environmental problems, drawing on ecology, chemistry, geology, biology, economics and other fields Environmental education (EE) "A process aimed at developing a world population that is aware of and concerned about the total environment and its associated problems, and which has the knowledge, attitudes, skills, motivation and commitment to work individually and collectively toward solutions of current problems and the prevention of new ones" (Belgrade Charter, 1975) Environmental literacy The capacity to perceive and interpret the relative health of environmental systems and to take appropriate action to maintain, restore or improve them (Roth, 1992). It has four components: knowledge, dispositions (attitudes, sensitivity, responsibility), competencies (skills) and environmentally responsible behaviour (Hollweg et al., 2011, NAAEE) Definition Environmental education (Stapp et al., 1969) : "Environmental education is aimed at producing a citizenry that is knowledgeable concerning the biophysical environment and its associated problems, aware of how to help solve these problems, and motivated to work toward their solution." This is often cited as the first formal definition.

t: 1.2 Aims and objectives of EE: attaining environmental literacy
x: The Tbilisi Declaration (UNESCO-UNEP Intergovernmental Conference on Environmental Education, 1977) set three goals and five categories of objectives that remain the foundation of EE. Goals: (1) to foster awareness of and concern about economic, social, political and ecological interdependence in urban and rural areas; (2) to provide every person with opportunities to acquire the knowledge, values, attitudes, commitment and skills needed to protect and improve the environment; (3) to create new patterns of behaviour towards the environment. Figure 1. The five Tbilisi objectives of environmental education (1977) Education about, in and for the environment Lucas (1979) and Palmer (1998) distinguished three dimensions of EE: Figure 2. Palmer's model: education about, in (through) and for the environment The Hungerford and Volk model (1990) Hungerford and Volk argued that knowledge alone does not change behaviour. Responsible environmental behaviour results from: Entry-level variables: environmental sensitivity (empathy with nature, often developed through significant outdoor experiences in childhood), knowledge of ecology, attitudes. Ownership variables: in-depth knowledge about issues and personal investment in them. Empowerment variables: knowledge of and skill in action strategies, locus of control (belief that one's actions make a difference), and intention to act. Figure 3. Hungerford and Volk's (1990) pathway to responsible environmental behaviour (built from the base up)

t: 1.3 Evolution of EE and its goals: from nature study to ESD
x: Figure 4. Evolution from nature study to education for sustainable development Nature study (late 19th century; Liberty Hyde Bailey, Anna Botsford Comstock): children observe and appreciate nature directly. Conservation education (1930s onward): wise use of natural resources (soil, forests, wildlife), stimulated by events such as the American Dust Bowl. Outdoor education: learning in natural settings. The environmental movement: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) on pesticides; the first Earth Day (1970). International EE: the UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm (1972) created UNEP and called for EE (Recommendation 96); the International Environmental Education Programme (IEEP, 1975); the Belgrade Charter (1975) ; the Tbilisi Conference (1977) . Sustainable development: Our Common Future (Brundtland, 1987). Rio Earth Summit (1992): Agenda 21, Chapter 36 ("Promoting education, public awareness and training") reoriented education towards sustainable development. Thessaloniki (1997) and the UN Decade of Education for Sustainable Development (DESD, 2005–2014) , led by UNESCO. Global Action Programme on ESD (2015–2019) and ESD for 2030 (2020–2030), with the Berlin Declaration on ESD (2021) . SDGs (2015): Target 4.7 calls for all learners to acquire knowledge and skills for sustainable development; SDG 13.3 calls for improved education on climate change mitigation, adaptation and early warning.

ESD is "an integral element of SDG 4 and a key enabler of all the other SDGs" (UNESCO, 2020). UNESCO's Education for Sustainable Development Goals: Learning Objectives (2017) specifies cognitive, socio-emotional and behavioural learning objectives for each of the 17 SDGs and eight key competencies for sustainability: systems thinking, anticipatory, normative, strategic, collaboration, critical thinking, self-awareness and integrated problem-solving. Basis Environmental education Education for sustainable development Focus Natural environment and environmental problems Environment, society and economy together Origin Belgrade (1975), Tbilisi (1977) Brundtland (1987), Rio (1992), DESD Goal Environmental literacy and responsible behaviour Sustainable lifestyles, societies and economies Scope Ecology, pollution, conservation Plus poverty, equity, peace, consumption, climate, health, gender

u: Unit 2: Environmental Education Curriculum and Implementation
t: 2.1 Guiding principles of the EE curriculum
x: The Tbilisi guiding principles (1977) state that EE should: Consider the environment in its totality: natural and built, technological and social. Be a continuous lifelong process, beginning at pre-school. Be interdisciplinary , drawing on the specific content of each discipline. Examine major environmental issues from local, national, regional and international points of view. Focus on current and potential environmental situations, with a historical perspective. Promote the value of local, national and international cooperation. Explicitly consider environmental aspects in plans for development and growth. Enable learners to have a role in planning their learning experiences. Relate environmental sensitivity, knowledge, problem-solving skills and values clarification to every age. Help learners discover the symptoms and real causes of environmental problems. Emphasise the complexity of environmental problems and the need for critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Use diverse learning environments and approaches, with emphasis on practical activities and first-hand experience.

u: Unit 2: Environmental Education Curriculum and Implementation
x: Objectives should span the Tbilisi categories (awareness, knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation) and Bloom's three domains, and be appropriate to learners' development (e.g. sensitivity and wonder in early years; issue investigation and action in adolescence). Examples: Class III: "Students will identify five sources of water pollution in their locality." Class VIII: "Students will investigate a local waste problem, analyse its causes and propose a feasible solution." Affective: "Students will demonstrate concern for plants by caring for a school garden."

u: Unit 2: Environmental Education Curriculum and Implementation
x: Approaches to placing EE in the curriculum: Infusion / integration (multidisciplinary): EE content is infused into existing subjects (science, geography, language, social studies). This is the most common approach, including in Bangladesh. Interdisciplinary (separate subject): EE as a distinct subject or course (e.g. Environmental Science). Cross-curricular theme: environment as a theme that runs across all subjects. Whole-school approach: sustainable school management (energy, waste, gardens, procurement), curriculum, community links (e.g. Eco-Schools programme). Content areas: ecosystems and biodiversity; natural resources (water, soil, forests, energy); pollution (air, water, soil, noise); waste management; climate change; population and environment; health and environment; disasters; sustainable agriculture; consumption and lifestyles; environmental ethics and policy. Sequencing: from local to global, concrete to abstract, awareness to action, and a spiral organisation that revisits concepts at greater depth.

u: Unit 2: Environmental Education Curriculum and Implementation
x: Principles: experiential and outdoor learning; inquiry and problem solving; local relevance; learner participation and action; interdisciplinarity; values clarification; systems thinking; cooperation; reflection. Strategy Description and example Field trips and outdoor learning Visit a river, park, wetland or the Sundarbans; nature walks; schoolyard ecology Project-based learning Students carry out a school waste audit and design a recycling plan Issue investigation and action training (Hungerford) Identify an issue, research it, evaluate options and take citizenship action (persuasion, consumer action, eco-management) Experiments and demonstrations Testing water quality; making a compost pit; demonstrating the greenhouse effect Case studies The Buriganga river pollution; arsenic contamination; the Rana Plaza collapse and industrial safety Role-play and simulation A mock public hearing on building a brick kiln near a school Games Ecosystem food-web games; carbon footprint calculators Storytelling and arts Folk songs about rivers; environmental drama; poster campaigns Community service and citizen science Tree planting, clean-up drives, bird counts, monitoring air quality Values clarification and dilemma discussion "Should a factory that provides jobs be allowed to pollute the river?" ICT and media Documentaries, GIS maps, online data (air quality index apps) Experiential learning cycle (Kolb, 1984) is especially relevant: concrete experience → reflective observation → abstract conceptualisation → active experimentation. Figure 5. Kolb's experiential learning cycle applied to environmental education

u: Unit 2: Environmental Education Curriculum and Implementation
x: Natural objects (leaves, soil samples, specimens); local environment as a resource; charts, maps and models; field guides; water and soil testing kits; videos and documentaries; ICT (GIS, simulations, apps); newspapers; textbooks and supplementary readers; low-cost, recycled materials (which themselves teach reuse); and community resource persons (farmers, fishermen, forest officials).

u: Unit 2: Environmental Education Curriculum and Implementation
x: EE should assess knowledge, attitudes, skills and behaviour , not only knowledge. Knowledge: tests, concept maps, essays. Attitudes and values: attitude scales (e.g. the New Ecological Paradigm (NEP) scale ; Dunlap et al., 2000), questionnaires, reflective journals. Skills: performance assessments (conducting a water test, mapping), project reports. Behaviour and participation: observation checklists, self-reports, portfolios, records of action projects. Authentic assessment: presentations to community members, action project outcomes. Programme evaluation: pre- and post-tests, follow-up of behaviour change.

u: Unit 2: Environmental Education Curriculum and Implementation
t: 2.7 Challenges in teaching and learning EE
x: Overloaded curricula and examination focus; EE treated as content rather than action; lack of teacher training and confidence; limited time and resources for field work; large classes and safety concerns; weak interdisciplinary coordination; gap between knowledge and behaviour; and the complexity and controversy of environmental issues. Solutions include teacher professional development, whole-school approaches, partnerships with NGOs and local government, integrating EE into assessment, and using the local environment as a low-cost resource.

u: Unit 3: Environmental Education in the Context of Bangladesh
x: Figure 6. Major environmental issues in Bangladesh Ecosystem imbalance: loss of forest cover (hill forests of Chittagong Hill Tracts, Sal forests of Madhupur), pressure on the Sundarbans (the world's largest mangrove forest and a UNESCO World Heritage Site), loss of wetlands and haors , declining fish and wildlife populations, river encroachment. Water pollution: untreated industrial effluents (textile dyeing, tanneries; the Buriganga, Turag and Shitalakshya rivers around Dhaka are severely polluted), sewage, agricultural chemicals, and naturally occurring arsenic in groundwater (affecting tens of millions of people since its discovery in the 1990s), plus increasing salinity in coastal areas. Air pollution in cities: Dhaka regularly ranks among the most polluted cities in the world for PM2.5. Main sources: brick kilns, vehicle emissions, construction dust, road dust and industry. Health effects include respiratory disease and premature deaths. Climate change: Bangladesh is among the most vulnerable countries (Germanwatch Climate Risk Index). Impacts: sea-level rise, stronger cyclones (Sidr 2007, Aila 2009, Amphan 2020), floods, river erosion, drought in the north-west, heat waves, salinity intrusion, climate-induced migration. Sound (noise) pollution: traffic horns, construction and loudspeakers; urban noise levels often exceed the standards in the Noise Pollution (Control) Rules 2006, causing hearing loss and stress. Soil pollution: overuse of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, industrial waste, salinity, loss of organic matter, topsoil removal for brick-making. Waste management: rapid urbanisation produces large volumes of solid waste; plastic pollution (despite the 2002 ban on polythene bags), e-waste, medical waste and inadequate landfill and recycling.

u: Unit 3: Environmental Education in the Context of Bangladesh
x: Strategies: protected areas (national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, ecologically critical areas); social forestry and coastal afforestation; wetland management (community-based fisheries); renewable energy (solar home systems); cleaner production and effluent treatment plants (ETPs); waste reduction, reuse and recycling (the 3Rs); environmentally friendly brick kilns; sustainable agriculture (integrated pest management); and public awareness. Community-based conservation and indigenous knowledge are important.

u: Unit 3: Environmental Education in the Context of Bangladesh
t: 3.3 EE in the curricula of Bangladesh
x: Intended learning objectives across the curriculum include awareness of the environment, understanding of natural resources and pollution, appreciation of biodiversity, skills for conservation, and participation in environmental protection. Content and organisation: Bangladesh largely uses the infusion approach : Primary: environmental content in Primary Science, Bangladesh and Global Studies, and in Bangla readings (trees, water, cleanliness, disasters). Secondary: Science, Geography and Environment, Biology, Agriculture, and Bangladesh and Global Studies cover ecosystems, pollution, climate change and disasters. NCF 2021 integrated environment and climate change across subjects such as Science and "Life and Livelihood". Higher education: Environmental Science departments in many universities. Comparison with other curricula: Country Approach Bangladesh Infusion into science and social studies; growing climate change content; limited outdoor and action learning India Supreme Court directive (1991, M. C. Mehta case) made EE compulsory at all levels; separate EVS subject in primary classes Australia Sustainability as a cross-curriculum priority in the national curriculum Finland Sustainability integrated across the national core curriculum; strong outdoor learning tradition England Eco-Schools programme; a climate education strategy in recent years

u: Unit 3: Environmental Education in the Context of Bangladesh
t: 3.4 EE through non-formal education in Bangladesh
x: NGOs and government agencies run community-based EE: BRAC, Bangladesh Centre for Advanced Studies (BCAS), IUCN Bangladesh, WildTeam (Sundarbans tiger conservation), the Department of Environment's awareness campaigns, community radio programmes, environmental clubs, adult literacy programmes with environmental content, and climate change awareness programmes in coastal areas. Mass media campaigns (tree planting fairs, World Environment Day) also play a role.

u: Unit 4: Health Education, Population Education and Disaster Risk Reduction
x: Population growth, development and environment Bangladesh's population was about 170 million in the 2022 census, making it one of the most densely populated countries in the world (about 1,100 people per km²). The total fertility rate fell from about 6.3 in the mid-1970s to about 2.0 recently, a demographic transition achieved through family planning, women's education and empowerment, and health programmes. Figure 7. Links between population, development and environment Concept: population education is "an educational programme which provides for a study of the population situation of the family, the community, the nation and the world, with the purpose of developing in the students rational and responsible attitudes and behaviour towards that situation" (UNESCO, 1970s). Population policy: Bangladesh's Population Policy 2012 aims to reduce fertility to replacement level, improve maternal and child health, promote family planning, and harness the demographic dividend. Population education in the curriculum: topics such as population growth and its effects, family size and quality of life, adolescent reproductive health, gender equality and population, urbanisation and migration, appear in Bangladesh and Global Studies, Science, and Physical Education and Health.

u: Unit 4: Health Education, Population Education and Disaster Risk Reduction
x: Environment and health The WHO estimates that around a quarter of the global disease burden is attributable to modifiable environmental factors. Key links: unsafe water and sanitation (diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid); air pollution (respiratory disease, heart disease); vector-borne diseases linked to environment (dengue, malaria); chemical exposure (arsenicosis, lead poisoning); noise (hearing loss, stress); and climate change (heat stress, new disease patterns). Health issues due to environmental pollution in Bangladesh Arsenicosis from arsenic-contaminated groundwater (skin lesions, cancers). Respiratory diseases from air pollution in cities. Water-borne diseases during floods. Dengue outbreaks in urban areas, linked to stagnant water and urbanisation (record outbreaks in 2019 and 2023). Lead exposure (from batteries, spices and paints) affecting children's cognitive development. Hearing problems among traffic police and urban residents. Health education in the curriculum Health education aims to develop knowledge, attitudes and practices for healthy living: personal hygiene, safe water, sanitation, nutrition, disease prevention, mental health, adolescent and reproductive health, first aid, and substance abuse prevention. In Bangladesh it is taught through "Physical Education and Health", Science, and NCF 2021's "Wellbeing" subject, and through school health programmes (deworming, vitamin A, WASH in schools). The WHO Health-Promoting Schools framework (and the 2021 Global Standards for Health-Promoting Schools ) recommends a whole-school approach.

u: Unit 4: Health Education, Population Education and Disaster Risk Reduction
x: Key concepts Hazard: a potentially damaging event (cyclone, flood, earthquake). Vulnerability: susceptibility to harm because of physical, social, economic or environmental factors. Capacity: resources and skills to cope. Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability ÷ Capacity. Disaster: a serious disruption of a community's functioning that exceeds its capacity to cope. Figure 8. The disaster management cycle Education in emergencies EiE ensures that learning continues safely during and after crises (see PC 112). It includes temporary learning spaces, psychosocial support, teacher support, and protection of schools. Education for reducing risks for children The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 calls for DRR knowledge in formal and non-formal education. The Comprehensive School Safety Framework (GADRRRES): (1) safe learning facilities; (2) school disaster management; (3) risk reduction and resilience education. Bangladesh: Disaster Management Act 2012; Standing Orders on Disaster (2010, revised 2019) assign roles to education officials and schools; schools used as cyclone and flood shelters; DRR content in textbooks (cyclones, floods, earthquakes, fire safety); school safety drills; Cyclone Preparedness Programme volunteers. Classroom DRR activities: hazard and risk mapping of the school and community; evacuation drills; making a family emergency kit; learning warning signals; first aid; swimming lessons (drowning is a leading cause of child death in Bangladesh). Exam Focus Likely questions: "Explain the goals and objectives of EE according to the Tbilisi Declaration." "Discuss the major environmental problems of Bangladesh and the role of education." "What is DRR education? How can schools reduce disaster risks for children?"

The term "non-formal education" became prominent with Philip H. Coombs's The World Educational Crisis: A Systems Analysis (1968), which argued that formal school systems in developing countries could not meet growing demand, were costly and often irrelevant, and that alternative forms of organised learning were needed. Coombs and Manzoor Ahmed developed the formal/non-formal/informal typology in studies for the World Bank and ICED (Coombs, Prosser & Ahmed, 1973; Coombs & Ahmed, 1974). Influences included Freire's popular education, Illich's Deschooling Society (1971), the Faure Report Learning to Be (1972), and the community development and adult literacy movements.

Definition Non-formal education (Coombs & Ahmed, 1974) : "Any organised, systematic, educational activity carried on outside the framework of the formal system to provide selected types of learning to particular subgroups in the population, adults as well as children." Definition Non-formal education (UNESCO ISCED, 2011) : Education that is institutionalised, intentional and planned by an education provider, and whose defining characteristic is that it is an addition, alternative and/or complement to formal education within the process of lifelong learning of individuals. Bangladesh's NFE Act 2014 defines non-formal education as education provided outside the formal system for out-of-school children, adolescents, youth and adults through flexible approaches, including basic literacy, life skills, livelihood skills and continuing education.

Organised and purposeful, but flexible in time, place, curriculum and duration. Learner-centred and need-based : content drawn from learners' lives and needs. Short-cycle and part-time , compatible with work and family. Low cost : uses community facilities and local facilitators. Participatory : learners and communities involved in planning. Diverse providers : government, NGOs, community organisations, employers. Focus on disadvantaged groups : out-of-school children, illiterate adults, women, the poor, working children. May or may not lead to certification ; increasingly linked to equivalency with formal education.

Literacy and numeracy; post-literacy and continuing education; second-chance primary education; life skills; livelihood and vocational skills; health, nutrition, population and family life education; agricultural extension; civic and rights education; environmental education; early childhood development; and community development. Figure 1. The scope of non-formal education

t: 1.5 Goals, objectives, significance and target people
x: Goals: provide basic education and learning opportunities to those excluded from formal education; reduce illiteracy; enhance skills for livelihood; empower individuals and communities; and support lifelong learning. Objectives: literacy and numeracy; life and livelihood skills; awareness of rights and responsibilities; improved health and quality of life; and pathways back into formal education. Significance: complements formal education; reaches the hardest to reach; cost-effective; relevant to local needs; supports national development and the SDGs. Target people: out-of-school children (8–14); adolescents and youth who dropped out; illiterate and neo-literate adults; women; working children; urban slum dwellers; ethnic minorities; persons with disabilities; refugees and people affected by disasters.

Second-chance education gives learners who missed or dropped out of school a new opportunity to acquire basic education and qualifications, often through accelerated learning programmes that compress the primary curriculum (e.g. five years into three or four). NFE is the main delivery mode for SCE. In Bangladesh, the Out-of-School Children (OoSC) Programme under BNFE and earlier programmes such as ROSC (Ananda schools) and BRAC's non-formal primary schools are examples. SDG 4.1 and 4.6 call for such pathways.

t: 1.7 Education in emergencies: local and global perspectives
x: Global: INEE Minimum Standards (2010); the Education Cannot Wait fund (2016); the Global Education Cluster; refugee education strategies (UNHCR's Refugee Education 2030 ). Non-formal approaches (temporary learning spaces, accelerated learning, radio education) are often the first response when formal schools are disrupted. Local (Bangladesh): learning centres for Rohingya children (LCFA, Myanmar Curriculum Pilot); continuity of learning during floods (boat schools such as Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha's floating schools); and remote learning during COVID-19.

t: 1.8 NFE in relation to EFA, UPE, CPE, OoSC and CE
x: Term Meaning Relation to NFE EFA (Education for All) Global commitment (Jomtien 1990, Dakar 2000) to meet the basic learning needs of all children, youth and adults NFE was recognised as essential for reaching EFA goals 3 (youth and adult learning) and 4 (adult literacy) UPE (Universal Primary Education) All children of primary age enrolled in and completing primary school (MDG 2) NFE provides alternative routes for children who cannot attend formal schools CPE (Compulsory Primary Education) Primary education made compulsory by law (Bangladesh, 1990) NFE helps those who fall outside compulsory schooling (e.g. over-age children) OoSC (Out-of-School Children) Children of school age not enrolled or who have dropped out The main target of second-chance NFE CE (Continuing Education) Learning after initial education NFE often provides post-literacy and continuing education

t: 1.9 Achieving skills and the role of NFE
x: NFE develops foundational skills (literacy, numeracy, digital literacy), life skills (WHO's ten core life skills: decision-making, problem-solving, creative thinking, critical thinking, effective communication, interpersonal skills, self-awareness, empathy, coping with emotions and coping with stress), livelihood and vocational skills (tailoring, poultry, mobile repair, handicrafts), and entrepreneurial and financial skills . It contributes to SDG target 4.4 (skills for employment) and 4.6 (literacy).

t: 2.1 Concept, definition, aims, purpose and importance
x: Definition Continuing education : Learning activities undertaken after the completion of initial education, by people who have left the formal system, to update, broaden or deepen knowledge and skills for personal, professional or social purposes. In developing countries, continuing education also refers to post-literacy and follow-up programmes that prevent neo-literates from relapsing into illiteracy and help them apply literacy to life (UNESCO's continuing education framework; Ahmed & Ouane, 1987). Aims: maintain and enhance literacy; upgrade skills; support career development; enable personal growth; promote active citizenship; and support community development. Importance: rapid change in knowledge and technology makes initial education insufficient; workers need reskilling; neo-literates need reinforcement; and societies need informed, adaptable citizens.

t: 2.2 CE in relation to education, NFE and further learning
x: CE is part of the broader concept of lifelong learning. It can be formal (evening degree courses, open university programmes), non-formal (training workshops, community learning centre courses) or informal (self-study, reading). Further learning includes further education (post-secondary, non-university) and higher education for adults.

Clientele: neo-literates; school dropouts; workers and professionals; women; farmers; the unemployed; senior citizens; and community leaders. Types (UNESCO's typology for post-literacy and continuing education, Ahmed & Ouane, 1987; Ouane, 1989): Post-literacy programmes: consolidating literacy skills. Equivalency programmes: alternatives to formal education leading to equivalent certificates. Income-generating programmes: vocational skills for earning. Quality-of-life improvement programmes: health, nutrition, environment. Individual interest promotion programmes: hobbies, culture, religion, sports. Future-oriented programmes: new skills and technologies. Figure 2. Types of continuing education programmes (after UNESCO, Ouane, 1989)

t: 2.4 CE in relation to CPD and HRD
x: Continuing Professional Development (CPD): the systematic maintenance, improvement and broadening of knowledge and skills throughout a professional's working life (e.g. teacher CPD, medical CPD). CE provides much of CPD. Human Resource Development (HRD): organisational and national processes to develop people's capacities. CE is a key strategy for HRD, turning population into productive human capital.

CE enables upskilling (improving current skills) and reskilling (learning new skills for new jobs). In the Fourth Industrial Revolution, automation and AI make reskilling essential. Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) allows skills gained informally to be certified (in Bangladesh, under the National Skills Development Authority's RPL system).

t: 2.6 CE, the SDGs, lifelong education and the knowledge economy
x: SDG 4 promotes lifelong learning opportunities for all; targets 4.3, 4.4 and 4.6 are directly linked to CE. Lifelong education (LE): the principle that education should be available throughout life (Faure, 1972; Delors, 1996). Knowledge economy (KE): an economy in which growth depends on the production, distribution and use of knowledge (OECD, 1996). Knowledge-based society (KBS): a society that generates, shares and uses knowledge for prosperity and wellbeing (UNESCO, 2005, Towards Knowledge Societies ). CE is essential for both. Figure 3. Lifelong learning encompasses formal, non-formal and informal learning across the whole life span

u: Unit 3: NFE and CE in Developing Countries
t: 3.1 Concept and characteristics of developing societies
x: Developing societies are characterised by lower per-capita incomes, large rural and informal sectors, rapid population growth or large youth populations, high poverty and inequality, limited infrastructure and public services, high illiteracy, gender disparities, vulnerability to disasters, and dependence on primary production (Todaro & Smith, 2020). Implications for education: large numbers of out-of-school children and illiterate adults; limited public funds; competing demands of work and survival; and the need for relevant, flexible, low-cost education.

u: Unit 3: NFE and CE in Developing Countries
t: 3.2 Learning needs, demands and opportunities in Bangladesh
x: Needs: basic literacy and numeracy (adult literacy around three-quarters of adults aged 15+ in recent BBS estimates, leaving tens of millions non-literate); second-chance education for millions of out-of-school children; skills for a large youth population; digital literacy; life skills (health, nutrition, rights, disaster preparedness); and financial literacy. Demands: rising aspirations for certificates and jobs; migrant workers' skill needs; women's demand for income-generating skills. Opportunities: BNFE programmes; NGO schools; community learning centres; TVET short courses; open and distance learning (Bangladesh Open University); online platforms (Muktopaath); mobile phone penetration; and the NFE Act 2014 equivalency framework.

u: Unit 3: NFE and CE in Developing Countries
t: 3.3 Linkage and equivalency of NFE and CE with formal education
x: Equivalency means recognising non-formal learning outcomes as equal to defined levels of formal education, enabling learners to move between systems. The NFE Act 2014 provides for equivalency between NFE and formal education levels and for a legal basis for BNFE. Pathways: graduates of NFE primary programmes can enter formal secondary schools (e.g. BRAC NFPE graduates entering Class VI); Bangladesh Open University's SSC and HSC programmes; TVET certificates under BNQF/NSQF; and RPL. Challenges: quality assurance, social perception of NFE as "second-class", weak coordination between MoPME, MoE and NSDA. Figure 4. Building pathways between non-formal and formal education

u: Unit 3: NFE and CE in Developing Countries
t: 3.4 Role of NFE and CE in national development
x: Dimension Contributions Social Literacy, health and hygiene awareness, reduced child marriage, women's empowerment, community participation Economic Livelihood skills, productivity, income generation, entrepreneurship, migrant workers' skills, microfinance linked with education Cultural Preservation of local culture and languages, folk media, community libraries, cultural identity Ethical and moral Values education, civic responsibility, tolerance, social harmony Political Rights awareness, informed voting, local governance participation Environmental Disaster preparedness, climate adaptation, environmental conservation

u: Unit 4: Non-formal and Lifelong Education (NFLE) Programmes in Bangladesh
x: Figure 5. Milestones of non-formal and lifelong education in Bangladesh 1970s: after independence, mass literacy campaigns; NGOs such as BRAC, Dhaka Ahsania Mission and FIVDB began adult literacy and functional education programmes. 1980: Mass Education Programme (MEP). 1985: BRAC launched the Non-Formal Primary Education (NFPE) programme, one-room schools for out-of-school children, mostly girls, with a female teacher from the community; it became a globally recognised model. 1991–1997: Integrated Non-Formal Education Programme (INFEP) . 1995: Directorate of Non-Formal Education (DNFE) created; the Total Literacy Movement (TLM) district-based campaigns. 2001 onward: Post-Literacy and Continuing Education (PLCE) projects for neo-literates. 2003: DNFE dissolved; 2005: Bureau of Non-Formal Education (BNFE) established. 2004–2017: Reaching Out-of-School Children (ROSC) Ananda schools. 2006: Non-Formal Education Policy . 2014: Non-Formal Education Act . 2014 onward: Basic Literacy Project (64 districts) ; 2019 onward: Out-of-School Children Education Programme (second-chance primary for 8–14-year-olds). Lifelong learning increasingly integrated into national policy (NEP 2010, 8th Five-Year Plan, BNQF 2021).

u: Unit 4: Non-formal and Lifelong Education (NFLE) Programmes in Bangladesh
x: Community learning centres (CLCs) and ganokendras (people's centres; Dhaka Ahsania Mission); NGO schools; BNFE literacy centres; TVET short courses (BMET technical training centres, Youth Development Department); Bangladesh Open University; agricultural extension (DAE) farmer field schools; health and nutrition education through community clinics; public and community libraries; media-based learning (radio, TV, mobile apps); and digital centres (Union Digital Centres).

u: Unit 4: Non-formal and Lifelong Education (NFLE) Programmes in Bangladesh
t: 4.3 Major government and non-government NFLE programmes
x: Provider Programmes BNFE (MoPME) Basic Literacy Project (64 districts); Out-of-School Children Education Programme; Second Chance Education; Lifelong learning centres DPE (MoPME) ROSC (Ananda schools), pre-primary for disadvantaged children Other ministries Youth Development Department training; Women and Children Affairs skills training; Social Welfare programmes; DAE farmer field schools BRAC Non-formal primary schools, adolescent development programme (clubs), BRAC pre-primary schools, skills development Dhaka Ahsania Mission Ganokendras (community learning centres), literacy, skills FIVDB Functional literacy, community learning centres CAMPE Network, advocacy and Education Watch research UCEP Technical and general education for working children Save the Children, Plan, UNICEF, UNESCO Early learning, literacy, life skills, EiE, CLC support

u: Unit 4: Non-formal and Lifelong Education (NFLE) Programmes in Bangladesh
x: Bangladesh's NFE has been built on extensive GO–NGO collaboration : the government provides policy, funding and coordination, while NGOs implement programmes at scale. Forms: contracting NGOs for programme delivery (e.g. Basic Literacy Project, OoSC programme); joint policy dialogue (CAMPE); and public–private partnerships (PPP) with businesses for skills training and digital learning. Challenges: sustainability after project funding ends, uneven quality, weak monitoring and accountability, delayed funding, and coordination among many actors.

u: Unit 4: Non-formal and Lifelong Education (NFLE) Programmes in Bangladesh
x: NFLE has shifted from literacy campaigns to lifelong learning : from basic literacy to functional, digital and financial literacy; from "remedial" second chance to recognised pathways (equivalency, RPL); from project-based to system-based provision (NFE Act 2014, BNQF); from adults only to all ages; and from face-to-face to blended and technology-enabled learning.

u: Unit 4: Non-formal and Lifelong Education (NFLE) Programmes in Bangladesh
t: 4.6 Changing modality of SCE: media and technology
x: Radio and television programmes (e.g. Amar Ghore Amar School , Ghore Boshe Shikhi ); mobile-phone based learning (SMS, IVR, apps); online platforms (Muktopaath, Kishore Batayon); open educational resources; community radio; video-based lessons in learning centres; tablets in Rohingya learning centres; and blended models. Challenges: the digital divide by income, gender and location; electricity and connectivity; digital skills of facilitators; and learner motivation without face-to-face support.

t: 5.1 Role of MoPME, BNFE, DPE and other organisations
x: Organisation Role MoPME Policy, legislation (NFE Act 2014), budget, coordination BNFE Planning and implementation of NFE programmes; registration of NFE providers; curriculum and materials; monitoring; equivalency DPE Pre-primary and primary, ROSC; coordination with NFE for transition of learners NCTB Curriculum and equivalency standards NSDA, BTEB Skills qualifications, RPL Local government Community mobilisation, facilities, monitoring Development partners (UNESCO, UNICEF, World Bank, ADB) Funding, technical assistance

t: 5.2 Major actors of NFLE in Bangladesh
x: Government (MoPME, BNFE, other ministries), INGOs (UNICEF, UNESCO, Save the Children, Plan, World Vision), national NGOs (BRAC, DAM, FIVDB, UCEP, Gonoshahajjo Sangstha), community-based organisations, the private sector, media, and learners and communities themselves.

t: 5.3 Programme implementation process: planning, management and leadership
x: Figure 6. The NFE programme implementation cycle Planning: participatory needs assessment (surveys, Participatory Rural Appraisal); setting objectives; designing curriculum and materials; deciding location, timing and duration; budgeting; partner selection. Management: recruitment and training of facilitators (often local, with short training); supervision; materials supply; MIS and record-keeping; financial management; monitoring of attendance and learning. Leadership: community leadership and ownership (learning centre management committees); transformational leadership by programme managers; and coordination across agencies. Common challenges: high facilitator turnover and low honoraria; irregular attendance of learners due to work; inadequate monitoring; short programme duration; relapse into illiteracy without post-literacy follow-up.

t: 5.4 Practising pedagogy, andragogy and heutagogy in NFLE
x: Figure 7. Matching approach to learners in NFLE Pedagogy suits out-of-school children in SCE: structured, activity-based, joyful learning, an accelerated curriculum and close teacher guidance. Andragogy (Knowles) suits adult literacy and livelihood programmes: learners' experience as a resource, problem-centred content (e.g. reading a fertiliser label, calculating loan interest), mutual respect, participation in planning and immediate application. Freire's dialogic, problem-posing method and the REFLECT approach (Regenerated Freirean Literacy through Empowering Community Techniques, ActionAid, 1990s), which was piloted in Bangladesh, combine literacy with community analysis. Heutagogy (Hase & Kenyon) suits motivated youth and professionals in continuing education: self-determined goals, online resources, reflection and capability building.

u: Unit 6: Future Education, Quality of Life and Lifelong Learning
t: 6.1 Concept, meaning, development and components of quality of life
x: Definition Quality of life : "An individual's perception of their position in life in the context of the culture and value systems in which they live and in relation to their goals, expectations, standards and concerns" (WHOQOL Group, 1995). Quality of life (QoL) developed from purely economic measures (income) to multidimensional measures including health, education, environment, social relationships, security and subjective wellbeing (e.g. the Physical Quality of Life Index, the HDI, the OECD Better Life Index, the World Happiness Report). Components (WHOQOL domains): physical health; psychological wellbeing; level of independence; social relationships; environment (safety, housing, services); and spiritual/personal beliefs. Other frameworks add material living conditions, education, work, governance and leisure. Figure 8. Components of quality of life

u: Unit 6: Future Education, Quality of Life and Lifelong Learning
t: 6.2 Empowering disadvantaged people for quality of life
x: Ways and means: literacy and life skills; livelihood training and access to credit (microfinance linked to education, as in BRAC and Grameen); health and nutrition education; legal and rights awareness; social safety nets; community organisation (self-help groups, cooperatives); access to information and digital services; inclusive education for persons with disabilities; and participation in local governance.

u: Unit 6: Future Education, Quality of Life and Lifelong Learning
t: 6.3 Role of LLL and SCE in improving quality of life
x: Lifelong learning and second-chance education improve QoL by raising incomes and employability, improving health practices, strengthening self-confidence and agency, enabling civic participation, supporting family wellbeing (children of literate mothers are healthier and more likely to attend school), and enabling adaptation to change. UNESCO's Global Report on Adult Learning and Education (GRALE) documents wide-ranging benefits of adult learning for health, employment and civic life. International frameworks: CONFINTEA (International Conferences on Adult Education): the Belém Framework for Action (2009) and the Marrakech Framework for Action (CONFINTEA VII, 2022) , which calls for a "culture of lifelong learning"; UNESCO's Recommendation on Adult Learning and Education (2015); the UNESCO Global Network of Learning Cities ; and the 2021 UNESCO report Reimagining Our Futures Together: A New Social Contract for Education .

u: Unit 6: Future Education, Quality of Life and Lifelong Learning
x: Digital learning: MOOCs, micro-credentials, mobile learning, AI-based adaptive learning and tutoring, virtual and augmented reality. Flexible pathways: stackable credentials, RPL, digital badges. Learning cities and community learning hubs. Digital inclusion: closing the digital divide (gender, rural, disability); digital literacy as a core lifelong skill (UNESCO's Digital Literacy Global Framework). Risks: inequality, data privacy, misinformation, screen overuse, weakening of human relationships in learning.

u: Unit 6: Future Education, Quality of Life and Lifelong Learning
t: 6.5 NFE in emergency and refugee settings
x: NFE is often the only education available in emergencies and refugee settings because formal systems are absent or inaccessible. Characteristics: temporary learning spaces; flexible, accelerated curricula; psychosocial support; volunteer or refugee teachers; life skills and protection messages; and pathways towards certification. In Bangladesh's Rohingya camps, learning centres using the LCFA and later the Myanmar Curriculum Pilot illustrate the move from emergency NFE towards recognised education. Disaster-affected communities in Bangladesh have used boat schools, radio lessons and community learning centres to maintain learning. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Define NFE and distinguish it from formal and informal education." "Discuss the role of continuing education in building a knowledge-based society." "Trace the development of NFE in Bangladesh and evaluate GO–NGO collaboration." "Explain how andragogy and heutagogy can be applied in NFLE programmes."
