u: Unit 2: Inclusion from the Perspective of Social Justice
x: Definition Inclusive education (UNESCO, 2009) : "Inclusive education is a process of strengthening the capacity of the education system to reach out to all learners… An 'inclusive' education system can only be created if ordinary schools become more inclusive — in other words, if they become better at educating all children in their communities." Definition Inclusion (UNESCO, 2005) : "A process of addressing and responding to the diversity of needs of all learners through increasing participation in learning, cultures and communities, and reducing exclusion within and from education." Ainscow (2005) identifies four elements of inclusion: (1) it is a process , a never-ending search for better ways of responding to diversity; (2) it is concerned with the identification and removal of barriers ; (3) it is about the presence, participation and achievement of all students; and (4) it places particular emphasis on learner groups at risk of marginalisation, exclusion or underachievement . Figure 5. Exclusion, segregation, integration and inclusion (UN CRPD General Comment No. 4, 2016) Booth and Ainscow's Index for Inclusion (2002) The Index guides school self-review in three dimensions: creating inclusive cultures (building community, establishing inclusive values), producing inclusive policies (developing a school for all, organising support for diversity) and evolving inclusive practices (orchestrating learning, mobilising resources).

u: Unit 2: Inclusion from the Perspective of Social Justice
t: 2.2 Social justice framework for equity, equality and inclusion
x: Social justice in education means that every learner has a fair chance to access, participate in and benefit from quality education. Theorist Idea Relevance to inclusion John Rawls ( A Theory of Justice , 1971) Justice as fairness; the difference principle : inequalities are acceptable only if they benefit the least advantaged; the "veil of ignorance" Allocate more resources to disadvantaged learners, including CWDs Amartya Sen ( The Idea of Justice , 2009; capability approach) Justice is about expanding people's capabilities , their real freedoms to be and do what they value Education should develop each learner's capabilities; disability limits conversion of resources into capabilities, so more support is needed Martha Nussbaum (2006) List of central human capabilities; extends justice to people with disabilities Dignity and full participation Nancy Fraser (1997, 2008) Three dimensions of justice: redistribution (economic), recognition (cultural respect), representation (political voice) Inclusion needs resources, respect for identity, and the voice of disabled people ("Nothing about us without us") Paulo Freire (1970) Critical pedagogy; education for liberation of the oppressed Challenge structures that marginalise learners Figure 6. Fraser's three dimensions of social justice applied to inclusive education

u: Unit 2: Inclusion from the Perspective of Social Justice
x: Figure 7. Key international milestones towards inclusive education Salamanca Statement and Framework for Action (1994) Adopted at the World Conference on Special Needs Education: Access and Quality , Salamanca, Spain (7–10 June 1994), by representatives of 92 governments and 25 international organisations, organised by UNESCO and the Government of Spain. Every child has a fundamental right to education and unique characteristics, interests, abilities and learning needs. Education systems should be designed to take into account the wide diversity of these characteristics and needs. Those with special educational needs must have access to regular schools, which should accommodate them within a child-centred pedagogy. "Regular schools with this inclusive orientation are the most effective means of combating discriminatory attitudes, creating welcoming communities, building an inclusive society and achieving education for all; moreover, they provide an effective education to the majority of children and improve the efficiency and ultimately the cost-effectiveness of the entire education system." — Salamanca Statement, para. 2 (UNESCO, 1994) UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD, 2006) Adopted by the UN General Assembly on 13 December 2006; entered into force in 2008. Bangladesh ratified it in 2007 , among the early ratifying states. Its principles (Article 3) include respect for inherent dignity, non-discrimination, full participation, respect for difference, equality of opportunity, accessibility, gender equality and respect for the evolving capacities of children. Article 24 (Education): States Parties shall ensure an inclusive education system at all levels and lifelong learning; persons with disabilities are not excluded from the general education system on the basis of disability; children can access inclusive, quality, free primary and secondary education in their communities; reasonable accommodation of individual requirements is provided; effective individualised support measures are provided; learning of Braille, sign language and alternative communication is facilitated; teachers, including teachers with disabilities, are trained. General Comment No. 4 (2016) clarified that inclusion requires systemic reform and that placing students in mainstream classes without structural changes is integration, not inclusion. SDG 4 (2015) "Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all." Target 4.5 calls for eliminating gender disparities and ensuring equal access at all levels for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations. Target 4.a calls for disability- and gender-sensitive, safe, inclusive learning environments.

u: Unit 2: Inclusion from the Perspective of Social Justice

Law or policy Key provisions for inclusive education National Education Policy 2010 Commits to education for all children irrespective of disability, gender, ethnicity and socio-economic status; calls for identifying CWDs, admission to mainstream schools where possible, special care and facilities, accessible infrastructure (ramps, toilets), teacher training in special needs, and special schools for those who need them; mother-tongue education for ethnic minorities Salamanca Statement 1994 Bangladesh is a signatory; it shaped the shift from special to inclusive education, reflected in PEDP II onwards UN CRPD 2006 Ratified in 2007; national laws were revised to align with it, leading to the 2013 Act Rights and Protection of Persons with Disabilities Act 2013 Replaced the Disability Welfare Act 2001; adopts a rights-based approach; recognises 12 types of disability : autism spectrum disorder, physical, mental illness leading to disability, visual, speech, intellectual, hearing, deaf-blindness, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, multiple disability and other disabilities; rights to education in mainstream institutions, accessibility, employment, health and participation; no educational institution may refuse admission on the grounds of disability ; provision for extra time and support in examinations; identification and registration of persons with disabilities Neuro-Developmental Disability Protection Trust Act 2013 Establishes a trust to protect and support persons with neuro-developmental disabilities (NDD) : autism, Down syndrome, intellectual disability and cerebral palsy; supports education, care, rehabilitation and guardianship Gender policy framework (2013 as listed in the syllabus) Within the National Women Development Policy 2011 and related gender strategies: equal access of girls and women, including women and girls with disabilities, to education; gender-responsive and safe schools; elimination of discrimination. t: 3.2 Educational approaches for children with SEN
x: Figure 8. Historical shift in approaches to educating children with disabilities (a) Special education Education in separate special schools or institutions designed for one type of disability (e.g., schools for the blind, schools for the deaf, schools for children with intellectual disabilities). In Bangladesh, the Department of Social Services operates government schools for visually and hearing-impaired children and special schools for intellectual disabilities, and many NGOs run special schools. Advantages: specialist teachers, specialised equipment and methods, small classes. Limitations: segregation, stigma, limited access (few schools, mainly urban, residential), limited curriculum, poor preparation for life in the community. (b) Integrated education Children with disabilities attend regular schools , often with a resource teacher or resource room , but are expected to adapt to the existing system. The Integrated Education Programme for visually impaired children in Bangladesh, which places them in regular secondary schools with resource teachers and hostels, is a well-known example. Advantages: social contact with peers; less costly than special schools. Limitations: the school does not change; children may be physically present but not participating ("locational" integration). (c) Inclusive education The school changes its culture, policies and practices to welcome and respond to all learners in age-appropriate regular classes in their neighbourhood schools, with necessary support. Form Meaning Full inclusion The child attends the regular class for the whole school day with support provided in the class Partial inclusion The child spends part of the day in the regular class and part in a resource room or special class for specialised instruction Reverse inclusion Children without disabilities join a class or programme designed for children with disabilities (e.g., in a special school), for shared learning and friendship Social inclusion Children with disabilities participate with peers in non-academic activities: assembly, play, lunch, sports, cultural programmes, clubs Vocational inclusion Youth with disabilities take part in mainstream technical and vocational education and training and workplaces with accommodations, leading to employment Figure 9. Special, integrated and inclusive education compared (d) Home-based education Education delivered at home for children with severe or multiple disabilities, chronic illness or those living where no accessible school exists. Itinerant teachers, community-based rehabilitation (CBR) workers or trained parents provide learning, therapy and daily living skills, with the goal of transition to school where possible. Limitations include isolation from peers and dependence on family capacity.

Evelyn Deno (1970) proposed a cascade of services : a range of placements from the most inclusive (most common) to the most restrictive (least common). The principle is that children should be placed in the least restrictive environment and moved towards more inclusive settings as soon as possible. Figure 10. The continuum of placement (after Deno, 1970): from the most restrictive to the most inclusive Key Point Under the CRPD, the goal is a fully inclusive system. The continuum is now seen as a set of supports that can be brought to the child in regular schools, rather than a set of places to which children are sent. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Who are children with special educational needs? Describe the characteristics of any three types." "Compare special, integrated and inclusive education." "Explain full, partial, reverse, social and vocational inclusion." "What is the continuum of placement?"

t: 4.1 Factors and challenges of inclusive classrooms
x: Figure 11. Factors influencing inclusion in the classroom Common challenges in Bangladesh: large classes (often 60 or more students), negative attitudes and low expectations, inadequate pre-service and in-service training, inaccessible buildings and toilets, lack of assistive devices and accessible materials, a rigid, exam-oriented curriculum, limited specialist support, and weak coordination between the education and social welfare ministries.

Inclusive pedagogy is an approach in which teachers extend what is ordinarily available to everyone, rather than providing different activities for "most" and "some" learners (Florian & Black-Hawkins, 2011). It rejects fixed-ability thinking and believes every child can learn. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Developed by CAST (Rose & Meyer, 2002), UDL applies the architectural idea of universal design to curriculum: design from the start for the widest range of learners. Figure 12. The three principles of Universal Design for Learning (CAST) Differentiated instruction Tomlinson (2001) describes differentiation of content (what learners learn), process (how they learn), product (how they show learning) and learning environment , according to learners' readiness, interests and learning profiles . Other effective strategies Cooperative learning and peer tutoring (e.g., think-pair-share, jigsaw, buddy system). Multi-level teaching: one lesson with tasks at different levels. Task analysis: breaking skills into small steps. Multisensory teaching: seeing, hearing, touching and doing. Scaffolding (Vygotsky's zone of proximal development). Reasonable accommodations in assessment: extra time, a scribe or reader, Braille or large-print papers, oral tests, separate room.

Physical: accessible seating, clear pathways, good lighting and acoustics, materials within reach, displays at eye level. Social and emotional: warm relationships, a sense of belonging, anti-bullying rules, celebrating differences, buddy systems. Instructional: clear routines and visual schedules, varied materials, high expectations, positive feedback.

t: 4.4 Assistive devices for children with SEN
x: Assistive technology (AT) is any item, equipment or system used to increase, maintain or improve the functional capabilities of persons with disabilities. t: 4.5 Effective classroom management for inclusive education
x: Strategy Practice Clear expectations and routines Few, positively stated rules; visual reminders; consistent routines Positive behaviour support Praise specific behaviour; token systems; focus on prevention rather than punishment Seating arrangements Flexible groups; children with visual or hearing needs near the teacher; avoid isolating any child Proximity and movement Circulate around the room; non-verbal cues Structured transitions Advance warnings and timers, particularly for children with autism Functional behaviour assessment Understand the ABC (antecedent–behaviour–consequence) of challenging behaviour and its purpose Large-class strategies Group work with roles, peer tutors, class monitors, choral responses, simple materials Time management Short varied activities; brain breaks Positive teacher–student relationships Know each learner's name, strengths and needs; be fair and consistent

Burnout is a psychological syndrome arising from prolonged work stress. Maslach and Jackson (1981) identify three dimensions: Emotional exhaustion: feeling drained and overextended. Depersonalisation (cynicism): detached, negative attitudes towards students. Reduced personal accomplishment: feelings of incompetence and lack of achievement. Causes in inclusive classrooms: large classes, lack of support and training, heavy workload and paperwork, behaviour challenges, low self-efficacy, isolation, and lack of recognition. Figure 13. Strategies for preventing and addressing teacher burnout

t: 4.7 Classroom communication strategies for educating CWDs
x: General: speak clearly and at a moderate pace; use simple language; check understanding; give instructions in more than one form (oral, written, visual, demonstration); allow extra response time; use the child's name; respect preferred communication methods. With deaf and hard-of-hearing learners: face the class; do not speak while writing on the board; good lighting on your face; use Bangla Sign Language (Bangla Sign Language Day is observed on 7 February), gestures, finger spelling, written words and pictures; repeat other students' answers; caption videos. With learners with visual impairment: say your name when approaching; describe visuals aloud; read board writing aloud; use tactile materials; orient the child to the classroom; avoid "this" and "there" without description. With learners with intellectual disabilities: short, concrete sentences; one instruction at a time; demonstrations; repetition; visual cues. With learners with autism: literal, clear language; visual supports; warn about changes; reduce sensory overload; give processing time. Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC): picture boards, PECS (Bondy & Frost), symbols and speech-generating devices for learners with limited speech. Respectful language: "a student with a hearing impairment", not "the deaf-mute boy"; avoid pity and labels. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Discuss the challenges of inclusive classrooms in Bangladesh." "What is Universal Design for Learning?" "Describe assistive devices for learners with visual and hearing impairments." "Explain the causes of teacher burnout and suggest remedies." "What communication strategies would you use with deaf learners in a regular classroom?"

u: Unit 5: Transforming Schools for Inclusive Education
t: 5.2 Accessibility for diverse learners: getting school buildings right
x: Accessibility follows the principles of universal design : equitable use, flexibility, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and appropriate size and space (Center for Universal Design, 1997). Figure 15. The accessibility chain: every link from home to classroom must be accessible Ramps with a gentle slope (about 1:12) and handrails; level entrances. Doors at least 900 mm wide; lever handles. Accessible toilets with grab bars and space for wheelchair turning; separate toilets for girls with menstrual hygiene facilities. Classrooms on the ground floor when lifts are absent; adequate lighting; good acoustics; tactile flooring and colour contrast for visually impaired learners. Signage in large print, Braille and pictures; safe water points at accessible height. Information accessibility: accessible textbooks, websites and notices.

u: Unit 5: Transforming Schools for Inclusive Education
x: Inclusion can be monitored through four indicators, often called the 4 As , widely used in Bangladeshi inclusive education training materials: Figure 16. The four indicators of inclusion Indicator Guiding question Example evidence Access Are all children in the catchment area enrolled and able to reach and enter the school and its information? Enrolment of CWDs; ramps; accessible textbooks; no admission refusal Acceptance Are all learners welcomed and valued by teachers, peers and community? Attitude surveys; friendships; no bullying; respectful language Active participation Do all learners take part fully in learning and school life? Continuous assessment records; IEP goal attainment; completion and transition rates Study tip Remember the sequence: a child must first get in (access), be welcomed (acceptance), take part (participation) and learn (achievement). Presence alone is not inclusion.

Community-based rehabilitation (CBR): community workers identify children with disabilities, link them to services and support enrolment. School Management Committees (SMCs) and local government (Union Parishad) can mobilise resources for ramps, toilets and transport. u: Unit 5: Transforming Schools for Inclusive Education
x: Emergencies (floods, cyclones, river erosion, conflict, pandemics, displacement) hit children with disabilities, girls and the poorest hardest: they are more likely to be left behind in evacuation, lose assistive devices, be excluded from temporary learning spaces and drop out permanently. The INEE Minimum Standards for Education: Preparedness, Response, Recovery (Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies) require that education in emergencies is accessible, safe, protective and inclusive. Figure 17. Disability-inclusive education in emergencies Practical strategies: Include children with disabilities in school disaster management plans and drills (see PC 123). Ensure cyclone shelters used as schools have ramps and accessible toilets. Provide information in accessible formats (sign language, pictures, audio). Train teachers in psychosocial support and inclusive teaching in temporary settings. During school closures (as in COVID-19), provide accessible remote learning and check on CWDs. In the Rohingya humanitarian response in Cox's Bazar, learning centres have sought to include children with disabilities through identification, referral and teacher training. Exam Focus Likely questions: "What is ILFE? Describe its characteristics and the strategies for creating it." "Explain the four indicators of inclusion with examples." "How can parents and the community help to transform schools for inclusion?" "Discuss government and non-government initiatives for inclusive education in Bangladesh." "How can inclusion be ensured in emergencies?"

u: Unit 1: Conceptualizing Educational Change in Global Perspective
x: Global change refers to the large-scale, interconnected transformations in economy, technology, politics, culture and environment that cut across national boundaries and alter the conditions under which people live, work and learn. In education the term covers both external drivers (globalisation, migration, digital technology, climate change, demographic transition) and internal responses of education systems (reforms in curriculum, assessment, governance and teacher education). Definition Globalisation (Giddens, 1990): "The intensification of worldwide social relations which link distant localities in such a way that local happenings are shaped by events occurring many miles away and vice versa." Definition Globalisation and education (Carnoy, 1999): Globalisation is an economy whose strategic core activities, including innovation, finance and corporate management, work as a unit on a world scale in near real time. Its effects on education come through three channels: finance-driven reforms, competitiveness-driven reforms and equity-driven reforms. Carnoy's (1999) typology remains one of the clearest lenses for analysing reform in developing countries such as Bangladesh: Type of reform Driving logic Typical measures Bangladesh illustration Competitiveness-driven Raise productivity of labour for a global economy Decentralisation, standards, better management, improved teacher recruitment, curriculum for skills Competency-based curriculum, TVET expansion, skills development projects Finance-driven Reduce public spending and shift costs Cost-recovery, shifting spending from higher to basic education, privatisation, larger class sizes Growth of private universities after the Private University Act 1992; fee-based private schools and coaching Equity-driven Increase equality of opportunity Targeted programmes for low-income, rural, girls, disabled learners Female Secondary School Stipend, primary stipend, school feeding, inclusive education Table 1. Carnoy's three types of globalisation-driven education reform

u: Unit 1: Conceptualizing Educational Change in Global Perspective
x: The syllabus asks for a chronological reading of how education became "global". The following periods are analytic, not watertight. Period Core features Implications for education Pre-modern (before c. 1500) Religious and scholarly networks: Nalanda and Vikramashila, Al-Azhar, Bologna, Paris; travelling scholars; manuscripts Education elite, religious, oral and text-based; knowledge travelled along trade and pilgrimage routes (e.g., Xuanzang's visit to Nalanda) Modernism (c. 1500 to 1945) Enlightenment, print, nation-states, industrialisation Mass compulsory schooling (Prussia, 1763 onwards; England 1870, 1880), state curricula, normal schools for teachers; schooling as nation-building Colonialism (16th to mid-20th century) European empires export institutions Macaulay's Minute (1835), Wood's Despatch (1854), University of Calcutta (1857), University of Dhaka (1921); English-medium elite, vernacular masses; dual systems persist Post-colonial and development era (1945 to 1980s) UN system, human capital theory, aid Universal Declaration (1948), UNESCO (1945), World Bank lending to education from 1962; manpower planning; expansion of primary schooling Postmodernism (late 20th century) Questioning grand narratives, identity, plural knowledges Multicultural and critical pedagogies, recognition of indigenous knowledge, learner-centred and constructivist approaches Globalisation (1990s onwards) ICT, liberalised trade, neoliberal governance, international testing EFA (1990), GATS and trade in education services (1995), PISA (2000), MDGs (2000), SDGs (2015); global benchmarking and policy borrowing Table 2. Periods in the development of global education Figure 1. Chronology of global education from pre-modern to globalised eras Bangladesh Context The Indian subcontinent illustrates every stage. The ancient Buddhist viharas of Paharpur (Somapura Mahavihara) and Mainamati in present-day Bangladesh belonged to a pre-modern international learning network. Colonial rule produced the English-medium, examination-oriented system whose legacy is still visible in public examinations, the Bangla-English-Madrasah triple stream and the prestige of English. Post-1971 Bangladesh entered the development era through the Qudrat-e-Khuda Commission and heavy donor involvement, and since 1990 it has been strongly shaped by EFA, the MDGs and the SDGs.

u: Unit 1: Conceptualizing Educational Change in Global Perspective
t: 1.3 Relationship between global change and education
x: The relationship is two-way. Global change shapes education (demands for new skills, new technologies, migration, climate risk) and education shapes global change (human capital, innovation, citizenship, sustainability). Figure 2. Channels through which global change reaches education Four theoretical lenses help explain this relationship at Master's level: Theory Key thinkers Core claim Critique Human capital theory Schultz (1961); Becker (1964) Education is an investment that raises productivity and earnings; justifies public spending Reduces education to economic value; ignores signalling and credentialism World culture / world polity theory Meyer, Ramirez, Boli Education systems converge because nation-states adopt global scripts of modern schooling Explains isomorphism but neglects local agency and power World-systems and dependency theory Wallerstein; Carnoy (1974); Altbach Core countries dominate the periphery through knowledge, language and aid; education reproduces dependency Can be deterministic; underplays real gains in the South Culturalist / critical theory Anderson-Levitt; Steiner-Khamsi; Appadurai Global ideas are locally re-interpreted; "vernacular globalisation" Harder to generalise; needs ethnographic evidence Table 3. Theories of education and global change Key Point Global convergence at the level of policy talk (everyone speaks of competencies, quality and accountability) often coexists with divergence at the level of classroom practice . This distinction between "talk", "action" and "practice" is central to comparative education (Steiner-Khamsi, 2004).

u: Unit 1: Conceptualizing Educational Change in Global Perspective
x: Neoliberalism is a political-economic philosophy that favours free markets, privatisation, deregulation, competition and a smaller state. In education it appears as school choice, vouchers, performance-based pay, standardised testing, league tables, public-private partnerships and the treatment of education as a tradable service. Definition Neoliberalism (Harvey, 2005): "A theory of political economic practices that proposes that human well-being can best be advanced by liberating individual entrepreneurial freedoms and skills within an institutional framework characterized by strong private property rights, free markets, and free trade." Sahlberg (2011, 2021) named the resulting global reform package the Global Educational Reform Movement (GERM) : standardisation of teaching and learning, focus on core subjects (literacy, numeracy), test-based accountability, market-style school choice and corporate management models. He contrasts GERM with Finland's emphasis on trust, collaboration, equity and teacher professionalism. GERM Alternative (e.g., Finland) Standardising teaching and learning Customising teaching and learning Focus on literacy and numeracy Focus on broad, creative learning Test-based accountability Trust-based responsibility Competition and school choice Collaboration and equity Corporate management models Professional leadership by educators Table 4. GERM compared with an alternative reform model (after Sahlberg, 2021) Network governance and global education Ball (2012) and Ball and Junemann (2012) describe a shift from government (hierarchical, state-run) to network governance , where policy is made through webs of state agencies, international organisations, philanthropic foundations, consultancies, edu-businesses and NGOs. Policy knowledge travels through conferences, reports, consultants and "best practice" toolkits. Figure 3. Actors in global network governance of education Bangladesh Context Bangladesh's education sector is a clear example of network governance. Sector-wide programmes such as PEDP (primary) and SESIP or SEDP (secondary) are co-financed and co-monitored by government and development partners (World Bank, ADB, EU, JICA, UNICEF and others) through joint annual reviews. BRAC, the largest NGO provider of non-formal primary education, and CAMPE as a civil society coalition are also influential policy actors. International education International education has several meanings: (a) education about other countries and global issues (international understanding, peace education); (b) cross-border movement of students, teachers, programmes and institutions; (c) international schools and curricula (IB, Cambridge, Edexcel); and (d) development cooperation in education. UNESCO's 1974 Recommendation concerning Education for International Understanding, Co-operation and Peace is an early normative text for the first meaning. Critical Perspective Critics argue that globalisation in education produces homogenisation (one model fits all), commodification (education as a product), brain drain from the South, and epistemic injustice (Southern knowledge marginalised). Defenders point to rapid expansion of access, cross-border research collaboration and the spread of rights-based norms. A balanced Master's answer acknowledges both and stresses that outcomes depend on how national actors mediate global pressures. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Explain Carnoy's typology of globalisation-driven reforms with examples from Bangladesh." "What is GERM? Critically compare it with the Finnish model." "Discuss the relationship between global change and education using at least two theoretical perspectives." "What is network governance in education?"

Key international instruments on education Verify Before Use The syllabus lists "UN-UHRC". This is usually read as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR, 1948), although the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC, established 2006) also reviews states' education rights through its Universal Periodic Review. Confirm with your department which is meant and prepare both. The four pillars of learning (Delors, 1996) Figure 5. Delors Commission: four pillars of learning The Commission, chaired by Jacques Delors, also identified seven tensions to be overcome: global and local, universal and individual, tradition and modernity, long-term and short-term considerations, competition and equality of opportunity, expansion of knowledge and our capacity to assimilate it, and the spiritual and the material. SDG 4 and its targets Target Focus 4.1 Free, equitable, quality primary and secondary education leading to relevant and effective learning outcomes 4.2 Access to quality early childhood development, care and pre-primary education 4.3 Equal access to affordable quality TVET and tertiary education, including university 4.4 Increase youth and adults with relevant skills, including ICT, for employment, decent jobs and entrepreneurship 4.5 Eliminate gender disparities and ensure equal access for the vulnerable, including persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and children in vulnerable situations 4.6 All youth and a substantial proportion of adults achieve literacy and numeracy 4.7 Knowledge and skills for sustainable development, human rights, gender equality, culture of peace, global citizenship, cultural diversity 4.a Build and upgrade education facilities that are child, disability and gender sensitive; safe, non-violent, inclusive learning environments 4.b Expand scholarships for developing countries for higher education 4.c Increase the supply of qualified teachers, including through international cooperation Table 6. SDG 4 targets (Education 2030) Key Point The Education 2030 Framework for Action set two financing benchmarks: public education expenditure of at least 4 to 6% of GDP and/or at least 15 to 20% of total public expenditure . Bangladesh has persistently spent around 2% of GDP or less on education, one of the lowest ratios in South Asia, which is a frequent exam point. Verify Before Use Check the current education share of GDP and of the national budget for the latest fiscal year (Ministry of Finance budget documents; UNESCO UIS). Figures vary depending on whether technology ministries' allocations are bundled with education.

x: The Constitution Article Provision Article 15 Basic necessities, including education, as a fundamental responsibility of the state Article 17 State to establish a uniform, mass-oriented and universal system of education; free and compulsory education for all children to a stage determined by law; relate education to the needs of society; remove illiteracy within a determined time Article 19 Equality of opportunity for all citizens Article 23 Preservation of national culture and language Article 28 No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, including access to educational institutions; special provision for women, children and backward sections allowed Article 41 Freedom of religion; no one attending an educational institution required to receive religious instruction of another religion Table 7. Education-related provisions of the Constitution of Bangladesh (1972) Note that Article 17 is in Part II (Fundamental Principles of State Policy), which is not judicially enforceable, while Article 28 is a fundamental right. This distinction is often examined. Education commissions and policies, 1972 to 2010 Commission / policy Year Key recommendations Bangladesh Education Commission (Qudrat-e-Khuda) 1972 to 1974 Free, compulsory primary to Grade 5 by 1980 and Grade 8 by 1983; Bangla as medium; secular, science-oriented, work-oriented education; universal eight-year primary Interim Education Policy / National Curriculum and Syllabus Committee 1976 to 1979 Curriculum reform; detailed syllabi for primary and secondary Mofizuddin Ahmed Education Commission 1987 to 1988 Eight-year primary; emphasis on vocational and religious education Shamsul Haque Education Policy Committee 1997 Draft policy (2000) with eight-year primary; largely adopted later MA Bari Commission 2002 Reforms in higher and secondary education Moniruzzaman Miah Commission 2003 Comprehensive report; never implemented Kabir Chowdhury Committee: National Education Policy (NEP) 2010 2009 to 2010 One-year pre-primary; primary extended to Grade 8; secondary Grades 9 to 12; common core curriculum across streams; creative questions; stipends; permanent education commission; Education Act; teacher training; ICT; inclusive and indigenous language education Table 8. Major education commissions and policies of Bangladesh Verify Before Use Dates and chairs of the intermediate commissions (1976 to 2003) are reported differently across sources. Cross-check with the Ministry of Education NEP 2010 document (its introduction lists previous commissions) and BANBEIS publications before quoting precise years. Laws, plans and other national commitments Compulsory Primary Education Act 1990 (CPEA): made primary education (age 6 to 10) compulsory; phased implementation from 1992 and nationwide from 1993. Draft Education Act: prepared from 2011 onwards to give legal backing to NEP 2010 (regulating coaching, notebooks, private tuition, teacher recruitment, compulsory education to Grade 8). Several drafts have been circulated; at the time of writing it had not been enacted. National Children Policy 2011: child rights, early childhood development, protection, education for disadvantaged children. National Women Development Policy 2011 and gender strategies in education. Persons with Disabilities Rights and Protection Act 2013: right to inclusive education, accessible institutions and reasonable accommodation. Neuro-Developmental Disability Protection Trust Act 2013 (NDD Act): protection, education and care of persons with autism, Down syndrome, cerebral palsy and intellectual disability. Five-Year Plans: the Seventh (2016 to 2020) and Eighth (2020/21 to 2025) Five-Year Plans align education targets with the SDGs (quality, TVET expansion, digital skills). Perspective Plan 2021 to 2041 (Vision 2041): aims for upper-middle income status by 2031 and high income by 2041; stresses quality, skills, STEM, TVET and a knowledge economy. Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 (adopted 2018): long-term water, climate and land plan; implications for disaster-resilient schools, climate education and education in emergencies. Verify Before Use The status of the Draft Education Act, the Five-Year Plan in force, and any post-2024 policy reviews or new education commission should be checked against current Ministry of Education and Planning Commission sources before the exam. u: Unit 2: Global Declarations and National Commitments
x: Policy borrowing is the conscious adoption in one context of policy observed in another (Phillips & Ochs, 2003). Policy lending is the active promotion of policies by donors. Policy travelling is a broader term for the movement of ideas across borders without implying conscious, rational transfer (Steiner-Khamsi, 2004). Figure 7. Phillips and Ochs (2003): four stages of policy borrowing Reason Explanation Problem-solving Genuine search for a solution that worked elsewhere Legitimation Reference to "international best practice" to justify a reform that is politically contested at home Externalisation Invoking foreign examples to break domestic deadlock (Schriewer) Donor conditionality Policies attached to loans or grants Symbolic modernity Signalling that the country is modern and globally aligned Table 9. Why governments borrow policy (Steiner-Khamsi, 2004) Bangladesh Context Examples for critical examination in Bangladesh include: (a) creative (structured) questions introduced in 2008 to 2010, inspired by Bloom-based structured questioning, which teachers struggled to implement and which fuelled guidebooks and coaching; (b) school-based assessment (SBA) piloted in 2007 and withdrawn; (c) the competency-based National Curriculum Framework 2021 with experiential learning and continuous assessment, rolled out in 2023 to 2024 and then reversed for secondary in 2025 amid public controversy; (d) Grade 5 PECE and Grade 8 JSC public exams introduced in 2009 and 2010 and later discontinued. Each case shows the importance of teacher readiness, public acceptance, assessment alignment and resources. Verify Before Use Confirm the current status of the 2021 curriculum framework and of public examinations at Grades 5 and 8 with the latest NCTB and Ministry announcements; this area has changed frequently since 2023. Critical Perspective Policy borrowing fails when (1) the context of origin is ignored (Finland's results rest on teacher selectivity, equity and social trust); (2) only the surface is borrowed (the form of a policy without its supporting conditions); (3) teachers are not engaged; and (4) "best practice" becomes a slogan. A good Master's answer proposes contextual adaptation : pilot, evaluate, build capacity, involve stakeholders and scale gradually. Exam Focus Expect: "Critically examine the influence of EFA and SDG 4 on education policy in Bangladesh." "Discuss constitutional provisions on education." "What is policy borrowing? Explain Phillips and Ochs's model with a Bangladesh example." "Write short notes: Salamanca Statement; Incheon Declaration; four pillars of learning."

u: Unit 3: Global and National Progress in Education
x: Definition Global Citizenship Education (UNESCO, 2015): GCED "aims to empower learners of all ages to assume active roles, both locally and globally, in building more peaceful, tolerant, inclusive and secure societies." It is grounded in human rights and is one of the two named elements of SDG target 4.7. UNESCO organises GCED learning around three core conceptual dimensions : Figure 9. UNESCO's three domains of learning in GCED Values and principles: human rights, respect for diversity, peace and non-violence, social justice, sustainability, solidarity and shared responsibility. Implementation strategies: whole-school approach; integration across subjects (social studies, languages, science); stand-alone courses; extra-curricular clubs and service learning; teacher education; participatory pedagogy (dialogue, project-based learning, simulations such as Model UN); partnerships with communities. Implementing GCED through ESD approaches Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) empowers learners with knowledge, skills, values and attitudes to take informed decisions for environmental integrity, economic viability and a just society. UNESCO led the UN Decade of ESD (2005 to 2014), the Global Action Programme (2015 to 2019) and now ESD for 2030 (2020 to 2030). ESD's five priority action areas are: advancing policy; transforming learning environments; building capacities of educators; empowering and mobilising youth; and accelerating local-level action. u: Unit 3: Global and National Progress in Education
x: Definition Internationalisation of higher education (Knight, 2004): "The process of integrating an international, intercultural or global dimension into the purpose, functions or delivery of post-secondary education." Knight distinguishes internationalisation at home (curriculum, intercultural learning, foreign faculty, virtual exchange) from internationalisation abroad or cross-border education (mobility of students, programmes, providers). De Wit et al. (2015) extended the definition to emphasise "intentional" internationalisation that enhances quality "for all students and staff" and makes "a meaningful contribution to society". Criteria often used: international students and staff ratios, joint degrees, international research collaboration and co-authorship, internationalised curricula, MoUs, language of instruction, mobility opportunities. Politics: internationalisation can become revenue-seeking (recruiting fee-paying foreign students), status-seeking (ranking-driven), or a tool of soft power (scholarships, branch campuses). It can widen inequality between globally connected elite universities and local institutions.

u: Unit 4: Paradigm Shift in Educational Practices
t: 4.1 The idea of a paradigm shift
x: Thomas Kuhn (1962) used paradigm to mean the shared assumptions, methods and exemplars of a scientific community; a paradigm shift occurs when anomalies accumulate and a new framework replaces the old. In education the term describes the move from a teaching paradigm (instruction, transmission, teacher-centred) to a learning paradigm (learning, construction, learner-centred) (Barr & Tagg, 1995). Dimension Instruction paradigm Learning paradigm Mission Provide instruction Produce learning Knowledge Transferred from teacher to student Constructed by learners Teacher's role Lecturer, expert Designer of learning environments, facilitator Assessment End-of-course, ranking Continuous, for learning Success criterion Inputs and coverage Learning outcomes and growth Learning environment Classroom, fixed time Any time, any place, flexible Table 14. From the instruction paradigm to the learning paradigm (adapted from Barr & Tagg, 1995)

u: Unit 4: Paradigm Shift in Educational Practices
x: Pedagogy (Greek paid , child; agogos , leading) traditionally means the art and science of teaching children. Andragogy , popularised by Malcolm Knowles (1970, 1980), is "the art and science of helping adults learn". Heutagogy (Hase & Kenyon, 2000) extends this to self-determined learning. Assumption Pedagogical model Andragogical model Self-concept Dependent Increasingly self-directed Experience Of little worth as a resource Rich resource for learning Readiness to learn Determined by age and curriculum Arises from life tasks and problems Orientation Subject-centred Problem- or life-centred Motivation External (grades, approval) Internal (self-esteem, quality of life) Need to know Learners learn what the teacher teaches Adults need to know why they should learn something Table 15. Knowles's assumptions of andragogy compared with pedagogy Figure 10. Continuum from pedagogy to heutagogy Inclusive pedagogy Florian and Black-Hawkins (2011) define inclusive pedagogy as an approach that extends what is ordinarily available to everyone rather than making "different" provision for "some". It rejects deterministic beliefs about fixed ability and treats difficulties in learning as professional challenges for teachers. Related approaches include Universal Design for Learning (UDL) (CAST) with its three principles: multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression. Blended pedagogy Blended learning integrates face-to-face and online learning in a planned, pedagogically valuable way (Garrison & Kanuka, 2004). Models include rotation (station, lab, flipped), flex, à la carte and enriched virtual (Staker & Horn, 2012). The COVID-19 school closures in Bangladesh (March 2020 to September 2021, among the longest globally) pushed TV-based (Sangsad TV "Amar Ghore Amar School"), radio, mobile and online instruction, revealing both possibilities and the digital divide.

t: 4.3 Shifts in teaching-learning, management and assessment
x: Area From To Teaching-learning Lecture, rote memorisation, whole-class Participatory, interactive, cooperative, inquiry and project-based learning Learner Passive recipient Active constructor, agent Personalisation Uniform pace Personalised learning : pace, path and support tailored using data and technology; differentiation Management Bureaucratic, input control Performance-based management (PBM) : goals, indicators, results; participatory monitoring and management (PMM) : SMCs, PTAs, community scorecards Assessment Summative, norm-referenced, exam-centred Formative, criterion-referenced, assessment for and as learning, portfolios, authentic tasks Supervision Inspection and fault-finding Mentoring, coaching, professional learning communities Teacher development One-off training Continuous professional development (CPD), lesson study, communities of practice Table 16. Major shifts in educational practice Verify Before Use The syllabus abbreviations "PBM" and "PMM" are not defined in the document. These notes interpret them as performance-based management and participatory monitoring and management; confirm the intended meaning with the course teacher. Monitoring to mentoring Traditional monitoring checks compliance against rules (attendance, syllabus coverage, records). Mentoring is a developmental relationship in which a more experienced professional supports a less experienced one's growth through observation, feedback, reflection and modelling. The shift reflects research showing that teacher learning improves when feedback is formative, sustained and trust-based. In Bangladesh, academic supervisors (AUEOs/Upazila Academic Supervisors) and cluster-based subject trainings are being reoriented from inspection towards mentoring, and initiatives such as teacher mentoring under PEDP4 and the Teach for Bangladesh fellowship illustrate this.

Figure 11. Bangladesh's Bangladesh National Qualifications Framework (BNQF) , approved around 2021, has ten levels covering general, TVET and higher education, building on the earlier NTVQF for skills. u: Unit 4: Paradigm Shift in Educational Practices
x: Definition Education in emergencies (INEE): "Quality learning opportunities for all ages in situations of crisis, including early childhood development, primary, secondary, non-formal, technical, vocational, higher and adult education." It provides physical, psychosocial and cognitive protection that can be both life-sustaining and life-saving. Types of emergency relevant to Bangladesh: Pandemic: COVID-19 closed schools for about 18 months; learning loss, dropout, child marriage and child labour risks rose; remote learning reached fewer poor and rural learners. Climate change and disasters: cyclones (Sidr 2007, Aila 2009, Amphan 2020), floods (Sylhet 2022), riverbank erosion; schools used as shelters; the Comprehensive School Safety Framework (GADRRRES) offers three pillars: safe learning facilities, school disaster management, and risk reduction and resilience education. Forced displacement: over 900,000 Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar since the 2017 influx. Verify Before Use Update the Rohingya population figure and the number of learners in camp education from current UNHCR/UNICEF/Joint Response Plan data. INEE Minimum Standards The Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies (INEE, founded 2000) published Minimum Standards in 2004, revised in 2010 and again in 2024. They are a companion to the Sphere humanitarian standards. Figure 13. INEE Minimum Standards: domains (2010 edition structure) Refugee education in global perspective UNHCR's Refugee Education 2030: A Strategy for Refugee Inclusion (2019) shifted policy from parallel camp schooling to inclusion of refugees in national education systems . The Global Compact on Refugees (2018) commits states to support refugee education. Key principles: access, quality, continuity, certification, protection, and inclusion. Bangladesh Context For Rohingya children, Bangladesh did not permit Bangladeshi curriculum or formal certification. Education was first provided through the informal Learning Competency Framework and Approach (LCFA) in learning centres and, from 2021 to 2022, through the phased Myanmar Curriculum Pilot , to prepare children for eventual return. This illustrates the tension between the global inclusion norm and host-state policy. Critical Perspective EiE debates include: inclusion versus return-oriented parallel education; the "humanitarian-development nexus" (short-term relief versus long-term system strengthening); underfunding (education receives a small share of humanitarian appeals); and the protection of teachers and schools from attack (Safe Schools Declaration, 2015). Exam Focus Expect: "Explain the paradigm shift from teaching to learning." "Differentiate pedagogy and andragogy with reference to Knowles." "What is education in emergencies? Discuss INEE Minimum Standards with reference to Rohingya children." "Discuss the redefinition of quality indicators in education."

u: Unit 6: Successful Education Practices in Selected Countries
x: Comparative education studies education systems across countries to understand, explain and improve them. Its classic phases are: travellers' tales; borrowing (Jullien, 1817, "father of comparative education"); factors and forces (Sadler, Kandel, Hans); social science methods (Noah & Eckstein, Bereday); and contemporary critical, globalisation and ILSA-based approaches. Definition Sadler's dictum (1900): "The things outside the schools matter even more than the things inside the schools, and govern and interpret the things inside." No system can be understood, let alone borrowed, without its social context. Figure 15. Bereday's (1964) four steps of comparative analysis Bray and Thomas's (1995) cube reminds us to compare across geographic/locational levels (world, region, country, state, district, school, classroom, individual), non-locational demographic groups (ethnic, gender, religious, age) and aspects of education and society (curriculum, finance, management, teaching methods, labour market).

Career education helps learners understand themselves, explore the world of work and plan learning and career pathways. Career development theories include Super's life-span, life-space theory, Holland's RIASEC typology (realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising, conventional), and Krumboltz's planned happenstance. Entrepreneurship education develops entrepreneurial mindsets (opportunity recognition, creativity, risk management, resilience) and practical venture skills. The EU's EntreComp framework (2016) lists 15 competences in three areas: ideas and opportunities, resources, and into action. Freelancing is the gig-based, often online, sale of services (writing, design, programming, digital marketing). Bangladesh has one of the world's largest online freelance workforces; government programmes such as the Learning and Earning Development Project trained youth in IT freelancing. Verify Before Use Bangladesh is often reported to rank second globally in supply of online labour (Oxford Internet Institute Online Labour Index). Confirm the latest ranking and freelancer estimates before quoting.

Collaborative research (between universities, countries, disciplines and practitioners) increases relevance and capacity, but raises ethical issues: Power and equity: "helicopter" or "parachute" research in which Northern researchers collect data in the South without genuine partnership or credit. Authorship and credit: criteria such as the ICMJE guidelines; fair recognition for local researchers and data collectors. Data ownership and sharing: agreements on who holds and can use data. Informed consent and cultural sensitivity: across languages and power differences; extra care with children and refugees. Ethical review: approval from both partner institutions' review boards. Conflicts of interest and funding influence. Benefit sharing and capacity building: collaboration should leave lasting research capacity in partner institutions. The Swiss Commission for Research Partnerships with Developing Countries (KFPE) published 11 Principles (2012, 2018) for fair partnerships, including setting the agenda together, mutual trust, sharing information, shared responsibility, creating transparency, monitoring and evaluating, disseminating results, applying results, sharing profits equitably, increasing research capacity and building on achievements.

u: Unit 1: Introduction to Policies in Education
x: The word policy derives from the Greek polis (city-state) and Latin politia (state, administration). In everyday administrative usage, a policy is a statement of intent that guides decisions and actions towards stated goals. Definition Public policy (Dye, 1972): "Whatever governments choose to do or not to do." Dye's definition reminds us that inaction (for example, not regulating private coaching) is also policy. Definition Policy (Easton, 1953): "The authoritative allocation of values" for a society. Education policy decides whose values (equity, efficiency, excellence, religious or secular identity, national language) shape schooling. Definition Policy as text and as discourse (Ball, 1993): Policy is both text (documents that are encoded by authors and decoded, often differently, by readers such as teachers) and discourse (frameworks of meaning that set limits on what can be thought and said, for example "quality", "accountability" or "skills"). Definition Education policy (Bell & Stevenson, 2006): Education policy is "about the power to determine what gets done, or not done" in education; it is "the operational statement of values" that emerges from contestation between different groups. Characteristics of a good educational policy Goal-oriented and grounded in national values and the Constitution. Evidence-informed and contextually feasible. Coherent with other sectoral policies (finance, labour, ICT, gender, disability). Flexible and periodically reviewed. Inclusive and equitable; developed with stakeholder participation. Clear on responsibilities, resources and timelines. Accompanied by a legal framework and a monitoring mechanism. Types of policy Basis Types Educational example Lowi's (1964) policy arenas Distributive, redistributive, regulatory, constitutive Free textbooks (distributive); stipends for poor girls (redistributive); rules on coaching centres (regulatory); creating a new university commission (constitutive) Substance Substantive versus procedural Curriculum content versus rules for teacher recruitment Level Macro (national), meso (directorate, board, district), micro (institution) NEP 2010; DSHE circular; school admission policy Effect Material versus symbolic Budget for school feeding versus declaring a "year of quality" Formality Explicit (written) versus implicit (practice, tradition) Written assessment guidelines versus informal promotion practices Table 1. Classifications of public and educational policy

u: Unit 1: Introduction to Policies in Education
x: A decision is a choice among alternatives at a particular moment; a policy is a standing guide that frames many decisions. Simon (1947) described organisations as decision-making systems in which policies set the value premises within which officials decide. Policy Decision Broad, general guideline Specific choice Long-term and continuing Often one-off or short-term Framed at higher levels Made at all levels Sets premises and limits for action Applies the policy to a case Example: "All primary-age children shall attend school free of charge" Example: "Admit this child without a birth certificate under the policy" Table 2. Policy versus decision Key Point Policies are implemented through thousands of decisions by officials, head teachers and teachers. This is why Lipsky (1980) called front-line public servants "street-level bureaucrats": their discretionary decisions effectively become policy in practice.

t: 1.7 Development of educational policy-making and implementation in Bangladesh
x: The usual sequence for a major education policy in Bangladesh is: Figure 5. Typical education policy process in Bangladesh Commitment Status (indicative) One-year pre-primary education Introduced in government primary schools from 2010 onward; expansion to two years for age 4+ planned Extension of primary education to Grade 8 Not implemented system-wide; piloted in a limited number of schools Single common curriculum to Grade 10 Attempted through NCF 2021 (removing streams in Grades 9 and 10) and reversed in 2025 Permanent Education Commission Not established Education Act Draft not yet enacted Free textbooks Implemented: free textbooks distributed nationwide each January since 2010 Creative (structured) questions Implemented 2008 to 2010 onward; widely criticised for guidebook dependence Teacher recruitment through a separate commission Partially: NTRCA for non-government teachers Table 7. Implementation status of selected NEP 2010 commitments (indicative) Verify Before Use Treat the "status" column as indicative and update it from the latest Ministry of Education and NCTB documents and news before using it in an exam; several items have changed since 2023. Why policies fail in implementation Fullan (2016) argues that change fails when it is overloaded, fragmented, under-resourced and poorly understood by implementers. In Bangladesh the common causes of the policy-practice gap are: frequent policy reversals; centralised top-down design with limited teacher involvement; inadequate training and resources; examination-driven incentives (coaching, guidebooks); weak monitoring; political interference; and insufficient financing. u: Unit 1: Introduction to Policies in Education
t: 1.8 Globalisation and the educational policy context
x: Rizvi and Lingard (2010) argue that education policy is now made in a global context : national governments still decide, but the "social imaginary" of neoliberal globalisation, international organisations (OECD, World Bank) and policy networks shape what counts as a problem and a solution. Convergence of policy discourse around human capital, skills, quality and accountability. Policy borrowing and lending (see ED 501), including donor conditionality. Datafication : global indicators (SDG 4) and comparative assessments drive policy priorities. Marketisation : growth of private higher education and private tutoring. Vernacularisation : global ideas are reinterpreted locally (Appadurai's "vernacular globalisation"). Critical Perspective A critical policy analysis asks: Whose problem? Whose solution? Who benefits? Who is silenced? For example, a competency-based curriculum may be framed globally as modernisation but experienced locally as a burden on under-resourced rural schools. Policy sociology (Ball, Whitty) encourages students of policy to examine power, discourse and inequality, not only efficiency. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Define policy. Distinguish policy from decision." "Explain the ecology of educational policy with reference to Bell and Stevenson's model." "Who are the actors in education policy-making in Bangladesh? Analyse their roles." "Describe the policy cycle and critically discuss the incremental and multiple-streams models." "Why do education policies fail in implementation in Bangladesh?"

The term strategy comes from the Greek strategos (general, the art of the general). It entered management through business and military thinking. Definition Strategy (Chandler, 1962): "The determination of the basic long-term goals and objectives of an enterprise, and the adoption of courses of action and the allocation of resources necessary for carrying out these goals." Definition Strategy (Johnson, Scholes & Whittington, 2008): "The direction and scope of an organisation over the long term, which achieves advantage in a changing environment through its configuration of resources and competences with the aim of fulfilling stakeholder expectations." Mintzberg (1987) proposed five Ps of strategy: strategy as plan (intended course of action), ploy (manoeuvre to outwit), pattern (consistency in behaviour over time, the "emergent" strategy), position (place in the environment), and perspective (an organisation's ingrained way of seeing the world). Figure 7. Deliberate and emergent strategy (Mintzberg & Waters, 1985)

Definition Leadership (Northouse, 2021): "A process whereby an individual influences a group of individuals to achieve a common goal." Four components: leadership is a process; involves influence; occurs in groups; and involves common goals. Definition Leadership (Stogdill, 1950): "The process of influencing the activities of an organized group toward goal setting and goal achievement." Definition Educational leadership (Bush, 2020): Leadership is "a process of influence leading to the achievement of desired purposes", grounded in personal and professional values and articulated as a clear vision for the school. Different ideas about leadership treat it as a trait (born leaders), a behaviour (what leaders do), a relationship (between leaders and followers), a process of influence, a position (formal authority) or a distributed property of an organisation (shared across many people). Leadership compared with management (Kotter, 1990; Bennis & Nanus, 1985) Bush (2020) argues that effective educational institutions need both: leadership without management lacks implementation; management without leadership lacks direction. Cuban (1988) linked leadership to change and management to maintenance.

Nature: leadership is relational, contextual, value-laden, purposeful and both formal and informal; it can be exercised by anyone, not only by the principal. Importance in education: Leithwood et al. Trait theories Early "great man" theories assumed leaders are born. Stogdill's reviews (1948, 1974) found traits associated with leadership (intelligence, self-confidence, determination, integrity, sociability) but showed that traits alone do not predict leadership across situations. Later research linked the Big Five personality factors to leadership emergence and effectiveness: extraversion strongest, followed by conscientiousness and openness (Judge et al., 2002). (2000) proposed a skills model with competencies (problem-solving, social judgement, knowledge), individual attributes and career experiences. Behavioural theories Ohio State studies: two dimensions, initiating structure (task) and consideration (relationship). University of Michigan studies: production orientation versus employee orientation . Blake and Mouton's Managerial (Leadership) Grid (1964): concern for production versus concern for people produces five styles: impoverished (1,1), country club (1,9), authority-compliance (9,1), middle-of-the-road (5,5) and team management (9,9). Figure 13. Contingency and situational theories Fiedler's contingency theory (1967): effectiveness depends on the match between leader style (measured by the Least Preferred Co-worker scale: task- or relationship-motivated) and situational favourableness (leader-member relations, task structure, position power). Hersey and Blanchard's Situational Leadership: leaders adapt directive and supportive behaviour to followers' development level. Figure 14. Leader-member exchange (LMX) theory: quality of dyadic relationships (in-group and out-group) affects outcomes. Research on gender and leadership examines whether women and men lead differently and why women are under-represented in senior positions. Eagly and Johnson (1990) meta-analysis: women tended to adopt a more democratic, participative style and men a more autocratic, directive style; differences in task versus interpersonal orientation were small in organisational settings. Eagly, Johannesen-Schmidt and van Engen (2003): women were somewhat more transformational and used more contingent reward, both associated with effectiveness. Role congruity theory (Eagly & Karau, 2002): prejudice arises because leadership roles are stereotyped as masculine, so women leaders are evaluated less favourably. Glass ceiling and the labyrinth metaphor (Eagly & Carli, 2007): women face multiple barriers (family responsibilities, networks, stereotypes) rather than one barrier at the top; the glass cliff (Ryan & Haslam, 2005) describes women appointed to precarious leadership roles. Bangladesh Context In Bangladesh, women form a majority of government primary teachers because of the female recruitment quota, yet they are under-represented as head teachers, education officers, principals of colleges and university vice-chancellors. Barriers include social norms on mobility, family responsibilities, transfer postings, sexual harassment and male-dominated networks. Affirmative action, mentoring, flexible postings and leadership training (e.g., through NAEM) are strategies to address the gap. Critical Perspective Avoid essentialism: the variation within each gender is larger than the difference between genders, and leadership style depends heavily on context, culture and organisational expectations. Intersectionality (gender with class, ethnicity, disability, location) matters. Exam Focus Expect: "Define leadership. Differentiate leadership from management." Leadership skills can be developed through structured learning combined with practice. The widely cited 70:20:10 model (McCall, Lombardo & Eichinger) suggests that roughly 70% of leadership learning comes from challenging experience, 20% from relationships (mentoring, coaching, feedback) and 10% from formal training. Conflict management Conflict is a process that begins when one party perceives that another has negatively affected, or is about to affect, something the first party cares about (Robbins & Judge). Conflict can be functional (improves decisions, innovation) or dysfunctional (damages relationships and performance). Sources of conflict in educational institutions: scarce resources, role ambiguity, differences in values or goals, communication failures, personality clashes, workload and timetable allocation, promotion, political affiliations, and disputes between management committees and heads. Understanding ICT begins with the difference between data and information. Data are raw, unprocessed facts (marks, attendance ticks, numbers). Information is data processed into a meaningful form (a class average, an attendance rate). Knowledge is information understood and applied in context, and wisdom is the judicious use of knowledge. Figure 1. The DIKW hierarchy (after Ackoff, 1989) Communication is the process of sharing information and meaning between senders and receivers through a channel. Education is a structured communication process in which teachers and learners exchange, construct and evaluate knowledge. ICT therefore sits at the intersection of all four: it captures data, processes it into information, communicates it, and supports the construction of knowledge.

Definition Information Technology (IT): The use of computers, storage, networking and other physical devices, infrastructure and processes to create, process, store, secure and exchange electronic data. Definition Information and Communication Technology (ICT) (UNESCO): "A diverse set of technological tools and resources used to transmit, store, create, share or exchange information", including computers, the internet, live broadcasting (radio, television), recorded broadcasting (podcasts, audio and video players) and telephony (fixed, mobile, video-conferencing). Definition ICT in Education (ICTE): The use of ICT to support, enhance and transform teaching, learning, assessment, educational management and teachers' professional development. ICTE covers both learning about ICT (ICT as a subject) and learning with/through ICT (ICT as a tool across subjects). Aspect IT ICT ICTE Focus Computing and data processing Information processing plus communication Educational use of ICT Components Hardware, software, data, networks IT plus telecommunications, broadcast media, internet ICT plus pedagogy, curriculum, management Typical users IT professionals, organisations Everyone Teachers, learners, administrators Example Database server Mobile phone, internet, TV Online class, EMIS, digital content Table 1. IT, ICT and ICTE compared

Definition Information literacy (ALA, 1989): "To be information literate, a person must be able to recognize when information is needed and have the ability to locate, evaluate, and use effectively the needed information." The ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education (2016) presents six frames: authority is constructed and contextual; information creation as a process; information has value; research as inquiry; scholarship as conversation; and searching as strategic exploration. Digital literacy is broader: the ability to use digital technologies to find, evaluate, create and communicate information, requiring both cognitive and technical skills. The European DigComp 2.2 framework (2022) defines five areas: information and data literacy; communication and collaboration; digital content creation; safety; and problem solving. UNESCO's Digital Literacy Global Framework (2018) adds devices and software operations and career-related competences. Figure 2. Five competence areas of DigComp 2.2

Definition Blended learning (Garrison & Kanuka, 2004): "The thoughtful integration of classroom face-to-face learning experiences with online learning experiences." Mishra and Koehler (2006), building on Shulman's (1986) pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) , proposed Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) : effective technology integration requires teachers to understand the complex interplay of three primary knowledge bases. Figure 3. The TPACK framework (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) Domain Meaning Example (Grade 8 geometry) CK Knowledge of subject matter Properties of triangles PK Knowledge of teaching and learning methods Inquiry learning, questioning TK Knowledge of technologies Using GeoGebra PCK Teaching particular content effectively Using paper folding to discover angle sum TCK How technology represents content Dynamic geometry shows angle sum stays 180° as the triangle changes TPK How technology changes teaching Using online polls for formative assessment TPACK Integrated knowledge of using technology to teach specific content with appropriate pedagogy Students explore triangles in GeoGebra, conjecture, then justify in groups Table 3. The seven knowledge domains of TPACK Key Point TPACK's central message is that technology integration is not a generic skill . A teacher who can operate PowerPoint (TK) is not automatically able to teach mathematics better with it. The surrounding circle in the diagram represents context (school, students, culture), which Mishra (2019) relabelled as contextual knowledge (XK) . E-education (e-learning) is learning facilitated and supported through ICT. Key concepts: Synchronous (real time: live classes on Zoom/Meet) versus asynchronous (anytime: recorded videos, discussion forums). Learning Management System (LMS): software for delivering, tracking and managing learning (Moodle, Google Classroom, Canvas, Blackboard). Virtual Learning Environment (VLE) and Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) . E-content: text, audio, video, simulations, interactive modules. E-assessment: online quizzes, e-portfolios, automated feedback. Learning analytics: measurement and analysis of data about learners to understand and optimise learning.

Definition Mobile learning (UNESCO, 2013): "Mobile learning involves the use of mobile technology, either alone or in combination with other ICT, to enable learning anytime and anywhere." UNESCO's Policy Guidelines for Mobile Learning (2013) list benefits such as expanding reach and equity, facilitating personalised learning, providing immediate feedback, enabling anytime-anywhere learning, supporting situated learning and building bridges between formal and informal learning. Challenges include small screens, distraction, cost of data, privacy and unequal access, especially for girls. Bangladesh Context In Bangladesh, mobile phone penetration is very high and mobile internet is the main mode of internet access. During COVID-19, mobile-based learning (Muktopaath, 10 Minute School, Facebook Live classes, and the 333 call-based support) and feature-phone-based interactive voice response complemented TV and radio lessons. t: 2.1 ICTE in global and local perspective
x: Globally, ICTE has moved through phases: computer-assisted instruction (1960s to 1980s), multimedia and the internet (1990s), Web 2.0 and one-to-one device programmes (2000s, e.g., One Laptop Per Child), mobile and cloud learning (2010s), and emergency remote teaching and AI (2020s). UNESCO's GEM Report 2023, Technology in Education: A Tool on Whose Terms? , warns that evidence on technology's added value is thin and context-dependent, that technology should be used only where it improves learning, and that one in four countries had banned smartphones in schools. t: 2.3 Current practices of ICTE by government and NGOs
x: Government initiatives a2i (Aspire to Innovate) , formerly Access to Information, under the ICT Division and Cabinet Division with UNDP support: drove multimedia classrooms, teacher-led content development and digital services. Multimedia Classrooms (MMC): laptop, projector, internet modem and speakers provided to secondary and primary schools; teachers trained to develop digital content. Shikkhok Batayon (Teachers' Portal): an online platform where teachers share and rate digital content; recognised internationally. Muktopaath: a Bangla e-learning platform for free online courses, including teacher professional development and skills courses. Kishore Batayon (Konnect): an edutainment portal for adolescents. Sheikh Russel Digital Labs and School of Future (ICT Division): computer labs in secondary institutions; some have been renamed after 2024. ICT as a compulsory subject at secondary and higher secondary levels; ICT teachers recruited for some schools. Sangsad TV "Amar Ghore Amar School" and Bangladesh Betar lessons during COVID-19. Bangladesh Open University (BOU): TV, radio and online distance programmes; BOU's e-learning platform. Online admission and results: college admission (XI class) online; result publication via SMS and web. BdREN: Bangladesh Research and Education Network connecting universities. NGO and private initiatives BRAC: BRAC IED, digital literacy, computer-aided learning in BRAC schools; online learning during COVID-19. JAAGO Foundation: online schools connecting urban teachers with rural classrooms. 10 Minute School: large private online learning platform with free and paid content. D.Net, Save the Children, UNICEF: digital content, mobile learning, Rohingya learning centres. Telecom operators: zero-rated educational content during COVID-19. Verify Before Use Names and status of government labs and portals (e.g., Sheikh Russel Digital Labs, Kishore Batayon) may have changed after August 2024; confirm current names before an exam. Bangladesh Context Research on multimedia classrooms in Bangladesh found that they increased student attention and teacher motivation, but often amounted to substitution in SAMR terms (slides replacing the board), with limited interactive or student-centred use, frequent equipment breakdowns, and insufficient time for teachers to prepare content.

t: 2.4 Relationship between ICTE curriculum and instruction
x: ICT appears in the curriculum in two ways: as a subject (ICT curriculum for Grades 6 to 12, digital technology in the 2021 framework) and as a cross-curricular tool . Synchronising curriculum and instruction requires: Alignment of curriculum objectives, ICT tools and assessment (constructive alignment, Biggs). Teacher guides that show how to use technology for particular content (TPACK). Time in the timetable for lab work. Assessment that rewards ICT-enabled skills (projects, portfolios), not only written exams. Professional development in pedagogy, not just in operating devices.

t: 2.5 Future modalities of ICTE in Bangladesh

Future modalities of ICTE in Bangladesh Critical Perspective Technology-led reforms often fail when they are hardware-centred (buy devices first, think about pedagogy later), lack maintenance budgets, or ignore teachers' workload. Cuban's (2001) Oversold and Underused showed that computers in US schools were rarely used to change teaching. The 2023 GEM Report urges asking: is it appropriate , equitable , scalable and sustainable ?
