t: 3.1 Technology as a tool in education
x: Jonassen (1996) distinguished learning from computers (computers as tutors delivering instruction) and learning with computers (computers as mindtools that learners use to construct knowledge: databases, spreadsheets, concept maps, simulations). Contemporary practice emphasises technology as a tool for active , collaborative , constructive , authentic and reflective learning.

u: Unit 3: Internet and Technology Assisted Learning in Education
x: Definition Distance education (Moore & Kearsley, 2012): "Teaching and planned learning in which teaching normally occurs in a different place from learning, requiring communication through technologies as well as special institutional organization." Distance education has evolved through generations: correspondence; broadcast radio and TV; teleconferencing; computer-based and internet learning; and online, mobile and AI-supported learning. Moore's theory of transactional distance argues that the psychological distance between teacher and learner depends on dialogue , structure and learner autonomy . Cloud computing delivers computing services (storage, software, platforms) over the internet. Models: SaaS (software as a service, e.g., Google Workspace), PaaS (platform), IaaS (infrastructure). In education, cloud tools allow real-time collaboration (Google Docs), storage (Drive, OneDrive), and LMS access from any device. Advantages Limitations Access from anywhere and any device Requires reliable internet Real-time collaboration Data privacy and ownership concerns Automatic updates, low local maintenance Dependence on vendors Scalable and often free for education Account management for minors Easy sharing of resources Digital literacy needs Table 9. Advantages and limitations of cloud-based learning

u: Unit 3: Internet and Technology Assisted Learning in Education
x: Google Classroom Google Classroom is a free LMS within Google Workspace for Education that lets teachers create classes, share materials, assign and grade work, give feedback and communicate with students. Features include Stream, Classwork, People and Grades tabs; integration with Docs, Forms, Meet and Drive; originality reports; and rubrics. Flipped learning Definition Flipped learning (Flipped Learning Network, 2014): "A pedagogical approach in which direct instruction moves from the group learning space to the individual learning space, and the resulting group space is transformed into a dynamic, interactive learning environment where the educator guides students as they apply concepts and engage creatively in the subject matter." The four pillars of flipped learning (F-L-I-P): F lexible environment, L earning culture (learner-centred), I ntentional content, P rofessional educator. Bergmann and Sams (2012) popularised the approach. Figure 6. Traditional and flipped classroom Web 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 Figure 7. Evolution of the web and its educational uses Open Educational Resources (OER) Definition Open Educational Resources (UNESCO, 2019 Recommendation): "Learning, teaching and research materials in any format and medium that reside in the public domain or are under copyright that have been released under an open license, that permit no-cost access, re-use, re-purpose, adaptation and redistribution by others." The term was coined at a UNESCO forum in 2002. Wiley's 5Rs describe openness: Retain, Reuse, Revise, Remix, Redistribute . Creative Commons licences enable this. Element Meaning BY (Attribution) Credit the creator SA (ShareAlike) Adaptations must use the same licence NC (NonCommercial) No commercial use ND (NoDerivatives) No adaptations allowed CC0 Public domain dedication; no rights reserved Table 10. Creative Commons licence elements Examples: MIT OpenCourseWare (2001), OpenStax textbooks, Khan Academy, Wikipedia, UNESCO OER, Bangladesh's NCTB e-textbooks and Shikkhok Batayon content. MOOCs Massive Open Online Courses became prominent in 2012 ("the year of the MOOC"): Coursera, edX, Udacity, FutureLearn, and India's SWAYAM. cMOOCs (connectivist, Siemens and Downes, 2008) emphasise networks; xMOOCs follow structured instruction. Completion rates are typically low (often under 10%), raising questions about their democratising promise. Other provisions Video conferencing (Zoom, Meet, Teams), podcasts, digital libraries (e.g., JSTOR, ERIC, institutional repositories), virtual labs (PhET simulations), educational games, AI chatbots and generative AI tools (with guidance on academic integrity). Key Point UNESCO's Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research (2023) recommends a human-centred approach: age limits (suggesting 13 as a minimum for independent use), data privacy protection, validation of AI tools, capacity building for teachers and students, and rethinking assessment.

t: 3.4 Scope and challenges of digital media
x: Scope: multimodal learning (text, image, audio, video), wider access to experts and resources, collaboration across distances, creativity (digital storytelling, podcasts), personalisation and data-informed feedback. Definition Management Information System (MIS): An integrated system of people, procedures, data and technology that collects, processes, stores and disseminates information to support decision-making, coordination, control and analysis in an organisation. Definition EMIS (UNESCO): "A system for the collection, integration, processing, maintenance and dissemination of data and information to support decision-making, policy analysis and formulation, planning, monitoring and management at all levels of an education system." It is "a system of people, technology, models, methods, processes, procedures, rules and regulations that function together". Figure 9. u: Unit 5: Ethics and Laws of ICTE
x: Computer ethics studies moral issues arising from ICT. Moor (1985) argued that computers create "policy vacuums" in which rules for conduct are unclear. Mason's (1986) PAPA framework names four ethical issues of the information age: Privacy, Accuracy, Property and Accessibility . Figure 12. Major e-ethical issues in education Viruses and malware Malware is malicious software: virus (attaches to files and spreads when run), worm (self-replicating across networks), Trojan horse (disguised as useful software), ransomware (encrypts data for ransom, e.g., WannaCry 2017), spyware , adware and phishing (fraudulent messages to steal credentials). Ethical use means not creating or spreading malware and protecting institutional systems. Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) IPR protects creations of the mind: copyright (literary, artistic, software works), patents (inventions), trademarks (brands), industrial designs and geographical indications (e.g., Jamdani, Hilsa and Fazli mango are registered GIs of Bangladesh). Educators must respect copyright while using exceptions such as fair use / fair dealing for teaching, criticism and research, and should prefer open licences. Plagiarism Definition Plagiarism: Presenting someone else's words, ideas, data or work as one's own without proper acknowledgement. Types include direct (verbatim) plagiarism, mosaic or patchwriting, self-plagiarism, paraphrasing without citation, and contract cheating; using AI-generated text without disclosure is increasingly treated as a form of academic misconduct. Prevention: teaching academic writing and citation (APA 7th), designing authentic assessments, using similarity checkers (Turnitin, iThenticate) as learning aids, clear institutional policies. In Bangladesh, the UGC and universities have adopted plagiarism policies and similarity-check requirements for theses. Verify Before Use Check the current UGC plagiarism guidelines or policy and your university's thesis similarity threshold. Technology addiction Problematic internet use, gaming disorder (recognised in the WHO ICD-11, 2019) and social media overuse affect sleep, attention, physical health and academic performance. Strategies: digital well-being education, screen-time agreements, parental guidance, balanced activities, counselling. Digital crime (cybercrime) Hacking, identity theft, online fraud, child sexual exploitation material, cyberstalking, sextortion, spreading malware, defamation and hate speech. Students and teachers need awareness of reporting channels (e.g., the police cyber units and the national helpline 999). Cyberbullying Definition Cyberbullying (Hinduja & Patchin, 2015): "Willful and repeated harm inflicted through the use of computers, cell phones, and other electronic devices." Forms include harassment, flaming, outing, exclusion, impersonation and cyberstalking. Schools respond through anti-bullying policies, digital citizenship education, reporting mechanisms, support for victims, restorative approaches and cooperation with parents. Censorship and privacy Censorship restricts access to information or expression; in education it raises questions of filtering harmful content versus protecting academic freedom. Privacy concerns personal data: students' records, photos on social media, surveillance software, data collected by EdTech companies. Figure 13. Ribble's nine elements of digital citizenship

Objectives Plan, record and edit a short lesson-based video tutorial (5 to 10 minutes) with screen capture, webcam and interactive elements. Tools ActivePresenter (Atomi Systems; free edition available): screen recording, slides, interactive quizzes, export to video or HTML5. OBS Studio (free, open-source): recording and live streaming with scenes and sources. Others: ScreenFaceCam, Debut video capture. Procedure 1. Plan: choose one learning objective; write a script or storyboard (introduction, explanation, example, check for understanding, summary). 2. Prepare slides with large fonts, minimal text, visuals (Mayer's multimedia principles: coherence, signalling, redundancy, spatial contiguity, temporal contiguity, segmenting, pre-training, modality, multimedia, personalisation, voice and image principles). 3. Set up OBS: add a scene; add sources (Display Capture or Window Capture, Video Capture Device for webcam, Audio Input); position webcam in a corner; set output to MP4 and 1080p or 720p. 4. Record in short segments; speak clearly and conversationally. 5. Edit in ActivePresenter (or another editor): trim, add captions, zoom-n-pan, callouts, background music at low volume. 6. Add interactivity (ActivePresenter): insert quiz slides (multiple choice, drag-and-drop) with feedback; export as HTML5 for an LMS. 7. Publish: upload to YouTube (unlisted) or Google Classroom; add captions and a description. Key Point Mayer's research suggests keeping instructional videos short and segmented, using narration with visuals rather than on-screen text duplicating narration, and removing extraneous material. Guo, Kim and Rubin (2014) found median engagement time for MOOC videos was around six minutes regardless of video length.

t: 1.1 What is a worldview or paradigm?
x: Every researcher brings assumptions about what reality is, how it can be known and what is valuable in inquiry. Creswell and Creswell (2018) call these assumptions a philosophical worldview : "a basic set of beliefs that guide action". Kuhn (1962) used paradigm for the shared beliefs and practices of a scientific community, and Guba and Lincoln (1994) defined a paradigm as "the basic belief system or worldview that guides the investigator, not only in choices of method but in ontologically and epistemologically fundamental ways".

Element Question it answers Example of positions Ontology What is the nature of reality? Single objective reality (realism) versus multiple constructed realities (relativism) Epistemology What is the relationship between knower and known? How do we know? Objective, detached researcher versus subjective, co-created knowledge Axiology What is the role of values in research? Value-free versus value-laden, ethical and political commitments Methodology How should we go about finding out? Experimental, survey, ethnography, action research, mixed methods Methods What techniques collect and analyse data? Tests, questionnaires, interviews, observation, documents Rhetoric (sometimes added) What language is used to report? Formal, impersonal versus personal, narrative voice Table 1. Elements of a research paradigm (Guba & Lincoln, 1994; Kivunja & Kuyini, 2017) Figure 1. From philosophy to methods: the logic of research design (after Crotty, 1998)

(i) Positivism and post-positivism Positivism (Comte) holds that the social world can be studied like the natural world through observation, measurement and the testing of hypotheses to discover general laws. Post-positivism (Popper, Phillips & Burbules) accepts that absolute truth cannot be proven; knowledge is conjectural and claims are tested through falsification and probability. Research is deterministic (causes probably determine effects), reductionist (reduce ideas into small testable variables) and focused on empirical observation and measurement. (ii) Interpretivism and constructivism Interpretivism (Weber's verstehen , Schutz, Gadamer) and social constructivism (Berger & Luckmann) hold that reality is socially constructed; researchers seek to understand the meanings people attach to their experiences. Research is inductive, context-bound and relies on participants' views, using open-ended questions, interviews and observation. (iii) Advocacy / participatory (transformative) The transformative worldview (Mertens, 2010) holds that research should be intertwined with politics and a political change agenda to confront social oppression. It includes critical theory (Habermas, Freire), feminist, critical race, queer, disability and indigenous perspectives, and participatory action research. Research is collaborative and aims at empowerment and emancipation. (iv) Pragmatism Pragmatism (Peirce, James, Dewey; in methodology, Morgan, Tashakkori and Teddlie) focuses on the research problem and the consequences of actions rather than on prior metaphysical positions. "What works" to answer the question guides the choice of methods; it underpins mixed methods research. Feature Post-positivism Constructivism / interpretivism Transformative / participatory Pragmatism Ontology One reality, known imperfectly (critical realism) Multiple, socially constructed realities Realities shaped by power, social, political, gender, ethnic values Reality is what works; singular and multiple Epistemology Objective; researcher independent Subjective; co-constructed with participants Collaborative; researcher works with communities Practical; whatever answers the question Axiology Value-neutral, bias controlled Values acknowledged; reflexivity Research must advance social justice Values shape choices about what to study Logic Deductive, theory-testing Inductive, theory-generating Varies; action-oriented Abductive; both Typical methodology Experiments, surveys, correlational studies Ethnography, phenomenology, grounded theory, case study, narrative Participatory action research, critical ethnography Mixed methods Typical question in Bangladesh Does teacher training increase Grade 5 maths scores? How do madrasah teachers experience the new curriculum? How can Dalit or Rohingya communities shape their children's schooling? What explains dropout, and how do families and teachers describe it? t: 1.4 Role of worldviews in educational research
x: They shape what questions are asked and how problems are framed. They guide the choice of design and methods. They determine criteria for quality (validity and reliability versus trustworthiness). They make researchers reflexive about their position and assumptions. They help readers evaluate whether the study's claims are consistent with its philosophy.

Figure 3. Linking worldviews to research approaches and designs (after Creswell & Creswell, 2018) Critical Perspective The "paradigm wars" of the 1980s (quantitative versus qualitative) have given way to more pluralist positions, but the incompatibility thesis (that paradigms cannot be mixed) still has defenders (Guba & Lincoln). Many methodologists now prefer to see paradigms as heuristic frames rather than rigid camps, and emphasise coherence between question, philosophy and method. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Explain ontology, epistemology and axiology with examples." "Compare positivism, interpretivism, transformative and pragmatic worldviews." "How does a researcher's worldview influence the selection of research design?"

u: Unit 2: Developing Theoretical and Conceptual Framework of a Research
x: Definition Theory (Kerlinger, 1986): "A set of interrelated constructs (concepts), definitions, and propositions that present a systematic view of phenomena by specifying relations among variables, with the purpose of explaining and predicting the phenomena." Definition Theoretical framework: The structure that holds or supports a theory of a research study; it introduces and describes the existing theory (or theories) that explain why the research problem exists and guides the study (Grant & Osanloo, 2014). It is borrowed from established literature. Definition Conceptual framework (Miles & Huberman, 1994): "Explains, either graphically or in narrative form, the main things to be studied: the key factors, constructs or variables, and the presumed relationships among them." It is the researcher's own synthesis, often drawing on several theories and empirical studies. Aspect Theoretical framework Conceptual framework Source An established theory (e.g., Bandura's self-efficacy theory) Researcher's synthesis of theories, literature and experience Scope Broad, general Specific to the study Purpose Explains phenomena; provides lens Maps variables or concepts and their relationships for this study Typical use Deductive, quantitative studies (also qualitative as lens) Both quantitative and qualitative studies Form Narrative description of theory Diagram plus narrative Analogy The blueprint of a house design style The specific floor plan of this house Table 3. Theoretical versus conceptual framework

u: Unit 2: Developing Theoretical and Conceptual Framework of a Research
x: Connects the study to existing knowledge and positions it in scholarship. Clarifies key concepts and variables; supports operational definitions. Guides formulation of research questions and hypotheses. Informs the design, instruments and analysis. Provides a lens for interpreting findings and explaining results. Helps generalisation (quantitative) or transferability (qualitative). In qualitative research, a framework can be developed or refined inductively (grounded theory) rather than fixed in advance.

Definition Research design (Creswell & Creswell, 2018): "Types of inquiry within qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods approaches that provide specific direction for procedures in a research study." A researchable problem is significant, feasible, ethical, clearly defined, and answerable with data. Sources include classroom experience, policy debates, theory, literature gaps and replication. t: 3.3 Selecting an appropriate design with justification
x: Figure 7. Decision path for selecting a research design A justification paragraph should state: (1) the research question and its nature; (2) the worldview; (3) why the design fits better than alternatives; (4) its known limitations and how they will be addressed.

t: 3.4 Complexity in selecting a research design
x: Multiple questions may require different designs (hence mixed methods). Ethical constraints (e.g., cannot withhold a beneficial programme) push towards quasi-experiments or waitlist designs. Practical constraints: access to schools, time, cost, language, gatekeepers. Researcher skills and supervisor expertise. Political sensitivity of topics (e.g., question leaks, corruption). Ambiguity of design labels across textbooks. Critical Perspective Correlation does not prove causation; causal language ("effect", "impact") should be used only with designs that support causal inference. Many Bangladeshi theses overclaim causality from cross-sectional surveys. Examiners appreciate cautious language: "is associated with" rather than "causes". Exam Focus Expect: "Discuss the major research designs with examples." "Explain the notation of experimental designs and identify threats to validity in O X O." "How would you select a design for studying dropout in rural Bangladesh? Justify."

t: 4.2 Sample size estimation with statistical formulae
x: Cochran's formula for proportions (large population) n₀ = Z² p q / e² where Z = 1.96 for 95% confidence, p = estimated proportion (use 0.5 if unknown), q = 1 − p, e = margin of error Worked Example For 95% confidence, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05: n₀ = (1.96)² × 0.5 × 0.5 / (0.05)² = 3.8416 × 0.25 / 0.0025 = 384.16, so 385 respondents. Finite population correction n = n₀ / [1 + (n₀ − 1) / N] Worked Example If the population is N = 2,000 teachers: n = 384.16 / [1 + 383.16 / 2000] = 384.16 / 1.1916 = 322.4, so 323 teachers. (Krejcie and Morgan's (1970) table gives 322 for N = 2,000.) Yamane's (1967) simplified formula n = N / (1 + N e²) Worked Example N = 2,000, e = 0.05: n = 2000 / (1 + 2000 × 0.0025) = 2000 / 6 = 333.3, so 334 . Sample size for estimating a mean n = (Z σ / e)² Worked Example To estimate mean test score within ±2 marks when σ ≈ 10: n = (1.96 × 10 / 2)² = (9.8)² = 96.04, so 97 students. Power analysis For experiments and comparisons, sample size depends on effect size , significance level (α) , power (1 − β) and the test. With α = .05 and power = .80, an independent-samples t-test needs about 64 per group to detect a medium effect (d = 0.5) and about 26 per group for a large effect (d = 0.8) (Cohen, 1988). G*Power software calculates these. Key Point Adjust for non-response (divide by expected response rate: 323 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 380 questionnaires) and for cluster sampling (multiply by the design effect, DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ, where m is cluster size and ρ the intraclass correlation).

Non-probability and qualitative sampling techniques Sample size in qualitative research Qualitative sample size is guided by saturation (no new information or themes emerge), information power (Malterud et al., 2016: narrower aims, dense specificity, established theory, strong dialogue and focused analysis need fewer participants) and design norms: phenomenology often 3 to 10 or more; grounded theory 20 to 30; case study 1 to 5 cases (Creswell & Poth, 2018).

A justification should link the sampling technique to the research question, design, population characteristics and generalisation claim. Complexities include: no reliable sampling frame (e.g., unregistered Qawmi madrasahs), access and gatekeepers, non-response, hidden populations, ethical issues of selecting vulnerable groups, and multistage designs requiring weighting. Worked Example Sampling plan for a national teacher survey: Stage 1, randomly select 4 of 8 divisions; Stage 2, randomly select 2 districts per division; Stage 3, stratify secondary schools by management (government, non-government) and location (urban, rural) and randomly select 6 schools per district; Stage 4, select all Bangla, English and mathematics teachers in each school. Total ≈ 48 schools × 6 teachers ≈ 288 teachers. Exam Focus Expect: "Calculate the sample size for a population of 5,000 at 95% confidence and 5% margin of error." "Compare stratified and cluster sampling." "What is saturation in qualitative sampling?" "Explain multistage sampling with a Bangladesh example."

Nature: a written set of questions that respondents answer themselves (self-administered), on paper or online. Types: structured (closed), unstructured (open), semi-structured (mixed); by mode: mailed, group-administered, online (Google Forms, KoBoToolbox), telephone-assisted. Item type Example Dichotomous Do you use multimedia in class? Yes / No Multiple choice Highest qualification: B.Ed / M.Ed / Other Rating scale (Likert) "Inclusive education benefits all learners": SD, D, N, A, SA Rank order Rank these five training needs from 1 to 5 Checklist Tick all ICT tools you use Semantic differential Teaching is: boring 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 interesting Open-ended What challenges do you face in continuous assessment? Table 11. Types of questionnaire items Construction steps: (1) define objectives and variables; (2) review existing instruments; (3) draft items aligned to each variable (item blueprint); (4) decide format, order and layout (general to specific; sensitive items later); (5) write clear instructions; (6) expert review for content validity; (7) translate and back-translate (Bangla/English); (8) cognitive interview and pilot test; (9) item analysis and reliability; (10) finalise. Item-writing rules: avoid double-barrelled questions ("Is the training useful and enjoyable?"), leading or loaded words, double negatives, jargon, ambiguous time frames and assumptions; keep items short; provide exhaustive and mutually exclusive options. Scope and limitations: economical, wide reach, anonymity and standardisation; but low response rates, misunderstanding, literacy demands, social desirability bias and no chance to probe.

Nature: a purposeful conversation in which the researcher asks questions and records answers. Types: structured (fixed questions, like an oral questionnaire), semi-structured (guide with flexible probes), unstructured (in-depth, conversational); individual or group; face-to-face, telephone or online. Construction: develop an interview protocol with introduction and consent script, warm-up questions, main questions linked to research questions, probes ("Can you give an example?"), closing question ("Is there anything else?"). Pilot it. Conducting: build rapport, listen actively, avoid leading, use silence, take notes, audio-record with consent, transcribe verbatim. Scope and limitations: depth, clarification, non-verbal cues, suitable for low-literacy participants; but time-consuming, costly, interviewer effects, smaller samples, and analysis is labour-intensive.

Nature: systematic watching and recording of behaviour in natural or controlled settings. Types: participant versus non-participant; structured (with schedule/checklist) versus unstructured (field notes); overt versus covert; natural versus contrived. Role Description Complete participant Researcher is a full member; identity concealed (ethical concerns) Participant as observer Researcher participates; role known Observer as participant Limited participation; mainly observing Complete observer No participation; e.g., video or one-way mirror Table 12. Observer roles (Gold, 1958) Construction: define behaviours operationally; choose recording method (event recording, interval/time sampling, duration, rating scales, anecdotal records); prepare a schedule (e.g., Flanders Interaction Analysis Categories for classroom talk, Stallings snapshot for time-on-task); train observers; establish inter-observer agreement. Scope and limitations: captures actual behaviour rather than reports; but observer effect (Hawthorne/reactivity), observer bias, time cost, cannot access thoughts.

Likert scale Developed by Rensis Likert (1932), a summated rating scale in which respondents indicate agreement with a series of statements, typically on 5 points (Strongly disagree to Strongly agree). Scores are summed across items, with negatively worded items reverse-scored . Statement SD (1) D (2) N (3) A (4) SA (5) Students with disabilities should learn in regular classrooms Inclusion reduces the quality of teaching for other students (reverse-scored) I feel confident adapting lessons for diverse learners Table 13. Example Likert items: attitudes towards inclusive education Construction: generate a large pool of positive and negative statements; expert review; pilot; item analysis (item-total correlations, discrimination between high and low scorers); retain items with good discrimination; compute Cronbach's alpha. Thurstone scale Developed by L. L. Thurstone (Thurstone & Chave, 1929), the method of equal-appearing intervals : (1) write many statements (often 100+) about the attitude object; (2) a panel of judges sorts each statement into 11 piles from least to most favourable; (3) compute each statement's scale value (median of judges' ratings) and spread (Q, interquartile range); (4) select about 20 statements with low Q spread across the scale range; (5) respondents tick statements they agree with; their score is the mean or median scale value of endorsed items. Feature Likert Thurstone Construction Simpler; no judges Laborious; requires judges Response Degree of agreement with each item Agree / disagree with items Scoring Sum of item scores Mean or median of scale values of endorsed items Assumption Ordinal; summed scores treated as interval Equal-appearing intervals Reliability Usually high with fewer items Comparable Use today Very common Rare Table 14. Likert and Thurstone scales compared Other scales: Guttman (cumulative) scaling, semantic differential (Osgood: evaluation, potency, activity), Bogardus social distance scale .

Nature: standardised instruments that measure psychological constructs (intelligence, aptitude, achievement, personality, interests, attitudes) by sampling behaviour under controlled conditions. Types: achievement versus aptitude; speed versus power; individual versus group; verbal versus non-verbal; norm-referenced versus criterion-referenced; objective versus projective (Rorschach, TAT). Construction: define construct and purpose; prepare a test blueprint (table of specifications); write items; expert review; try-out; item analysis (difficulty index p, discrimination index D); assemble final test; establish reliability, validity and norms; prepare manual. Scope and limitations: objective and comparable data; but cultural bias, test anxiety, misuse by untrained users, and ethical issues of labelling.

Nature: a moderated group discussion (usually 6 to 10 participants) on a focused topic, using group interaction to generate data (Krueger & Casey, 2015). Purpose: explore perceptions, norms, language and reasons; generate items for questionnaires; interpret survey results; evaluate programmes. Construction and conduct: define purpose; select homogeneous groups (e.g., separate groups for mothers and fathers; teachers and SMC members); prepare a question route (opening, introductory, transition, key, ending questions); recruit; arrange a neutral venue; moderator facilitates, note-taker records; obtain consent and confidentiality agreement; audio-record; debrief immediately; analyse transcripts across groups. Scope and limitations: efficient, rich interaction, useful with low-literacy groups; but dominant voices, conformity, confidentiality limits, difficult analysis, not suitable for sensitive personal topics.

Nature: a technique developed by Jacob L. Moreno (1934) to measure social relationships, attraction and rejection within a group. Members nominate peers according to a criterion ("Whom would you most like to work with on a project?"). Construction: state a meaningful criterion; ask for 1 to 3 choices (positive and possibly negative); tabulate choices in a sociomatrix ; draw a sociogram showing stars (highly chosen), isolates (unchosen), mutual pairs, cliques and rejectees. Figure 9. A simplified sociogram (lines represent nominations): Student A is a "star" Scope and limitations: identifies isolated or rejected children for support, informs group work and inclusion; but ethical sensitivity (negative nominations), changes over time, does not explain why .

t: 5.8 Validity, reliability and usefulness of tools
x: Validity of instruments Definition Validity (AERA, APA & NCME, 2014): "The degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses of tests." Validity is a property of interpretations, not of the instrument itself. Type Meaning How established Content validity Items adequately represent the domain Table of specifications; expert judgement; Content Validity Index (CVI; Lawshe's CVR) Face validity Appears to measure what it should Informal review (weakest form) Criterion validity: concurrent Correlates with an established measure at the same time Correlation with existing test Criterion validity: predictive Predicts a future criterion SSC scores predicting HSC results Construct validity Measures the theoretical construct Factor analysis (EFA/CFA), convergent and discriminant validity, known-groups Table 15. Types of validity evidence Reliability of instruments Definition Reliability: The consistency of scores across occasions, forms, items or raters. Classical test theory: Observed score = True score + Error (X = T + E); reliability = variance of T / variance of X. Method Procedure Coefficient Test-retest (stability) Same test twice after an interval Pearson r Parallel / alternate forms (equivalence) Two equivalent forms Pearson r Split-half Split into halves (odd-even); correct with Spearman-Brown r(full) = 2r(half) / (1 + r(half)) Internal consistency Inter-item consistency Cronbach's alpha; KR-20 (dichotomous items) Inter-rater Agreement between raters Percentage agreement; Cohen's kappa; ICC Table 16. Methods of estimating reliability Cronbach's α = [k / (k − 1)] × [1 − (Σ s²ᵢ / s²ₜ)] where k = number of items, s²ᵢ = variance of each item, s²ₜ = variance of total scores Worked Example If a split-half correlation is 0.70, the Spearman-Brown corrected reliability is 2(0.70) / (1 + 0.70) = 1.40 / 1.70 = 0.82 . Key Point Common rules of thumb for Cronbach's alpha: ≥ .90 excellent; .80 to .89 good; .70 to .79 acceptable; .60 to .69 questionable; < .60 poor (George & Mallery, 2003). Very high alpha (> .95) may indicate redundant items. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Figure 10. Reliability and validity illustrated with a target Usefulness (practicality): ease of administration, time, cost, scoring, interpretability, acceptability to respondents. u: Unit 6: Validity and Reliability of Research Outcomes
x: According to John Stuart Mill's logic as adopted by Shadish et al. (2002), a causal relationship requires: (1) the cause precedes the effect (temporal precedence); (2) the cause and effect covary ; and (3) alternative explanations are ruled out. Experiments achieve this by manipulating the cause, observing the effect, and using control groups and randomisation to rule out alternatives.

x: Threats include: interaction of selection and treatment (results apply only to the type of participants studied), interaction of setting and treatment (urban versus rural schools), interaction of history and treatment (effects during COVID-19 may not hold later), reactive arrangements / Hawthorne effect , and multiple-treatment interference . External validity is supported by random sampling, diverse samples, replication and clear description of context.

u: Unit 6: Validity and Reliability of Research Outcomes
x: Lincoln and Guba (1985) proposed parallel criteria to replace conventional validity and reliability: Criterion Parallel to Strategies Credibility Internal validity Prolonged engagement, persistent observation, triangulation, peer debriefing, negative case analysis, member checking Transferability External validity Thick description of context, purposive sampling Dependability Reliability Audit trail, code-recode, stepwise replication Confirmability Objectivity Audit trail, reflexive journal, triangulation Authenticity (later added) — Fairness, ontological, educative, catalytic and tactical authenticity Table 19. Trustworthiness criteria (Lincoln & Guba, 1985) Triangulation (Denzin, 1978) includes data triangulation (different sources), investigator triangulation (multiple researchers), theory triangulation and methodological triangulation. Maxwell (1992) proposed descriptive, interpretive, theoretical, generalisability and evaluative validity for qualitative work.

u: Unit 6: Validity and Reliability of Research Outcomes
x: Onwuegbuzie and Johnson (2006) used the term legitimation , including sample integration, inside-outside (emic-etic) legitimation, weakness minimisation, sequential legitimation, conversion legitimation, paradigmatic mixing, commensurability, multiple validities and political legitimation. Creswell and Plano Clark (2018) emphasise threats such as inadequate integration, unequal samples when merging, and failure to follow up contradictory results. Figure 12. Quality criteria in quantitative and qualitative research Exam Focus Expect: "Explain threats to internal and external validity with examples." "What are the conditions for inferring causality?" u: Unit 7: Data Analysis: Descriptive and Inferential Statistics
x: Frequency distribution A frequency distribution organises raw scores into classes with frequencies (f), relative frequencies (%) and cumulative frequencies (cf). Figure 13. Histogram and frequency polygon of students' marks Measures of central tendency Mean x̄ = Σx / n Median = middle value of ordered data (grouped: Md = L + [(n/2 − cf) / f] × i) Mode = most frequent value (grouped: Mo = L + [(f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × i) Worked Example Scores: 12, 15, 15, 18, 20. Mean = 80 ÷ 5 = 16 ; median = 15 ; mode = 15 . Measures of variation Range = Highest − Lowest Quartile deviation Q = (Q₃ − Q₁) / 2 Sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)] Coefficient of variation CV = (s / x̄) × 100 Worked Example For 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 (mean 16): deviations −4, −1, −1, 2, 4; squared 16, 1, 1, 4, 16 = 38; s² = 38 ÷ 4 = 9.5; s = 3.08 . Shape of distribution Figure 14. Symmetric and asymmetric (skewed) distributions Skewness describes asymmetry: in a positively skewed distribution (e.g., a very difficult test), most scores are low with a long tail to the right; mean > median > mode. In a negatively skewed distribution (an easy test), mean < median < mode. Kurtosis describes peakedness: leptokurtic (peaked), mesokurtic (normal), platykurtic (flat).

u: Unit 7: Data Analysis: Descriptive and Inferential Statistics
x: Figure 15. Scatter plots showing positive, negative and zero correlation Pearson's r = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / √[Σ(x − x̄)² × Σ(y − ȳ)²] Spearman's ρ = 1 − [6Σd² / n(n² − 1)] Worked Example X = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (hours of study) and Y = 3, 5, 4, 8, 10 (test score). x̄ = 6, ȳ = 6. Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 12 + 2 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 34; Σ(x − x̄)² = 40; Σ(y − ȳ)² = 34. r = 34 / √(40 × 34) = 34 / 36.88 = 0.92 : a very strong positive correlation. r (absolute) Interpretation 0.00 to 0.19 Very weak / negligible 0.20 to 0.39 Weak 0.40 to 0.59 Moderate 0.60 to 0.79 Strong 0.80 to 1.00 Very strong Table 22. Interpreting the size of r (common guideline) Key Point r² (coefficient of determination) gives the proportion of variance shared: r = 0.92 means r² = 0.85, so 85% of the variance in Y is associated with X. Correlation does not imply causation (third variables, reverse causation).

u: Unit 7: Data Analysis: Descriptive and Inferential Statistics
x: Regression predicts a dependent variable (Y) from one or more independent variables (X). Simple regression: Ŷ = a + bX, where b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ(x − x̄)² and a = ȳ − b x̄ Multiple regression: Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + ... + bₖXₖ Worked Example Using the data above: b = 34 / 40 = 0.85 ; a = 6 − 0.85 × 6 = 0.90 . Regression equation: Ŷ = 0.90 + 0.85X. A student who studies 7 hours is predicted to score 0.90 + 5.95 = 6.85 . Figure 16. Regression line of best fit with residuals Regression model concepts: the least-squares line minimises the sum of squared residuals; R² shows variance explained; standardised coefficients (β) compare predictors; assumptions include linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of residuals and absence of multicollinearity (check VIF). Logistic regression is used when Y is dichotomous (e.g., dropout yes/no). Multilevel (hierarchical linear) models handle students nested in schools.

u: Unit 7: Data Analysis: Descriptive and Inferential Statistics
x: Inferential statistics draw conclusions about populations from samples. The syllabus distinguishes (a) hypothesis testing and (b) interval estimation. (Strictly, point estimation means estimating a parameter with a single value, such as x̄ estimating μ; hypothesis testing is a decision procedure.) Steps in hypothesis testing Figure 17. Steps in testing a hypothesis Figure 18. Type I (α) and Type II (β) errors Decision H₀ true H₀ false Reject H₀ Type I error (α) Correct decision (power = 1 − β) Fail to reject H₀ Correct decision Type II error (β) Table 23. Decision errors in hypothesis testing Parametric tests Test Use Formula / note Z-test Compare means when σ known or n large (n > 30) z = (x̄ − μ) / (σ / √n) One-sample t-test Compare a sample mean with a known value t = (x̄ − μ) / (s / √n), df = n − 1 Independent-samples t-test Compare two independent group means t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) Paired-samples t-test Compare two related means (pre-post) t = d̄ / (s_d / √n) F-test / ANOVA Compare three or more means; ratio of variances F = MS between / MS within Table 24. Common parametric tests Worked Example Independent t-test: Group A (activity-based teaching) n = 30, x̄ = 72, s = 8; Group B (lecture) n = 30, x̄ = 66, s = 10. SE = √(64/30 + 100/30) = √5.467 = 2.34; t = 6 / 2.34 = 2.57 , df = 58. The critical value at α = .05 (two-tailed) ≈ 2.00, so H₀ is rejected. Effect size d = 6 / √[(64 + 100)/2] = 6 / 9.06 = 0.66 (medium to large). Assumptions of parametric tests: interval/ratio data, approximately normal distribution (or large n), homogeneity of variance (Levene's test), independence of observations. Non-parametric tests Used with nominal or ordinal data, small samples or violated assumptions. Purpose Parametric Non-parametric alternative Two independent groups Independent t-test Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum Two related groups Paired t-test Wilcoxon signed-rank test Three or more independent groups One-way ANOVA Kruskal-Wallis H Three or more related groups Repeated-measures ANOVA Friedman test Association Pearson r Spearman's rho; Kendall's tau Categorical association — Chi-square test Table 25. Parametric tests and their non-parametric alternatives Chi-square χ² = Σ [(O − E)² / E], where E = (row total × column total) / N; df = (r − 1)(c − 1) Worked Example 100 students (50 male, 50 female) are asked whether they prefer online classes. Males: 30 Yes, 20 No; females: 20 Yes, 30 No. Each expected frequency = (50 × 50) / 100 = 25. χ² = (30−25)²/25 + (20−25)²/25 + (20−25)²/25 + (30−25)²/25 = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.00 ; df = 1; critical value at .05 = 3.84. Since 4.00 > 3.84, preference is associated with gender. Confidence intervals Definition Confidence interval: A range of values, computed from sample data, that is likely to contain the population parameter with a stated level of confidence. A 95% CI means that if the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter. 95% CI for the mean = x̄ ± 1.96 (σ / √n) [use t instead of 1.96 for small samples] Worked Example x̄ = 72, s = 8, n = 64: SE = 8 / 8 = 1; 95% CI = 72 ± 1.96 = 70.04 to 73.96 . Critical Perspective Statistical significance is not practical significance. The American Statistical Association (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) warned against relying solely on p < .05; researchers should report effect sizes and confidence intervals , and interpret results in context. APA (2020) requires effect sizes for primary analyses. Exam Focus Expect: "Differentiate univariate, bivariate and multivariate analysis." "Compute Pearson's r and the regression equation from given data." "Explain Type I and Type II errors." "When would you use a non-parametric test? Explain the chi-square test with an example." "What is a confidence interval?"

Data interpretation is the process of assigning meaning to analysed data: explaining what the results say about the research questions, relating them to theory and previous research, and drawing implications. Analysis answers "What did we find?"; interpretation answers "What does it mean, and why does it matter?" Importance: it connects findings to the problem; it avoids misleading conclusions; it shows the study's contribution; it informs policy and practice; and it reveals limitations. Figure 19. From data to conclusions

Principles: 1. Return to each research question or hypothesis in turn. 2. Report the statistic, direction, significance and effect size (e.g., "Students taught through activity-based methods scored significantly higher, t(58) = 2.57, p = .013, d = 0.66"). 3. Interpret magnitude, not only significance (Cohen's d: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large; r: .1 small, .3 medium, .5 large). 4. Compare with previous research and theory: consistent or contradictory? Why? 5. Consider alternative explanations and threats to validity. 6. Avoid over-generalisation beyond the sample and causal claims from correlational data. 7. State practical implications. Worked Example Finding: r = −.45 between hours of private tutoring and SSC GPA in a sample of rural students. Weak interpretation: "Tutoring reduces achievement." Better interpretation: "A moderate negative association was observed; this may reflect that lower-achieving students seek more tutoring (reverse causation) or that tutoring quality varies. Causal conclusions cannot be drawn from this cross-sectional design."

Qualitative interpretation moves from codes to categories to themes to assertions or theory , supported by participants' voices. Raw data (quote) Code Category Theme "I have 70 students; I cannot do group work every day." Large class size Structural constraints Implementing activity-based learning under constraint "The guidebook gives all creative answers; students memorise them." Guidebook dependence Examination culture Assessment drives practice "Our head teacher asked us to try it in one class first." Supportive leadership Enabling conditions Leadership mediates reform Table 26. From qualitative codes to interpretation: an illustration Principles: use thick description ; present themes with illustrative quotations; show diversity and negative cases; relate to theory (e.g., Spillane's sense-making); state the researcher's reflexive position; and discuss transferability. Key Point Wolcott (1994) described three moves in transforming qualitative data: description (what is going on), analysis (how things work, identifying key factors and relationships) and interpretation (what it all means). Strong theses balance all three. Exam Focus Expect: "What is data interpretation? Distinguish it from analysis." "Discuss guidelines for interpreting quantitative results with examples." "How are qualitative findings interpreted? Illustrate with codes and themes."

Research is incomplete until it is reported. Reporting: makes findings available for scrutiny and replication; contributes to the body of knowledge; informs policy and practice; fulfils obligations to participants and funders; and builds the researcher's career.

Various aspects (preliminary, main body, reference matter) Part Contents Preliminary pages Title page; declaration; certificate of supervisor; acknowledgements; abstract (150 to 300 words); table of contents; list of tables; list of figures; abbreviations Chapter 1: Introduction Background; statement of the problem; purpose; research questions / hypotheses; significance; scope and delimitations; operational definitions Chapter 2: Literature review Theoretical/conceptual framework; review of empirical studies; research gap Chapter 3: Methodology Worldview; design; population and sample; instruments; validity and reliability; data collection; analysis; ethical considerations Chapter 4: Results / findings Presented by research question; tables and figures; qualitative themes Chapter 5: Discussion, conclusions and recommendations Interpretation linked to literature; conclusions; implications; limitations; recommendations for practice and further research Reference matter References (APA 7th); appendices (instruments, consent forms, permission letters, extra tables) Table 27. Components of a thesis or research report Pagination Preliminary pages are numbered in lower-case Roman numerals (i, ii, iii); the main text begins with Arabic numeral 1 on the first page of Chapter 1. APA student papers place page numbers at the top right. Tables and figures (APA 7th) Number tables and figures consecutively in bold (Table 1, Figure 1). Give an italicised title in title case on the line below the number. Tables use minimal horizontal lines and no vertical lines. Notes go below the table or figure (general, specific, probability notes). Refer to every table and figure in the text; do not repeat all numbers in prose. Report statistics in APA format: M = 72.00, SD = 8.00; t (58) = 2.57, p = .013; r (48) = .45, p < .001. Writing style and language Clear, concise, objective and formal; avoid bias in language (APA 7th guidelines on bias-free language: person-first or identity-first language as appropriate; singular "they"); use past tense for methods and results, present tense for discussing implications; avoid anthropomorphism; define abbreviations at first use. Referencing APA 7th edition uses the author-date system. Source Reference list format Book Creswell, J. W., & Creswell, J. D. (2018). Purposes of evaluation: judge credibility and quality; decide whether to use findings; identify contributions and weaknesses; learn research skills; peer review for publication; examine theses. Section Guiding questions Title and abstract Is the title concise and informative? Does the abstract summarise purpose, method, results and conclusions? Problem and purpose Is the problem significant and clearly stated? Are questions or hypotheses clear and researchable? Literature review Is it current, relevant, critical and synthesised? Is there a clear gap and framework? Method Is the design appropriate and justified? Is the sample adequate and described? Are instruments valid and reliable? Are procedures replicable? Were ethics addressed? Analysis Are analyses appropriate to questions and data? Are assumptions checked? Are effect sizes reported? Results Are results clearly presented and accurately reported? Discussion Are interpretations supported by data? Are findings related to literature? Are limitations acknowledged? Conclusions and recommendations Do conclusions follow from findings? Are recommendations feasible? References and presentation Are references complete and consistent (APA)? Is the writing clear and well organised? Table 29. Checklist for evaluating a research report Study tip Practise report evaluation the way a journal club does: read one published Bangladeshi article (e.g., Malak et al., 2018, in the Cambridge Journal of Education), evaluate it with the checklist, then note its strengths, weaknesses and how you would improve it. Exam Focus Expect: "Describe the format of a research report." "Explain APA 7th guidelines for tables, figures and referencing." "Prepare a checklist for evaluating a research report and apply it to a study you know."

The word statistics comes from the Latin status (state) and the Italian statista (statesman), reflecting its origin in state record-keeping. Today it has two meanings: (a) numerical facts (e.g., enrolment statistics), and (b) the science of collecting, organising, analysing and interpreting data. Definition Statistics (Croxton & Cowden): "The collection, presentation, analysis and interpretation of numerical data." Definition Statistics (Garrett, 1973): Statistical methods are "the techniques used in the collection, classification, analysis and interpretation of quantitative data" which help us "to describe and to draw inferences" from observed facts in education and psychology. Nature of statistics: it deals with aggregates, not single cases; with numerically expressed facts; facts affected by many causes; collected systematically for a purpose; with reasonable accuracy; and placed in relation to each other for comparison. Statistics is both a science (it has methods and principles) and an art (it requires judgement in application).

t: 1.2 Role of statistics in educational research
x: Figure 1. Functions of statistics in educational research Describing student performance, attendance and teacher characteristics. Measuring reliability and validity of tests (correlations, factor analysis). Comparing teaching methods, schools or groups (t-test, ANOVA). Exploring relationships (correlation) and predicting outcomes (regression). Generalising from samples to populations (inference). Evaluating programmes and policies.

t: 1.3 Contribution of educational statistics to improving education in Bangladesh
x: Bangladesh Context Statistics underpin planning and accountability in Bangladesh: the Annual Primary School Census (DPE) and BANBEIS statistics guide teacher allocation, school construction and budgeting; the National Student Assessment (NSA) and LASI measure learning outcomes; public examination statistics (pass rates, GPA-5) inform debates on quality; household surveys (HIES, MICS) reveal equity gaps by income, gender and location; and SDG 4 indicators track national commitments. Weaknesses include delays in publishing data, limited learning-outcome data at secondary level, inconsistent definitions across agencies, and limited use of data by schools. Verify Before Use Check the most recent APSC, BANBEIS and NSA releases for current indicator values and publication years.

u: Unit 2: Recapitulation: Data Organization, Summarization and Presentation
x: Raw data / raw scores: data in the form originally collected, unorganised. Organised data: arranged in order (array) or grouped into classes. Data summarisation: reducing data to a few meaningful numbers or tables. Distribution of measures: the pattern of scores across the range.

u: Unit 2: Recapitulation: Data Organization, Summarization and Presentation
x: Definition Frequency distribution: A table that shows the number of times (frequency, f) each score or class of scores occurs. It may also show relative frequencies (proportions or percentages) and cumulative frequencies. Purposes: organise raw data; reveal the shape, centre and spread; provide the basis for graphs and computations; allow comparison between groups. Steps in constructing a grouped frequency distribution 1. Find the range = highest score − lowest score. 2. Decide the number of classes (usually 5 to 20; Sturges' rule k ≈ 1 + 3.322 log₁₀N). 3. Determine the class interval (i) ≈ range ÷ number of classes; choose a convenient size (2, 3, 5, 10). 4. Write class limits starting from a multiple of i at or below the lowest score. 5. Tally scores and count frequencies. 6. Add columns for midpoints (x), cumulative frequency (cf) and percentages as needed. Worked Example Marks of 50 M.Ed students were grouped with i = 10: Class Exact limits Midpoint (x) f cf % 30-39 29.5-39.5 34.5 2 2 4 40-49 39.5-49.5 44.5 5 7 10 50-59 49.5-59.5 54.5 9 16 18 60-69 59.5-69.5 64.5 14 30 28 70-79 69.5-79.5 74.5 10 40 20 80-89 79.5-89.5 84.5 6 46 12 90-99 89.5-99.5 94.5 4 50 8 Total 50 100 Table 6. Grouped frequency distribution of 50 students' marks Characteristics of a good frequency distribution: classes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, of equal width, neither too many nor too few, and clearly labelled.

t: 2.4 Using graphs to determine the characteristics of a distribution
x: Graphs reveal four characteristics: central tendency (where scores cluster), variability (spread), skewness (symmetry) and kurtosis (peakedness), as well as modality (unimodal, bimodal) and outliers . u: Unit 3: Recapitulation: Univariate Measures: Central Tendency and Variability
t: 3.1 Central tendency: meaning, use and importance
x: Central tendency is a single value that represents the centre or typical value of a distribution. It summarises data, allows comparison between groups and forms the basis for further analysis.

u: Unit 3: Recapitulation: Univariate Measures: Central Tendency and Variability
x: Ungrouped mean x̄ = Σx / N Grouped mean x̄ = Σfx / N, or by assumed mean: x̄ = A + (Σfd / N) × i Grouped median Md = L + [(N/2 − cf) / f] × i Grouped mode Mo = L + [(f₁ − f₀) / (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × i Empirical relation (moderately skewed): Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean where L = exact lower limit of the median (or modal) class, cf = cumulative frequency below that class, f = frequency of that class, f₁ = frequency of the modal class, f₀ and f₂ = frequencies of the preceding and following classes, and i = class interval. Worked Example For the table in Unit 2 (N = 50): Mean: Σfx = 3,315, so x̄ = 3315 ÷ 50 = 66.30 . Using assumed mean A = 64.5 with d = (x − A)/i: Σfd = 9, so x̄ = 64.5 + (9/50) × 10 = 66.30 . Median: N/2 = 25; median class 60-69 (cf below = 16, f = 14, L = 59.5): Md = 59.5 + [(25 − 16)/14] × 10 = 65.93 . Mode: modal class 60-69 (f₁ = 14, f₀ = 9, f₂ = 10): Mo = 59.5 + [(14 − 9)/(28 − 9 − 10)] × 10 = 59.5 + 5.56 = 65.06 . Measure Strengths Limitations Use when Mean Uses all scores; algebraically manipulable; stable across samples Affected by extreme scores Interval/ratio data, symmetric distributions Median Not affected by extremes; usable with open-ended classes Ignores actual values Skewed data (income), ordinal data Mode Easy; usable with nominal data May not exist or be multiple; unstable Nominal data; most common category Table 8. Comparing mean, median and mode

u: Unit 3: Recapitulation: Univariate Measures: Central Tendency and Variability
x: Variability (dispersion) is the extent to which scores differ from each other and from the centre. Two classes may have the same mean (60) but very different spreads; a teacher's strategy for a homogeneous class differs from that for a heterogeneous one. Variability is also the basis of reliability, correlation and inferential statistics.

u: Unit 3: Recapitulation: Univariate Measures: Central Tendency and Variability
x: Range = H − L Quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) Q = (Q₃ − Q₁) / 2, where Q₁ = L + [(N/4 − cf)/f] × i and Q₃ = L + [(3N/4 − cf)/f] × i Mean deviation MD = Σ|x − x̄| / N Standard deviation (grouped, assumed mean) σ = i × √[Σfd²/N − (Σfd/N)²] Coefficient of variation CV = (σ / x̄) × 100 Worked Example For the same data: Q₁: N/4 = 12.5; class 50-59 (L = 49.5, cf = 7, f = 9): Q₁ = 49.5 + (5.5/9) × 10 = 55.61. Q₃: 3N/4 = 37.5; class 70-79 (L = 69.5, cf = 30, f = 10): Q₃ = 69.5 + 7.5 = 77.00. Q = (77.00 − 55.61)/2 = 10.69 . SD: Σfd = 9, Σfd² = 117: σ = 10 × √(117/50 − 0.0324) = 10 × √2.3076 = 15.19 . CV = 15.19/66.3 × 100 = 22.9% . Measure Merits Demerits Range Simple, quick Based on two extreme values; unstable Quartile deviation Not affected by extremes; for open-ended data Ignores 50% of data Mean deviation Uses all scores Ignores signs; less used in inference Standard deviation Uses all scores; mathematically sound; basis for inference Affected by extremes; harder to compute by hand Table 9. Comparing measures of dispersion

u: Unit 3: Recapitulation: Univariate Measures: Central Tendency and Variability
x: Raw scores from different tests cannot be compared directly. Standard scores express a score's position relative to the mean in SD units. z = (X − x̄) / s T = 50 + 10z Stanine ≈ 5 + 2z (rounded, range 1 to 9) Deviation IQ = 100 + 15z Worked Example Rina scored 75 in Bangla (class mean 60, SD 10) and 80 in mathematics (mean 70, SD 20). z(Bangla) = (75 − 60)/10 = 1.5 ; z(Maths) = (80 − 70)/20 = 0.5 . Relative to her class, Rina performed better in Bangla, despite a lower raw score. T-scores: 65 and 55. Figure 5. The normal curve with standard deviation areas Key Point In a normal distribution, approximately 68.26% of scores lie within ±1 SD, 95.44% within ±2 SD and 99.74% within ±3 SD of the mean. Exam Focus Expect: "Compute the mean, median and mode from a grouped distribution." "Calculate the quartile deviation and standard deviation." "Compare measures of central tendency and variability." "What is a standard score? Convert raw scores into z and T-scores and interpret."

u: Unit 4: Bivariate Measures: Study of Relationship
x: Educational questions often concern relationships: Is time spent reading related to vocabulary? Do SSC results relate to university performance? Is teacher experience related to student achievement? Correlation helps in prediction, test validation (criterion validity), reliability estimation and theory building.

u: Unit 4: Bivariate Measures: Study of Relationship
x: Two variables are related (correlated) when changes in one tend to be accompanied by systematic changes in the other. The coefficient of correlation expresses the direction (+ or −) and strength (0 to 1) of the relationship. Figure 6. Positive, negative and zero correlations

u: Unit 4: Bivariate Measures: Study of Relationship
x: Correlation does not imply causation. A correlation between X and Y may arise because X causes Y, Y causes X (reverse causation), a third variable causes both (spurious correlation), or by chance. For example, the number of private tutors and SSC GPA may correlate because both depend on family income. Figure 7. Correlation versus causation

u: Unit 4: Bivariate Measures: Study of Relationship
x: Simple (bivariate) correlation: between two variables. Multiple correlation (R): between one variable and a combination of two or more others. Partial correlation: between two variables with the effect of a third removed. Positive: both increase together; negative: one increases as the other decreases; zero: no linear relationship. Linear versus curvilinear (e.g., anxiety and performance follow an inverted U, Yerkes-Dodson).

u: Unit 5: Sampling Distribution and its Use
t: 5.1 Concept, role and use of sampling distribution
x: Definition Sampling distribution: The probability distribution of a statistic (such as the mean) obtained from all possible samples of a given size drawn from a population. It shows how a statistic varies from sample to sample due to chance. The sampling distribution is the bridge between descriptive statistics and inference. It tells us how much a sample statistic is expected to differ from the population parameter ( sampling error ) and allows us to compute probabilities, confidence intervals and significance tests. Figure 8. From population to sampling distribution

u: Unit 5: Sampling Distribution and its Use
x: Statistic Standard error (SE) Note Mean (x̄) SE = σ / √n (estimated s / √n) Most widely used Median SE ≈ 1.253 σ / √n Larger than SE of mean for normal data Difference between two means SE = √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂) Basis of the t-test Proportion (p) SE = √[p(1 − p)/n] Surveys Correlation coefficient (r) SE ≈ (1 − ρ²) / √n; Fisher's z' transformation with SE = 1 / √(n − 3) Testing and CIs for r Variance (s²) Related to chi-square distribution with n − 1 df Testing variances Table 13. Common sampling distributions and their standard errors

u: Unit 5: Sampling Distribution and its Use
t: 5.3 The central limit theorem and properties of normality
x: Definition Central limit theorem (CLT): For samples of size n drawn randomly from any population with mean μ and finite standard deviation σ, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n as n increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution. In practice n ≥ 30 is often sufficient. Figure 9. The central limit theorem: means of samples from a skewed population become normal as n increases Properties of the normal distribution: bell-shaped and symmetric; mean = median = mode; asymptotic (tails approach but never touch the x-axis); total area = 1; defined by μ and σ; fixed proportions within SD units (68-95-99.7 rule); inflection points at μ ± σ.

u: Unit 5: Sampling Distribution and its Use
t: 5.4 Distribution of sample means and standard error
x: The mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean (x̄ is an unbiased estimator of μ). The standard error of the mean (SEM) measures the uncertainty of the sample mean. SE(x̄) = σ / √n (estimated: s / √n) Worked Example If the SD of Grade 8 mathematics scores is 12 and a sample of 144 students is drawn, SE = 12 / √144 = 12 / 12 = 1 . About 95% of sample means will lie within ±1.96 marks of the population mean. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error. Key Point The standard error (variability of a statistic across samples) is different from the standard deviation (variability of individual scores) and from the standard error of measurement (variability of an individual's observed scores around the true score in test theory).

u: Unit 5: Sampling Distribution and its Use
x: The standard normal distribution has μ = 0 and σ = 1. Any normal variable is converted to z = (X − μ)/σ, and probabilities are read from the z-table. Worked Example SSC mathematics scores in a district are approximately normal with μ = 60 and σ = 10. (a) What proportion scored above 75? z = (75 − 60)/10 = 1.5; area beyond z = 1.5 is 0.0668 , so about 6.7%. (b) What proportion scored between 50 and 70? z = −1 to +1, area = 0.6827 (about 68%). (c) What score marks the top 10%? z = 1.28, so X = 60 + 1.28 × 10 = 72.8 . Applications: converting scores to percentiles; setting cut-off scores; grading on the curve (with caution); checking normality assumptions; computing probabilities in inference. Exam Focus Expect: "What is a sampling distribution? Explain its role in inference." "State and explain the central limit theorem." "Distinguish standard deviation and standard error." "Solve problems using the normal curve table."

t: 6.1 Rationale for studying probability in research
x: Research uses samples; samples vary by chance. Probability quantifies uncertainty, enabling researchers to decide whether an observed difference is likely to be real or due to chance (significance), to estimate parameters with stated confidence, and to model outcomes (e.g., guessing on MCQs).

t: 6.2 Concept, meaning and types of probability
x: Definition Probability: A numerical measure of the likelihood that an event will occur, ranging from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). P(A) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. Approach Definition Example Classical (a priori) Based on logical analysis of equally likely outcomes, before observation P(head) = 1/2; P(guessing correctly on a 4-option MCQ) = 1/4 Empirical / relative frequency (a posteriori) Based on observed frequencies over many trials If 180 of 1,000 students dropped out, P(dropout) ≈ 0.18 Subjective Based on personal judgement A principal estimates a 70% chance of passing inspection Axiomatic Based on Kolmogorov's axioms Mathematical foundation for all approaches Table 14. Approaches to probability Key Point The syllabus terms a priori and a posteriori probability refer to probability determined before experience (by reasoning) versus after experience (from observed frequencies). In Bayesian statistics, a prior probability is updated with evidence to give a posterior probability.

Addition (mutually exclusive events): P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) General addition: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) Multiplication (independent events): P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) General multiplication: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A) Complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) Bayes' theorem: P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B) Worked Example (1) A student guesses on two 4-option MCQs. P(both correct) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16 = 0.0625 . P(at least one correct) = 1 − (3/4)² = 1 − 0.5625 = 0.4375 . (2) In a class, 40% are girls and 25% wear glasses, 10% are girls with glasses. P(girl or glasses) = 0.40 + 0.25 − 0.10 = 0.55 . Worked Example Bayes' theorem in screening: 5% of children have a reading disability. A screening test detects 90% of affected children (sensitivity) but also flags 10% of unaffected children (false positives). If a child is flagged, P(disability | flagged) = (0.90 × 0.05) / (0.90 × 0.05 + 0.10 × 0.95) = 0.045 / 0.140 = 0.32 . Only about one in three flagged children actually has the disability: a key lesson for teachers about screening.

Binomial distribution Applies when there are n independent trials, each with two outcomes (success/failure) and a constant probability p of success. P(X = k) = ⁿCₖ pᵏ (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ Mean = np; SD = √[np(1 − p)] Worked Example A student guesses all 5 four-option MCQs. P(exactly 3 correct) = ⁵C₃ (0.25)³ (0.75)² = 10 × 0.015625 × 0.5625 = 0.088 . Expected number correct by guessing = 5 × 0.25 = 1.25. This is the basis of correction for guessing formulas. Normal distribution Continuous, symmetric distribution used for many educational measures and as the approximation for many sampling distributions (see Unit 5). The binomial approaches the normal when np and n(1 − p) are both ≥ 5. Other distributions t-distribution (Gosset, "Student", 1908) for small-sample means; chi-square for categorical data and variances; F-distribution (Fisher) for ratios of variances (ANOVA); Poisson for counts of rare events. Point estimates A point estimate is a single value used to estimate a parameter: x̄ estimates μ, s estimates σ, p̂ estimates the population proportion. Good estimators are unbiased , consistent , efficient and sufficient . An interval estimate (confidence interval) supplements a point estimate with a range. 95% confidence interval for μ: x̄ ± t(0.025, n − 1) × s / √n (for large n, use 1.96) Worked Example A sample of 100 teachers has mean job-satisfaction score 3.6 (SD 0.8). SE = 0.08. 95% CI = 3.6 ± 1.96 × 0.08 = 3.44 to 3.76 . Exam Focus Expect: "Explain a priori and a posteriori probability." "State the laws of probability with examples." "Solve a binomial probability problem related to guessing in MCQs." "What are point and interval estimates?"

u: Unit 7: Testing Hypotheses and Making Decisions
x: A statistical hypothesis is a statement about a population parameter. The null hypothesis (H₀) states no effect or no difference (μ₁ = μ₂); the alternative hypothesis (H₁) states that an effect exists (μ₁ ≠ μ₂, two-tailed; or μ₁ > μ₂, one-tailed). Because decisions are based on samples, they carry risks of error. Decision H₀ actually true H₀ actually false Reject H₀ Type I error (probability α, "false positive") Correct (power = 1 − β) Retain H₀ Correct (1 − α) Type II error (probability β, "false negative") Table 15. Accuracy and errors in statistical decisions Figure 10. Type I and Type II errors and the critical region Factors increasing power : larger sample size, larger effect size, higher α, one-tailed test (when justified), reduced variability (reliable measures, homogeneous samples), and matched or repeated-measures designs.

u: Unit 7: Testing Hypotheses and Making Decisions
x: Parametric tests make assumptions about population parameters and distributions: interval/ratio DV, normality (or large n), homogeneity of variances, independence. They are more powerful when assumptions hold. t, Z and F statistics Test Use Formula df Z-test for a mean Large sample or known σ z = (x̄ − μ) / (σ/√n) — One-sample t Compare x̄ with a hypothesised value t = (x̄ − μ) / (s/√n) n − 1 Independent t Two independent means t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / s_diff, s_diff from pooled variance n₁ + n₂ − 2 Paired t Two related means t = d̄ / (s_d / √n) n − 1 F-test Ratio of two variances; ANOVA F = s₁² / s₂² or MS_between / MS_within (df₁, df₂) Table 16. t, Z and F tests Worked Example Paired t-test: Eight students' reading scores before and after a phonics programme: Student 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 Pre 10 12 9 14 11 13 8 15 Post 13 14 9 18 12 17 11 14 d = Post − Pre 3 2 0 4 1 4 3 −1 Table 17. Data for a paired t-test d̄ = 16/8 = 2.0 ; s_d = 1.85; SE = 1.85/√8 = 0.655; t = 2.0/0.655 = 3.06 , df = 7. Critical t (α = .05, two-tailed, df = 7) = 2.365. Since 3.06 > 2.365, H₀ is rejected: reading scores improved significantly. Effect size d = d̄/s_d = 2.0/1.85 = 1.08 (large). Analysis of variance (ANOVA) ANOVA (R. A. Fisher) tests differences among three or more means by partitioning total variance into between-groups and within-groups components. Using multiple t-tests instead inflates the Type I error rate (with three tests at α = .05, the familywise error ≈ 1 − 0.95³ = .14). SS_total = SS_between + SS_within SS_between = Σ nⱼ(x̄ⱼ − x̄_G)² ; SS_within = ΣΣ(x − x̄ⱼ)² MS = SS / df ; F = MS_between / MS_within df_between = k − 1 ; df_within = N − k Worked Example One-way ANOVA: scores of students taught by three methods (n = 5 each): Method A: 6, 8, 7, 9, 10 (mean 8); Method B: 4, 5, 6, 5, 5 (mean 5); Method C: 7, 9, 8, 8, 8 (mean 8). Grand mean = 7. Source SS df MS F Between groups 30 2 15.00 12.86 Within groups 14 12 1.17 Total 44 14 Table 18. ANOVA summary table Critical F(2, 12) at α = .05 = 3.89. Since 12.86 > 3.89, the method means differ significantly. Effect size η² = SS_between / SS_total = 30/44 = 0.68 . Post hoc tests (Tukey HSD, Scheffé, Bonferroni) then identify which pairs differ (here, B differs from A and C). Two-way and multi-factor ANOVA Two-way ANOVA examines two independent variables (factors) simultaneously, e.g., teaching method (A, B) × location (urban, rural). It tests two main effects and their interaction (whether the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other). Figure 12. Interaction in two-way ANOVA: parallel lines show no interaction; crossing lines show interaction Multiple-factor (factorial) ANOVA extends this to three or more factors (e.g., method × gender × location). Repeated-measures ANOVA handles the same participants measured several times; MANOVA handles several dependent variables. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) ANCOVA combines ANOVA with regression: it compares group means on the DV after statistically adjusting for one or more covariates (e.g., pretest scores, IQ). It increases power and reduces bias from initial differences, especially in quasi-experiments with intact classes. Additional assumptions: linear relationship between covariate and DV, and homogeneity of regression slopes across groups. One-way, two-way and multi-factor ANCOVA follow the same logic as ANOVA.

u: Unit 7: Testing Hypotheses and Making Decisions
x: Non-parametric (distribution-free) tests make fewer assumptions about population distributions. They are used with nominal or ordinal data, small samples, skewed data or outliers. They are less powerful than parametric tests when parametric assumptions hold. Situation Test One sample, nominal Chi-square goodness of fit; binomial test Two independent samples, ordinal Wilcoxon rank-sum / Mann-Whitney U Two related samples, ordinal Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-ranks (T); sign test Three or more independent samples Kruskal-Wallis H Three or more related samples Friedman test Association, nominal Chi-square test of independence; phi; Cramér's V Association, ordinal Spearman's rho; Kendall's tau Table 19. Types of non-parametric tests Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U) Compares two independent groups by ranking all scores together and comparing rank sums. U₁ = R₁ − n₁(n₁ + 1)/2 ; U₂ = R₂ − n₂(n₂ + 1)/2 U = the smaller of U₁ and U₂ ; check: U₁ + U₂ = n₁n₂ Worked Example Creativity scores: Group A (art club) 12, 15, 18, 20, 22; Group B (no club) 8, 10, 11, 14, 16. Ranking all ten: B's scores 8, 10, 11 get ranks 1, 2, 3; A's 12 gets 4; B's 14 gets 5; A's 15 gets 6; B's 16 gets 7; A's 18, 20, 22 get 8, 9, 10. R_A = 37, R_B = 18. U_A = 37 − 15 = 22; U_B = 18 − 15 = 3; U = 3 . Critical U (n₁ = n₂ = 5, α = .05 two-tailed) = 2. Since 3 > 2, H₀ is retained (p ≈ .056): the difference is not significant with such small groups. Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-ranks test (T) For two related samples: compute differences, drop zero differences, rank the absolute differences, attach signs, and sum positive and negative ranks; T = the smaller sum. Worked Example Using the pre-post reading data above: differences 3, 2, 0, 4, 1, 4, 3, −1. Drop the zero (n = 7). Absolute values ranked: 1, 1 → ranks 1.5, 1.5; 2 → 3; 3, 3 → 4.5, 4.5; 4, 4 → 6.5, 6.5. The only negative difference (−1) has rank 1.5. T⁻ = 1.5; T⁺ = 26.5; T = 1.5 . Critical T (n = 7, α = .05 two-tailed) = 2. Since 1.5 ≤ 2, H₀ is rejected (p ≈ .047), consistent with the paired t-test. Kruskal-Wallis test Non-parametric equivalent of one-way ANOVA for three or more independent groups. H = [12 / N(N + 1)] Σ (Rⱼ² / nⱼ) − 3(N + 1), df = k − 1 (compare with chi-square) For the three-method data above, H = 9.29 (corrected for ties) > χ²(2) critical 5.99, so the groups differ significantly. Chi-square (χ²) test Definition Chi-square test: A non-parametric test that compares observed frequencies with expected frequencies under H₀. χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E. It is used as a goodness-of-fit test (one variable) and a test of independence (two variables in a contingency table). Limitations: requires frequencies (not percentages or means); observations must be independent; expected frequencies should generally be at least 5 in each cell (otherwise combine categories or use Fisher's exact test); sensitive to sample size; shows association, not its strength or direction (use phi or Cramér's V). #### Chi-square as a goodness-of-fit test Worked Example 60 HSC students choose among three streams. H₀: choices are equally distributed. Observed: Science 28, Humanities 18, Business 14. Expected = 20 each. χ² = (28 − 20)²/20 + (18 − 20)²/20 + (14 − 20)²/20 = 3.2 + 0.2 + 1.8 = 5.20 , df = 2. Critical value = 5.99. Since 5.20 < 5.99, H₀ is retained (p ≈ .074). #### Contingency tables and Yates's correction for continuity For 2 × 2 tables (df = 1), especially with small expected frequencies, Yates's correction subtracts 0.5 from each |O − E| to adjust for using a continuous distribution for discrete counts. Yates: χ² = Σ (|O − E| − 0.5)² / E Shortcut for a 2 × 2 table with cells a, b, c, d: χ² = N(|ad − bc| − N/2)² / [(a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d)] Worked Example 40 students: of 20 who attended remedial classes, 12 passed and 8 failed; of 20 who did not, 5 passed and 15 failed. Without correction: χ² = 40(12 × 15 − 8 × 5)² / (20 × 20 × 17 × 23) = 40 × 19,600 / 156,400 = 5.01 . With Yates: χ² = 40(|180 − 40| − 20)² / 156,400 = 40 × 14,400 / 156,400 = 3.68 . Critical value (df = 1, α = .05) = 3.84. The uncorrected test is significant but the corrected one is not: a reminder that small samples call for caution (Fisher's exact test is a better choice here). #### Chi-square test of independence Worked Example 100 students (50 male, 50 female) are asked if they prefer online classes. Males: 30 yes, 20 no; females: 20 yes, 30 no. Expected for each cell = (50 × 50)/100 = 25. χ² = 4 × (5²/25) = 4.00 , df = 1 > 3.84, so preference is associated with gender (uncorrected). Cramér's V = √(χ²/N) = √0.04 = 0.20 (weak to moderate association).
