t: 8.1 Importance of prediction in educational research
x: Prediction helps in admission and selection (predicting university success from HSC results and admission test scores), early warning systems (predicting dropout from attendance and achievement), guidance and counselling, programme planning and theory testing. Single prediction uses one predictor; multiple prediction uses two or more.

Concept: simple linear regression models the relationship between one predictor (X) and one criterion (Y) with a straight line. Regression equation: Ŷ = a + bX b = Σxy / Σx² (deviation form) = r (s_Y / s_X) a = Ȳ − b X̄ The regression line (line of best fit) is determined by the least-squares criterion : it minimises the sum of squared residuals Σ(Y − Ŷ)². Worked Example Using the six students' data from Unit 4 (Σxy = 425, Σx² = 437.5, X̄ = 57.5, Ȳ = 53): b = 425 / 437.5 = 0.971 ; a = 53 − 0.971 × 57.5 = −2.86 . Regression equation: Ŷ = −2.86 + 0.971X. A student with a class-test score of 62 is predicted to score −2.86 + 60.20 = 57.3 in the final exam. Figure 13. Regression line, predicted values and residuals

t: 8.3 Coefficient of determination and standard error of estimate
x: Coefficient of determination R² (= r² in simple regression) = SS_regression / SS_total Standard error of estimate SEE = √[Σ(Y − Ŷ)² / (N − 2)] = s_Y √(1 − r²) × √[(N − 1)/(N − 2)] Worked Example For the example, r = 0.954, so r² = 0.91 : 91% of the variance in final scores is explained by class-test scores. The residual sum of squares is 41.14, so SEE = √(41.14 / 4) = 3.21 marks: predictions are typically within about ±3.2 marks (about 68% within ±1 SEE, assuming normal residuals).

Multiple regression predicts Y from two or more predictors. Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + ... + bₖXₖ Two uses: 1. Predicting the dependent variable: e.g., predicting first-year university GPA from HSC GPA, admission test score and English proficiency. 2. Assessing the effect of independent variables: the partial regression coefficient bⱼ shows the change in Y for a one-unit change in Xⱼ, holding other predictors constant . Standardised coefficients (β) allow comparison of predictors' relative importance. Worked Example Illustrative output: Ŷ(SSC mathematics score) = 22.5 + 0.45(attendance %) + 3.2(hours of home study per day) + 4.8(mother's education, years ÷ 4). R² = .38, F(3, 296) = 60.3, p < .001. Interpretation: together the three predictors explain 38% of the variance in mathematics scores. Holding the others constant, each additional percentage point of attendance is associated with 0.45 more marks; each additional daily hour of home study with 3.2 more marks. (Numbers are illustrative only.) Concept Meaning Multiple correlation (R) Correlation between observed Y and predicted Ŷ R² Proportion of variance in Y explained by all predictors Adjusted R² R² corrected for number of predictors and sample size F-test for the model Tests whether R² is significantly greater than zero t-tests for coefficients Test whether each predictor contributes significantly Standardised β Coefficients in SD units; compare relative importance Multicollinearity High correlation among predictors; inflates SEs (check VIF > 10 or tolerance < .1) Methods of entry Enter (simultaneous), hierarchical (blocks by theory), stepwise (statistical, criticised) Assumptions Linearity, independence of errors (Durbin-Watson), homoscedasticity, normality of residuals, no influential outliers (Cook's distance) Sample size Rule of thumb N ≥ 50 + 8k for testing R² (Green, 1991), where k is the number of predictors Table 21. Key concepts in multiple regression Critical Perspective Regression shows prediction and association, not causation, unless the design supports causal inference. Stepwise selection capitalises on chance and is discouraged; theory-driven hierarchical regression is preferred. For students nested in schools, multilevel models avoid underestimated standard errors. Study tip Practise the full workflow with free software such as JASP or jamovi (menu-driven, APA-style output), and R if you want to go further: enter data, check assumptions with plots, run the analysis, and write an APA-style results paragraph. Make sure you can explain each number in the output table. Exam Focus Expect: "Explain the importance of prediction in educational research." "Fit a regression line to given data and predict Y for a given X." "Explain the coefficient of determination and the standard error of estimate." "Distinguish simple and multiple regression; interpret a multiple regression output."

u: Unit 1: Introduction to Philosophical Worldview of Research
t: 1.1 Research traditions in science, social science and education
x: Natural science established the model of empirical, experimental, hypothesis-testing research (Bacon, Newton, the "scientific method"). Social science adopted this model in the 19th century (Comte's positivism, Durkheim's social facts) but also developed interpretive traditions (Weber's verstehen , Dilthey's hermeneutics) arguing that human action must be understood through meanings. Educational research grew out of psychology (Thorndike's measurement, experimental pedagogy), philosophy (Dewey's pragmatism and inquiry) and sociology, and today draws on all of these. Phase Period Dominant features Experimental pedagogy and measurement c. 1900 to 1950 Thorndike, Binet, testing movement; "scientific" management of schools Behavioural science and positivist dominance 1950s to 1970s Psychometrics, large surveys (Coleman Report, 1966), process-product research Interpretive and qualitative turn 1970s to 1980s Classroom ethnography, curriculum evaluation (Stenhouse, Parlett & Hamilton), teacher thinking Critical and action research revival 1980s onwards Carr & Kemmis (1986), feminist and critical theory, practitioner research Paradigm pluralism and mixed methods 1990s onwards Pragmatism, mixed methods, design-based research, evidence-based policy and RCTs Contemporary 2010s onwards Implementation science, research-practice partnerships, improvement science, big data and learning analytics Table 1. Phases in the history of educational research

u: Unit 1: Introduction to Philosophical Worldview of Research
t: 1.2 Brief description of dominant educational research
x: Dominant educational research has been largely quantitative : surveys of achievement and attitudes, correlational studies of factors affecting achievement, experiments comparing methods, and large-scale assessments. In Bangladesh, a large proportion of M.Ed and M.Phil theses are descriptive surveys using questionnaires with teachers and students.

u: Unit 1: Introduction to Philosophical Worldview of Research
x: Positivist paradigm: characteristics and role in education Characteristics: a single objective reality; knowledge through observation and measurement; researcher detachment and value-neutrality; hypothesis testing and generalisation; quantification, control and causal explanation. Role in education: standardised testing, experimental evaluation of programmes, large-scale surveys, and evidence-based policy (e.g., randomised controlled trials of interventions). It provides generalisable evidence about "what works" on average. Interpretive paradigm: characteristics and role in education Characteristics: reality is socially constructed; knowledge is understanding of meanings from participants' perspectives; researcher is an instrument; context is central; inductive, qualitative methods. Role in education: understanding classroom culture, teacher beliefs, student experiences, how policies are interpreted; giving voice to marginalised groups. Constructivist and postmodern paradigms Constructivism (Guba & Lincoln) emphasises that knowledge is co-constructed between researcher and participants; multiple realities exist; hermeneutic-dialectical methods are used. Postmodernism (Lyotard: "incredulity toward metanarratives"; Foucault: knowledge-power) rejects universal truths and grand theories, focusing on discourse, power, difference and the deconstruction of taken-for-granted categories (e.g., "normal child", "quality"). u: Unit 1: Introduction to Philosophical Worldview of Research
t: 1.4 Failure of these paradigms to bring change in practice
x: Carr and Kemmis (1986) argued that both positivist and interpretive research fail to change education: Positivist research treats teachers as objects of research and consumers of findings produced by outsiders; it separates theory from practice; generalisations ignore context; findings are written for academics, not teachers. Interpretive research helps us understand practice but tends to leave it unchanged; it accepts participants' self-understandings without questioning distortions created by ideology and power. Both create a theory-practice gap (Hargreaves, 1996, described educational research as a "private, esoteric activity"). Figure 1. Why traditional research often fails to change practice and how action research responds Critical Perspective Carr and Kemmis's critique is influential but contested. Defenders of large-scale research argue that systemic change requires generalisable evidence (e.g., effects of class size or structured pedagogy), while action research may lack rigour and generalisability. A sophisticated view sees different traditions serving different purposes, and builds research-practice partnerships connecting them.

u: Unit 1: Introduction to Philosophical Worldview of Research
t: 1.5 Critical review of prevailing educational research in Bangladesh
x: Common limitations identified in reviews of Bangladeshi educational research (to be examined with the course teacher's guidance): Over-reliance on descriptive surveys with self-report questionnaires. Weak theoretical framing and literature reviews. Limited use of experimental, longitudinal, qualitative or mixed designs. Small, convenience samples and weak sampling justification. Inadequate reporting of validity and reliability. Over-generalised recommendations not linked to findings. Limited dissemination to teachers and policymakers; findings rarely used. Few studies initiated by practising teachers. Study tip Pick one recent M.Ed or M.Phil thesis or BANBEIS/NAEM study. Analyse its paradigm, design, sample, tools and the extent to which its findings could change practice, using the checklist in Unit 7. This makes critique concrete. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Compare positivist, interpretive and constructivist research paradigms." "Why have dominant research paradigms failed to bring change in educational practice? Discuss with reference to Carr and Kemmis." "Critically review the state of educational research in Bangladesh."

Definition Action research (Carr & Kemmis, 1986): "A form of self-reflective enquiry undertaken by participants in social situations in order to improve the rationality and justice of their own practices, their understanding of these practices, and the situations in which the practices are carried out." Definition Action research (Elliott, 1991): "The study of a social situation with a view to improving the quality of action within it." Definition Action research (Mills, 2018): "Any systematic inquiry conducted by teacher researchers, principals, school counselors, or other stakeholders in the teaching/learning environment to gather information about how their particular schools operate, how they teach, and how well their students learn." Figure 2. The basic action research cycle Types of action research Type Interest (Habermas) Purpose Facilitator role Technical Technical interest in control Improve effectiveness of practice; test a predetermined intervention Outside expert directs Practical Practical interest in understanding Improve understanding and practitioners' professional judgement Facilitator encourages reflection Emancipatory / critical Emancipatory interest in freedom Transform practice and its conditions; challenge constraints and injustice Group takes collective responsibility Table 3. Types of action research (Grundy, 1982; Carr & Kemmis, 1986) Other forms include individual teacher research , collaborative action research (teams of teachers), school-wide action research , district-wide action research (Calhoun, 1994) and participatory action research (PAR) (Fals-Borda, Freire, Kemmis).

Characteristics: Practical and problem-focused: starts from a real problem in practice. Cyclical / spiral: plan, act, observe, reflect, repeated. Participatory and collaborative: practitioners are researchers. Reflective: systematic reflection on practice. Situational: findings apply to the specific context. Change-oriented: aims at improvement, not only knowledge. Emergent and flexible: plans evolve. Uses multiple data sources and both qualitative and quantitative data. Scope: teaching methods, classroom management, assessment, curriculum adaptation, inclusion, student motivation, school-community relations, professional development, leadership and school improvement. Rationale: bridges theory and practice; empowers teachers as knowledge creators; improves student learning in context; develops reflective professionals (Schön, 1983); supports school-based professional development; democratises knowledge production.

t: 2.4 Teachers' role in the classroom: behind the scene
x: Behind every visible lesson lies invisible professional work: planning, interpreting the curriculum, knowing learners, assessing and giving feedback, reflecting, managing relationships and emotions, and making hundreds of decisions (Jackson's Life in Classrooms , 1968, estimated around 1,000 interpersonal interactions a day for elementary teachers). Action research makes this hidden work explicit and systematic: teachers become aware of their tacit knowledge (Polanyi), question routines, and gather evidence about the effects of their decisions.

t: 2.5 Teacher as researcher: political, professional and personal dimensions
x: Stenhouse (1975) argued that "it is not enough that teachers' work should be studied: they need to study it themselves". Elliott, Kemmis and others developed the political and professional dimensions. Figure 3. Three dimensions of teacher as researcher Dimension Meaning Example Political Teachers claim a voice in knowledge production and policy; challenge top-down reforms and unjust structures Teachers document the effects of large class sizes and present evidence to the upazila education office Professional Research as part of professional competence and accountability; evidence-informed practice; career development A teacher systematically tests strategies for improving English speaking and shares results in a cluster meeting Personal Self-understanding, reflection on values and identity, personal growth and satisfaction A teacher examines her own gendered expectations of boys and girls in science Table 5. Political, professional and personal dimensions of the teacher-researcher Bangladesh Context In Bangladesh, action research has been promoted in teacher education (B.Ed, M.Ed, Diploma in Primary Education), by NAEM and through projects (e.g., English in Action, subject-based trainings, BRAC IED). Begum and colleagues (2002) argued for problem-based school research by teachers. Barriers include heavy teaching loads, examination pressure, hierarchical supervision, lack of recognition, and the perception that research belongs to universities. Exam Focus Expect: "Define action research and explain its characteristics." "Distinguish technical, practical and emancipatory action research." "Discuss the uses and limitations of action research." "Explain the teacher as researcher in its political, professional and personal dimensions."

Kurt Lewin (1890 to 1947), a German-American social psychologist, coined the term action research in his 1946 paper "Action research and minority problems". He described it as "a comparative research on the conditions and effects of various forms of social action and research leading to social action", proceeding in "a spiral of steps, each of which is composed of a circle of planning, action, and fact-finding about the result of the action". He famously stated that "research that produces nothing but books will not suffice". Figure 4. Lewin's (1946) spiral of action research steps Lewin also contributed field theory , force-field analysis (driving and restraining forces for change) and the three-step model of change (unfreeze, change, refreeze), all widely used in planning educational change. Figure 5. Lewin's force-field analysis applied to introducing group work in a secondary school Stephen Corey (1953) introduced action research into American education at Teachers College, Columbia ("Action research to improve school practices").

t: 3.2 Ideas and influence of Lawrence Stenhouse
x: (The syllabus spells his name "Lawrence steakhouse"; the correct name is Lawrence Stenhouse , 1926 to 1982.) Stenhouse, director of the Humanities Curriculum Project (1967 to 1972) and founder of the Centre for Applied Research in Education (CARE) at the University of East Anglia, revived action research in Britain through the idea of the teacher as researcher . Key ideas: Curriculum as hypothesis: "A curriculum is an attempt to communicate the essential principles and features of an educational proposal in such a form that it is open to critical scrutiny and capable of effective translation into practice." Each classroom is a laboratory where the teacher tests curricular proposals. Process model of curriculum (in contrast to the objectives model of Tyler), emphasising principles of procedure. Extended professionalism: teachers' commitment to systematic questioning of their own teaching, the skills to study it, and the concern to question and test theory in practice. Research as "systematic enquiry made public".

t: 3.3 Schemes of Stephen Kemmis and John Elliott
x: Kemmis and McTaggart's action research spiral Kemmis and McTaggart (1988; Kemmis, McTaggart & Nixon, 2014) represented action research as a self-reflective spiral of cycles: plan, act and observe, reflect , then revised plan , and so on. They emphasised critical participatory action research that is collective, aimed at changing practices, understandings and the conditions of practice ("practice architectures"). Figure 6. Kemmis and McTaggart's self-reflective spiral of action research John Elliott's model Elliott (1991), working in the Ford Teaching Project, refined Lewin's model, arguing that the "general idea" should be allowed to shift, that reconnaissance should involve analysis as well as fact-finding, and that implementation of action steps should be monitored before evaluating effects. Figure 7. John Elliott's (1991) action research model (simplified)

t: 3.4 Jack Whitehead's notion of living educational theory
x: Jack Whitehead (1989) proposed living educational theory : the explanations that individual practitioners create for their own educational influence in their own learning, in the learning of others and in the social formations in which they live and work. The central question is "How do I improve what I am doing?" Practitioners experience themselves as "living contradictions" when their values are denied in practice; action research helps resolve this. Step Question 1 What is my concern? 2 Why am I concerned? (values) 3 What experiences can I describe to show why I am concerned? 4 What can I do about it? What will I do about it? 5 What kind of data will I gather to show the situation as it unfolds? 6 How will I explain my educational influences in learning? 7 How will I ensure that any conclusions I reach are reasonably fair and accurate (validation)? 8 How will I evaluate the evidence-based account of my learning? 9 How will I modify my concerns, ideas and practice in light of my evaluation? Table 6. Whitehead's action-reflection cycle (McNiff & Whitehead, 2011)

Definition Participatory Rural Appraisal (Chambers, 1994): "A growing family of approaches and methods to enable local (rural or urban) people to share, enhance, and analyze their knowledge of life and conditions, to plan and to act." It evolved from Rapid Rural Appraisal (RRA) in the 1980s and 1990s. Principles: handing over the stick (local people lead); optimal ignorance and appropriate imprecision; triangulation; learning from and with local people; self-critical awareness; sharing. t: 4.1 Concept and emergence of qualitative research
x: Definition Qualitative research (Denzin & Lincoln, 2018): "A situated activity that locates the observer in the world. It consists of a set of interpretive, material practices that make the world visible... qualitative researchers study things in their natural settings, attempting to make sense of, or interpret, phenomena in terms of the meanings people bring to them." Definition Qualitative research (Creswell & Poth, 2018): Qualitative research begins with assumptions and interpretive frameworks that inform the study of problems addressing the meaning individuals or groups ascribe to a social or human problem, using an emerging approach, data collection in natural settings sensitive to participants, and inductive and deductive analysis that establishes patterns or themes. Emergence: roots in anthropology (Malinowski's fieldwork), Chicago School sociology (1920s to 1930s), symbolic interactionism (Mead, Blumer), phenomenology (Husserl, Schutz) and hermeneutics. Denzin and Lincoln describe "moments" from the traditional period (1900 to 1950) through modernist, blurred genres, crisis of representation, postmodern, and post-experimental moments. In education, it grew from the 1970s with classroom ethnographies and illuminative evaluation.

t: 4.2 Role of qualitative research in researching education
x: Understanding how teaching and learning happen in real classrooms. Revealing participants' meanings, beliefs and experiences (teachers, students, parents). Explaining why and how policies are interpreted and implemented. Giving voice to marginalised groups (children with disabilities, ethnic minorities, refugees). Generating hypotheses and theories; developing instruments. Evaluating programmes in context (illuminative evaluation).

Patton (2015) identified key themes of qualitative inquiry grouped into design, data collection and analysis strategies: Group Theme Meaning Design Naturalistic inquiry Study real-world settings without manipulation Design Emergent design flexibility Adapt inquiry as understanding deepens Design Purposeful sampling Select information-rich cases Data collection Qualitative data Thick, detailed description; direct quotations Data collection Personal experience and engagement Researcher has direct contact with people and situations Data collection Empathic neutrality and mindfulness Understanding without judgement Data collection Dynamic systems Attention to process and change Analysis Unique case orientation Each case is special Analysis Inductive analysis and creative synthesis Immersion in details to discover patterns Analysis Holistic perspective The whole phenomenon as a complex system Analysis Context sensitivity Findings placed in social, historical, temporal context Analysis Voice, perspective and reflexivity Researcher owns and reflects on their voice Table 9. Major themes of qualitative inquiry (after Patton, 2015)

t: 4.4 Critical analysis of the contribution of quantitative research in education
x: Contributions: generalisable evidence on achievement gaps, effectiveness of interventions (e.g., meta-analyses such as Hattie's Visible Learning ), test development, large-scale monitoring, programme evaluation (RCTs on stipends, teacher training), efficiency and cost-effectiveness analyses. Limitations: reduces complex educational phenomena to variables; neglects context and meaning; may treat participants as objects; measurement validity issues (attitude scales, self-reports); "black box" problem (shows whether something works, not how or why ); limited usefulness for individual teachers; potential to reinforce performativity and narrow accountability.

t: 4.5 Rationale for qualitative research in education
x: Education is a human, social and moral practice embedded in culture. Qualitative research is needed when: the phenomenon is complex and poorly understood; context matters; we need to understand processes and meanings; the voices of participants are missing; quantitative findings require explanation; or theory needs to be developed.

Interpretive frameworks used in qualitative research (Creswell & Poth, 2018) include social constructivism , transformative frameworks , postmodern perspectives , pragmatism , feminist theories , critical theory and critical race theory , queer theory and disability theories . Approaches include symbolic interactionism, ethnomethodology, hermeneutics and narrative inquiry.

u: Unit 5: Data Collection and Making Sense of Data in Qualitative Research
t: 5.4 Content analysis, thematic analysis and interim analysis
x: Content analysis Definition Content analysis (Krippendorff, 2019): "A research technique for making replicable and valid inferences from texts (or other meaningful matter) to the contexts of their use." It can be quantitative (counting categories) or qualitative (interpreting meaning). Hsieh and Shannon (2005) distinguish conventional (categories derived from data), directed (categories from theory) and summative (counting keywords then interpreting) content analysis. Example: analysing gender representation in NCTB textbooks by counting male and female characters and roles. Thematic analysis Definition Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006): "A method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns (themes) within data." Braun and Clarke (2019, 2022) now call their approach reflexive thematic analysis , emphasising the researcher's active role in generating themes. Figure 12. Braun and Clarke's six phases of thematic analysis Data extract Initial code Theme "I have to keep records for 60 students in 6 subjects; it takes my evenings." Record-keeping burden Assessment as paperwork "Parents ask: where are the marks? They don't trust the new symbols." Parental distrust Legitimacy crisis of new assessment "When I give feedback, weak students try again. That is new for me." Feedback motivates Glimpses of assessment for learning Table 15. Thematic analysis illustration (teachers' experiences of continuous assessment) Interim analysis Interim analysis is the cyclical process of collecting and analysing data during a single study, so that early analysis guides further data collection (Johnson & Christensen, 2014). Miles, Huberman and Saldaña (2014) describe analysis as three concurrent flows: data condensation , data display (matrices, networks) and conclusion drawing/verification . Figure 13. Miles, Huberman and Saldaña's interactive model of data analysis

u: Unit 5: Data Collection and Making Sense of Data in Qualitative Research
t: 5.5 Interpreting findings in action research and qualitative research
x: In action research , interpretation asks: What changed? For whom? Why? What evidence shows improvement? What unintended consequences occurred? What did I learn about my practice and values? What next cycle is needed? Evidence is validated with critical friends and participants. In qualitative research , interpretation links themes to the research questions, theory and literature; shows how themes relate to each other (e.g., a thematic map or model); acknowledges alternative interpretations and negative cases; and discusses transferability. Key Point A good qualitative interpretation is plausible , grounded in data (quotations), theoretically informed , reflexive and useful . Avoid simply listing themes; explain their significance. Exam Focus Expect: "Describe the techniques of qualitative data collection." "What is triangulation? Explain its types." "Explain Braun and Clarke's six phases of thematic analysis." "Distinguish content analysis and thematic analysis." "How are findings interpreted in action research?"

u: Unit 6: Mixed Method Approach in Educational Research
x: Definition Mixed methods research (Johnson, Onwuegbuzie & Turner, 2007): "The type of research in which a researcher or team of researchers combines elements of qualitative and quantitative research approaches (e.g., use of qualitative and quantitative viewpoints, data collection, analysis, inference techniques) for the broad purposes of breadth and depth of understanding and corroboration." Definition Mixed methods research (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018): An approach in which the researcher collects and analyses both qualitative and quantitative data rigorously in response to research questions, integrates the two forms of data and their results, organises these procedures into specific designs, and frames them within theory and philosophy. Milestones in the development of mixed methods research

u: Unit 6: Mixed Method Approach in Educational Research
x: Educational problems are complex and multi-level; one method is rarely sufficient. Combines generalisability (QUAN) with depth and context (QUAL). Explains statistical results with participants' voices. Develops and validates instruments grounded in context. Evaluates programmes: whether they work and how/why. Useful for policy audiences who value both numbers and stories. Greene, Caracelli and Graham (1989) identified five purposes: Purpose Meaning Triangulation Seek convergence and corroboration of results from different methods Complementarity Seek elaboration, enhancement or clarification of results from one method with another Development Use results of one method to develop or inform the other (sampling, instruments) Initiation Discover paradox and contradiction leading to new questions Expansion Extend breadth and range of inquiry using different methods for different components Table 17. Purposes of mixed methods (Greene, Caracelli & Graham, 1989)

t: 6.4 Key characteristics of mixed methods design

x: Teddlie and Yu (2007) identified four mixed methods sampling strategies: Strategy Description Example Basic mixed methods sampling Combining probability and purposive features in one sample Stratified purposive sampling of schools Sequential mixed methods sampling Results of the first strand inform sampling for the second Select extreme-scoring teachers from the survey for interviews Concurrent mixed methods sampling Probability and purposive samples drawn at the same time, independently or as subsets Random sample for survey; purposive subsample for observation Multilevel mixed methods sampling Sampling at different levels of a hierarchy Random districts, purposive head teachers, random students Table 19. u: Unit 6: Mixed Method Approach in Educational Research
t: 6.7 Techniques to use different tools together and combine data
x: Integration strategies (Fetters, Curry & Creswell, 2013): Merging: bring QUAN and QUAL results together for comparison (convergent design). Connecting: results of one strand determine the sample for the other (explanatory sequential). Building: results of one strand inform data collection tools or interventions in the other (exploratory sequential). Embedding: data collection and analysis linked at multiple points (intervention designs). Joint displays present quantitative and qualitative results side by side. Survey result (QUAN) Interview theme (QUAL) Meta-inference Teachers in schools with high distributed leadership scores report 25% more weekly collaboration "Our head teacher gives us a period each week to plan together" Structural time for collaboration explains part of the relationship No significant difference between urban and rural schools "In rural schools, we are few, so we talk anyway" versus "In town, there is no time" Similar levels arise for different reasons: contextual mechanisms differ Table 20. Example joint display: teacher collaboration study Data transformation: quantitising qualitative data (counting theme frequencies) or qualitising quantitative data (creating profiles from scores) to compare strands. Critical Perspective Critics warn of "mixed methods lite", in which studies collect both kinds of data but never integrate them. Other debates concern paradigm compatibility, privileging quantitative strands, and the additional demands on novice researchers. Quality requires explicit integration and justification. Exam Focus Expect: "Define mixed methods research and trace its development." "Explain the purposes of mixed methods research (Greene et al.)." "Compare convergent, explanatory sequential and exploratory sequential designs with examples." "Discuss sampling and integration techniques in mixed methods research."

u: Unit 7: Writing Report and Evaluating Research
x: Different research traditions have different report structures, but all share the logic of problem → literature → method → findings → discussion .

u: Unit 7: Writing Report and Evaluating Research
x: Section Content Title and abstract Indicate the focus and context; summary of concern, actions, findings and learning Introduction / context School and classroom context; my role and values; the concern and why it matters Literature Relevant theory and research informing the action Research questions Usually "How can I improve...?" or "What happens when...?" Methodology Action research model; participants; cycles; data collection methods; ethics; validation procedures Cycle 1 Plan, action, observation (data), reflection Cycle 2 (and later) Revised plan, action, observation, reflection Findings and discussion Evidence of change; interpretation; unexpected outcomes; link to literature Learning and implications Personal and professional learning; implications for practice and others Limitations and next steps Honest account; plans for future cycles References and appendices Instruments, samples of student work, consent forms Table 21. Structure of an action research report Feldman and colleagues (University of Massachusetts) suggest writing an action research report as a narrative of practice and inquiry , using the first person, describing the researcher's thinking at each stage, and making the evidence visible.

u: Unit 7: Writing Report and Evaluating Research
x: Structure: introduction (problem, purpose, questions); literature review (often briefer and used as a sensitising frame); methodology (design rationale, researcher positionality, setting, participants and sampling, data collection, analysis procedures, trustworthiness, ethics); findings (organised by themes, with rich description and quotations); discussion (interpretation, relation to literature and theory, implications); conclusion. Writing features: thick description; participants' voices; reflexivity; first-person voice acceptable; narrative structures; careful anonymisation. The Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) (O'Brien et al., 2014) and COREQ (Tong et al., 2007) checklists support complete reporting.

u: Unit 7: Writing Report and Evaluating Research
x: Structure options: (1) separate QUAN and QUAL sections followed by an integration section; or (2) integrated by research question. Essential elements: rationale for mixed methods; design name and diagram; notation; procedures for each strand; integration procedures; joint displays; meta-inferences; legitimation. The Good Reporting of A Mixed Methods Study (GRAMMS) guidelines (O'Cathain et al., 2008) list six items: justify using mixed methods; describe the design (purpose, priority, sequence); describe each method (sampling, data collection, analysis); describe where and how integration occurred; describe limitations of one method associated with the other; describe insights gained from mixing.

u: Unit 7: Writing Report and Evaluating Research
t: 7.5 Evaluating the quality of your research report
x: Research type Quality criteria Action research Evidence of improvement; validated by critical friends; transparency of cycles; congruence with values; catalytic and democratic validity (Herr & Anderson, 2015: outcome, process, democratic, catalytic, dialogic validity) Qualitative Credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability (Lincoln & Guba); Tracy's (2010) eight "big-tent" criteria: worthy topic, rich rigour, sincerity, credibility, resonance, significant contribution, ethics, meaningful coherence Mixed methods Quality of each strand plus integration quality: legitimation types (Onwuegbuzie & Johnson, 2006); GRAMMS completeness Quantitative Internal, external, construct and statistical conclusion validity; reliability Table 22. Quality criteria for different research types Figure 16. Tracy's (2010) eight big-tent criteria for qualitative quality Self-evaluation checklist Is the problem significant and clearly linked to practice? Is the paradigm and design justified and consistent? Are methods described in enough detail to judge and replicate? Is the evidence sufficient and convincing? Are claims supported? Are participants' voices represented fairly? Is the analysis systematic and transparent? Are ethical issues addressed? Is the contribution to practice and knowledge clear? Is the writing clear, well-structured and correctly referenced?

u: Unit 7: Writing Report and Evaluating Research
x: Use APA 7th edition consistently. Key rules: author-date in-text citations; "et al." for three or more authors from the first citation; page numbers for direct quotations (Stenhouse, 1975, p. 143); reference list in alphabetical order with hanging indent; DOIs as URLs (https://doi.org/...); italics for book titles and journal names and volumes. Use reference managers (Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote) to manage citations. Study tip Swap draft reports with a classmate and evaluate each other's work using Tracy's criteria or GRAMMS, then revise. Peer evaluation builds the critical eye you need as a researcher and reviewer. Exam Focus Expect: "Describe the structure of an action research report." "How does a qualitative research report differ from a quantitative one?" "What should a mixed methods report include (GRAMMS)?" "Discuss criteria for evaluating the quality of action, qualitative and mixed methods research."

t: 1.1 Concept of learning, learning experience and learning outcome
x: Definition Learning: A relatively permanent change in behaviour, knowledge, skills, attitudes or capacity that results from experience or practice (not from maturation, fatigue or drugs). Constructivists add that learning is the active construction of meaning by the learner. Definition Learning experience (Tyler, 1949): "The interaction between the learner and the external conditions in the environment to which he can react." Learning takes place through the active behaviour of the student; it is what the learner does that he learns, not what the teacher does. Definition Learning outcome: A statement of what a learner is expected to know, understand and be able to do at the end of a period of learning (e.g., "Students will be able to explain the causes of the Liberation War using at least three sources"). Outcomes are written with observable action verbs. Figure 1. From intended outcomes to evidence of learning

t: 1.2 Types of learning outcomes: basic and higher-order
x: Bloom's taxonomy (cognitive domain) Bloom et al. (1956) classified cognitive objectives into six hierarchical levels; Anderson and Krathwohl (2001) revised them, using verbs and adding a knowledge dimension. Figure 2. Revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) Knowledge dimension Description Example Factual Basic elements: terminology, specific details Name the parts of a flower Conceptual Interrelationships: classifications, principles, theories Explain how pollination leads to fertilisation Procedural How to do something: skills, techniques, methods Use a microscope to observe pollen Metacognitive Knowledge of cognition and self-awareness Plan how to revise for a biology test Table 1. Revised taxonomy: knowledge dimension × cognitive process Basic (lower-order) outcomes: remember, understand, simple application. Higher-order outcomes: analyse, evaluate, create, problem-solving, critical and creative thinking. Other taxonomies Taxonomy Domain Levels Krathwohl, Bloom & Masia (1964) Affective Receiving, responding, valuing, organisation, characterisation by a value complex Simpson (1972) / Harrow (1972) / Dave (1970) Psychomotor Dave: imitation, manipulation, precision, articulation, naturalisation SOLO (Biggs & Collis, 1982) Structure of observed learning outcomes Prestructural, unistructural, multistructural, relational, extended abstract Webb's Depth of Knowledge (1997) Cognitive complexity Recall, skill/concept, strategic thinking, extended thinking Table 2. Other taxonomies of learning outcomes Figure 3. The SOLO taxonomy (Biggs & Collis, 1982)

t: 1.3 Learning theories and their implications for assessment
x: Theory View of learning Implications for assessment Behaviourism (Thorndike, Skinner) Change in observable behaviour through stimulus-response and reinforcement Objective tests of discrete skills; mastery learning; immediate feedback Cognitivism (Piaget, Ausubel, information processing) Mental structures and processes; schema building Assess understanding, misconceptions, problem-solving; concept maps Constructivism (Piaget, Bruner) Learners actively construct knowledge Performance tasks, projects, portfolios; assessment embedded in learning Social constructivism / sociocultural (Vygotsky) Learning through social interaction and mediation; ZPD Dynamic assessment; peer and self-assessment; scaffolding Humanism (Rogers, Maslow) Whole-person growth, self-direction Self-assessment, reflective journals, learner choice Connectivism (Siemens) Learning in networks Digital portfolios, assessing networked participation Table 3. Learning theories and assessment

Assessment drives learning: "Students can, with difficulty, escape from the effects of poor teaching; they cannot (by definition, if they want to graduate) escape the effects of poor assessment" (Boud, 1995). Backwash (washback): the effect of assessment on teaching and learning, which can be positive or negative (Biggs, 2003). Constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang, 2011): intended learning outcomes, teaching-learning activities and assessment tasks should be aligned. Figure 4. Constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang, 2011) Key Point Black and Wiliam's (1998) review Inside the Black Box found that formative assessment produced learning gains with effect sizes of about 0.4 to 0.7, larger than most educational interventions, with particular benefits for lower-achieving students. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Define learning, learning experience and learning outcome." "Explain basic and higher-order learning outcomes with reference to the revised Bloom's taxonomy and SOLO." "Discuss the relationship between learning theories and assessment." "What is constructive alignment?"

Definition Assessment (Harlen, 2007): "The process of gathering, interpreting and using evidence to make judgements about students' achievements in education." Definition Measurement, test and evaluation: Measurement assigns numbers to attributes according to rules; a test is an instrument or procedure for measuring a sample of behaviour; assessment is the broader process of gathering evidence by many methods; evaluation makes value judgements about worth or merit (of students, programmes or policies). Figure 5. Relationship among test, measurement, assessment and evaluation Aspects of assessment: purpose (why), content (what), method (how), timing (when), agent (who: teacher, self, peer, external), interpretation (norm-, criterion- or self-referenced), and use (feedback, grading, certification, selection, accountability).

t: 2.5 Side-effects of assessment and bias in assessment
x: Side-effects Negative washback: teaching to the test, narrowing the curriculum, rote memorisation. Shadow education: private coaching and guidebook dependence oriented to examinations. Stress and anxiety; fear of failure; suicide risk linked to high-stakes results in severe cases. Labelling and lowered self-esteem; self-fulfilling prophecies. Malpractice: cheating, question paper leaks, grade inflation, lenient marking. Campbell's law (1976): "The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor." Bangladesh Context Bangladesh illustrates many side-effects: the proliferation of coaching centres and guidebooks; question-paper leaks in public examinations (notably around 2012 to 2018); a dramatic rise in GPA-5 numbers that raised concerns about grade inflation; and the burden of multiple public examinations (PECE at Grade 5 and JSC at Grade 8, introduced in 2009 and 2010 and later discontinued). Mullick and Begum (2005) documented biases in secondary assessment practices. Bias in assessment Bias Example Content / cultural bias Items assume urban middle-class experiences (e.g., questions about lifts or shopping malls for rural children) Linguistic bias Complex language disadvantages second-language learners and indigenous children Gender bias Stereotyped contexts in items; differential item functioning Socio-economic bias Tasks requiring home resources (internet, materials) Rater biases Halo effect, leniency or severity, central tendency, contrast effect, handwriting and presentation effects, knowing the student's identity Disability bias Lack of accommodations (extra time, Braille, readers) Table 7. Sources of bias in assessment Remedies: blind marking; clear rubrics; moderation; diverse item review panels; differential item functioning (DIF) analysis; universal design of assessment; accommodations.

t: 3.2 Continuous assessment: concept, purpose and nature
x: Definition Continuous assessment: A systematic, ongoing process of gathering evidence of learners' achievement throughout a course, using varied methods (class tests, assignments, observation, projects, portfolios), and using it both to support learning and to contribute to final grades. Purposes: monitor progress, provide timely feedback, reduce dependence on one examination, assess a broader range of outcomes, motivate regular learning. Nature: cumulative, comprehensive, diagnostic, formative, guidance-oriented and systematic. Challenges: teacher workload, large classes, record-keeping, risk of becoming "continuous testing", reliability and favouritism concerns, parental distrust.

Definition Performance assessment: Assessment in which students demonstrate knowledge and skills by performing a task or creating a product , judged against criteria (e.g., conducting an experiment, delivering a speech, building a model). Steps: identify the performance outcome; design a realistic task; specify criteria; develop a rubric or checklist; train raters; give feedback.

x: Classroom assessment is assessment designed and used by teachers within their classrooms, mainly for formative purposes. Definition Authentic assessment (Wiggins, 1990): Assessment is authentic "when we directly examine student performance on worthy intellectual tasks", requiring students to use knowledge in realistic contexts, replicating the challenges faced by adults and professionals. t: 3.6 Role of different types of assessment for students' learning
x: Formative and authentic assessments promote deeper learning, motivation and self-regulation; summative and external assessments provide certification and accountability but can narrow learning if they dominate. A balanced assessment system combines classroom formative assessment, school-based summative assessment and external assessments, all aligned to the same learning goals. t: 4.2 Tests: nature, purpose, scope and limitations
x: A test is a systematic procedure for observing and describing one or more characteristics of a person with the aid of a numerical scale or category system (Cronbach). Good tests have validity , reliability , objectivity , usability (practicality) and discrimination . Limitations: sample only part of the domain; measurement error; may encourage memorisation; cultural bias; anxiety; inadequate for complex skills and attitudes. Short-answer (restricted response) limits content and form ("List three causes..."); long-answer (extended response) allows freedom to organise and develop ideas. Strengths: measure higher-order thinking, organisation, expression; easy to construct. Limitations: limited content sampling; subjective and unreliable scoring; time-consuming marking; bluffing. Principles of writing essay questions: 1. Use essays for outcomes that cannot be measured well by objective items. 2. Define the task clearly with specific verbs ("compare", "evaluate") and scope. 3. Indicate marks and suggested time. 4. Avoid optional questions when comparability matters (they reduce reliability). 5. Prepare a model answer or rubric in advance.

Item type Guidelines Common flaws Multiple choice (stem + key + distractors) Clear stem with a central problem; plausible, homogeneous distractors; one best answer; 3 to 4 options; avoid "all of the above"; avoid negatives or highlight them; options of similar length Grammatical cues, longest-option-correct, implausible distractors, overlapping options True-false Simple statements; one idea; avoid specific determiners ("always", "never"); balance true and false High guessing (50%), ambiguity Matching Homogeneous lists; more responses than premises; brief responses on the right; instructions on reuse Heterogeneous lists, clues Fill in the blank (completion) One blank near the end; only key words omitted; one correct answer Multiple acceptable answers, too many blanks Table 14. Objective item types and writing guidelines Research on MCQ item-writing flaws (e.g., Tarrant et al., 2006) shows flawed items are common in teacher-made and high-stakes tests and disadvantage high-achieving students. Well-written MCQs can assess application and analysis (context-dependent items using scenarios, data or passages). Item analysis Difficulty index p = (U + L) / (2n) Discrimination index D = (U − L) / n where U and L are the numbers answering correctly in the upper and lower groups (often top and bottom 27%), each of size n Worked Example With n = 20 in each group, if 16 in the upper group and 8 in the lower group answer an item correctly: p = 24 / 40 = 0.60 (moderate difficulty); D = (16 − 8) / 20 = 0.40 (very good discrimination). Ebel's guideline: D ≥ .40 very good; .30 to .39 reasonably good; .20 to .29 marginal; < .20 poor (revise or discard). Distractors chosen by no one or chosen more by the upper group should be revised.

t: 4.5 Structured / creative questions: principles and practices
x: Bangladesh Context Bangladesh introduced creative questions (srijonshil prosno) , a form of structured question, at SSC from 2008 and later across subjects and levels. Each question presents a stem (a scenario, passage, diagram or data) followed by four parts aligned to Bloom-based levels: (a) knowledge , (b) comprehension , (c) application , and (d) higher-order abilities (analysis, synthesis, evaluation), typically worth 1, 2, 3 and 4 marks. The aim was to reduce rote memorisation and guidebook dependence. Part Cognitive level Marks Example (Bangladesh and Global Studies) Stem — — A short scenario about a village where floods disrupt schooling every year (a) Knowledge 1 What is the Delta Plan? (b) Comprehension 2 Explain why floods affect school attendance. (c) Application 3 How can the village school apply disaster preparedness measures? (d) Higher-order 4 Evaluate the role of government and community in ensuring education during floods. Table 15. Structure of a creative (structured) question Critical Perspective Studies found that creative questions were poorly understood by many teachers, questions were often copied from guidebooks, and students memorised answers to anticipated stems, which reproduced the problem they were meant to solve. Begum and Ahmed (2007) questioned whether secondary assessment tools encouraged higher-order learning. Effective implementation requires teacher training in item writing, question banks, and novel stems in examinations.

To discourage guessing, a correction for guessing (formula scoring) may be applied. S = R − W / (k − 1) where S = corrected score, R = number right, W = number wrong (omitted items not counted), k = number of options per item Worked Example On a 60-item test with four options, a student answers 40 correctly, 16 wrongly and omits 4. S = 40 − 16 / 3 = 40 − 5.33 = 34.67 . With true-false items (k = 2), S = R − W. Critical Perspective Frary (1988) noted that correction for guessing changes rank order very little when nearly all items are attempted, may penalise risk-averse students (often girls) who omit items, and encourages test-wiseness strategies. Many testing programmes therefore advise students to answer every item and do not use correction. Bangladesh's public examinations do not apply negative marking at school level, while some admission tests (e.g., university entrance) use negative marking (e.g., 0.25 deducted per wrong answer). Verify Before Use Confirm current negative-marking rules for specific admission tests and the BCS preliminary examination, which change by year and institution.

1. Prepare a model answer or analytic rubric before marking. 2. Mark question by question (all students' Q1, then Q2) rather than script by script. 3. Avoid halo effects from handwriting, length or prior knowledge of the student. 7. Use double marking or moderation for high-stakes decisions. 8. Write constructive comments for feedback. t: 7.2 Public examinations: nature and critical analysis of tests
x: Nature: centrally set, board-administered, high-stakes, largely paper-based; mix of MCQ (objective) and creative (structured) questions; practicals in science subjects; results reported as GPA. Critical analysis: Validity: emphasis on recall even within creative questions; limited assessment of practical, oral, collaborative and higher-order skills. Reliability: marker inconsistency; limited moderation time; lenient marking instructions alleged in some years. Washback: coaching, guidebooks, memorisation; narrowing of curriculum to examinable subjects. Equity: urban and private schools perform better; costs of coaching disadvantage the poor. Integrity: question leaks undermined credibility (e.g., 2014 to 2018); countermeasures included question sets distributed digitally on exam morning. Grade inflation: rapid growth in GPA-5 numbers created a ceiling effect, reducing the discriminating power of results for admission.

x: Strengths Weaknesses Standardised and nationally recognised High stakes, single-shot Objective MCQ component improves reliability MCQ often recall-based; reduced later in weight Creative questions aim at higher-order thinking Implementation weaknesses; guidebook dependence Transparent GPA reporting Grade inflation; limited information on specific competencies Practical component in science Practical marks often inflated Table 26. Strengths and weaknesses of current SSC/HSC assessment scheme Bangladesh Context School-based assessment (SBA) was piloted at secondary level from around 2007 (with 30% weight for SBA proposed), but was withdrawn amid concerns about teacher capacity, fairness and workload (Begum & Farooqui, 2008). Lessons: SBA needs teacher training, moderation, manageable record-keeping and public trust.

t: 7.4 Continuous assessment at primary level: review and critique
x: Under PEDP II, PEDP3 and PEDP4, continuous assessment (CA) and competency-based approaches were promoted, with teacher guides and training (including in the Diploma in Primary Education, DPEd). Reviews found that CA was frequently implemented as additional tests and record-keeping rather than formative feedback; large class sizes, teacher shortages and examination pressure (especially while PECE existed) limited its effect. The 2021 National Curriculum Framework proposed that Grades 1 to 3 be assessed fully through continuous (learning-period) assessment and that higher grades combine continuous and summative assessment, reporting achievement through performance indicators and descriptors rather than marks. Public concern about the absence of marks and about record-keeping contributed to its reversal. Critical Perspective The Bangladesh experience shows that assessment reform succeeds only when teacher assessment literacy , public understanding , manageable workload , moderation systems and alignment with high-stakes examinations are all addressed together. Reforms imposed quickly, without piloting and communication, tend to be resisted or ritualised. Exam Focus Expect: "Describe the nature of student assessment at different levels in Bangladesh." "Critically analyse SSC and HSC examinations." "Review continuous assessment at primary level." "Why did school-based assessment fail in Bangladesh? What lessons can be learned?"

Definition Evaluation (Scriven, 1991): "The process of determining the merit, worth, or value of something, or the product of that process." Definition Evaluation (Stufflebeam, 1971): "The process of delineating, obtaining, and providing useful information for judging decision alternatives." Definition Evaluation (Tyler, 1949): "The process of determining to what extent the educational objectives are actually being realised by the programme of curriculum and instruction." Definition Evaluation (Weiss, 1972): "The systematic assessment of the operation and/or the outcomes of a program or policy, compared to a set of explicit or implicit standards, as a means of contributing to the improvement of the program or policy." Merit is intrinsic quality; worth is value in a particular context (Scriven). Evaluation thus combines evidence with judgement against criteria .

The syllabus lists models adapted from Hopkins (1989), Evaluation for School Development , which drew on Parlett and Hamilton (1972) and MacDonald and Walker. The classical / agricultural-botany model Derived from agricultural experiments (Fisher) in which plots receive different treatments and yields are measured. In education, students are given pretests, exposed to a programme, and given post-tests; results are compared with a control group. It emphasises objectives , measurement and experimental design (Tyler's objectives model is related). Strengths: rigour, quantifiable results. Limitations: Parlett and Hamilton (1972) criticised it as treating students like plants: it ignores context, process and participants' experience; assumes stable conditions; and focuses on narrow, measurable outcomes. The research and development (R&D) / industrial-factory model Treats curriculum development like industrial product development: define objectives, design materials, field-test, measure against specifications, revise, and disseminate. Evaluation checks whether the "product" meets its specifications (quality control). Common in large curriculum projects of the 1960s and 1970s. Limitations: assumes teachers are passive implementers; mechanistic view of education; ignores local adaptation. The illuminative / anthropological model Parlett and Hamilton (1972) proposed illuminative evaluation : "to study the innovatory programme: how it operates; how it is influenced by the various school situations in which it is applied; what those directly concerned regard as its advantages and disadvantages; and how students' intellectual tasks and academic experiences are most affected." It focuses on the instructional system (the formal plan) and the learning milieu (the social-psychological and material environment). Methods: observation, interviews, questionnaires and documents, in three overlapping stages: observe, inquire further, seek to explain ("progressive focusing"). The briefing decision-makers / political model (Included in Hopkins's list.) The evaluator provides information to decision-makers, often external, to support policy choices; MacDonald (1976) distinguished bureaucratic , autocratic and democratic evaluation according to whose interests the evaluation serves. The teacher as researcher / professional model Based on Stenhouse: teachers evaluate their own practice systematically as part of professional development (closely linked to action research). Evaluation is formative, internal and improvement-oriented. Strengths: ownership, relevance, professional growth. Limitations: time, skills, potential bias, limited external credibility. The case study / portrayal model Stake's responsive evaluation and portrayal aim to give a holistic, vivid account of a programme case, representing the perspectives of different stakeholders so that audiences can make their own judgements. MacDonald and Walker's democratic evaluation emphasises negotiation and access for all stakeholders. Quantitative: descriptive statistics, comparison of groups (t-tests, ANOVA), regression, effect sizes, cost-effectiveness ratios. Qualitative: thematic analysis of interviews and observations, case narratives, contribution analysis. Mixed: joint displays and triangulation.

Structure of an evaluation report Reports should be tailored to audiences: policy briefs for decision-makers, community feedback meetings, infographics, and technical reports for specialists.

Evaluation is valuable only when used. Types of use: instrumental (direct decisions), conceptual (changing understanding), process use (learning from participating in evaluation) and symbolic (legitimising decisions). Patton's (2008) utilisation-focused evaluation designs evaluations from the start for "intended use by intended users". Organisations learn through management response plans, follow-up of recommendations, dissemination, and building a culture of evidence. Bangladesh Context Large programmes in Bangladesh, such as PEDP, stipend programmes and school feeding, have been evaluated through joint annual reviews, mid-term reviews and impact evaluations (e.g., by the World Bank, BIDS and IFPRI). Evaluations of the school feeding programme, for example, found improvements in enrolment and attendance. Use of evaluation findings in policy has been uneven; strengthening the Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED) and institutional M&E capacity is an ongoing need. Verify Before Use Cite specific evaluation findings (e.g., attendance gains from school feeding or stipends) only after checking the original evaluation reports. Exam Focus Expect: "How would you design a programme evaluation? Explain evaluation questions, the evaluator's role, data collection, analysis and reporting." "What is utilisation-focused evaluation?" "Design an evaluation of a teacher training programme in Bangladesh."

Definition Quantitative research: An approach that investigates a problem by collecting numerical data from a sample, analysing them with statistics, and generalising findings to a population. It is based on a post-positivist view that reality can be measured, at least approximately, and that hypotheses can be tested (Creswell, 2008). Design Purpose Typical Master's project Analysis Descriptive survey Describe attitudes, practices, opinions or characteristics of a population Secondary teachers' use of formative assessment in Dhaka Frequencies, percentages, means, SD Correlational Examine the relationship between two or more variables Relationship between study habits and HSC GPA Pearson r, Spearman rho, regression Causal-comparative (ex post facto) Compare existing groups on an outcome Achievement of students who attend coaching vs. those who do not t-test, ANOVA, chi-square True experiment Test cause and effect with random assignment Effect of cooperative learning on Grade 8 science achievement t-test, ANCOVA Quasi-experiment Test an intervention with intact groups Effect of digital content on two existing sections of a class ANCOVA on post-test with pre-test as covariate Table 1. Quantitative designs suitable for a one-semester project Nature and sources of data Primary data : collected by the researcher through questionnaires, tests, rating scales, observation schedules or structured interviews. Secondary data : existing datasets such as BANBEIS statistics, board examination results, the National Student Assessment (NSA), school records, the Education Household Survey, or international datasets (e.g., MICS). Levels of measurement : nominal (gender, school type), ordinal (Likert items, ranks), interval (test scores, scale totals) and ratio (age, hours of study). The level decides the statistic. Key Point Every quantitative study rests on a chain: variable → operational definition → instrument → item → score → statistic → inference . A weak link anywhere (e.g., a vague construct, an unpiloted questionnaire) cannot be repaired by sophisticated analysis.

Figure 1. Workflow for a small-scale survey Writing research questions and hypotheses Descriptive RQ : "What is the level of ICT use in teaching among secondary teachers in Rajshahi city?" Comparative RQ : "Is there a significant difference in ICT use between government and non-government school teachers?" Relational RQ : "What is the relationship between teachers' ICT self-efficacy and their classroom ICT use?" Null hypothesis (H₀) : There is no significant difference in ICT use between male and female teachers. Determining sample size Cochran (infinite population): n₀ = Z² p q / e² = (1.96)² (0.5)(0.5) / (0.05)² ≈ 384 Finite population correction: n = n₀ / [1 + (n₀ − 1) / N] Yamane (1967): n = N / (1 + N e²) Worked Example A district has N = 1,200 secondary teachers. With 95% confidence and a 5% margin of error: Cochran gives n₀ = 384.16, and with the finite population correction n = 384.16 / [1 + 383.16 / 1,200] = 291 teachers. Yamane gives n = 1,200 / (1 + 1,200 × 0.0025) = 1,200 / 4 = 300 . For a one-semester Master's project, a smaller purposive or cluster sample (e.g., 100 to 150 teachers in 10 to 15 schools) is acceptable if the limitation on generalisation is clearly stated. Study tip Students often over-promise. Agree a feasible scope with your supervisor early: one upazila or city corporation area, one level of education, one or two key variables, and a sample you can reach within four weeks of fieldwork. Developing a questionnaire (Gillham, 2008; Cox & Cox, 2008) 1. List the constructs and sub-dimensions from the literature (a blueprint ). 2. Write 4 to 8 items per dimension; use simple Bangla or English, one idea per item, and avoid double-barrelled, leading and negative items. 3. Choose response formats: 5-point Likert (Strongly disagree to Strongly agree), frequency scales (Never to Always), checklists or short open items. 4. Add a demographic section (gender, experience, school type, training) at the end. 5. Have 3 to 5 experts judge content validity; compute a content validity index (CVI) if possible. 6. Translate and back-translate if an instrument is adapted from English. 7. Pilot with 20 to 30 respondents outside the sample; compute Cronbach's alpha (α ≥ .70 acceptable) and revise unclear items. Figure 2. True experiment vs. quasi-experiment 1. Choose an intervention that can be implemented in 3 to 6 weeks (e.g., concept mapping, cooperative learning, multimedia content, think-pair-share, formative feedback). 2. Define the dependent variable and develop a test aligned with the content taught (use a table of specifications; compute reliability). 3. Select the design : pre-test/post-test control group design is the most practical. 4. Select groups : two comparable sections (e.g., Class 8 A and Class 8 B) in the same school, taught by the same or similarly qualified teachers. 5. Prepare lesson plans for both groups covering identical content; only the method differs. 6. Administer the pre-test , implement the treatment, then the post-test under identical conditions. 7. Control threats : same content and time, same test, blind marking where possible, monitoring of implementation fidelity. 8. Analyse : independent-samples t-test on gain scores or ANCOVA on post-test scores with pre-test as covariate; report effect size. Pre-test/post-test control group design: R O₁ X O₂ (experimental group) R O₃ O₄ (control group) R = random assignment; O = observation (test); X = treatment Threat Example in a classroom study Control History A school event or coaching affects one group Run groups simultaneously; record events Maturation Students improve naturally over time Use a control group Testing Pre-test sensitises students to post-test Use parallel forms or longer gap Instrumentation Different markers or test versions Same test, marking scheme and marker Selection Sections differ in ability at the start Pre-test; ANCOVA; matching Mortality (attrition) Students absent at post-test Track attendance; analyse completers and report losses Diffusion of treatment Control students borrow materials Separate schedules; brief teachers Experimenter effect Researcher's enthusiasm boosts results Use regular teacher; standard scripts Table 3. Threats to internal validity and how to handle them in a school experiment Worked Example Effect of cooperative learning on Grade 8 science achievement. Experimental group (n = 30): post-test M = 68.4, SD = 9.2. Control group (n = 30): M = 62.1, SD = 10.1. Independent-samples t-test: t(58) = 2.53, p = .014 . Pooled SD ≈ 9.66, so Cohen's d = 6.3 / 9.66 ≈ 0.65 , a medium-to-large effect. Report: "Students taught through cooperative learning scored significantly higher than those taught through the lecture method, t(58) = 2.53, p = .014, d = 0.65." If pre-test means differed, ANCOVA would be preferred.

Choosing a statistic for a Master's quantitative project Critical Perspective Common weaknesses in student surveys: unpiloted instruments, no reliability evidence, convenience samples described as "random", treating each Likert item as interval data without justification, reporting only percentages, and interpreting correlation as causation. In experiments: no pre-test, unequal teaching time, a test that does not match the treatment, and ignoring effect size. Study tip Self-check list for Unit 1: (1) your research questions are answerable with numbers; (2) constructs are operationally defined; (3) the instrument has a blueprint, expert review, pilot and alpha; (4) sampling is described honestly; (5) data are cleaned and coded with a codebook; (6) each RQ is matched to an analysis; (7) tables follow APA format; (8) findings are discussed against the literature. x: Qualitative problems are framed around a central phenomenon and use open, exploratory language: explore , understand , describe , discover . A good test is whether the question begins with "how" or "what" and cannot be answered with a number. Weak : "What percentage of teachers use multimedia?" (quantitative) Better : "How do secondary teachers in a rural upazila experience the use of multimedia classrooms?" Central question : "How do head teachers make sense of their role in school-based teacher professional development?" Sub-questions : What practices do they describe? What constraints do they face? What support do they value? x: Figure 4. Workflow for a small-scale qualitative study Purposeful sampling Qualitative studies select information-rich cases. Strategies include maximal variation, typical case, extreme case, homogeneous, snowball and criterion sampling. For a semester project, 6 to 12 interview participants, or 1 to 3 cases, is realistic. Saturation (when new data add no new themes) guides when to stop. Interview protocol (sample) Section Questions and probes Opening Tell me about your teaching career and the subjects you teach. Experience Can you describe a recent lesson in which you used the multimedia classroom? What happened? How did students respond? Meaning What does using digital content mean for you as a teacher? Has it changed how you see your role? Challenges What difficulties do you face (electricity, devices, training, time)? Can you give an example? Support What support have you received from the head teacher, upazila office or colleagues? Closing Is there anything else you would like to tell me? May I contact you to check my interpretation? Table 7. Semi-structured interview protocol: teachers' experience of multimedia classrooms Study tip Practise probing: "Can you tell me more?" "Can you give an example?" "How did you feel about that?" Silence is also a probe. Record with permission, take brief notes, and write a contact summary within 24 hours of each interview. Observation protocol and field notes Field notes have two columns: descriptive notes (what was seen and heard, with time, setting, people, actions, quotations) and reflective notes (the researcher's thoughts, hunches, questions and feelings). Spradley's (1980) nine dimensions (space, actors, activities, objects, acts, events, time, goals, feelings) help beginners decide what to observe. Focus groups (Barbour, 2007) A focus group of 6 to 8 participants discusses a topic guided by a moderator. It is useful for exploring shared views and how opinions form through interaction, e.g., students' views on guidebooks or parents' views on the new curriculum. Plan a topic guide of 5 to 7 questions, a note-taker, seating in a circle and a 60 to 90 minute session. Be careful with sensitive topics, since participants hear each other.
