From data to themes: a worked coding example Coding approaches : in vivo codes (participants' words), descriptive codes and process codes; open coding followed by grouping into categories (axial coding). Tools : manual coding with colour highlighters or a spreadsheet; software such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti or the free QDA Miner Lite and Taguette. Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006): familiarisation, generating codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes, and writing up. Trustworthiness Criterion Parallel concept Strategies Credibility Internal validity Prolonged engagement, triangulation, member checking, peer debriefing Transferability External validity Thick description of setting and participants Dependability Reliability Audit trail, consistent protocols, code-recode Confirmability Objectivity Reflexive journal, audit trail, quotations supporting claims Table 9. Lincoln and Guba's (1985) criteria and strategies Critical Perspective Common weaknesses: "qualitative" studies that merely tabulate open-ended answers; leading interview questions; no description of how codes became themes; long quotations with no interpretation; claiming generalisation from four interviews; and no reflexivity about the researcher's position (e.g., a teacher studying colleagues in her own school). Bangladesh Context Positionality matters in Bangladesh: hierarchy (a junior researcher interviewing a head teacher or officer), gender norms (male researchers interviewing female participants in rural settings), and language (Bangla dialects, Indigenous languages such as Chakma or Santali) all shape data. Interviewing in the participant's language, choosing a comfortable venue and reassuring participants about anonymity improve data quality. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Distinguish case study, ethnography and narrative research." "Design a qualitative study on a problem of your choice, with an interview protocol." "Explain the process of coding and theme development with an example." "How do you establish trustworthiness in qualitative research?"

Definition Mixed methods research: A design in which the researcher collects, analyses and integrates both quantitative and qualitative data within a single study or series of studies, to gain a more complete understanding of a research problem than either approach alone could provide (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018; Johnson & Christensen, 2008). Why mix methods? Triangulation : corroborate findings from different data (e.g., survey and interviews). Complementarity : elaborate or explain results (e.g., why scores rose). Development : use one method to build the other (e.g., interviews to develop a questionnaire). Expansion : extend the breadth and range of inquiry. Initiation : discover contradictions that generate new questions (Greene, Caracelli & Graham, 1989). Figure 6. The three core mixed methods designs (Creswell & Plano Clark, 2018) Design Sequence Purpose Example Convergent (parallel) QUAN + QUAL at the same time, then merge Compare and validate results Survey of 120 students on writing anxiety plus interviews with 8 students; compare (cf. Rezaei & Jafari, 2014) Explanatory sequential QUAN → qual Explain quantitative results Survey of teachers' assessment practices, then interviews with high and low scorers to explain differences Exploratory sequential QUAL → quan Develop an instrument or test a theory Focus groups with students on causes of dropout, then a questionnaire based on the themes Embedded / intervention QUAL inside an experiment Understand how an intervention works Writing-to-learn experiment with student interviews (cf. Hohenshell & Hand, 2006) Table 10. Core designs and their use in a semester project Key Point Notation (Morse, 1991): capital letters show priority (QUAN, QUAL), lower case shows less weight (quan, qual), "+" means concurrent, "→" means sequential. QUAN → qual is an explanatory design with quantitative priority.

A mixed methods problem is one where one type of data is not enough . Students should be able to write a mixed methods question that states how the two strands connect, e.g., "To what extent do the interview findings explain the survey results about why teachers rarely use peer assessment?" Levels, types and causes of writing anxiety among EFL students in a Bangladeshi university. Teachers' perceptions and practice of classroom assessment techniques (cf. Muhammad, Hafsa & Iqra, 2018). Effect of a reading programme on Grade 3 fluency, and teachers' and parents' experiences of it. Causes of student dropout in a haor-area secondary school: survey plus case narratives.

Figure 7. Workflow for an explanatory sequential study Integration: the heart of mixed methods Integration can happen at the level of design (sequencing), methods (connecting the sample of one strand to the other, building an instrument), analysis (merging, joint displays) and interpretation (discussing convergence, complementarity or discordance). Survey result (n = 140) Interview theme (n = 10) Integrated interpretation Only 18% use peer assessment often "Students cannot judge each other fairly" Low use linked to doubts about students' competence Use is higher among trained teachers (M = 3.4 vs. 2.6) Trained teachers describe rubrics as making peer assessment possible Training with rubrics may enable practice (confirming) Class size not significantly related to use Teachers still name large classes as a barrier Perceived and statistical barriers diverge: discuss why (discordant) Table 11. Joint display example: teachers' use of peer assessment Study tip A table of the type above is the single best way to show examiners that your study is genuinely mixed, rather than two separate studies stapled together. Critical Perspective Common weaknesses: no rationale for mixing; the qualitative strand reduced to a few open-ended survey items; the two strands reported separately without integration; and inconsistent paradigms. Pragmatism (what works for the question) is the usual philosophical justification. Exam Focus Likely questions: "What is mixed methods research? Why is it used?" "Compare convergent, explanatory and exploratory designs with diagrams." "Design an explanatory sequential study on a problem in Bangladesh." "What is integration in mixed methods research? Explain joint displays."

t: 4.1 Review of concepts, nature and scope
x: Definition Action research: A form of self-reflective inquiry undertaken by practitioners in social situations in order to improve the rationality and justice of their own practices, their understanding of these practices, and the situations in which the practices are carried out (Carr & Kemmis, 1986). In education it is research by teachers, for teachers, about their own practice (McNiff & Whitehead, 2005). Figure 8. Kemmis and McTaggart's self-reflective spiral of action research Aspect Conventional research Action research Who External researcher Teacher or practitioner as researcher Purpose Generate generalisable knowledge Improve own practice and local situation Design Fixed in advance Cyclical and emergent Sample Representative sample Own class, school or group Validity Statistical and design rigour Usefulness, credibility, triangulation, critical friends Output Journal article, thesis Improved practice, report, shared learning Table 12. Action research compared with conventional research Types and scope Technical (improve effectiveness of a practice), practical (improve understanding and judgement) and emancipatory or critical (challenge constraints and inequities) (Grundy, 1982). Individual , collaborative (a group of teachers) and school-wide action research. Scope in education: teaching methods, classroom management, assessment, student motivation, attendance, homework, parental involvement, inclusive practice, school leadership. Bangladesh Context Action research has been encouraged in B.Ed and M.Ed programmes, in PTI and TTC training, and in initiatives such as lesson study and teacher learning circles under PEDP and secondary projects. It suits Bangladesh classrooms because it needs few resources and addresses problems teachers actually face, such as large classes, absenteeism, weak reading or low participation of girls in discussion.

t: 4.2 Selecting a problem and designing a framework
x: A good action research problem is within the teacher's control , important to students' learning , and small enough to change in 4 to 8 weeks. The question usually takes the form "How can I improve ...?" (McNiff & Whitehead, 2005). Concern Action research question Possible action Many students do not complete homework How can I increase homework completion in my Class 7 English class? Shorter, differentiated tasks; homework diary; parent SMS Students are silent in class How can I encourage more students to participate in discussion? Think-pair-share; wait time; random calling sticks Weak reading fluency in Grade 3 How can I improve the reading fluency of my weakest readers? Paired reading; graded readers; daily 10-minute practice Back-benchers disengaged How can I engage back-bench students in mathematics? Rotating seating; group work with roles Low use of feedback How can I help students use my feedback to improve their writing? Two stars and a wish; redrafting time Table 13. Turning concerns into action research questions Figure 9. The action research cycle used in the course project Data collection tools for action research Baseline and post data : attendance or homework registers, short tests, reading-fluency counts (words correct per minute), participation tallies. Observation : a colleague as critical friend uses a simple checklist; video with permission. Teacher research journal : daily reflections on what happened and why. Student voice : exit tickets, short questionnaires, drawings or group discussions. Artefacts : students' work samples before and after. Worked Example A Class 7 English teacher found that only 42% of 50 students completed homework over two baseline weeks. Cycle 1 introduced shorter differentiated tasks and a homework diary checked daily: completion rose to 58% . Reflection and student exit tickets showed that students without help at home struggled, so Cycle 2 added a 10-minute "homework start" session at the end of class and peer buddies: completion rose to 71% . The teacher triangulated the register data with journal notes and student comments and concluded that support at the point of starting the task mattered more than reminders. (Illustrative example.) Figure 10. Homework completion across cycles (illustrative)

Section Content Context School, class, the researcher's role and why the problem matters Concern and question How the problem was identified; the "How can I...?" question Literature What others have found about similar problems and actions Baseline Data showing the situation before action Action plan What was done, when and with whom Cycles For each cycle: action, observation data, reflection, changes Evidence and validation Triangulation; critical friend; validation group Learning and claims What improved, what the teacher learned, limits of the claims Next steps Further cycles and sharing with colleagues Table 14. Structure of an action research report Key Point Validity in action research is established through triangulation , critical friends and validation meetings where colleagues examine the evidence for the claims (McNiff & Whitehead, 2005). Claims should be modest: "In my class, this action was associated with ...", not "this method improves homework everywhere". Critical Perspective Common weaknesses: choosing a problem outside the teacher's control (e.g., "lack of government funding"); only one cycle with no real reflection; no baseline data; collecting data only from the teacher's impressions; and confusing action research with a small experiment. Ethical issues also arise because the teacher is also the assessor, so students must be able to decline without penalty. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Define action research and explain its characteristics." "Explain Kemmis and McTaggart's action research spiral." "Design an action research project to solve a classroom problem in Bangladesh." "Distinguish action research from conventional research." "How is validity established in action research?"

Recommended monograph structure (about 10,000 to 15,000 words) Study tip For an action research monograph, Chapters 3 and 4 are often merged into chapters describing each cycle. For a qualitative study, Chapter 4 is organised by themes rather than statistical tests.

u: Writing the Monograph: Timeline, Ethics and Assessment
x: Informed consent : a plain-language information sheet and signed consent; for children, parental consent and child assent. Voluntary participation : participants may withdraw at any time without penalty; especially important when the researcher is also the teacher. Confidentiality and anonymity : use pseudonyms for schools and people; store data securely; avoid identifying details in small communities. Do no harm : avoid sensitive questions without support; take special care with vulnerable groups (children with disabilities, refugees, survivors of abuse). Honesty : no fabrication, falsification or plagiarism; cite all sources in APA style; check similarity with plagiarism software if the university provides it. Reciprocity : share findings with the school and thank participants. Element Wording Purpose I am a Master of Education student at the Department of ... I am studying how teachers use assessment in their classrooms. What is involved You will be asked to fill in a questionnaire / take part in a 40-minute interview, which will be audio-recorded with your permission. Voluntary Your participation is voluntary. You may refuse to answer any question or withdraw at any time without any consequence. Confidentiality Your name and school will not be used in the report. Data will be kept securely and used only for this study. Contact If you have any questions, contact the researcher or the supervisor (phone/email). Consent I have read this information and agree to take part. Signature and date. Table 17. Sample consent statement (adapt and translate into Bangla) Verify Before Use Confirm whether the department requires a formal ethics clearance form for M.Ed monographs, and the word limit, formatting and binding requirements in the current M.Ed regulations.

u: Unit 1: Concept and Foundations of Open and Distance Learning
x: Distance education (DE) is any planned educational process in which the teacher and the learner are separated in space and often in time for most of the learning, and the gap is bridged by learning materials, media and two-way communication organised by an educational institution. The learner studies mainly at home or at work, at their own pace, with occasional contact with tutors. Definition Distance education (Keegan, 1996) : Education characterised by the quasi-permanent separation of teacher and learner throughout the length of the learning process; the influence of an educational organisation in planning and preparing learning materials and providing student support; the use of technical media to unite teacher and learner and carry content; the provision of two-way communication; and the quasi-permanent absence of the learning group, so that people are taught as individuals rather than in groups, with the possibility of occasional meetings. Definition Distance education (Moore & Kearsley, 2012) : Teaching and planned learning in which teaching normally occurs in a different place from learning, requiring communication through technologies as well as special institutional organisation. Definition Distance education (Holmberg, 1977) : The various forms of study at all levels which are not under the continuous, immediate supervision of tutors present with their students in lecture rooms or on the same premises, but which, nevertheless, benefit from the planning, guidance and teaching of a tutorial organisation. Figure 1. Keegan's defining elements of distance education (Keegan, 1980; 1996)

u: Unit 1: Concept and Foundations of Open and Distance Learning
x: Open learning is a philosophy, not a delivery method. It aims to remove barriers to learning: entry qualifications, age, place, time, pace, cost and fixed curricula. A system is more or less open according to how many choices it gives the learner (Rumble, 1989; Lewis & Spencer, 1986). Openness can apply to who may enter, what is learned, where , when , how and at what pace learning occurs, and how and when it is assessed. Definition Open learning (Lewis & Spencer, 1986) : A term used to describe courses flexibly designed to meet individual requirements. It is often applied to provision which tries to remove barriers that prevent attendance at more traditional courses, but it also suggests a learner-centred philosophy. Definition Open and distance learning (UNESCO, 2002) : Approaches to learning that focus on freeing learners from the constraints of time and place while offering flexible learning opportunities to individuals and groups of learners. Key Point Distance describes the mode (separation of teacher and learner); open describes the philosophy (removal of barriers). A course can be distance but not open (strict entry requirements, fixed timetable) or open but not distance (an open-entry evening class). ODL combines the two and is the term used by UNESCO, COL and BOU.

u: Unit 1: Concept and Foundations of Open and Distance Learning

u: Unit 1: Concept and Foundations of Open and Distance Learning
x: Separation of teacher and learner in space and/or time. Institutional planning: courses designed by a course team, not by an individual teacher in a classroom. Mediated teaching through print, audio, video, broadcast, Internet and mobile. Two-way communication via tutorials, assignments with feedback, phone, e-mail, LMS forums. Self-learning materials that teach on their own ("teacher in print"). Learner autonomy : the learner manages time, pace and place. Industrialised production: division of labour, mass production of materials, economies of scale (Peters). Learner support through regional and study centres, tutors and counsellors. Open admission and flexible duration (e.g. BOU B.Ed: 1 year, up to 5 years to complete). Large scale : mega-universities with over 100,000 learners (Daniel, 1996).

u: Unit 1: Concept and Foundations of Open and Distance Learning
x: ODL rests on the ideas of education as a human right (UDHR Art. 26), lifelong learning (Faure, 1972; Delors, 1996), equity and social justice (reaching those excluded by geography, poverty, gender, disability or work), learner-centredness and adult learning (Knowles's andragogy: self-concept, experience, readiness, problem-centred orientation, internal motivation). Its guiding principles include openness, flexibility, learner autonomy, interaction, quality equal to conventional education, and cost-effectiveness.

u: Unit 1: Concept and Foundations of Open and Distance Learning
x: Access and equity : reaches rural people, women, working adults, people with disabilities, prisoners and the poor. Lifelong and continuing education : in-service upgrading without leaving the job (e.g. teachers' B.Ed through BOU). Massification of higher education where campus capacity is limited. Second chance : SSC/HSC for dropouts and over-age learners. Cost-effectiveness : lower cost per learner at scale. Human resource development and national development goals (SDG 4: inclusive, equitable quality education and lifelong learning). Resilience : continuity of learning in disasters and pandemics.

u: Unit 1: Concept and Foundations of Open and Distance Learning
x: Single-mode : teach only at a distance (e.g. BOU, UK Open University, IGNOU, AIOU). Dual-mode : conventional universities that also offer distance programmes (e.g. University of Delhi School of Open Learning; in Bangladesh, some private universities' online/blended programmes where permitted). Mixed-mode / multi-mode : on-campus students may take distance courses and vice versa. Consortium : several institutions share courses and materials (e.g. SAARC Consortium on ODL; Commonwealth Executive MBA/MPA delivered with COL support). Exam Focus Likely questions: "Define distance education. Distinguish it from open learning." "Discuss Keegan's elements of distance education." "Compare ODL with conventional education." "Why is ODL important for a developing country like Bangladesh?"

Keegan (1996) grouped the theories of distance education into three families: theories of independence and autonomy (Wedemeyer, Moore), theory of industrialisation (Peters) and theories of interaction and communication (Holmberg, Bååth, Daniel & Marquis). Later, online learning added community and connectivist theories (Garrison et al., Anderson, Siemens).

Charles A. Wedemeyer (University of Wisconsin), the father of American independent study, argued in Learning at the Back Door (1981) that education should be available to anyone, anywhere, at any time. His system emphasised learner independence : learners should be able to start at any time, pace themselves, choose goals and use many media. He proposed the separation of teaching and learning, the teacher–learner–communication–content system, and led the AIM (Articulated Instructional Media) Project (1964–68), which inspired the UK Open University.

Michael G. Moore (1973, 1993) argued that distance is pedagogical, not geographical . Transactional distance (TD) is the psychological and communication space between teacher and learner that can create misunderstanding. It depends on three variables: Dialogue : purposeful, constructive two-way interaction between teacher and learner. Structure : rigidity or flexibility of objectives, content, methods and evaluation; how far the course can respond to individual needs. Learner autonomy : the extent to which the learner, not the teacher, determines goals, methods and evaluation. Key Point More structure and less dialogue = greater transactional distance ; greater TD demands greater learner autonomy. A broadcast TV lecture has high structure and no dialogue (high TD); a live tutorial has high dialogue (low TD). Figure 3. Moore's theory of transactional distance: dialogue, structure and resulting distance Moore's three types of interaction (1989) : learner–content, learner–instructor and learner–learner. Hillman, Willis and Gunawardena (1994) added learner–interface interaction (using the technology itself).

Otto Peters (1967/1973, FernUniversität Hagen, Germany) described distance education as the most industrialised form of education . Like factory production, it uses rationalisation, division of labour (authors, editors, designers, media producers, tutors), mechanisation, assembly-line methods, mass production, standardisation, planning, centralisation and economies of scale . Peters later (2001) discussed the move to "post-industrial" digital learning environments. Criticism : it can treat learners as products, reduce teacher autonomy and lead to impersonal learning.

Börje Holmberg (Sweden, Germany) proposed that distance teaching should be a guided didactic conversation : materials and tutor comments should be written in a friendly, personal, conversational style ("you", "we"), with easy language, explicit advice, invitations to exchange views and emotional involvement. He held that feelings of personal relation between teaching and learning parties promote study pleasure and motivation , which improve learning (Holmberg, 1983; 2005). His later term was teaching–learning conversation .

t: 2.5 Keegan: reintegration of the teaching act
x: Desmond Keegan argued that in distance education the teaching acts are separated from the learning acts, so the institution must artificially reintegrate them: at the course-development stage through well-designed materials, and during delivery through two-way communication and student support. If reintegration fails, learning is weak and dropout high.

Theorist Theory / idea Core message Bååth (1979) Two-way communication Assignments and tutor feedback are the core of teaching in DE. Daniel & Marquis (1979) Independence vs interaction Balancing independent study (cheap) and interaction (costly) is the key design decision. Sewart (1978) Continuity of concern Students need continuing human support; materials alone cannot teach. Garrison (1985); Garrison & Shale Generations & control Control = independence + power + support; technology shapes generations of DE. Garrison, Anderson & Archer (2000) Community of Inquiry (CoI) Deep online learning needs cognitive, social and teaching presence . Anderson (2003) Interaction equivalency theorem Deep learning occurs if one of the three interactions (S–T, S–S, S–C) is high; the others can be reduced. Siemens (2005); Downes Connectivism Learning is building and navigating networks of people and information; basis of cMOOCs. Saba & Shearer (1994) Systems dynamics Tested Moore's theory: dialogue and structure vary dynamically over time. Figure 4. Generations of distance education: each new technology adds rather than replaces earlier media Nipper (1989) described three generations: correspondence, multimedia, and computer-mediated communication. Taylor (2001) extended this to five (Figure 4). Anderson & Dron (2011) described three generations of pedagogy : cognitive-behaviourist, social-constructivist and connectivist. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Explain Moore's theory of transactional distance with examples." "Discuss Peters's industrialisation theory and its relevance to BOU." "What is guided didactic conversation? How should SLM be written in this light?" "Explain the Community of Inquiry framework."

u: Unit 3: Historical Development of ODL: Global and Bangladesh
x: Year Milestone 1728 Caleb Phillips advertises shorthand lessons by mail in the Boston Gazette (often cited as the earliest example). 1840 Isaac Pitman teaches shorthand by post in England (penny post), the first systematic correspondence course. 1856 Charles Toussaint and Gustav Langenscheidt teach languages by correspondence in Berlin. 1858 University of London External System : degrees by examination for students anywhere. 1873 Anna Eliot Ticknor's Society to Encourage Studies at Home (USA), mainly for women. 1892 University of Chicago (William Rainey Harper) correspondence department; University of Wisconsin extension. 1938 International Council for Correspondence Education founded (now ICDE , Oslo). 1946 University of South Africa (UNISA) becomes a distance-teaching university. 1960s Wedemeyer's AIM project; radio and TV education spread. 1969 UK Open University receives Royal Charter; first students 1971. Model for the world's open universities. 1972–74 Korea National Open University (1972); Spain's UNED (1972); Allama Iqbal Open University , Pakistan (1974); FernUniversität, Germany (1974). 1978 Sukhothai Thammathirat Open University (STOU), Thailand. 1984–85 Universitas Terbuka, Indonesia (1984); IGNOU , India (1985). 1987 Commonwealth of Learning (COL) established; Asian Association of Open Universities ( AAOU ) founded. 1992 Bangladesh Open University established. 1990s–2000s Internet and online learning; virtual universities; UNESCO coins OER (2002). 2008 First MOOC (Siemens & Downes, "Connectivism and Connective Knowledge", CCK08). 2012 "Year of the MOOC": Coursera, edX, Udacity; UNESCO Paris OER Declaration . 2019 UNESCO Recommendation on OER . 2020–21 COVID-19: emergency remote teaching worldwide; ODL institutions lead recovery. 2023–26 Generative AI enters teaching, tutoring and assessment; micro-credentials expand. Mega-universities : Daniel (1996) defined them as distance-teaching universities with over 100,000 students in degree programmes. Examples: IGNOU, AIOU, Anadolu University (Turkey), Universitas Terbuka, UNISA, KNOU, STOU and BOU.

CEMCA (1994, New Delhi) COL's Commonwealth Educational Media Centre for Asia; SLM and media training. AAOU (1987) Asian Association of Open Universities; BOU is a member. u: Unit 3: Historical Development of ODL: Global and Bangladesh
t: 3.3 Development of distance education in Bangladesh
x: Year Development 1956–62 Early radio education programmes; Audio-Visual Education Centre (AVEC) set up in 1962. 1978 School Broadcasting Programme (SBP) launched to support classroom teaching by radio. 1983 AVEC and SBP merged into the National Institute of Educational Media and Technology (NIEMT) . 1985 Bangladesh Institute of Distance Education (BIDE) created; offered B.Ed by distance mode for in-service teachers (from 1986). 1992 BOU Act 1992 passed by Parliament; BOU established on 21 October 1992 by absorbing BIDE (and NIEMT's functions). 1990s BOU launches SSC, HSC, BA/BSS, B.Ed, certificate and non-formal programmes; radio and BTV broadcasts. 2000s Expansion of regional and sub-regional centres; MBA, M.Ed, M.Phil/Ph.D; COL-supported programmes. 2010 National Education Policy 2010 recognises distance education for access and teacher training. 2014–20 Digital platforms: a2i's Muktopaath (2016) online teacher training; BOU e-books, YouTube and BOUTube. 2020–21 COVID-19: Sangsad TV lessons ("Amar Ghore Amar School"), radio and online classes; UGC permits online classes and exams. 2021–26 UGC blended learning policy initiatives for higher education; BOU online admission, results and digital content. Verify Before The Exam Check dates for SBP (1978), NIEMT (1983), BIDE (1985) and the UGC blended learning policy against BOU's "About BOU" page and the UGC website. BOU's own profile states that AVEC (1962), NIEMT (1983) and BIDE (1985) were its predecessor bodies. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Trace the historical development of distance education in the world." "Describe the evolution of distance education in Bangladesh leading to the establishment of BOU." "What is a mega-university? Give examples."

u: Unit 4: Bangladesh Open University: Structure, Programmes and Delivery System
x: BOU was established by the Bangladesh Open University Act, 1992 and started on 21 October 1992 . It is the country's only public single-mode distance-teaching university , with its main campus at Board Bazar, Gazipur (35 acres). The President of the Republic is the Chancellor; the Vice-Chancellor is its chief executive and academic officer. Objectives (based on the BOU Act 1992) : to provide higher, technical, professional and general education through distance and open methods; to upgrade the quality of education; to train teachers; to provide continuing, non-formal and lifelong education; to use mass media for education; to widen access for people who cannot attend conventional institutions; and to conduct research in ODL.

u: Unit 4: Bangladesh Open University: Structure, Programmes and Delivery System
x: Statutory bodies : Board of Governors, Academic Council, Finance Committee, Planning Committee and the Selection Boards. Academic schools (each headed by a Dean): Open School; School of Agriculture and Rural Development (SARD); School of Business; School of Education (SOE) ; School of Social Sciences, Humanities and Languages (SSHL); School of Science and Technology (SST); and School of Law (newer). Administrative divisions (11), including Admission, Examination, Media, Publishing-Printing-Distribution (PPD), Student Support Services, Regional Services, Planning, ICT, Finance and Registrar's office. Field network : Regional Centres, Sub-Regional Centres and study (tutorial) centres hosted in schools and colleges across the country. Figure 5. BOU's ODL delivery system: from the main campus to the learner Verify Before The Exam BOU's e-book portal profile (2026) lists: 6 academic schools (the website menu shows 7 including Law), 11 administrative divisions, 12 Regional Centres , 80 Sub-Regional Centres , 1,835 study centres , 67 formal and 19 non-formal programmes, 147 full-time teachers, 22,961 adjunct teachers/tutors, and 3,68,328 learners in formal programmes (session 2023–24). The 12 RCs are Dhaka, Chattogram, Rajshahi, Khulna, Sylhet, Barishal, Rangpur, Mymensingh, Cumilla, Bogura, Jashore and Faridpur. Confirm figures on bou.ac.bd before quoting.

u: Unit 4: Bangladesh Open University: Structure, Programmes and Delivery System
x: 1. Self-learning materials (SLM) : printed modular textbooks written by course teams (BOU faculty and subject experts), now also available free as e-books (ebookbou.edu.bd). 2. u: Unit 4: Bangladesh Open University: Structure, Programmes and Delivery System
x: Second chance to millions of dropouts through SSC and HSC. Teacher professionalisation (B.Ed, B.M.Ed, M.Ed) on a national scale. u: Unit 4: Bangladesh Open University: Structure, Programmes and Delivery System
x: Delays in printing and distributing SLM; outdated modules. Shortage of full-time faculty compared with learners; heavy reliance on adjunct tutors with little ODL training. Low tutorial attendance and weak learner–tutor interaction. Limited use of interactive online learning; digital divide in rural areas. High dropout and low completion rates; weak learner tracking. Examination management, session delays and social perception of BOU degrees. Weak quality assurance and research culture; inadequate funding.

u: Unit 4: Bangladesh Open University: Structure, Programmes and Delivery System
x: Move to a blended model: an LMS for every course, mobile apps, WhatsApp/Facebook study groups, recorded tutorials. Revise SLM regularly and release them as OER with interactive digital versions. Train tutors and staff in ODL pedagogy and online facilitation; reward good tutoring. Strengthen learner support: early-alert systems, counselling, helpline, learning analytics. Accreditation and QA through IQAC and the Bangladesh Accreditation Council (BAC). Partnerships with COL, AAOU, IGNOU, AIOU and industry; credit transfer and recognition of prior learning. u: Unit 5: Instructional Design and Self-Learning Materials (SLM)
x: Because the teacher is absent, all teaching must be planned in advance and built into the materials and support system. Instructional design (ID) is the systematic process of analysing needs, setting outcomes, designing content and activities, developing materials, delivering and evaluating. The best-known model is ADDIE : Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation. Others: Dick & Carey's systems approach, Gagné's nine events of instruction, Kemp's model, Merrill's first principles, and backward design (Wiggins & McTighe) used in outcome-based education (OBE).

u: Unit 5: Instructional Design and Self-Learning Materials (SLM)
x: Approach Description Strengths / weaknesses Course team (UKOU model) Academics, instructional designer, editor, media producer, graphic artist and administrator develop the course together. High quality; slow and costly. Author–editor model A subject expert writes; an editor/ID shapes it into SLM. Faster, cheaper; quality depends on the editor. Adoption / adaptation Existing materials or OER are adopted or adapted with a study guide. Very cheap and quick; fit to context may be weak. Consultancy / transnational Materials are bought or co-developed with another institution. Shares cost; may not suit local learners.

u: Unit 5: Instructional Design and Self-Learning Materials (SLM)
x: SLM are self-instructional materials designed so that a learner can learn without a teacher present. Rowntree (1994) called them a "tutorial in print" ; Holmberg called them a guided didactic conversation . Good SLM are: Feature Meaning Self-explanatory Content is clear without outside help; jargon explained; examples given. Self-contained Everything needed is in the material or clearly referenced. Self-directed Objectives, advice and signposts guide the learner through the content. Self-motivating Conversational style, relevance to life, curiosity and encouragement. Self-evaluating Self-assessment questions (SAQs), activities and feedback let learners check progress. Self-learning Overall: the material teaches. Key Point Remember the "self" features : self-explanatory, self-contained, self-directed, self-motivating, self-evaluating and self-learning. These are common short-answer questions in Indian and Bangladeshi ODL exams. Figure 6. Typical structure of a unit/lesson in self-learning material

u: Unit 5: Instructional Design and Self-Learning Materials (SLM)
x: 1. Title and introduction : what the unit is about and why it matters; links to earlier units (advance organiser). 2. Learning outcomes stated in measurable terms (Bloom's revised taxonomy: remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, create). 3. Study time estimate. 4. Content in short sections with headings, examples, diagrams, case studies and local references. 5. Activities and self-assessment questions (SAQs) placed within the text ("in-text questions"), with space to write. 6. Feedback / answers to SAQs at the end of the unit. 7. Summary , key terms/glossary and further reading . 8. Final evaluation / assignment linked to the TMA.

u: Unit 5: Instructional Design and Self-Learning Materials (SLM)
x: Use a personal, conversational tone ("you", "we"): Holmberg. Short sentences and paragraphs; plain language; readability suited to the learner (readability formulae such as Flesch). Access devices (Rowntree): contents list, objectives, headings, summaries, glossary, index, icons and signposts. Generous white space, margins for notes, visuals and tables. Culturally relevant Bangladeshi examples; gender-sensitive and inclusive language; accessible formats for learners with disabilities. Bangla-medium modules for most BOU programmes, with English technical terms in brackets.

u: Unit 5: Instructional Design and Self-Learning Materials (SLM)
x: Definition Open Educational Resources (UNESCO, 2019) : Learning, teaching and research materials in any format and medium that reside in the public domain or are under copyright that have been released under an open license, that permit no-cost access, re-use, re-purpose, adaptation and redistribution by others. Wiley's 5Rs : retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute. Creative Commons licences : CC BY, BY-SA, BY-NC, BY-ND and their combinations. Benefits for ODL : lower cost of materials, faster course development, quality through sharing, access for learners. MOOCs : Massive Open Online Courses. cMOOCs (connectivist, Siemens & Downes, 2008) emphasise networks; xMOOCs (Coursera, edX, SWAYAM in India) follow a structured video-and-quiz model. Weaknesses: very low completion rates (often under 10%). Bangladesh: Muktopaath (a2i) provides free online courses and teacher training; BOU's e-books are freely available online. Exam Focus Likely questions: "What are self-learning materials? Discuss their characteristics." "Describe the steps of SLM development." "Explain the course team approach." "What are OER? How can BOU benefit from OER?"

u: Unit 6: Media and Technology in ODL
x: In ODL, media are the carriers of teaching and the bridge between teacher and learner . Media present content, provide interaction, motivate, give feedback and support administration. The choice of media determines access, cost and the kind of learning possible (Bates, 2019).

u: Unit 6: Media and Technology in ODL
t: 6.3 Media selection: Bates's ACTIONS and SECTIONS models
x: Tony Bates (1995) proposed ACTIONS for selecting technology: A ccess, C osts, T eaching and learning, I nteractivity and user-friendliness, O rganisational issues, N ovelty, S peed. In Teaching in a Digital Age (2015/2019) he updated it to SECTIONS : S tudents, E ase of use, C ost, T eaching functions, I nteraction, O rganisational issues, N etworking, S ecurity and privacy. Key Point Access comes first in Bates's model: the best technology is useless if learners cannot reach it. For BOU's rural learners, print plus mobile phone remains the most accessible combination, with online media as an addition.

u: Unit 6: Media and Technology in ODL
x: Synchronous (same time) Asynchronous (different time) Live tutorial, video-conference, webinar, chat, phone E-mail, discussion forum, recorded lecture, SLM, assignments Immediacy, motivation, social presence Flexibility, time to reflect, suits working adults Scheduling and bandwidth problems Delayed feedback, possible isolation

u: Unit 6: Media and Technology in ODL
x: A Learning Management System (LMS) such as Moodle, Canvas or Google Classroom hosts content, discussion, quizzes, assignments, grades and analytics. Blended learning combines the best of face-to-face and online learning; Garrison and Kanuka (2004) called it transformative for higher education. Models include rotation, flex, flipped classroom and enriched virtual models. TPACK (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) and SAMR (Puentedura) help teachers integrate technology meaningfully.

u: Unit 6: Media and Technology in ODL
x: Access to electricity, devices, connectivity and digital skills is unequal by location, income, gender, age and disability . ODL planners should use low-bandwidth, mobile-first and offline-capable designs; provide content in multiple formats (print, audio, video with captions); and follow accessibility standards (WCAG; UDL principles). Bangladesh Context During COVID-19 school closures (2020–21), Bangladesh used a multi-channel approach: recorded lessons on Sangsad Bangladesh TV ("Amar Ghore Amar School" for secondary and "Ghore Boshe Shikhi" for primary), Bangladesh Betar and community radio, mobile phone helplines and online platforms such as Muktopaath and Konnect/Kishore Batayon . Surveys found that a large share of rural and poor students could not access TV or online lessons, showing the digital divide. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Discuss the role of media in distance education." "Explain Bates's ACTIONS model of media selection." "Distinguish synchronous and asynchronous learning." "How can mobile learning improve BOU's programmes?"

u: Unit 7: Learner Support, Assessment and Quality Assurance
x: Most ODL learners are adults , part-time , employed , with family responsibilities, diverse ages and backgrounds, often from rural or disadvantaged groups and returning to study after a gap. They are usually goal-oriented and motivated but short of time, and many lack study skills and confidence. Andragogy (Knowles), self-directed learning and heutagogy (self-determined learning; Hase & Kenyon, 2000) explain how such learners learn best.

u: Unit 7: Learner Support, Assessment and Quality Assurance
x: Definition Learner support (Tait, 2000) : The range of services, both for individuals and for students in groups, which complement the course materials or learning resources that are uniform for all learners. Its three functions are cognitive (supporting and developing learning), affective (a supportive environment that builds commitment and self-esteem) and systemic (effective, transparent and learner-friendly administrative processes). Figure 7. Tait's three functions of learner support in ODL Type of support Examples Academic / tutorial Tutorials, tutor comments on assignments, discussion forums, helpdesk for content questions, library and e-resources Counselling and guidance Pre-admission advice, study-skills and time-management guidance, career counselling, personal counselling Administrative Admission, registration, fees, materials distribution, examination and results, transcripts Technical LMS and portal help, digital literacy orientation Peer support Study groups, alumni mentors, social media groups Special needs Accessible materials (Braille, audio), examination accommodation, support for prisoners and remote learners

u: Unit 7: Learner Support, Assessment and Quality Assurance
t: 7.3 The role of the tutor / counsellor
x: Facilitator of learning rather than lecturer: clarifies difficult points, leads discussion, uses learners' experience. Assignment marker : gives detailed, timely, encouraging written feedback ("teaching through assignments"). Motivator and counsellor: monitors progress, contacts inactive learners. Link between learner and institution: reports problems and feedback on materials. Online moderator: Salmon's (2000) five-stage e-moderating model : access and motivation, online socialisation, information exchange, knowledge construction, development.

u: Unit 7: Learner Support, Assessment and Quality Assurance
x: Dropout is the biggest weakness of ODL. Kember's (1989) model explains it through the learner's social integration (balancing study with family, work and social life) and academic integration , leading to a cost–benefit decision to continue or leave. Tinto's (1975) student integration model, Rovai's (2003) composite persistence model and Simpson's (2013) work on proactive motivational support are also cited. Causes : time pressure from job/family, financial problems, isolation, weak study skills, poor or delayed materials, weak feedback, difficult courses, health, lack of motivation, unclear goals. Remedies : pre-admission counselling, orientation, early contact by tutors, early-alert analytics, flexible deadlines, peer groups, timely materials, quality feedback, financial support, recognition of progress.

u: Unit 7: Learner Support, Assessment and Quality Assurance
x: Component Purpose and features Self-assessment (SAQs, activities) Formative; not graded; learners check their own understanding. Tutor-marked assignments (TMA) Formative and summative; teaching through feedback; counts toward continuous assessment (BOU uses assignments in each course). Computer-marked assignments (CMA) / online quizzes Objective items marked automatically; instant feedback; large scale. Practical / project / teaching practice Skills-based; for B.Ed, practice teaching observed by supervisors. Term-end / semester-final examination Summative, proctored at examination centres; main weight in grade. E-portfolio, online proctoring, viva Newer methods; authenticity checks; academic integrity. Issues : maintaining validity, reliability and fairness across thousands of tutors; preventing plagiarism, impersonation and AI-assisted cheating; quick return of assignments; aligning assessment with outcomes ( constructive alignment , Biggs).

u: Unit 7: Learner Support, Assessment and Quality Assurance
x: Definition Quality in ODL : Fitness for purpose and fitness of purpose; providing learning experiences and outcomes at least equal to conventional education while meeting the needs of distance learners efficiently. Areas of quality (COL, AAOU QA Framework): vision and mission; management and planning; programme design and curriculum; course materials; learner support; assessment; staff development; infrastructure and technology; research; feedback and continuous improvement. COL Review and Improvement Model (COL-RIM) : institutional self-review for continuous improvement. AAOU Quality Assurance Framework (2010) and ICDE quality network. E-xcellence (EADTU) benchmarks for e-learning quality; Quality Matters rubric for online course design. Bangladesh : UGC's Institutional Quality Assurance Cells (IQAC) established under HEQEP; Bangladesh Accreditation Council Act 2017 created BAC to accredit programmes and institutions; BOU has an IQAC. Tools: learner feedback, tutor evaluation, materials review, programme review, tracer studies, external examiners. Verify Before The Exam Confirm the current status of BOU's IQAC and BAC accreditation guidelines for ODL programmes on ugc.gov.bd and bac.gov.bd. Exam Focus Likely questions: "What is learner support? Explain Tait's functions." "Discuss the causes of dropout in distance education and suggest remedies." "Describe the role of a tutor in ODL." "How can quality be assured in BOU's programmes?"

u: Unit 8: Management, Economics, Policy and Future of ODL
x: ODL management differs from campus management because it runs a production system (materials), a delivery system (distribution, media, logistics), a learner support system (regional network, tutors) and an assessment system at scale. Rumble (1986; 1992) identified the key subsystems: course development, materials production, distribution, student administration, regional services and evaluation. Planning : needs assessment, enrolment projection, budgeting, scheduling of course development and delivery. Organising : centralised vs decentralised models; regional centres; partnerships with host institutions for study centres. Staffing and staff development : core faculty, adjunct tutors, media and ICT staff; training in ODL. Logistics : printing, warehousing and distribution of SLM; examination management. Information systems : student records, ERP, LMS, learning analytics. Monitoring and evaluation and leadership for change.

u: Unit 8: Management, Economics, Policy and Future of ODL
x: ODL has high fixed costs (course development, media production, systems) and low variable (marginal) costs per extra learner. As enrolment rises, average cost per learner falls (economies of scale). Rumble (1997) and Daniel (1996) showed that mega-universities can teach at a fraction of conventional per-student cost. Cost-effectiveness depends on enrolment size, course life (years before revision), media chosen, completion rates and support costs . High dropout raises the cost per graduate. Figure 8. The "iron triangle" of access, quality and cost (Daniel, Kanwar & Uvalić-Trumbić, 2009) Key Point Iron triangle : in conventional education, increasing access or quality raises cost, and cutting cost harms quality. Daniel, Kanwar and Uvalić-Trumbić (2009) argue that well-designed ODL and technology can increase access, improve quality and reduce cost at the same time .

u: Unit 8: Management, Economics, Policy and Future of ODL
x: Global : UDHR (1948) Art. 26; EFA (Jomtien 1990, Dakar 2000); SDG 4 (2015) and targets 4.3 (equal access to tertiary education) and 4.4 (skills); UNESCO OER Recommendation (2019); Marrakech Framework for Action (CONFINTEA VII, 2022). Bangladesh : BOU Act 1992; National Education Policy 2010 (distance education for access, teacher training and lifelong learning); Non-Formal Education Act 2014; National Skills Development Policy 2022; ICT in education master plans; UGC's strategic plans and blended learning guidelines for higher education; National Teacher Education/Training policies that recognise BOU B.Ed. Verify Before The Exam Check the latest UGC blended/online learning policy and any 2025–26 changes under the current government before quoting names and years.

u: Unit 8: Management, Economics, Policy and Future of ODL
x: Trend What it means for ODL Online and blended learning Open universities move from print-based to digital-first or blended delivery. Emergency remote teaching (ERT) COVID-19 showed the difference between quickly moving classes online and designed ODL (Hodges et al., 2020). OER and open textbooks Lower costs; sharing across universities; adaptation to Bangla and local contexts. MOOCs and micro-credentials Short, stackable, credit-bearing courses; digital badges; recognition of prior learning (RPL). Learning analytics Data on learner activity predict risk of dropout; requires privacy safeguards. Artificial intelligence AI tutors, automated feedback, translation, content generation; risks to academic integrity and equity. Mobile-first design Most learners use smartphones; content must be short, low-data and responsive. Flexible, lifelong pathways Credit transfer, national qualifications frameworks (BNQF), skills for the 4th Industrial Revolution. Internationalisation Cross-border ODL, partnerships, joint programmes and quality concerns.

u: Unit 8: Management, Economics, Policy and Future of ODL
x: ODL can help Bangladesh widen tertiary participation, upgrade its teaching workforce, reskill workers and reach marginalised groups (women, char and haor communities, people with disabilities, migrants and Rohingya-affected host communities). For this, BOU and other providers need digital transformation (LMS, mobile apps, e-SLM), quality assurance and accreditation, trained tutors , research-based improvement , parity of esteem with campus degrees, and sustainable funding . ODL should not be seen as a second-best option but as a mainstream form of lifelong learning. Exam Focus Likely questions: "Why is ODL considered cost-effective? Explain economies of scale." "Explain the iron triangle." "Discuss current trends in ODL and their implications for BOU." "Suggest a plan to transform BOU into a digital open university."

u: 1. The Big Picture: SDG 4 at the Countdown to 2030
t: 1. The Big Picture: SDG 4 at the Countdown to 2030
x: Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) commits the world to "ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all" by 2030. It was adopted in 2015 through the Incheon Declaration and Education 2030 Framework for Action . With four years left, the global conversation has shifted from ambition to accountability: which countries are on track, which are not, and what has actually worked. (Links to ED 501 Education in Global Perspective and PC 119 Education and Development.)

u: 1. The Big Picture: SDG 4 at the Countdown to 2030
t: 1.1 The 2026 GEM Report: Access and equity
x: The Global Education Monitoring (GEM) Report is UNESCO’s independent annual report that tracks SDG 4. The 2026 edition, Access and equity: countdown to 2030 , is the first of a three-part "Countdown to 2030" series. The next two will cover quality and learning (2027) and relevance of education (2028) (UNESCO, 2026a). MUST REMEMBER: 2026 GEM REPORT HEADLINE FIGURES 273 million children, adolescents and youth are out of school, a number that has risen for the seventh consecutive year ; about one in six of the age group is excluded. There are 327 million more students in primary and secondary school than in 2000, so access has expanded even as the absolute out-of-school number rises with population growth. 27% of five-year-olds are already in primary school instead of pre-primary (too early), and six in ten who enrol in university never graduate. Countries with 12 years of compulsory education rose from 8% (1998) to 26% (2023). Countries with inclusive education laws rose from 1% to 24% since 2000. A new Equitable Financing in Education (EFE) Index finds fewer than one in ten countries’ funding mechanisms have a strong equity focus. Fast progress is possible: Madagascar, Togo, Morocco, Viet Nam, Georgia and Türkiye cut out-of-school rates by at least 80% for some age groups since 2000; Côte d’Ivoire halved its rates. The report’s main message is that progress comes from sustained, country-owned policy over decades, not quick fixes . It draws four policy principles: (1) mix policies (no single intervention works alone), (2) target financing to disadvantaged groups, (3) localise policies, and (4) think long term . On monitoring, it asks countries to measure participation by age, completion and repetition rather than enrolment alone, and notes that one in three countries do not report urban-rural gaps and one in two do not report wealth gaps.

u: 1. The Big Picture: SDG 4 at the Countdown to 2030
t: 1.2 The 2025 SDG 4 Scorecard: Are countries on track?
x: Since 2022, countries have set their own national SDG 4 benchmarks for seven or eight indicators (for example, early childhood participation, out-of-school rate, completion, minimum proficiency, trained teachers and public spending). About 80% of countries have now set at least one benchmark. The 2025 SDG 4 Scorecard (UNESCO GEM Report & UIS, 2025) found that the indicators furthest off track are: Minimum reading proficiency at the end of primary: about 11 percentage points behind national targets, partly because many countries lack data. Early childhood education participation : about 9 points behind (a COVID-19 effect). Trained teachers in pre-primary : about 7 points behind. Public spending : in 2023 countries were further from the twin benchmarks of 4–6% of GDP and 15–20% of total public expenditure than they were in 2015. The Scorecard estimated 272 million out of school in 2023 and called this an undercount, since the ten most conflict-affected countries could add at least 13 million more (UNESCO GEM Report & UIS, 2025). Key Terms Education 2030 Framework for Action (2015): the roadmap for SDG 4. It sets the financing benchmarks of 4–6% of GDP and/or 15–20% of public expenditure on education. SDG 4 benchmarks: national targets set by each country for 2025 and 2030 on a common set of indicators, so that progress can be compared with the country’s own promise. Learning-adjusted thinking: the shift from counting enrolment ("schooling") to measuring whether children actually learn ("learning"). See Chapter 2.

u: 1. The Big Picture: SDG 4 at the Countdown to 2030
t: 1.3 The Transforming Education Summit and its legacy
x: The UN Secretary-General convened the Transforming Education Summit (TES) in September 2022, after COVID-19 had closed schools for about 1.6 billion learners. It produced national statements of commitment and five thematic "action tracks": inclusive, equitable, safe and healthy schools; learning and skills for life, work and sustainable development; teachers and the teaching profession; digital learning and transformation; and financing of education. Several follow-up initiatives grew from it, including the Greening Education Partnership , the Global Initiative on Digital Learning (Gateways to Public Digital Learning) , the International Finance Facility for Education , and the UN High-Level Panel on the Teaching Profession (Chapter 11). Critical Perspective Critics argue that SDG 4 has become a "monitoring industry": more reports than results. The GEM Report itself admits the 2030 targets will not be met. A strong viva answer acknowledges this but points out that country-set benchmarks make governments answerable to their own citizens, and that examples such as Viet Nam or Côte d’Ivoire show steady policy does move the numbers. Bangladesh Angle Bangladesh achieved near gender parity in primary and secondary enrolment early, a celebrated success. Its weaker points against SDG 4 are learning quality , pre-primary quality , teacher shortages and public spending , which has stayed around 2% of GDP or below for many years, well under the 4–6% benchmark. The FY2026–27 budget raised education to about 2% of GDP, with a stated aim of reaching 5% in phases (Chapter 14). Verify Before Use The 2026 GEM Report figures above are taken from UNESCO’s explainer article (September 2026). The out-of-school figure appears as 273 million in the 2026 report and 272 million (2023 data) in the 2025 Scorecard. Check the latest figure on the GEM Report or UIS website before quoting.

u: 2. The Learning Crisis, Recovery and Foundational Learning
t: 2. The Learning Crisis, Recovery and Foundational Learning
x: The single most important idea of the past decade in international education is that schooling is not the same as learning . The World Bank’s World Development Report 2018: Learning to Realize Education’s Promise popularised the phrase "learning crisis" : millions of children attend school for years without learning to read a simple text or do basic arithmetic. (Links to PC 119, PC 117 and ED 501.) Definitions Learning poverty (World Bank & UIS, 2019): the share of 10-year-olds who cannot read and understand a simple, age-appropriate text. It combines being out of school with being in school but not reading. Foundational learning: basic literacy, numeracy and transferable socio-emotional skills that are the base for all later learning. Learning recovery: policies to make up for learning lost during COVID-19 closures and other disruptions. Learning-adjusted years of schooling (LAYS): years of schooling adjusted for how much students actually learn. A country where children spend 11 years in school but learn as much as in 6.5 "quality" years has a large gap. The World Bank and partners estimated that learning poverty in low- and middle-income countries rose from about 57% before the pandemic to around 70% in 2022 (World Bank et al., 2022). COVID-19 closures were longest in South Asia and Latin America; Bangladesh kept schools closed for about 18 months, one of the longest closures in the world.

u: 2. The Learning Crisis, Recovery and Foundational Learning
x: The Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel (GEEAP) , convened by the World Bank, FCDO, UNICEF and USAID, rates interventions by cost-effectiveness. Its 2023 report Cost-Effective Approaches to Improve Global Learning lists as "great buys" : giving parents and students information on the benefits, costs and quality of education, and supporting teachers with structured pedagogy , targeting teaching by learning level , and (in some settings) structured lesson plans with linked materials and ongoing teacher support (GEEAP, 2023). Table 1. High-impact approaches for foundational learning Approach What it means Example Structured pedagogy A coherent package of lesson plans, student materials and teacher coaching aligned to clear learning goals. Kenya’s Tusome literacy programme; Sobral in Brazil. Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) Group children by current level (not grade) for part of the day and teach to that level. Pratham (India); scaled in Zambia and elsewhere. Science of reading Explicit, systematic phonics plus vocabulary, fluency and comprehension. England’s phonics screening check; reforms in many US states. Coaching teachers Regular, practical in-class feedback instead of one-off workshops. Common across successful literacy programmes. Mother-tongue early literacy Start reading in a language the child speaks, then bridge to others. MTB-MLE programmes; indigenous-language books in Bangladesh. Exam Focus Explain the difference between "schooling" and "learning" with the concept of learning poverty. Why is Teaching at the Right Level considered cost-effective? (It addresses the mismatch between an over-ambitious curriculum and children’s actual level.) Link to curriculum theory: Pritchett and Beatty (2015) argued that "overambitious curricula" make children fall further behind each year, because the curriculum moves faster than learning. Bangladesh Angle National Student Assessments by the Directorate of Primary Education have repeatedly shown that many Grade 3 and Grade 5 pupils do not reach expected competencies in Bangla and mathematics, and that results fell after COVID-19. In February 2026, the new Education Minister named "getting students back to class" as one of three immediate priorities, and the HSC 2026 results (Chapter 14) were read by many commentators as a sign of unrecovered learning loss. Verify Before Use Learning-poverty figures (57% and 70%) come from the 2022 State of Global Learning Poverty update; the World Bank may have published newer estimates. Check the latest DPE National Student Assessment report for exact Bangladesh percentages before quoting them.

International large-scale assessments (ILSAs) are the main source of comparable evidence on learning. A student of education should know what each one measures, who runs it, and its latest headline. (Links to PC 117, EER 582 and ED 501.) Table 2. Major international assessments Assessment Run by Who is tested Latest cycle PISA OECD 15-year-olds: reading, maths, science + an innovative domain 2025 (results 8 Sep 2026) TIMSS IEA Grades 4 and 8: maths and science 2023 (results Dec 2024) PIRLS IEA Grade 4 reading 2021; next 2026 PIAAC (Survey of Adult Skills) OECD Adults 16–65: literacy, numeracy, adaptive problem solving Cycle 2, results Dec 2024 TALIS OECD Teachers and principals 2024 (results 2025) ICILS IEA Grade 8 computer and information literacy 2023

PISA 2025 results were launched by the OECD on 8 September 2026 . About 91 countries and economies took part, with science as the major domain and "Learning in the Digital World" as the innovative domain. An optional foreign language assessment (English) was also introduced. Figure 3. OECD average PISA scores, 2018–2025. Reading and mathematics are now at their lowest ever recorded levels. Source: OECD PISA 2025 Results (Volume I), as reported by the OECD press release (Sept 2026) and secondary summaries. Must Remember: Pisa 2025 The OECD average fell to about 463 in mathematics (472 in 2022; 489 in 2018), 461 in reading (476 in 2022) and 482 in science (485 in 2022). Reading and maths are the lowest averages ever recorded by PISA. One in five 15-year-olds in OECD countries is now a low performer in all three subjects, up from 16% in 2022. East Asian systems still lead: Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang (China) , Singapore , Macao , Chinese Taipei , Japan and Korea . Singapore topped reading; B-S-J-Z topped maths and science. Estonia is again Europe’s best performer. Because the decline began before COVID-19 (it was visible from about 2012 in many countries), the OECD links it not only to the pandemic but also to digital distraction , reduced reading for pleasure and wellbeing issues. Other PISA 2025 findings worth quoting Devices and distraction: students who use digital devices for leisure at school score much lower; moderate use for learning is linked to better results. About 28% of students say classmates are distracted by devices in most science lessons, compared with fewer than 10% in the top East Asian systems. Clear phone policies are linked to less distraction. AI use: students who frequently use general AI tools for schoolwork tend to score lower than those who do not, while students who also get chances to learn AI literacy do slightly better; those chances are more common among advantaged students. Gender: girls outperform boys in reading by about 30 points, boys lead in maths by about 13 points, and science is near parity. Equity: socio-economic status explains about 12% of the variation in science performance within countries. Canada, Estonia, Ireland, Japan, Korea and Macao combine high performance with equity. LEARNING IN THE DIGITAL WORLD (PISA 2025 INNOVATIVE DOMAIN) Measures students’ capacity to build knowledge and solve problems iteratively using computational tools (for example, simulations and block-based programming), while regulating their own learning . It brings together computational thinking and self-regulated learning (OECD, 2026a). Critical Perspective PISA has been criticised for narrowing education to what is measurable, encouraging "league table" policy borrowing, and ignoring local purposes of schooling (Sellar & Lingard, 2013; Zhao, 2020). Defenders reply that it gives low- and middle-income countries an external mirror. A balanced viva answer: use PISA as a diagnostic , not a ranking . Bangladesh Angle Bangladesh has not taken part in PISA or TIMSS. Its learning evidence comes from national assessments (NSA by DPE; LASI for secondary by DSHE/MoE) and regional studies. A possible viva question is: "Should Bangladesh join PISA?" Arguments for: international benchmark, data quality, pressure for reform. Arguments against: cost, test-curriculum mismatch, risk of teaching to the test, and the fact that PISA for Development -type options exist for lower-income systems. Verify Before Use PISA 2025 averages and findings above are drawn from the OECD press release and secondary summaries (OECD pages could not be read in full when this note was written). Confirm figures in PISA 2025 Results (Volume I) on oecd.org before quoting exact numbers.

u: 4. Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI in Education
t: 4. Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI in Education
x: Since ChatGPT was released in November 2022, generative AI (GenAI) has become the fastest-moving topic in education. Every examiner now expects a student to hold an informed, balanced view. (Links to ED 503 ICT in Education and PC 114 Instructional Technology.) Definitions Artificial intelligence (AI): computer systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as recognising patterns, predicting, or generating language. Generative AI (GenAI): AI that creates new content (text, images, audio, code) in response to prompts, based on large language models (LLMs) trained on huge datasets. AI literacy: the knowledge, skills and attitudes needed to understand, use, evaluate and question AI responsibly. Cognitive offloading: handing mental work to an external tool. Helpful when it frees attention for deeper thinking; harmful when it replaces the very thinking a learner needs to practise.
