u: 4. Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI in Education
t: 4.2 What the evidence says: OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026
x: The OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026: Exploring Effective Uses of Generative AI in Education (January 2026) is the most important recent evidence review. Its central finding is a distinction between performance and learning (OECD, 2026b): Students using general-purpose chatbots often produce better work , but the advantage disappears or even reverses when AI is removed , for example in exams. Offloading thinking to chatbots can cause "metacognitive laziness" , reducing engagement and long-term skill development. GenAI tools designed for learning (for example, AI tutors that give hints instead of answers, or AI that supports structured group argumentation) show more lasting benefits. According to TALIS 2024 , about 37% of lower-secondary teachers used AI in their work; 57% of users said it helped with lesson planning, and 72% worried about academic integrity. Figure 5. Two ways GenAI can be used: offloading thinking versus augmenting it The OECD recommends: (1) human-centred use that enriches rather than replaces cognitive effort ; (2) investment in rigorously evaluated educational AI; (3) policy for trustworthy AI (privacy, safety, bias, transparency, age-appropriateness); and (4) inclusive infrastructure and teacher professional learning.

u: 4. Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI in Education
x: Table 4. GenAI in education at a glance Opportunities Risks Sensible responses Personalised tutoring and feedback at scale Lesson planning, question generation, rubrics Support for learners with disabilities and second-language learners Administrative time saved Plagiarism and academic dishonesty Hallucinations (confident but false answers) Bias and cultural misrepresentation (weak Bangla content) Data privacy, surveillance Widening digital divide Deskilling of teachers and learners Redesign assessment (oral defence, process portfolios, in-class writing) Teach AI literacy and verification Clear institutional AI policies (allowed / allowed with disclosure / not allowed) Keep humans in the loop Invest in teacher AI competency Critical Perspective AI detectors are unreliable and can unfairly flag non-native English writers (Liang et al., 2023), so many universities now focus on assessment redesign instead of detection. Scholars such as Selwyn (2024) warn against "AI hype" and remind us that past technologies (radio, TV, MOOCs) promised revolutions that did not arrive. Regulation is growing: the EU AI Act (2024) classifies AI used for admissions, assessment and proctoring as "high-risk" . Bangladesh Angle Bangladesh’s 2026 government plans include "One Teacher, One Tab" , multimedia classrooms, free Wi-Fi in institutions, and making digital literacy, AI awareness and cyber safety mandatory at school level in partnership with the ICT Division. Challenges: device and connectivity gaps between urban and rural schools, limited Bangla-language AI resources, and no comprehensive national AI-in-education policy yet. Universities (for example, through UGC guidance) are beginning to set rules on AI use in assignments and theses. Verify Before Use The "age 13" suggestion and the three level names (Acquire/Deepen/Create; Understand/Apply/Create) come from the UNESCO PDFs; confirm the wording on unesdoc.unesco.org. Check whether UGC or the Ministry of Education has issued a formal AI policy since November 2026.

Alongside AI, the most visible global policy trend of 2023–2026 is restricting smartphones in schools . UNESCO’s 2023 GEM Report, Technology in Education: A Tool on Whose Terms? , concluded that there is little robust evidence of technology’s added value in many settings, warned about distraction, and recommended that technology be used only where it improves learning. (Links to ED 503 and PC 113.) Figure 6. Share of education systems with a national law or policy banning phones in school Source: UNESCO GEM Report phone-ban tracker, as reported in March 2026 (114 education systems, 58%). In June 2023 about 24% of countries had a national school phone ban; by March 2026 the figure was about 58% (114 education systems) . Examples: the Netherlands, France, Italy, Finland, Sweden (from August 2026), Brazil, China, and many US states; England issued guidance; Australian states banned phones in public schools. Evidence is mixed but growing. A large randomised trial in Odisha, India (about 17,000 college students) found that collecting phones during class raised grades by about 0.09 standard deviations overall and 0.16 SD for lower-achieving students (reported in Hendrick, 2026). PISA 2025 links leisure device use at school with lower scores. Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation (2024) popularised the claim that smartphones and social media drove a youth mental-health crisis; critics (for example Odgers, 2024) argue the causal evidence is weaker. Present both sides in an exam answer. Key Ideas Digital wellbeing: healthy, balanced and safe use of digital technologies. Digital citizenship: responsible, ethical participation online, including privacy, safety and respectful communication. Screen time vs screen use: researchers increasingly argue that what a child does on screen matters more than the total minutes. Bangladesh Angle Mobile phone use among Bangladeshi adolescents rose sharply during COVID-19 closures. Several board officials explaining the poor HSC 2026 results mentioned students’ phone use and dependence on coaching. A balanced policy would combine in-class restrictions with digital literacy teaching , since phones are also many rural learners’ only access to online resources.

The "science of learning" (also called cognitive science in the classroom or learning sciences ) applies findings from cognitive psychology and neuroscience to teaching. It is one of the strongest movements in teacher education today, especially in England, Australia and the US, and is now entering South Asian teacher training. (Links to PC 113 Educational Psychology.) Figure 7. A simplified model of memory and the strategies that act on each stage (after Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968; Sweller, 1988)

Table 5. Principles from the science of learning Principle What it says Classroom use Cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988) Working memory is small; learning fails when it is overloaded. Reduce extraneous load, manage intrinsic load, foster germane processing. Worked examples, step-by-step instructions, remove clutter from slides, teach in small steps. Retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) Recalling information strengthens memory more than rereading (the "testing effect"). Low-stakes quizzes, brain dumps, flashcards, exit tickets. Spaced practice (Ebbinghaus; Cepeda et al., 2006) Learning spread over time lasts longer than massed "cramming". Revisit topics after days and weeks; cumulative tests. Interleaving (Rohrer & Taylor, 2007) Mixing problem types improves the ability to choose the right method. Mixed practice sets in maths and science. Dual coding (Paivio, 1971; Mayer, 2009) Words plus well-chosen visuals help memory. Diagrams with narration; avoid reading slides aloud. Elaboration and concrete examples Asking "why" and "how" and linking to examples deepens understanding. Self-explanation prompts. Desirable difficulties (Bjork, 1994) Some effort during learning (retrieval, spacing, variation) improves long-term retention even if it feels harder. Do not over-scaffold; let students struggle productively. Metacognition and self-regulation Learners who plan, monitor and evaluate their learning do better. EEF toolkit rates this one of the highest-impact, lowest-cost approaches (about +7 months). Teach planning, monitoring and evaluation explicitly.

Barak Rosenshine’s (2012) Principles of Instruction combine cognitive science, classroom research and expert teacher studies into ten principles that are now widely taught: begin with a short review ; present new material in small steps ; ask many questions ; provide models (worked examples); guide student practice ; check for understanding ; obtain a high success rate (about 80%); provide scaffolds for difficult tasks; require independent practice ; and engage in weekly and monthly review .

A 2025 meta-analysis of pre-questions (55 studies, about 12,000 participants) found strong effects on remembering the questioned material, especially with feedback, but little effect on new material ( Educational Psychology Review , 2025). Retrieval practice benefits are smaller with complex, real texts and with strong explanations: one 2025 study with 213 undergraduates found no advantage over rereading for a journal article, warning against treating retrieval as a magic bullet ( Instructional Science , 2025). Kalyuga (2025) proposed adding "explicit intention to learn" as a principle in cognitive load theory. A PISA 2022 re-analysis of 507,588 students in 74 countries found growth mindset was positively linked to achievement in 50 countries, with socio-economic status moderating the link ( PLOS ONE , 2025). Earlier meta-analyses found growth-mindset interventions have small average effects (Sisk et al., 2018; Macnamara & Burgoyne, 2023). Neuromyths To Avoid Popular but unsupported ideas you should not repeat: "learning styles" (matching teaching to visual/auditory/kinaesthetic learners: no good evidence; Pashler et al., 2008); "we only use 10% of our brain"; "left-brain vs right-brain learners"; and "Brain Gym" exercises improve learning. Howard-Jones (2014) showed that a majority of teachers in several countries believe some of these myths. Exam Focus Explain cognitive load theory and give two classroom implications. Distinguish retrieval practice from rereading, and spaced from massed practice. Critically evaluate "learning styles" as a neuromyth. Compare explicit (direct) instruction with inquiry-based learning; mention Kirschner, Sweller and Clark’s (2006) critique of minimally guided instruction and Kapur’s productive failure as a middle path.

The B.Ed and M.Ed syllabi cover classical theorists (Piaget, Vygotsky, Bruner, Dewey, Skinner, Bloom, Gagné). Examiners often ask about newer ideas to test whether a student reads beyond the textbook. The table below gives the "must know" set with the key name and year. (Links to PC 113, PC 115, PC 120, ED 503.) Table 6. Newer theories and approaches to know Theory or approach Key figure(s), year Core idea in one line Connectivism George Siemens (2005); Stephen Downes Learning is the ability to build and navigate networks of people, information and technology. Heutagogy Hase & Kenyon (2000) Self-determined learning: learners decide what and how to learn (beyond andragogy). Productive failure Manu Kapur (2008, 2016) Let students attempt problems before instruction; the struggle prepares them to learn the concept. Self-determination theory Deci & Ryan (1985, 2000) Motivation grows when needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness are met. Visible Learning John Hattie (2009; 2023 "The Sequel") Synthesis of meta-analyses: effect sizes above 0.40 worth attention; teacher clarity and feedback high. Culturally responsive / sustaining pedagogy Gloria Ladson-Billings (1995); Django Paris (2012) Teaching that values and sustains students’ languages and cultures. Translanguaging Ofelia García (2009) Bilingual learners use their whole language repertoire; teachers can allow it strategically. Critical pedagogy (renewed) Paulo Freire (1970); bell hooks (1994) Education for critical consciousness and freedom; renewed in debates on decolonising curricula. TPACK and SAMR Mishra & Koehler (2006); Puentedura (2006) Teachers need technology, pedagogy and content knowledge together; tech use from substitution to redefinition. Universal Design for Learning CAST (Rose & Meyer, 2002; v3.0 2024) Design for learner variability from the start (Chapter 9). Social-emotional learning CASEL (1994; framework 2020) Five SEL competencies taught alongside academics (Chapter 9). Phenomenon-based learning Finland national core curriculum (2014/2016) Study real-world phenomena across subjects in multidisciplinary modules. Flipped and blended learning Bergmann & Sams (2012); Garrison & Kanuka (2004) Content online before class; class time for active learning. Microlearning and gamification Various (2010s–) Short focused units; game elements for motivation. Embodied cognition Wilson (2002); Glenberg (2010) Thinking is grounded in bodily action and perception; gestures and movement aid learning. Positive education Seligman et al. (2009); PERMA model Teach wellbeing skills alongside academic skills. Two Short Definitions To Memorise Connectivism (Siemens, 2005): "Learning is a process that occurs within nebulous environments of shifting core elements… focused on connecting specialised information sets." In plain words: in a digital age, knowing where to find and how to connect knowledge matters as much as knowing facts. Heutagogy: the study of self-determined learning. Pedagogy is teacher-directed, andragogy is self-directed within a teacher’s frame, and heutagogy lets the learner set the goals and path. It suits lifelong and online learning. Critical Perspective There is a long-running debate between explicit instruction (supported by cognitive load theory and Rosenshine) and constructivist/inquiry approaches (supported by Dewey, Bruner and project-based learning). Current consensus leans to "explicit for novices, more open for experts" (the expertise reversal effect , Kalyuga et al., 2003) and to a sequence: explicit teaching → guided practice → open application.

Most curriculum reforms of the last decade, including Bangladesh’s 2021 framework, are competency-based : they define what learners should be able to do with knowledge, not just what they should know. (Links to PC 120 Introduction to Curriculum and ED 502.) Definitions Competency: an integrated combination of knowledge, skills, attitudes and values applied to perform effectively in a context (OECD, 2019). Competency-based education (CBE): learners progress by demonstrating mastery of competencies, with flexible time and authentic assessment. 21st-century skills / 4Cs: critical thinking, creativity, collaboration and communication (P21 Framework). Transferable skills: skills useful across contexts, such as problem solving, self-management and digital literacy.

OECD Learning Compass 2030 (2019): learners need knowledge, skills, attitudes and values to develop student agency and co-agency with teachers; "transformative competencies" are creating new value, reconciling tensions and dilemmas, and taking responsibility. WEF Education 4.0 (2020): eight characteristics of learning for the Fourth Industrial Revolution (see the figure below). UNESCO’s Futures of Education report, *Reimagining Our Futures Together: A New Social Contract for Education* (2021): calls for education as a global common good, built on cooperation, solidarity and care for the planet. Delors Report pillars (1996) remain the foundation: learning to know, to do, to live together and to be (with "learning to become" added in later UNESCO work). Figure 8. World Economic Forum Education 4.0: four content and four experience shifts (WEF, 2020)

The Future of Jobs Report 2025 surveyed over 1,000 employers. They expect 39% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030 (down from 44% in 2023). AI and big data , networks and cybersecurity and technological literacy are the fastest-growing skills, followed by creative thinking, resilience, flexibility and agility, and curiosity and lifelong learning. Manual dexterity is the fastest-declining (WEF, 2025). Figure 9. Top ten core skills employers rated most important in 2025 (WEF, 2025) Exam Focus Define competency-based curriculum and compare it with a content-based curriculum. What is "student agency" in the OECD Learning Compass? Explain why the WEF predicts that analytical thinking and AI literacy will be core skills by 2030, and what this means for teacher education. Critical Perspective Critics warn that skills frameworks written by business forums can turn education into "human capital production" and neglect citizenship, culture and personal flourishing (Biesta, 2010, on qualification, socialisation and subjectification). Competency-based reforms also need major teacher training and assessment capacity, which was one reason Bangladesh’s 2021 framework faltered.

u: 9. Inclusion, Equity and Wellbeing: UDL 3.0, SEL and Beyond
t: 9. Inclusion, Equity and Wellbeing: UDL 3.0, SEL and Beyond
x: Inclusion has moved from a special-education topic to a whole-system principle: every school should plan for the full diversity of learners. (Links to PC 127 Inclusion in Education, PC 122 Gender Education and PC 121 Value Education.)

u: 9. Inclusion, Equity and Wellbeing: UDL 3.0, SEL and Beyond
x: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) , developed by CAST, asks teachers to design lessons that work for the widest range of learners from the start, instead of retrofitting adjustments. UDL Guidelines 3.0 were released in July 2024 after a four-year community review. The three principles remain engagement (the why), representation (the what) and action and expression (the how), but version 3.0: changes the goal from "expert learners" to "learner agency" (purposeful and reflective, resourceful and authentic, strategic and action-oriented); adds attention to identity, belonging, joy and play , and to biased or exclusionary practices ; stresses collective as well as individual learning and draws on culturally sustaining pedagogy. Figure 10. The three principles of Universal Design for Learning, version 3.0 (CAST, 2024)

u: 9. Inclusion, Equity and Wellbeing: UDL 3.0, SEL and Beyond
x: SEL is "the process through which all young people and adults acquire and apply the knowledge, skills and attitudes to develop healthy identities, manage emotions and achieve personal and collective goals, feel and show empathy for others, establish and maintain supportive relationships, and make responsible and caring decisions" (CASEL, 2020). A widely cited meta-analysis of 213 programmes found SEL improved academic achievement by about 11 percentile points (Durlak et al., 2011). Figure 11. CASEL’s five core SEL competencies

u: 9. Inclusion, Equity and Wellbeing: UDL 3.0, SEL and Beyond
x: Table 7. Inclusion and equity trends Trend What to know Mental health and wellbeing Post-COVID rise in student anxiety and depression; school counsellors, whole-school approaches and teacher wellbeing are growing priorities. Trauma-informed teaching Recognising how adverse childhood experiences affect behaviour and learning; safe, predictable classrooms. Mother-tongue-based multilingual education UNESCO: about 40% of learners are not taught in a language they speak or understand. Start in the home language and bridge. Gender equality, both ways Girls still excluded in some regions (e.g., Afghanistan’s ban on girls’ secondary and higher education since 2021–22), while boys now lag in many middle-income countries, including in Bangladesh’s secondary results. Disability inclusion UNCRPD Article 24; inclusive education laws rose from 1% to 24% of countries since 2000 (GEM 2026). Assistive technology and AI captioning are new tools. Refugee and crisis education Education in emergencies; Bangladesh hosts about one million Rohingya refugees, with Myanmar-curriculum learning centres in Cox’s Bazar. Bangladesh Angle The 2026 budget promised free education for girls up to undergraduate level , inclusive education with assistive technology for children with disabilities, and expanded mid-day meals . In HSC 2026, girls passed at a higher rate than boys for the sixth straight year (55.45% vs 47.14% in the general boards), raising the emerging issue of boys’ disengagement . The Persons with Disabilities Rights and Protection Act 2013 and the National Education Policy 2010 already promise inclusion; implementation is the gap.

Around the world, systems are trying to reduce the dominance of high-stakes, memory-based public examinations and build balanced assessment systems . Two new pressures have accelerated this: GenAI, which makes many take-home tasks unreliable, and competency-based curricula, which need assessment of performance, not recall. (Links to PC 117 and EER 582.) Figure 12. Assessment of, for and as learning (Earl, 2003; Black & Wiliam, 1998) Table 8. Assessment trends Trend Description Formative assessment / assessment for learning Black and Wiliam’s (1998) "Inside the Black Box" showed large gains from formative feedback. Dylan Wiliam’s five strategies: clarify learning intentions; elicit evidence; give feedback that moves learners forward; activate peers; activate students as owners of their learning. School-based assessment (SBA) Teachers assess continuously across the year; often combined with fewer, shorter public exams. Competency and performance assessment Projects, portfolios, practicals and rubrics that show what learners can do. Authentic and "AI-resilient" assessment Real-world tasks, oral defences (viva), in-class writing, process evidence (drafts, reflections), and assessments that require personal context. Digital and adaptive testing Computer-based tests that adjust difficulty; PISA has been computer-based since 2015 and adaptive since 2018. Item banks and blueprints Calibrated question banks and test specification tables to improve validity and reduce rote "suggestion" culture. Programmatic assessment Many low-stakes data points combined for high-stakes decisions (from medical education). Two-lane approach to AI (Univ. of Sydney, 2024) "Lane 1": secure, supervised assessment of learning; "Lane 2": open assessment where AI use is allowed and taught. Bangladesh Angle Bangladesh has swung between models. The 2021 curriculum framework removed exams up to Grade 3, abolished PSC (2022) and JSC/JDC (2023) , and introduced continuous assessment with behavioural indicators and a year-end summative assessment, which parents and teachers found confusing. After its withdrawal in 2024, the traditional exam system returned. In February 2026 a consultation committee recommended limiting SSC written exams to five core subjects (Bangla, English, mathematics, science and social science), with ICT, religion, physical education and arts assessed by schools. The new government’s 12-point agenda promises item banks, test blueprints, moderation and school-based assessment guidelines in phases, while the reintroduction of a primary scholarship examination was criticised by educationists. Exam Focus Compare assessment of, for and as learning with examples. Why did continuous assessment under the 2021 curriculum face resistance in Bangladesh? (Teacher capacity, unclear indicators, parental trust in exams, coaching culture, short preparation time.) How should universities redesign assessment in the age of GenAI?
Teachers are the single most important school-level factor in learning, and the profession faces a global crisis of shortage, status and wellbeing. (Links to ED 502 and PC 118.)

UNESCO’s Global Report on Teachers (2024) estimated that 44 million additional teachers are needed by 2030 to achieve universal primary and secondary education, 15 million of them in sub-Saharan Africa. By the time of the 2025 World Summit, education leaders were citing a need for about 50 million teachers, with attrition doubling in some regions since 2015.

t: 11.2 UN High-Level Panel and the Santiago Consensus
x: In February 2024 the UN Secretary-General’s High-Level Panel on the Teaching Profession issued 59 recommendations on dignity, status, pay, working conditions, professional development and teacher participation in policy. In August 2025 (28–29 August) , UNESCO and Chile hosted the first World Summit on Teachers in Santiago de Chile , which adopted the Santiago Consensus . Its six priority areas are: 1. Comprehensive teacher policies covering the whole career, from recruitment to retirement; 2. Lifelong professional development that links initial training, induction, mentoring and continuing development; 3. Social dialogue : permanent participation of teachers and unions in policymaking; 4. Sustainable financing , in line with SDG target 4.c (supply of qualified teachers); 5. Future-ready teaching , including digital and AI competencies, and adoption of UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Teachers; 6. Inclusion and equity , including a more diverse teaching workforce. The Consensus also stated that education technologies must serve humanity and should not undermine the essential role of human interaction in education.

Teacher professional learning communities (PLCs) and lesson study (Japanese jugyou kenkyuu ) replace one-off workshops. Instructional coaching : a meta-analysis by Kraft, Blazar and Hogan (2018) found coaching improved instruction (0.49 SD) and achievement (0.18 SD). Teacher wellbeing and workload : TALIS 2024 and national surveys show high stress; AI may reduce paperwork. Teacher agency and research-informed practice : teachers as researchers (Stenhouse, 1975), action research and evidence hubs such as the UK’s Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) Teaching and Learning Toolkit. Bangladesh Angle In 2026 the Education Minister told parliament that at least 92,081 teacher posts were vacant, and around 34,000–35,000 primary schools lacked head teachers (press reports, May 2026). Recruitment runs through the NTRCA for non-government secondary schools and colleges and through the DPE for government primary schools. Teacher training reforms promised in 2026 include mandatory subject knowledge and assessment literacy , "One Teacher, One Tab" , and strengthening teacher training colleges (TTCs) and PTIs. Low pay, MPO-related protests and heavy dependence on private tuition remain sensitive issues. Verify Before Use Vacancy numbers and training plans are from press reports (Bonik Barta, Feb 2026; The Daily Star, May 2026). Check the latest NTRCA circular and Ministry statements.

u: 12. Climate, Green and Global Citizenship Education
t: 12. Climate, Green and Global Citizenship Education
x: Climate change is now treated as an education issue, not only an environmental one. (Links to PC 123 Environmental Education and ED 501.) Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) for 2030 (UNESCO, 2020) and the Berlin Declaration on ESD (2021) call for ESD to be a core component of all education systems by 2025. The Greening Education Partnership , launched at the 2022 Transforming Education Summit, has four pillars: greening schools, greening curriculum, greening teacher training and education systems, and greening communities . UNESCO published a Greening Curriculum Guidance (2024). A UNESCO review found that nearly half of national curricula made no reference to climate change (UNESCO, 2021). Global Citizenship Education (GCED) and the 2023 UNESCO Recommendation on Education for Peace, Human Rights and Sustainable Development (replacing the 1974 Recommendation) define what learners need for a just, peaceful and sustainable world. Climate-resilient schools: extreme heat and floods are closing schools; in 2024 Bangladesh closed schools during record heatwaves, and many schools in the north and north-east flood every year. Bangladesh Angle Bangladesh is among the most climate-vulnerable countries. Climate change and disaster topics appear in science and Bangladesh and Global Studies textbooks. Researchers have called for a dedicated climate-education strategy, heat-safe school calendars, and climate-resilient school buildings in coastal and haor areas. Verify Before Use The "nearly half of curricula" figure comes from UNESCO’s 2021 Learn for Our Planet review; newer monitoring may update it.

As you are applying to teach at a university, expect questions about higher education itself. (Links to ED 502 and ED 501.) Table 9. Higher education trends Trend Key points Outcome-based education (OBE) Programmes defined by programme and course learning outcomes, aligned with teaching and assessment (constructive alignment, Biggs, 1996). In Bangladesh, OBE curricula are promoted by the UGC and required for accreditation by the Bangladesh Accreditation Council (BAC, Act 2017) . Qualifications frameworks The Bangladesh National Qualifications Framework (BNQF) sets levels from school to doctorate; links to recognition of prior learning and TVET. Micro-credentials and stackable learning Short, certified units that can build into degrees; UNESCO and the EU have issued definitions (EU Council Recommendation, 2022). GenAI and academic integrity Universities are writing AI policies, redesigning assessment and teaching AI literacy (Chapter 4). Internationalisation and rankings Growth of transnational education; criticism of global rankings for distorting priorities. Open science and open educational resources UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science (2021) and on OER (2019). Completion and employability GEM 2026: six in ten university entrants never graduate globally. Graduate unemployment is a major concern in Bangladesh. Academic freedom and governance After 2024, debates on politicisation of campuses and appointment of vice-chancellors have been intense in Bangladesh. Exam Focus Be ready to explain constructive alignment and OBE with an example from a course you might teach (for example, writing a course learning outcome for PC 117 and showing how you would teach and assess it).

Bangladesh’s education system has gone through more policy turbulence between 2023 and 2026 than in any period since the 1970s. Examiners will almost certainly ask about it. Answer factually and without partisanship: describe what happened, give the educational arguments on each side, and propose a constructive way forward. (Links to PC 112 Education in Bangladesh, PC 120 and ED 502.) Figure 13. Bangladesh’s curriculum and policy timeline, 2010–2027

t: 14.1 The rise and withdrawal of the competency-based curriculum
x: National Education Policy 2010 and the National Curriculum 2012 shaped the system for a decade: subject streams (science, humanities, business) from Grade 9, and public exams at Grades 5 (PSC), 8 (JSC/JDC), 10 (SSC) and 12 (HSC). The National Curriculum Framework 2021 (often called "Curriculum 2022") introduced a competency-based, experiential model: no exams up to Grade 3, no PSC (dropped in 2022) or JSC (abolished 2023), no streams in Grades 9–10 , ten learning areas, and continuous assessment with a year-end summative assessment. It was rolled out in Grades 1, 6 and 7 in 2023 and Grades 2, 3, 8 and 9 in 2024. Criticism grew over teacher preparation , unclear assessment indicators , cost of activity materials, and parents’ fear that children were "not studying". After the July–August 2024 mass uprising and change of government, the Secondary and Higher Education Division declared the new curriculum "not implementable" (notification of 1 September 2024). For 2025 , secondary education returned to the 2012 curriculum with revised textbooks, streams and traditional exams, while primary continued with revised books based on the 2021/2022 framework. In July 2025 the NCTB said a new national curriculum would start at secondary level from 2027, beginning with Grade 6 and adding one grade per year. It reviewed models from about 16 countries (including Australia and the US, where assessment is continuous and school-based) and planned to blend elements of the 2012 and 2022 curricula (Dhaka Tribune, 17 July 2025). Critical Perspective: What Can We Learn? Most education researchers agreed the goals of the 2021 framework (less rote learning, more experiential and competency-based learning) were sound, but the implementation was rushed: limited piloting, short teacher training, and weak communication with parents. Fullan’s (2007) change theory reminds us that reform succeeds only when teachers understand and own it. The lesson for the 2027 curriculum: pilot, train, communicate, and keep it stable . Constant resets (2012 → 2021 → 2012 → 2027) themselves harm learning.

A new elected government took office in February 2026 , with Tarique Rahman as Prime Minister, Dr A N M Ehsanul Hoque Milon as Education Minister and Bobby Hajjaj as State Minister. On 19 February 2026 the Education Ministry presented a 12-point reform agenda in three phases : Table 10. Bangladesh’s 2026 education reform agenda Theme Main plans (as reported) Financing Raise education spending to 5% of GDP in phases; fix slow use of development budgets (about 53% of secondary development funds were reported unspent). Teachers Strengthen training; mandatory subject knowledge and assessment literacy; "One Teacher, One Tab" ; fill vacancies. Curriculum Review the national curriculum; sports, physical and mental health education and arts compulsory from Class IV; new subjects such as "Joyful Learning" and "Sports and Culture"; content on the July 2024 uprising. Skills Technical education from Grade 6 / secondary for all students; credit bridges with BTEB and NSDA; industry internships and career centres. Languages A compulsory third language in phases (e.g., Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, French, German) alongside Bangla and English. Digital Digital literacy, AI awareness and cyber safety mandatory; robotics and maker corners in each upazila; free Wi-Fi in institutions. Assessment Item banks, blueprints, moderation, school-based assessment; exam reform in phase 3 (12–36 months). Equity Nationwide mid-day meals; free girls’ education to undergraduate level; inclusive education and assistive technology; sanitation for girls. Madrasa Modernise with science, maths, English and ICT; recognition of Qawmi certificates; Minimum Learning Standards. Accountability Public dashboard and school report cards; university research grants. Commentators welcomed the ambition but questioned financing, sequencing and coherence . Professor Manzoor Ahmed (BRAC University) described the initiatives as "fragmented, separate and partial", and CAMPE’s Rasheda K. Choudhury warned that "only increasing the budget will not be enough" (The Daily Star, 28 May 2026).

The budget placed on 11 June 2026 allocated about Tk 1.37 lakh crore (Tk 1.37 trillion) to education and technology, about 14.6% of the total budget and close to 2% of GDP , up from a revised 1.39% of GDP in FY2025–26. The three education divisions received about Tk 1.22 lakh crore (bdnews24.com, 2026; Dhaka Tribune, 2026). This is a real increase, but still below the international benchmark of 4–6% of GDP.

Figure 14. HSC and equivalent results: GPA-5 holders, 2024–2026, and pass rates (Prothom Alo; The Daily Star) Results published on 31 October 2026 : pass rate 52.12% across 11 boards (58.83% in 2025), the lowest in about two decades; 40,084 GPA-5 holders (about 72,000 in 2025 and 145,911 in 2024). Pass rates fell in all nine general boards; humanities 42%, business 51%, science 73%; English and ICT results fell widely. Girls 55.45% vs boys 47.14% (general boards). Explanations offered: exams on the full syllabus and full marks for the first time since COVID-19, stricter script evaluation , identical question papers across boards, unrecovered learning loss , teacher shortages, irregular classes, coaching dependence and phone use. How To Discuss Hsc 2026 In A Viva Avoid simply blaming students. A balanced answer: (1) lower pass rates partly reflect more honest marking after years of grade inflation, which restores credibility; (2) they also reveal a real learning deficit carried from COVID-19 closures and curriculum instability; (3) the remedy is classroom teaching quality, remedial support and teacher recruitment , not lowering standards again.

Teacher vacancies (92,000+), NTRCA recruitment, MPO and non-government teachers’ pay demands. Coaching centres, guidebooks and the private tuition economy. University governance after 2024; student politics; quality assurance (BAC accreditation, OBE). Primary education: textbook delivery on 1 January, mid-day meals, a reintroduced scholarship exam, and World Bank-supported primary programmes. TVET expansion and the target of higher technical enrolment. Education in the Rohingya camps and in climate-vulnerable regions. Verify Before Use Names of office-holders, budget numbers and the 12-point agenda details come from newspapers (Bonik Barta, The Daily Star, Dhaka Tribune, bdnews24, Prothom Alo, Feb–Nov 2026). The two newspapers give slightly different HSC 2026 figures (52.12% all boards vs 51.62% in one report); the candidate counts support 52.12%. Check the Ministry of Education, NCTB, and Education Board websites for the latest official figures before an exam.

University examinations in Education typically combine a written paper (MCQ and/or descriptive) with a viva voce. In the viva, examiners often begin with your thesis or area of interest and then move to current issues. Use this chapter to practise.

t: 15.2 Likely viva questions with answer points
x: Table 12. Viva questions and model answer points # Question Points to make 1 What are the most important global trends in education right now? Name 4–5: learning crisis and foundational learning; AI and GenAI; phone restrictions and wellbeing; competency-based curricula and assessment reform; teacher shortage; inclusion and UDL; climate education. Give one source per trend. 2 What did PISA 2025 show? Lowest OECD averages ever in reading and maths; 1 in 5 low performers in all subjects; East Asia leads; decline predates COVID; links to digital distraction. Bangladesh does not participate. 3 Should Bangladesh participate in PISA? Pros: benchmark, data, reform pressure. Cons: cost, mismatch, test pressure. Middle path: strengthen national assessments first and consider PISA-style items. 4 How should teachers use ChatGPT and other GenAI tools? Human-centred: use for planning, differentiation, feedback drafts; teach AI literacy; never let it replace students’ thinking; redesign assessment; protect privacy. Cite UNESCO 2023 and OECD 2026. 5 What is "metacognitive laziness"? OECD 2026: offloading thinking to chatbots reduces effort and long-term learning; output improves but learning does not. 6 Explain UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Teachers. 5 dimensions: human-centred mindset, ethics of AI, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, AI for professional development; 3 levels: acquire, deepen, create. 7 Why did the 2021 curriculum fail in Bangladesh? Sound goals but rushed implementation: little piloting, weak teacher training, unclear assessment, parental distrust, resource costs, political context of 2024. Lesson: pilot, train, communicate, sustain. 8 What is your view on the decline in HSC 2026 results? Partly honest marking after grade inflation; partly real learning loss; solution = teaching quality, remedial support, teacher recruitment. 9 What is competency-based education? Integration of knowledge, skills, attitudes and values to perform tasks; mastery-based progression; authentic assessment; example from curriculum. 10 What is learning poverty? Share of 10-year-olds unable to read and understand a simple text (World Bank & UIS, 2019); ~70% in LMICs in 2022. 11 What is Teaching at the Right Level? Pratham’s approach: group by learning level, teach basics intensively; GEEAP "great buy". 12 What is cognitive load theory? Sweller: limited working memory; reduce extraneous load; worked examples; split-attention and redundancy effects. 13 Is "learning styles" a valid theory? No: a neuromyth (Pashler et al., 2008). Better: use multiple modes for everyone (dual coding). 14 What is UDL, and what changed in UDL 3.0? Design for variability; engagement, representation, action and expression; 3.0 aims at learner agency, adds identity, belonging, joy, anti-bias. 15 What is SEL and why does it matter? CASEL 5; Durlak et al. (2011) +11 percentile points; wellbeing after COVID. 16 What is the Santiago Consensus? World Summit on Teachers (Aug 2025): six priorities including career-long policy, PD, social dialogue, financing, AI competencies, inclusion. 17 How big is the global teacher shortage? 44 million needed by 2030 (UNESCO 2024), about 50 million cited in 2025; Bangladesh 92,000+ vacant posts. 18 What is Education 4.0? WEF (2020): 4 content shifts (global citizenship, innovation and creativity, technology, interpersonal skills) and 4 experience shifts (personalised, accessible, problem-based/collaborative, lifelong). 19 What are formative and summative assessment? Black & Wiliam (1998); assessment for vs of learning; Wiliam’s five strategies; assessment as learning. 20 How can assessment be made "AI-resilient" in a university course? In-class tasks, oral defence, drafts and reflections, personal or local data, two-lane approach, clear AI-use rules. 21 What is connectivism? Siemens (2005): learning in networks; relevance for digital age; criticised as not a full learning theory. 22 What is outcome-based education? Learning outcomes drive teaching and assessment; constructive alignment (Biggs); BAC and UGC require OBE curricula. 23 What is the Greening Education Partnership? Launched at TES 2022; four pillars: greening schools, curriculum, teacher training/systems, communities. 24 How much does Bangladesh spend on education? About 2% of GDP in FY2026–27 (up from 1.39% revised FY26), below the 4–6% benchmark; target 5%. 25 What would you change first in Bangladesh’s education system? Pick one and justify with evidence: e.g., teacher recruitment and coaching-based training focused on foundational learning, with stable curriculum and fair assessment. Viva Technique Structure every answer: define → explain with a source and year → give a Bangladesh example → offer a balanced view or your recommendation. Show you read beyond the syllabus : mention one recent report (GEM 2026, PISA 2025, OECD DEO 2026) by name. Be politically neutral : describe policies by what they do; evaluate them on educational evidence. Say "I am not sure of the exact figure, but…" rather than inventing a number.
